title: What We Do — ArmaturaSec d.o.o.
text:
ArmaturaSec builds network security appliances for operational technology environments. If you run a water treatment plant, an electricity distribution substation, or a manufacturing line and you need to control who can talk to your PLCs and whether that traffic looks legitimate, that is what our products are designed for.

We are not a general-purpose cybersecurity company. We do not sell endpoint agents, email filters, or cloud security platforms. Every product we have shipped since 2008 has been a hardware device that sits inside an industrial network and inspects or controls traffic at the protocol level.

Our NetGuard-OT appliance handles network access control: it enforces rules about which devices can communicate, blocks unauthorised connections, and logs everything in a format that your existing SCADA historian can ingest. The Mini variant fits on a standard DIN rail for installations where cabinet space is limited.

ProtoSense is our protocol inspection module. It understands Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP at the message level, not just the packet level, so it can tell you that a device sent a write command to a coil it has never written to before — not just that traffic occurred.

Our SecAudit service is a one-time on-site engagement. Two of our engineers spend two days on your site, map the network as it actually exists, identify the gaps between that and how it is supposed to be configured, and produce a written report with prioritised findings.

We work with clients in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. Most of our installations are in the energy and water sectors. A growing share are in food and beverage manufacturing.

If you want to talk about a specific installation or you have a question about whether our products fit your environment, contact our sales team in Zrenjanin.

title: Firmware Engineer — Network Protocols (Zrenjanin)
text:
ArmaturaSec is looking for a firmware engineer to join our core development team in Zrenjanin. We have a monthly release cycle across four hardware variants and we need someone who can contribute to protocol parsing, system integration, and the tooling that keeps the whole process running.

What the work looks like day to day: you will work on the firmware that runs on our NetGuard-OT appliances — mostly C with an increasing share of Rust for new components. You will work closely with the person responsible for our Yocto build system and with the QA team that tests each release on physical hardware.

We deal with Modbus TCP, BACnet/IP, and a few less common industrial protocols. You do not need to know all of them when you start. You do need to be comfortable reading protocol specifications and writing parsers from them.

The hardware side: our appliances are based on ARM Cortex-A SoCs. We have a bench in the office with physical boards, PLC simulators, and packet generators. You will spend time at that bench.

What we are looking for:
— At least three years writing firmware or embedded systems software in C
— Comfort with Linux networking internals (netfilter, raw sockets, that level)
— Experience debugging with JTAG or serial console, not just printf
— Some exposure to Rust is useful but not required

What we are not looking for: someone who wants to work on cloud infrastructure or web services. This is hardware-close work.

We offer a permanent contract, a salary in line with the Zrenjanin market for this experience level, and flexible hours within reason. The office is in the industrial zone on the north side of the city. Remote work is possible one or two days a week once you are settled in.

Send a CV and a short note about something you have built to posao@armaturesec.rs.

title: QA and Test Automation Engineer (Zrenjanin)
text:
Our QA team maintains a regression suite of around 1,400 test cases that runs against every firmware release on four hardware boards. The suite is written in Python and runs against physical hardware on a test bench. It works, but it is slow to extend and we are spending too much engineering time on it.

We are looking for someone who wants to take ownership of that suite and make it better. That means maintaining what is already there, finding ways to generate or scaffold new test cases faster, and reducing the manual effort involved in keeping tests up to date when firmware behaviour changes.

This is not a role where you will be asked to deploy a commercial test management platform and declare victory. We have specific constraints: the test runner is Python, the hardware is physical and will stay physical, and the timeline for releases is not going to change. What we need is someone who will sit with the existing code, understand why it is the way it is, and improve it incrementally.

Some things that would be useful background:
— Experience maintaining a large test suite in Python
— Familiarity with hardware-in-the-loop testing or any kind of test automation that involves real devices rather than simulators
— An opinion about why test suites grow brittle over time and what to do about it

Experience with industrial protocols is not required. You will learn what you need to know about Modbus and BACnet on the job.

The role is full-time in Zrenjanin. One or two days remote per week is possible. We expect some collaboration with our firmware engineers and some with the field support team who often find bugs first.

Questions and applications to posao@armaturesec.rs. We review applications on a rolling basis.

title: ArmaturaSec Completes Installation at Heating Utility in North Macedonia
text:
ArmaturaSec has completed the installation of NetGuard-OT appliances at three control network sites operated by a district heating utility in North Macedonia. The project began in October 2023 following a SecAudit engagement that identified uncontrolled lateral movement between the utility's corporate network and its SCADA segment.

The installation covers the main heat production facility and two distribution pump stations. Each site received a NetGuard-OT unit configured to enforce communication rules between engineering workstations, RTUs, and the SCADA server. ProtoSense modules were added at the main facility to provide visibility into Modbus TCP traffic on the primary production loop.

Miloš Anđić, who led the installation from our side, noted that the network topology at the pump stations differed significantly from the documentation provided before the site visit. 'We found three devices that were not on any diagram. Two were legacy HMI panels that had been connected years earlier and forgotten. One we could not identify at all. That kind of discovery is exactly why we do a physical walkthrough before we start configuring anything.'

The utility's IT manager confirmed that the project came in on the agreed timeline despite the additional scoping work required during installation.

This is our sixth active installation in North Macedonia. We are currently in early discussions with two other utilities in the region about similar projects.

For questions about projects in North Macedonia or other markets outside Serbia, contact our sales team at prodaja@armaturesec.rs.

title: Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection
text:
For about eighteen months we tried to build a detection component that could identify unusual Modbus traffic by training on labelled datasets published by research groups. We had four datasets we thought were credible. We spent a significant chunk of time getting them into a format our pipeline could use, training classifiers, and then testing them against real traffic from our own lab bench and from anonymised captures our clients had agreed to share with us.

The results were not good. False positive rates that looked acceptable on the test set turned into something much worse when we applied the model to a real site. A water treatment plant runs its Modbus polling on a rhythm that is specific to that plant — the scan rate, the register addresses, the devices on the bus, everything. A model trained on traffic from a research testbed in another country does not know that rhythm. It cannot know it.

We also noticed that the labelled datasets we were using represented attack scenarios that were either very obvious (flooding the bus with write commands) or very specific to hardware we do not see in the Balkans. Neither is particularly useful.

What we think actually works for our environment is learning what normal looks like on a specific site and flagging deviations from that. No labels, no pre-trained model from somewhere else. This is not a new idea. The challenge is doing it in a way that runs on our hardware, produces alerts that a plant operator can understand without a data science background, and does not require us to collect six months of clean traffic before it is useful.

We have not solved this yet. We have a set of traffic archives from our client base and one engineer who has been working on this part-time. If you have relevant experience or want to talk about it, we are interested.

title: What We Do — Zrenjanin Game Works
text:
We make educational browser games for primary schools. That is the whole job.

Our games run directly in a browser — Chrome, Firefox, Edge, it does not matter — on any device the school already has. There is nothing to install, no account for parents to create, and no advertisements. A teacher adds the game link to the classroom portal and children can start playing in the same lesson.

We currently cover mathematics for grades one through four, Serbian and Hungarian language literacy for early primary, and a set of natural-science quiz modules for grades three and four. All content is aligned with the Serbian national curriculum, and our language games are available in both Serbian and Hungarian to serve the bilingual communities of Vojvodina.

Our customers are municipalities, school boards, and NGOs. We do not sell directly to individual schools or parents. A typical contract covers a one or two-year licence for a defined set of schools, with a content-update and hosting service included. Prices are fixed at contract signing, so there are no surprises mid-year.

Before we build anything new, we talk to teachers. Our pedagogy consultant Tatjana Kovačević coordinates playtesting and curriculum-mapping sessions with classroom teachers, usually in Zrenjanin and the surrounding municipalities. We have been doing this since our first game in 2020 and it shapes everything from the difficulty curve to the visual design.

If you represent a municipality, school district, or NGO and want to discuss a contract, contact us at info@zrenjanin-gameworks.rs. We are a small team and we respond personally.

title: Junior Front-End Developer (Part-Time, Zrenjanin or Remote)
text:
Zrenjanin Game Works is looking for a junior front-end developer to join our small team on a part-time basis, around 20 hours per week. This can be done from Zrenjanin or fully remote.

We build browser-based educational games using HTML5, JavaScript, and the Phaser 3 game framework. Our backend is PHP with MySQL. We do not use large frameworks on the front end — everything is close to the metal, which means you will actually understand what your code is doing and why.

What we need from you:
- Solid working knowledge of JavaScript (ES6+)
- Some experience with or genuine curiosity about Phaser 3 or a comparable canvas-based game library
- Ability to read and work with JSON data structures
- Comfort working in a Git-based workflow (we use Gitea)
- Patience — educational games require a lot of iteration based on teacher and child feedback, which means things change

Nice to have but not required:
- Experience with PHP or MySQL
- Hungarian language skills (we have bilingual content)
- Any background in education or working with children

What the work looks like: You would work closely with Miroslav Kovačević, our lead developer, building and maintaining game modules, fixing bugs reported from live school deployments, and occasionally helping implement new content based on specs from our pedagogy team.

We are not a fast-growth startup. We are a small, stable company with real customers who use what we build every school day. If that sounds like a place where you would do good work, send a short message and any code samples or portfolio links to posao@zrenjanin-gameworks.rs.

title: New Contract: Subotica District Education Office Joins for 2024–25 School Year
text:
We are pleased to confirm that the Subotica District Education Office has signed a one-year contract with Zrenjanin Game Works for use of our math and language game modules across fourteen primary schools in the district.

This is our first contract in the Subotica area and our largest to date in terms of number of schools. The district serves a significant Hungarian-speaking population, which is part of why they approached us — our Hungarian-language content and the bilingual structure of our games matched what they were looking for.

The contract covers our full mathematics module for grades one through four and both the Serbian and Hungarian literacy games. Schools will be onboarded in September at the start of the new school year. We will run two short orientation sessions for teachers in August — one in Subotica and one online — to walk through how the platform works and how to read the session reports.

For us, this is a meaningful step. Most of our previous contracts have been in and around Zrenjanin, where we have existing relationships with schools and the education office. Expanding to Subotica means working with teachers we have not met before, in a district with a different demographic mix. We expect to learn a lot.

Tatjana Kovačević, who handles pedagogy and customer relationships, will be the primary contact for the Subotica schools throughout the year.

If you are a municipality or school district interested in similar arrangements, our contact address is info@zrenjanin-gameworks.rs.

title: Freelance Data Analyst — Learning Outcomes Project (Short-Term Contract)
text:
We are looking for a freelance data analyst for a defined short-term project, expected to run three to five months.

Background: We log clickstream events for every student session across our math games — question ID, answer, timestamp, attempt count, time-on-question. We have roughly 4,200 students' worth of data from the last two school years in CSV exports from our MySQL database. We want to build a simple, explainable method for identifying students who are likely guessing randomly rather than demonstrating understanding. The output needs to be something a classroom teacher can act on without needing to understand statistics.

What we are looking for:
- Experience working with behavioural or interaction log data
- Ability to work in Python or R — whichever you prefer
- Interest in making outputs readable for non-technical users (teachers, school coordinators)
- Clear communication — we need to understand what you are doing and why at each step

What this is not: This is not a machine-learning research project. We do not need a published paper. We need something that works reliably on the data we have and can be maintained by a small team. Interpretability matters more than accuracy metrics.

Data access: We will provide anonymised CSV exports. No personally identifiable information will be included — students are identified only by anonymised session IDs.

Budget: Modest. We are a small company. Please ask about the range before applying if that is a concern — we would rather have an honest conversation early.

If this sounds like work you would find interesting, write to us at info@zrenjanin-gameworks.rs with a short description of relevant experience.

title: What We Learned at the Novi Sad Education Technology Gathering
text:
In late August we attended the Novi Sad Education Technology Gathering, a small two-day event for people working on digital tools in Serbian and regional schools. It was the second year it ran and this time drew around ninety attendees — mostly teachers, a few NGO coordinators, a handful of small companies like us, and some people from municipal education offices.

We went mainly to listen. We had a small table where people could sit and try our games, and we talked to probably thirty or forty people over the two days.

A few things stood out.

First, the question of what students actually learn came up in almost every conversation. Teachers are used to seeing scores and completion rates, but several of them said directly that high scores do not always mean real understanding. One teacher from a school in Novi Sad described the same pattern we have been hearing from our own users — children who finish every level quickly but cannot do the same tasks on paper. We are working on this problem and it was useful to hear that it is not specific to our games.

Second, there was more interest in accessibility than we expected. Three teachers mentioned dyslexia or reading difficulties without us raising the topic. One asked specifically what we were doing about it. The honest answer is that we are still figuring it out, and we said so.

Third, we had a useful conversation with a representative from an NGO called Ravnica Learning Network, which works with schools in rural parts of Vojvodina. They are currently operating under a contract with a different provider but mentioned they would be open to talking in early 2025 when that contract ends.

Overall a worthwhile two days. We came back with a clearer picture of what teachers want and a list of conversations to follow up on.

title: Innovation Fund Voucher Application: Where We Are
text:
We want to be straightforward about something that has taken up more of our time than we expected this year.

In March 2024 we submitted an application for an Innovation Fund Voucher for Small Enterprises. The application was intended to fund a research collaboration focused on our student learning analytics work. The application was returned in May for corrections related to activity classification, resubmitted in June, returned again in July for a formatting issue in a financial attachment, and resubmitted in August. As of the end of October we are still waiting on a decision.

This process has cost us roughly six weeks of Miroslav's working time spread across the year — time that came directly out of product development. We delivered our Subotica contract obligations on schedule, but a planned update to the natural science modules was pushed back by two months as a result.

We are not writing this to complain about the fund or the process. The corrections requested were legitimate; we made mistakes in the original application. The problem is that we do not have someone on the team whose job is grant administration, and trying to build that capacity while also running a small software company is genuinely difficult.

If the application is approved, the funding would support the analytics work we have described elsewhere. If it is not approved, we will need to find another way to approach that problem, possibly through a partnership arrangement with a research institution that has more experience with public funding applications.

We are telling this story publicly because we suspect other small companies in the region are in the same position, and because honesty about how these things actually go seems more useful than pretending the process is smooth.

title: What We Do — Conveyor and Sorting Systems for Food and Beverage Producers
text:
AutomVoj a.d. designs and builds conveyor systems and automated sorting lines for food and beverage manufacturers who need equipment that works consistently in difficult conditions. We have been doing this since 1983 from our production site in Zrenjanin, and it is still the only thing we do.

A typical project starts with a customer's throughput requirement and floor plan and ends with a commissioned, tested line with full documentation and a trained operator team on site. We handle mechanical design, electrical panel assembly, PLC programming, and commissioning under one contract. Customers do not have to coordinate between a mechanical supplier and a controls integrator — that is our job.

Our systems run in ambient packaging halls, in cold stores operating close to freezing, in wet wash-down areas, and in high-dust grain and milling environments. We select materials and protection ratings to suit the actual operating conditions, not the easiest ones.

On the controls side, we work primarily on Siemens S7-1500 and S7-300 hardware with TIA Portal programming and Profinet networking. Most of our customers have Siemens infrastructure already, which makes spare parts and support straightforward for their maintenance teams. We also supply EPLAN-documented control panels and can integrate with existing SCADA or ERP systems where required.

After handover we offer maintenance contracts, remote support, and a spare-parts service with a 48-hour response commitment for any system we have installed. Our parts warehouse in Zrenjanin stocks the most failure-prone components for every active product generation.

Currently installed systems are operating in Serbia, Hungary, Romania, Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, and Slovakia. For inquiries about a specific project, contact our sales team in Zrenjanin.

title: Automation Engineer — PLC Programming and Commissioning
text:
AutomVoj a.d., Zrenjanin — Full-time, permanent

We are looking for an automation engineer to join our programming and commissioning team. This is a hands-on role: you will write and test PLC programs in our workshop, travel to customer sites for commissioning, and provide technical support during the warranty period. You will work on conveyor and sorting systems for food and beverage customers in Serbia and across Central Europe.

What the work looks like day to day:
— Writing and modifying ladder logic and structured text programs in Siemens TIA Portal

— Building and testing HMI screens in WinCC or Weintek
— Commissioning systems on customer sites, including network setup, I/O testing, and operator training

What we are looking for:

— Comfortable reading and producing electrical schematics

It would help if you also have:
— Experience with Profibus or Profinet network diagnostics
— Any exposure to modular or library-based programming practices
— Familiarity with food industry safety requirements (machine guarding, emergency stop categories)

We are a team of 212 people and most of our engineers have been here for more than five years. We offer a competitive salary, a travel allowance, and a tool budget. Send a CV and a short note about a project you have worked on to posao@automvoj.rs.

title: Structural Welder — Conveyor Frame Fabrication
text:
AutomVoj a.d., Zrenjanin — Full-time, permanent

We need an experienced structural welder for our frame fabrication workshop. We build mild steel and stainless steel conveyor frames to order, working from AutoCAD drawings. Quality matters: our frames ship to food production customers in several countries and have to meet their hygiene and structural requirements.

Daily work includes:
— MIG/MAG welding of hollow section and plate steel to drawing
— Fitting and tacking assemblies on jigs before final weld
— Visual and dimensional inspection of completed joints
— Light grinding and surface preparation before painting or passivation
— Working with the workshop supervisor and the engineering team when a drawing needs clarification

What we need:
— Qualified welder with a valid EN ISO 9606 certificate, preferably covering both mild steel and stainless steel
— At least four years of experience in structural or industrial fabrication
— Able to read workshop drawings independently
— Attention to fit-up quality before welding, not just the weld bead itself

Useful additional skills:
— Experience with low-temperature or food-grade stainless fabrication
— Familiar with welding procedure specifications and aware of how pre-heat and filler choice affect joint quality

We run a single day shift. The workshop is equipped and well-maintained. Salary is based on qualification and experience. Contact us at posao@automvoj.rs with your welding certificate and a brief work history.

title: AutomVoj Delivers Sorting Line to Kovačević Frozen Foods in Hungary
text:
AutomVoj a.d. has completed the commissioning of a new automated sorting and conveyor system at the Debrecen facility of Kovačević Frozen Foods Kft., a Hungarian producer of frozen vegetable products.

The project covered approximately 120 metres of PLC-controlled conveyor, three sorting stations with weight-based divert gates, and a new central control panel integrating the line into the customer's existing building management infrastructure. The system operates in a cold processing environment at approximately 4 °C and was designed and tested to run in those conditions continuously across two production shifts.

Project manager Slobodan Marković led the AutomVoj site team for the eight-week commissioning period. Handover took place in late March after a 72-hour acceptance run at full production throughput with no unplanned stoppages.

"The Kovačević project was technically straightforward in some ways and more demanding in others," said Marković. "The cold environment puts different demands on the mechanical side, and we were running electrical installation and PLC commissioning in parallel to meet the customer's production restart date. The team managed it."

Kovačević Frozen Foods is the third Hungarian customer AutomVoj has supplied in the past four years. The company currently has active installations in six EU member states in addition to its domestic market.

For information about project references or delivery timelines, contact AutomVoj sales at prodaja@automvoj.rs.

title: Why We Keep Getting Called Back to Fix the Same Electrical Noise Problem
text:
Over the past eighteen months we have had two separate customer complaints about interference affecting precision instruments on their production floors. In both cases, our conveyor systems — specifically the frequency drives running the main belt motors — were identified as a likely source.

We take these complaints seriously. Frequency drives generate harmonic currents by nature; it is a known property of variable-speed drive technology and it is not unique to the equipment we use. The question is always whether the emission level is within the limits set by applicable standards, and whether the installation has been designed to limit the problem spreading into the building's supply network.

Our standard response has been to fit line reactors at the drive input, which reduces harmonic injection and is the most common first step in the industry. In both cases the situation improved. But "improved" is not the same as "characterised and resolved", and we are honest enough to say that we do not currently have the measurement tools to tell a customer exactly what is happening on their grid and whether it meets EN 61000 limits.

That is a gap we want to close. We are looking for partners — whether test laboratories, technical institutions, or individuals with the right equipment — who could help us measure the emission spectrum from our drive configurations properly, compare it against applicable limits, and give us a design rule we can build into our standard installation practice going forward.

If you work in power electronics or electrical measurement and you think this is something you could help with, we would be glad to hear from you. Contact our chief engineer, Nikola Bošnjak, at tehnika@automvoj.rs.

title: OsiguroMi potpisao ugovor sa agro-platformom Polje.rs — pokrivenost za 1.200 gazdinstava
text:
OsiguroMi d.o.o. i platforma za upravljanje gazdinstvima Polje.rs potpisali su partnerski ugovor kojim se parametarsko osiguranje useva integriše direktno u Polje.rs mobilnu aplikaciju.

Prema uslovima saradnje, korisnici platforme Polje.rs mogu aktivirati vremensku polisu za svoju parcelu kroz dva klika u aplikaciji — bez odlaska kod agenta, bez papira. Polisa se vezuje za katastarsku parcelu korisnika i prati padavine na osnovu dostupnih meteoroloških podataka za odgovarajuću mikrozonu.

U prvoj fazi, koja je počela 1. novembra 2023, pokrivenost je dostupna za gazdinstva u Vojvodini i Mačvi. Planirano je proširenje na ostatak Srbije u drugoj polovini 2024.

Direktor Polje.rs platforme Aleksandar Mišković izjavio je: 'Naši korisnici su godinama tražili rešenje koje funkcioniše bez birokratije. Ovo je konkretno i merljivo.'

Prema internim podacima OsiguroMi tima, u prvih 30 dana od lansiranja aktivirano je oko 1.200 polisa. Okidačka sezona za zimsku pšenicu počinje u aprilu 2024.

Ova integracija je prva u agro-sektoru za OsiguroMi i označava ulazak kompanije na tržište koje do sada nije pokrila. Naredni korak je kalibracija modela na osnovu povratnih informacija koje stižu od gazdinstava u pilot periodu.

title: Šta radimo — OsiguroMi API platforma
text:
OsiguroMi je API-first platforma za ugradnju parametarskog mikro-osiguranja. Naši partneri su platforme, aplikacije i B2B servisi koji žele da ponude osiguranje kao deo svog proizvoda — bez potrebe da sami postanu osiguravač.

Kako funkcioniše: partner integriše naš API u svoju checkout ili booking stranicu. Kada korisnik završi rezervaciju, naš sistem automatski generiše polisu na osnovu parametara transakcije — destinacija, datum, vrednost, lokacija parcele i slično. Polisa se šalje korisniku u roku od nekoliko sekundi. Ako dođe do okidača — let kasni više od definisanog praga, padavine padnu ispod ugovorene granice, događaj se otkaže — isplata se pokreće bez ikakvog zahteva od strane korisnika.

Naši B2B partneri danas uključuju putničku agenciju MontFlite iz Beograda, agro-platformu Polje.rs i organizatora festivala SoundRavine Events. Kroz njihove kanale, naše polise su aktivne kod više od 40.000 krajnjih korisnika.

Tehničke karakteristike naše integracije:
— REST API, dokumentacija dostupna na developer portalu
— Sandbox okruženje za testiranje bez stvarnih podataka
— Webhookovi za obaveštenja u realnom vremenu
— SLA od 99,7% dostupnosti

Podržavamo integracije u roku od jednog radnog dana za standardne slučajeve upotrebe. Za nestandardne okidače ili nove tržišne segmente, radimo kroz pilot program koji traje četiri do šest nedelja.

Nismo broker niti posrednik u klasičnom smislu — mi smo tehnološki i aktuarski sloj koji stoji između reosiguravača i digitalnih kanala distribucije. Svaki naš proizvod je pokriven ugovorom sa reosiguravačem pre nego što izađe na tržište.

title: Zašto 3% grešaka u automatskim isplatama nije sitnica — i šta smo saznali iz revizije
text:
Kada smo u oktobru 2023. završili internu reviziju isplata za treće tromesečje, broj koji je iskočio bio je 3,1%. Toliko naših automatskih isplata za kašnjenje leta nije trebalo da bude aktivirano — ne zbog greške u polisi, ne zbog prevare korisnika, već zbog loših podataka koji su ušli u sistem pre nego što je okidač uopšte proverio bilo šta.

Naš mehanizam za obradu zahteva radi brzo jer mora. Korisnik koji kasni na letu treba obaveštenje dok je još na aerodromu. To znači da sistem donosi odluku za manje od 60 sekundi od momenta kada API za status letova javi promenu. Problem je što taj API ponekad javlja promene koje su artefakti sistema, a ne stvarnost — dupli unosi, let koji je preklasifikovan iz 'otkazano' u 'kasni' iz tehničkih razloga operatera, vremenski žigovi koji ne odgovaraju stvarnom stanju kapija.

U apsolutnim brojevima, 3,1% od 9.000 mesečnih zahteva znači oko 279 pogrešnih isplata mesečno. Svaka isplata u ovoj kategoriji iznosi između 15 i 60 EUR. To nije katastrofa, ali je sistematski odliv koji se akumulira.

Ono što nismo imali je filter koji bi proveravao konzistentnost dolaznih podataka pre okidača. Sada tražimo upravo to: ne sistem koji usporava obradu, već sloj validacije koji može da identifikuje neverovatne kombinacije podataka i da ih pošalje na kratak ručni pregled ili zadrži 90 sekundi dok ne stigne potvrda iz alternativnog izvora.

Ako radite na ovakvim problemima ili imate iskustvo sa detekcijom anomalija u API tokovima u realnom vremenu, otvoreni smo za razgovor.

title: What We Learned at Meditech Forum Vienna 2023
text:
Three of us from Kardiolink — Nenad Lazić from hardware, Milena Kovačević from clinical affairs, and myself from product — spent two days at Meditech Forum Vienna in October. It is a mid-size conference, more working meeting than showcase, and that suits us. Here is what we took away.

The storage problem is not ours alone. In three separate conversations with engineers from other patch and implantable monitoring companies, the same topic came up without us raising it: the cost of storing raw biosignal data in the cloud is becoming a real operating expense, and the standard compression approaches people adopted four or five years ago are not keeping up with the volume growth. One engineer from a company making implantable loop recorders mentioned they had started archiving processed feature vectors rather than raw signals for older recordings, which raises obvious questions about what you lose and whether regulators will eventually have a view on it. We are watching that conversation carefully.

MDR timelines are compressing everyone. Several smaller device companies said they had paused new product development to focus entirely on getting existing products through MDR certification. That is a reasonable short-term choice but it means the market for new devices is going to feel thin for another year or two while the backlog clears. For us, getting the KL-Patch 14 certified promptly is commercially important for exactly that reason: the window before competitors catch up is not infinite.

Cardiologists want simpler reports, not more data. Milena spent most of her time in the clinical sessions. The consistent message from cardiologists in primary and secondary care was that the value of remote monitoring is being diluted by platforms that surface too much raw information and not enough clear clinical signal. That is useful feedback for where we take KardioPortal's reporting module next year.

We will be back at Meditech Forum next year. If you are attending and want to talk patches, platform, or OEM manufacturing, reach out before the event.

title: About Kardiolink — Cardiac Monitoring Designed and Built in Novi Sad
text:
Kardiolink a.d. was founded in Novi Sad in 2004 by a group of engineers and cardiologists who had spent the previous decade working in hospital telemetry and wanted to move monitoring out of the ward and into patients' everyday lives. The company has remained headquartered in Novi Sad throughout, and all hardware design and manufacturing takes place at our facility on Futoška street.

Our main product line is the KL-Patch family of wearable ECG patches. The KL-Patch 72 is a 72-hour single-use device that sticks to the patient's chest, records a continuous three-channel ECG, and uploads data to our KardioPortal platform via Bluetooth when within range of a paired mobile phone or our KL-Reader clinic terminal. The KL-Patch 14 is a longer-wear variant for patients where a cardiologist needs a broader window to capture infrequent arrhythmia events. Both devices are cleared for use and are currently in use at more than 80 cardiology clinics and remote patient monitoring programmes across Serbia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, and Romania.

KardioPortal handles data ingestion, archiving, and clinical reporting. Clinicians log in through a web browser, review auto-generated reports, annotate events, and export findings in formats compatible with hospital electronic health record systems. We host the platform on AWS infrastructure with data residency options in Frankfurt to meet EU data protection requirements.

Our team of 112 covers hardware design, embedded firmware, signal processing, cloud software, clinical affairs, quality, and manufacturing. We do not outsource PCB fabrication for our core devices. Keeping production in-house means we can respond to component supply changes or clinical feedback without renegotiating with a third party.

If you are a cardiology clinic, a remote monitoring service operator, or a company looking for an OEM patch manufacturing partner, we are open to conversations. Contact us at info@kardiolink.rs.

title: Kardiolink Signs Supply Agreement with Medivera Remote Monitoring, Czech Republic

Under the agreement, Medivera will order a minimum of 400 KL-Patch 72 units per month, with option provisions for the KL-Patch 14 once that device completes its CE MDR certification process. Medivera's clinical coordinators will access patient data through KardioPortal, with a data residency configuration that keeps all patient records on AWS Frankfurt infrastructure to satisfy Czech and EU data protection requirements.

Lukáš Horváth, Operations Director at Medivera, said the decision came down to the combination of a manufacturable, field-tested device and an accessible reporting platform. He noted that previous patch vendors his organisation had evaluated required Medivera to integrate with separate data platforms, adding implementation time before the programme could start.

For Kardiolink, the agreement is the company's first direct customer relationship in the Czech market, where the company had previously sold only through a regional distributor. Gordana Ristić, Head of Commercial at Kardiolink, said the shift toward direct agreements with monitoring programme operators reflects where growth in the EU remote cardiology market is coming from: structured, programme-level deployments rather than single-clinic purchasing.

The first patch shipment under the Medivera agreement is scheduled for March 2024. Kardiolink's logistics partner for Czech deliveries is Transporto Balkan d.o.o., which also handles distribution to customers in Slovakia and Hungary.

text:

What you will work on:

Our patches run FreeRTOS on an ARM Cortex-M4, with a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 handling both application logic and BLE communication. The work involves writing and optimising firmware for real-time ECG acquisition at 250 Hz, managing BLE duty cycling to reduce active current draw, and maintaining the IEC 62304-compliant software lifecycle artefacts our notified body requires.

We have a specific near-term problem we need help with: our 72-hour patch consumes more current during BLE activity than we want, and we need an engineer who can dig into the power budget at the level of radio scheduler configuration, ADC sampling modes, DMA transfers, and sleep state transitions. We have a Keysight N6705C power analyser set up in the lab and a suite of instrumented reference boards ready to go.

What we are looking for:
- Three or more years writing firmware in C for Cortex-M microcontrollers
- Direct experience with Nordic nRF52 series and the nRF5 SDK or nRF Connect SDK
- Demonstrated work on BLE power optimisation: advertising intervals, connection parameters, PHY selection
- Familiarity with FreeRTOS task scheduling and its interaction with low-power modes
- Ability to write and maintain IEC 62304 software lifecycle documentation is a significant plus
- Experience with biosignal acquisition hardware is welcome but not required

The position is full-time, on-site in Novi Sad, with some flexibility for remote days after an initial settling-in period. Salary is negotiable based on experience. Send your CV and a short note about a power optimisation problem you have solved to careers@kardiolink.rs.

title: What PravniPilot Does — Platform and Services Overview
text:
PravniPilot gives lawyers faster access to the decisions and arguments that matter to their case.

Our platform holds over two million court decisions from Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Every document is parsed, indexed and linked to related cases so you can find relevant precedent in seconds rather than hours. Keyword search, Boolean filters, court-level filters and date ranges are all available from a single interface. No installation required — the platform runs in any modern browser.

The case-outcome prediction module analyzes the facts you enter and compares them against historical decisions in the same legal area. It returns a probability distribution across outcome categories, along with the decisions that influenced that estimate. The module currently covers commercial disputes, labor claims and property litigation. Prediction results include the number of supporting cases so you know how much data sits behind any estimate.

For firms that process high volumes of documents, our document annotation tool generates structured summaries of uploaded filings, extracts cited statutes and precedents, and flags arguments the opposing side has used in similar past cases.

Enterprise customers — insurers, banks and larger litigation practices — can access our full dataset through a bulk-export API. We also license cleaned, structured legal datasets to third parties under a separate data agreement.

All customer data is stored on our own infrastructure inside Serbia. We do not use customer documents or queries to train or update our models without explicit written consent.

For pricing, onboarding timelines or a demonstration, contact our sales team in Subotica or visit our development office at NTP Novi Sad.

title: Why our AI summaries cited a case that no longer applies — and what we are doing about it
text:
We want to be straightforward about something that happened twice in the past eight months.

Our platform generated research summaries that cited precedents which had been amended or effectively overturned by subsequent rulings. In both cases, a law firm user included the summary language in a draft brief. In one case the error was caught internally before filing. In the other, the brief went to opposing counsel with the outdated citation. No proceeding was harmed, but the firm was embarrassed and we were responsible.

We have spent time since the second incident understanding why this happened and what a real fix looks like.

The short version: our summarization model generates fluent text, but it does not inherently know whether the case it is citing is still good law. It picks the most statistically relevant decision for a given query, not the most current or most authoritative one. We have a recency filter in the search layer, but that filter does not feed back into the summary generation in a meaningful way. The result is a system that sounds confident and is sometimes wrong.

What we are doing now: we have added a visible warning banner on all AI-generated summaries that explicitly tells users to verify every cited decision before using it in a filing. That is not a technical fix — it is a patch. The real work is building sentence-level source provenance so that every claim in a summary links to a specific, datestamped decision and shows the user how many cases support that claim. We are actively working on this and will say more when we have something worth showing.

We are also reviewing whether our onboarding materials have been clear enough about the limitations of the summarization tool. Based on what we saw this year, they were not.

We think lawyers deserve tools that are honest about what they know and what they do not. We are not there yet on this feature, but we are working on it.

title: What We Do — Suncokret Eko d.o.o.
text:
Vojvodina produces hundreds of thousands of tonnes of agricultural residues every year. Sunflower husks come off the decorticating lines at oil mills. Maize cobs pile up after grain separation. Food processors generate wet organic fractions that mostly end up in landfill or are spread untreated on fields. We built Suncokret Eko to turn that material into something more useful.

Our main product line is biomass pellets. We collect husks and cobs from farms and processing plants across Vojvodina, dry and size them to a consistent specification, and press them into fuel pellets that meet the requirements of industrial and residential heating systems. Our pellets are wood-free, which matters for customers who need to demonstrate that their fuel supply does not contribute to deforestation.

Alongside pellet production we operate a slow-pyrolysis unit that converts a portion of our feedstock into biochar. Biochar applied to agricultural soil retains carbon for centuries and can improve water-holding capacity in the sandy soils common in this region. We sell biochar to farms, composting operations, and land reclamation projects. We are currently working through the documentation required to register our biochar production under a recognised carbon certification scheme so that buyers can use it toward carbon removal commitments.

Our facility is located on the campus of the NTP Novi Sad science and technology park, which gives us access to testing equipment and connects us with research groups working on related topics. We ship domestically and to buyers in Hungary, Romania, and Germany. Minimum order quantities and current pricing are available on request.

If you produce agricultural residues or food-processing waste and want to discuss a collection or co-processing arrangement, contact our procurement team at nabavka@suncokreteko.rs.

Experience with pyrolysis, biomass processing, or carbon certification is a plus but not expected at the junior level. This role has room to grow as our biochar business grows. Send applications to posao@suncokreteko.rs with the subject line 'Junior Analyst Application'.

title: Suncokret Eko Secures Supply Agreement with Toplana Zrenjanin
text:
We are pleased to confirm that Suncokret Eko has signed a two-year pellet supply agreement with Toplana Zrenjanin, a municipal district heating operator serving approximately 8,400 households. Deliveries under the agreement will begin in September 2024 ahead of the winter heating season.

The contract covers 1,200 tonnes of biomass pellets per year. Toplana Zrenjanin was looking for a locally produced, wood-free fuel that could be introduced gradually into their existing combustion system alongside their current fuel mix. Our sunflower husk pellets met their calorific value and ash-content requirements and the short transport distance from our facility in Novi Sad was a factor in their decision.

For us this is the largest single supply contract we have signed to date. It also creates a clear forward load on our pellet press line for the next two years, which affects how we plan maintenance and feedstock procurement. Our procurement manager, Milica Vranić, has already begun discussions with three additional farms in the Zrenjanin area to secure enough husk material to cover the increased volume without putting pressure on our existing suppliers.

Dragan Ostojić noted that running at higher sustained throughput will also give us better data on how our line performs over longer uninterrupted runs, which feeds directly into the work we are doing to reduce press downtime.

We thank the team at Toplana Zrenjanin for a straightforward and practical negotiation process. Questions about pellet supply availability can be directed to prodaja@suncokreteko.rs.

title: What We Learned at BioenergyEurope Showcase 2024 in Vienna
text:
Four of us from Suncokret Eko attended the BioenergyEurope Showcase in Vienna at the beginning of May. It was the first time we had taken a stand at an international trade event rather than just walking the floor, and it was worth the effort.

The conversations that were most useful were not with the large equipment suppliers or the established pellet producers. They were with two groups of buyers we had not had direct contact with before. The first were German agricultural input distributors who are looking for biochar they can blend into soil conditioner products. Three of them asked about our production capacity and our quality documentation. Two of those three specifically asked about European Biochar Certificate registration, which confirmed for us that this certification is becoming a practical requirement for that market, not just a nice-to-have.

The second group was buyers from the Netherlands running commercial greenhouse operations. They are interested in biochar as a growing medium component. Their fixed-carbon requirements were similar to the German buyers, and one of them was willing to discuss a pilot purchase even before full certification, on the condition that we could provide detailed lab analysis and a signed declaration of production method.

We also spent time at a session on feedstock pre-conditioning for pellet producers. A presenter from Slovakia described a system they use to homogenise cereal straw from multiple suppliers before it enters the press. The approach was not identical to our situation but some of the ideas were directly relevant to the sunflower husk consistency problems we have been dealing with.

We came back with a list of follow-up contacts and a clearer sense that the biochar market in Germany and the Netherlands is real and moving faster than the domestic Serbian market. Getting our certification documentation finished is no longer a background task — it is the main commercial bottleneck on that side of our business.

title: What We Make and Who We Make It For
text:
Elekron Sistemi has been building control electronics for municipal infrastructure since 1987. That is not a marketing line — it is the reason our engineering team thinks differently from companies that entered this market in the last decade.

Our core product is the ES-RTU series of remote terminal units. Each unit is designed to sit in an unheated, unattended substation, read sensors, control actuators, and report reliably to a SCADA system for years without intervention. We manufacture the enclosures that house them in our own sheet-metal workshop in Subotica, and we write the firmware that runs on them. When something goes wrong in the field, the person who answers the phone wrote some of the code.

Since 2021 we have been expanding into LoRaWAN-based metering. Municipal utilities across the region have tens of thousands of water and heat meters that were installed before wireless communication was practical. Replacing them is expensive. Our LoRaWAN collar device attaches to the existing meter body, reads the pulse output, and transmits daily consumption data to a cloud dashboard without replacing the meter itself. We have active deployments in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia.

Our customers are municipal water companies, district-heating operators, and the engineering integrators who serve them. They do not want innovation for its own sake. They want equipment that works on a Tuesday morning in February when the duty engineer is the only person on site. That requirement shapes every decision we make about materials, protocols, and firmware design.

Elekron Sistemi is employee-owned. The 117 people here have a direct interest in the company's reputation, and that shows in how we handle warranty calls and field failures. We hold framework agreements with seven municipal utilities and maintain a field-service team that covers the Western Balkans region.

title: Embedded Firmware Engineer — RTU and LoRaWAN Products

title: Process Engineer — Sheet-Metal Fabrication and Surface Finishing
text:

This is a hands-on position — you will spend time on the workshop floor, not just in front of a spreadsheet. Our workshop supervisor Branimir Talić will be your closest collaborator.

title: What We Learned Exhibiting at ENEX Beograd 2024
text:
Five of us travelled to Belgrade in April for the ENEX energy and infrastructure exhibition. We had a 12-square-metre stand, two working hardware demonstrations, and a stack of datasheets. Here is an honest account of what was useful and what was not.

The useful part was conversations with municipal utility engineers, not procurement people. The engineers who stopped at our stand had specific problems — a pump station with intermittent communication dropouts, a heat substation where the existing RTU had been discontinued by the original manufacturer and nobody could source spare parts, a metering project that needed to cover 400 basement locations on a fixed budget. These are exactly the conversations we came for. We collected 23 serious leads and have followed up on all of them.

The less useful part was the panel discussions. We sat through two sessions on the future of smart city infrastructure that spent most of their time on topics that have nothing to do with the practical reality of keeping a 1980s water network running reliably in a mid-sized Balkan city. We do not expect conference panels to solve our problems, but it would be good to hear more from operators and less from consultants.

Our LoRaWAN collar demonstration attracted more interest than we expected. We brought a live setup with a gateway and two collar units transmitting to a laptop dashboard. Several visitors had not seen a retrofit approach before and asked detailed questions about installation time and battery life. Average installation time in the field is 25 minutes per meter. Battery life at one transmission per hour is approximately five years on the standard AA cell pack.

We will exhibit at ENEX again next year. If you missed us in April and want to see a working demonstration, contact us to arrange a visit to our Subotica facility or a remote call with a hardware demo.

title: Elekron Sistemi Receives Provincial Innovation Fund Grant for LoRaWAN Signal Research
text:
Elekron Sistemi a.d. has been awarded a grant of 4.2 million dinars from the Vojvodina Development Fund's 2024 innovation support programme. The grant will part-fund a 14-month applied research project aimed at improving LoRaWAN read reliability in obstructed urban environments, specifically basement meter rooms with thick reinforced-concrete walls.

The project, internally called ReachRate, will combine antenna configuration testing, adaptive spreading-factor firmware logic, and evaluation of low-power mesh relay approaches. We are conducting the work with our own engineering team and are in early discussions with the Science and Technology Park Novi Sad about additional technical support for the signal propagation and firmware analysis components.

The grant covers approximately 55% of projected project costs. The remainder will be funded from our own operating budget. Project lead is our senior RF engineer Dragan Fekete, who has been with Elekron Sistemi for nine years and led the original LoRaWAN collar development.

We set a clear target for the project: reduce daily missed readings at our existing deployments from the current 9% to below 1% without replacing installed gateways. We have three live municipal sites in Bosnia and North Macedonia where we can test changes under real conditions, which is a significant practical advantage compared with laboratory-only research.

If the project produces firmware or hardware changes that meet the target, we will roll them out to existing collar deployments as an over-the-air firmware update and incorporate them into new production units from mid-2025 onward.

We thank the Vojvodina Development Fund for the support. Detailed project reporting will be submitted at the six-month and final milestones as required by the grant terms.

title: LinguaBot signs second telecom client, expands team by three
text:
LinguaBot d.o.o. has signed a contract with Mobilna Mreža Vojvodine d.o.o., a regional mobile network operator, to deploy LinguaBot Assist on their customer support web portal. The deployment is scheduled to go live in the second quarter of 2024.

The contract follows a four-month pilot in which LinguaBot handled a subset of billing and account queries for a test group of customers. During the pilot, the bot resolved 61% of sessions without agent handoff, against an internal baseline of 44% for the previous chat tool the operator was using.

This is LinguaBot's second telecom client after Telekomunikacije Srednje Srbije d.o.o., which has been using LinguaBot Assist since late 2022.

"The pilot gave us a clear picture of where the tool performs and where it needs more work," said Milena Kovačević, head of customer operations at Mobilna Mreža Vojvodine. "The morphology handling was noticeably better than what we had seen from other vendors. We still have gaps we want to close, but the baseline was good enough to move forward."

LinguaBot CEO Dragan Filipović said the win validates the company's focus on Serbian-language accuracy over breadth. "We are not trying to support forty languages. We are trying to make one language work properly. That is still a hard problem and there is still work to do, but clients notice the difference."

Alongside the contract announcement, LinguaBot confirmed three new hires: two ML engineers and one integration specialist. The company now employs 22 people, all based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad.

title: What We Do — LinguaBot d.o.o.
text:
LinguaBot builds customer support automation for companies that serve Serbian-speaking customers. That is a specific problem, and we treat it that way.

Most conversational AI tools are built around English and then stretched to cover other languages. Serbian does not stretch well. The grammar is complex, the script situation is unusual, and the training data available in the open market is thin. We have spent four years building around those constraints rather than ignoring them.

Our main product, LinguaBot Assist, handles multi-turn support conversations on web and mobile. It connects to a client's existing knowledge base and CRM, understands what a customer is asking even when they write in Cyrillic one moment and Latin the next, and hands off to a human agent when it genuinely cannot help — with a summary of what was already discussed.

LinguaBot Search sits underneath Assist and can also be licensed separately. It is a retrieval layer for internal knowledge bases that understands Serbian morphology, so a support agent searching for 'otkazivanje ugovora' will find documents that contain 'otkazati ugovor' or 'raskid ugovora' without anyone having to maintain a synonym list by hand.

LinguaBot Studio gives content teams at our client companies a way to update conversation flows, add new FAQ entries, and review bot performance without filing a ticket with us every time. Most of our clients have someone using it daily.

We work primarily with banks and telecoms in Serbia. Current clients include four retail banks and two mobile network operators. We process around 140,000 chat sessions per month and our uptime across all deployments last year was 99.91%.

Our team is based in the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad. If you want to talk about whether what we do fits your situation, write to us.

title: NLP / Search Engineer — LinguaBot d.o.o.
text:
We are looking for an engineer who wants to work on Serbian-language search and retrieval.

The core problem: our Elasticsearch-based search works, but it does not work well enough. Serbian morphology means the same concept appears in many surface forms, and our users mix Latin and Cyrillic script. We have measured a meaningful miss rate on real queries and we want to fix it properly.

What you would work on:
- Improving our indexing pipeline to handle morphological variation in Serbian, whether through better lemmatisation, morphological analysis, or a different retrieval approach entirely
- Building or integrating script normalisation that handles Latin/Cyrillic mixing reliably
- Evaluating changes against our labelled query dataset (around 85,000 query-response pairs)
- Working with our two in-house linguists, who can annotate and validate

What we are looking for:
- Solid experience with Elasticsearch or a comparable search system
- Python — we use it for everything in the pipeline
- Some practical experience with morphologically complex languages, or genuine interest in learning
- Comfort working with annotated datasets and running your own evaluations

Nice to have:
- Experience with spaCy or similar NLP libraries
- Familiarity with Serbian, Croatian, or another South Slavic language

What we do not need: a researcher who wants to publish. We need someone who wants to ship something that works and can tell when it does not.

This is a full-time position at our office in NTP Novi Sad. We offer a competitive salary by local market standards, flexible hours, and a small team where your work is visible. Send a CV and a short note about what you have worked on to posao@linguabot.rs.

title: Why our search still fails some of the time, and what we are doing about it
text:
We track every session where our bot returns no useful result. Last quarter, across all deployments, that number was higher than we want it to be — around 17% of sessions ended without the customer getting an answer.

We have looked at the logs carefully. Script mixing accounts for some of it: a user types 'kredit' in Latin and our index has the document filed under Cyrillic 'кредит', or the other way around. That is solvable with normalisation and we have a partial fix in place, but it is not complete.

The bigger problem is morphology. Serbian is an inflected language. The noun 'kartica' (payment card) appears in our users' queries as 'karticu', 'kartice', 'karticom', 'karticama', and a handful of other forms depending on what the user is trying to say. Our stemmer treats these as different words. Sometimes they land on the right document anyway because the document also uses multiple forms. Often they do not.

We have tried expanding synonym lists manually, but our clients add new product names and terms every quarter and we cannot keep up. We have also tried a retrieval approach that uses sentence embeddings rather than keyword matching, and it helps with paraphrase variation but does not reliably fix morphological mismatch — the embedding models available for Serbian are trained on limited data and have their own gaps.

What we have that could help: 85,000 labelled query-response pairs, two linguists who know Serbian morphology well, and a clear evaluation setup so we can measure whether a proposed change actually improves things before we deploy it.

We do not have a clean solution yet. We are talking to people who work on computational morphology for South Slavic languages and running our own experiments on lemmatisation pipelines. If you have worked on this problem — the practical engineering side, not just the theory — we are interested in talking. You can reach us at research@linguabot.rs.

title: Speech / ML Engineer (Voice Project) — LinguaBot d.o.o.
text:
We have a contract commitment to deliver a voice channel product by early 2027. We need an engineer who knows how speech recognition systems work and can help us figure out what is realistic for Serbian on telephony audio.

Background: we tested two commercial ASR APIs on a sample of real Serbian call recordings and got word-error rates above 38%. That is not usable. We have about 1,200 consented call recordings from a client, which is a start but not a lot. We need someone who can look at this situation clearly and tell us what is possible, then help build it.

What the role involves:
- Assessing what fine-tuning an existing multilingual speech model on our data would actually achieve
- Identifying what additional data we would need to collect and how
- Building a proof-of-concept pipeline: audio in, transcript out, good enough to run intent detection on
- Working with our ML engineers on integrating ASR output into the existing chat understanding stack

What we are looking for:
- Experience training or fine-tuning speech recognition models — we do not need someone who has only used APIs
- Python
- Honest about what is hard and what is not
- Able to work toward a fixed deadline without pretending uncertainty does not exist

Familiarity with Serbian is not required but would help. This is a full-time position in Novi Sad. The project has a real deadline and a real budget. If you have done this kind of work before and want a concrete problem to solve, write to posao@linguabot.rs with 'Voice' in the subject line.

title: Kredo Fintech Crosses 1,000-Loan Milestone
text:
Kredo Fintech announced this week that it has funded its 1,000th loan since launching its platform in late 2020. The milestone was reached with a loan to Braća Nikolić d.o.o., a small timber processing firm based near Sremska Mitrovica that used the funds to purchase a replacement band saw after their existing machine failed.

Milan Đorđević, one of Kredo's co-founders, described the number as meaningful but noted that the team was more focused on the quality of the portfolio than its size. "A thousand loans does not mean much if half of them are in trouble. What we are more interested in is that our default rate has stayed below what the banking sector reports for comparable SME lending. That tells us the model is doing its job."

The loan book spans 23 sectors, with the largest concentrations in food and beverage production, small logistics and transport, and e-commerce retail. Average loan size is approximately 8,400 euros, and average loan term is 22 months.

Kredo operates entirely from its office at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad and has no branch network. All applications, decisions, and repayments are handled through the Kredo Portal, the company's borrower-facing web platform.

The company said it plans to use 2024 to improve its scoring capability for early-stage businesses and to prepare the regulatory groundwork for expansion into North Macedonia. No date for the North Macedonia launch has been set.

title: About Kredo Fintech — Loans Built for Small Business Reality
text:
Kredo Fintech exists because the standard bank loan application was not designed for a business with seven employees and eighteen months of trading history. It was designed for someone who already had access to capital.

We opened our doors in Novi Sad in 2020 with one product and one question: can you build a credit decision that is fast, fair, and financially sound without requiring a business to jump through hoops it was never built to jump through? Four years and more than 1,400 funded loans later, we think the answer is yes.

Our lending process is entirely online. An applicant connects their business bank account, uploads a tax filing, and answers a short questionnaire. Our platform pulls that information into a scoring pipeline built in Python on a Snowflake data warehouse, and in most cases returns a decision within two business hours. For approved applicants, funds reach their account within one working day.

We lend to businesses across a wide range of sectors — food production, small logistics operators, printing and packaging, e-commerce, repair services. What they have in common is that they are real, operating businesses that need working capital or a small investment and do not want to wait six weeks to find out whether they qualify.

Our team of 26 is based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad. We are licensed and supervised by the National Bank of Serbia. We do not use third-party lead generators or commission-based brokers. Every borrower deals directly with Kredo.

If you run a small business in Serbia and you need financing, start an application. It takes about twelve minutes.

title: Why We Struggle to Score a One-Year-Old Business (And What We Are Doing About It)
text:
One of the more uncomfortable facts about our scoring model is that it works best for businesses that least need us.

A firm with two or three years of transaction data, a clean tax record, and stable monthly revenues is easy to score. We have plenty of examples like it in our training data. The model has seen the pattern before and it forms a confident view. These applicants get fast decisions and competitive rates.

The firms that are harder to score are the ones that are newer. A business that has been operating for eight months has less data. The seasonal patterns are not yet clear. There may be one large payment that looks unusual but is actually normal for the sector. Our model, trained mostly on older firms, tends to treat this uncertainty as risk and either rejects the application or prices it at a rate that makes the loan unworkable.

This is a problem we want to fix, because new businesses are often the ones that need capital most urgently and have the fewest alternatives.

We have tried a few approaches. Adding sector-level benchmarks as features — so the model can compare a young bakery against how bakeries of that size and age typically behave — helped a little. Incorporating payment regularity signals from connected bank accounts helped a little more. But the improvement has not been large enough to change our approval rate on this segment in a meaningful way.

What we think we need is a different approach to the thin-file problem: either a separate model trained specifically on young-firm applications with appropriate features, or a way to transfer learning from more data-rich segments to less data-rich ones. We have about 400 labeled examples from young-firm applicants where we now know the outcome. That is not a large dataset but it is something.

We are actively looking for people with experience in this area. If you work on credit scoring, alternative data, or machine learning for thin-file populations and you want to talk, our door is open. You can reach our data lead, Nemanja Stojanović, at podaci@kredofintech.rs.

title: What We Do — Velago Software
text:

Our clients are typically companies with between 50 and 500 employees that have outgrown generic platforms but do not want to build and manage a large internal IT function. They need software that fits their process exactly, and they need to be able to call someone when something breaks at 07:00 on a Monday.

We work in React, Node.js, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL for most projects, and we deploy on AWS. We manage our own CI/CD pipelines and we write tests. We can discuss the technical details with your internal team or your CTO — we are used to both.

title: Mid-Level DevOps / Test Infrastructure Engineer — Velago Software

You do not need to have worked on our specific stack, but you should have worked on a codebase where the test suite had grown faster than its architecture.

title: Why our defect escape rate went from 2% to 9% — and what we are doing about it
text:
We track defect escape rate — the share of bugs that reach a production environment rather than being caught in testing — as one of our main internal quality indicators. For most of our history it sat around 2 percent, which we considered acceptable given our project mix. Over the past six months it has climbed to around 9 percent. We have had two production incidents serious enough to require client communication. We think it is worth being honest about what happened.

The immediate cause is straightforward: our test suite now takes four and a half hours to run end to end. That is long enough that developers have started making rational, understandable decisions to skip the full run or push small changes without waiting. When you are trying to get a fix out before a client's morning standup, four hours is not a realistic wait time.

The slower cause is that the test suite grew without coordination. Over several years, different developers added tests that made sense at the time. Nobody was responsible for the overall structure. We now have significant overlap between unit tests and end-to-end scenarios covering the same logic, slow database fixtures that could be mocked, and Playwright tests that are essentially duplicating what Jest tests already verify at a lower level.

We tried parallelising more of the Playwright tests last autumn and got the time down from about six hours to four and a half, which tells us the architecture of the suite is the real problem rather than just the runner capacity.

We are currently hiring a DevOps and test infrastructure engineer specifically to address this. The goal is a restructured pipeline where the feedback loop for a typical push is under 45 minutes, and where the full suite is reserved for merge requests to main rather than every commit. We expect this to take three to four months to implement properly.

We are writing about this because we suspect we are not the only software company in this position. The test suite slowdown is a problem that grows invisibly until the consequences are hard to ignore.

title: Sentinel Byte completes first municipal engagement in Kanjiža
text:
We finished our first full security assessment for a municipal client in northern Vojvodina in October and we want to write briefly about what that experience taught us, without sharing any findings that belong to the client.

The engagement covered the municipality's internal network, their public-facing web presence, and the workstations used by administrative staff. The scope was agreed over two meetings with their IT coordinator, a practical person who was candid about the limits of what he could realistically fix given the municipality's maintenance budget and procurement constraints.

We found what we generally find in organisations of this type: a mix of well-maintained systems and systems that have not been touched in years because nobody flagged them as a priority. The report we delivered listed seventeen findings across four severity levels. The top three were straightforward to fix with no budget — configuration changes and a patching task that had been deferred.

The more interesting outcome came a month later. We followed up with the IT coordinator and learned that only four of the seventeen findings had been addressed. Not because the municipality disagreed with our recommendations, but because the remediation steps, written in our standard technical format, were not actionable for someone who manages IT part-time alongside other administrative duties.

We went back for a half-day session, went through each finding verbally, and helped prioritise. Within three weeks, eleven of the seventeen findings were resolved.

This is not a story about a client failing. It is a story about the gap between a technically correct report and a useful one. We are working on closing that gap as a formal part of what we offer. If you have had a similar experience with audit reports that did not lead anywhere, we are interested in talking.

title: Our Services
text:
Sentinel Byte is a Subotica-based security testing firm with six people and one straightforward focus: finding the gaps in your defences before someone else does.

**Network Penetration Testing**
We map your internal and external network, identify exposed services, and test whether those exposures can be turned into real access. You receive a written report in Serbian or English listing every finding, its severity, and a concrete remediation step written for your actual IT staff.

**Web Application Audit**
For companies running customer portals, internal tools, or any web-facing application, we conduct a structured audit covering authentication, authorisation, input handling, and session management. We follow the OWASP Testing Guide as a baseline and document every tested item.

**Municipal Security Assessment**
Local governments in Serbia have specific obligations under information security legislation. We understand those requirements and produce findings reports formatted to support compliance documentation. We also offer a follow-up session for your IT coordinators to walk through what the findings mean in practical terms.

**Phishing Simulation**
We send a controlled phishing campaign to your staff, measure click and credential-entry rates, and debrief your team on what the results mean. This is not about embarrassing employees; it is about giving management a realistic picture of social engineering risk.

**Remediation Support**
An audit report sitting unread helps nobody. We offer a structured session after delivery — in person or remote — to help your team prioritise and begin acting on findings.

All engagements begin with a scoping call at no charge. We will tell you honestly if your situation falls outside what a six-person firm can handle well.

title: Why we wrote our own reconnaissance scripts and why we are about to stop
text:
For the past two years, every penetration test we run has started the same way: Nikola sits down with a target scope, runs a set of Bash scripts that wrap Nmap and a few other tools, and spends most of a working day cleaning the output into something our testers can actually use. The scripts work. They are also held together with more string than we would like to admit.

We wrote them because we needed something faster than running tools manually and we could not justify the licensing cost of a commercial continuous scanning platform for a firm our size. The scripts do their job: they take a list of IP ranges or domains, run a structured scan sequence, and produce a text file organised by host with open ports, detected services, and Nessus findings cross-referenced. Nikola knows every line. Nobody else on the team fully does.

The problem has two parts. First, clients are starting to ask for something closer to continuous monitoring — not an annual test but a monthly or quarterly scan that shows what changed since last time. Our scripts were built for a single run, not for comparison across time. We have tried adding a diff step and it mostly works, but edge cases cause enough noise that someone still has to review everything manually before we trust the output.

Second, the scripts break when tool versions change. Nessus in particular has changed its output format twice since we wrote the parser. Each time, Nikola spends two days fixing things instead of running tests.

We are not complaining. We knew what we were building. But we have reached the point where maintaining this ourselves is not the best use of our time, and we are actively looking for a better approach — whether that is a different toolchain, a collaboration that could help us build something more robust, or a combination of the two. If you work on this kind of problem and want to compare notes, reach out.
