title: PlastiPak Vojvodina Signs Multi-Year Crate Supply Agreement with Balaton Pack Kft.
text:
PlastiPak Vojvodina has signed a multi-year supply agreement with Balaton Pack Kft., a packaging distributor based in Győr, Hungary. Under the agreement, PlastiPak will supply stackable polypropylene crates in three standard formats to Balaton Pack's retail and logistics customers in western Hungary, with volumes ramping up to approximately double our current crate-equivalent tray output by the third quarter of 2025.

The agreement represents the largest single customer commitment in the company's history for the tray and crate product lines. Negotiations began in the second half of 2023, following an introduction at the Packaging Solutions Central Europe trade fair in Vienna, where PlastiPak exhibited for the first time.

Direktor Miroslav Čović said the contract reflects the location advantage that the Subotica plant offers for Hungarian buyers. 'Our plant is forty minutes from the border crossing. For a Hungarian distributor that means reliable short-cycle delivery without the costs of warehousing large buffer stocks in Hungary. That is the argument we made in Vienna and Balaton Pack found it straightforward.'

Fulfilling the volume commitments in the agreement requires PlastiPak to expand its thermoforming capacity. The company submitted an application under the IPARD III rural development programme nine months ago to co-finance the necessary equipment purchase. That application remains under review. PlastiPak has stated that it is monitoring the application status closely and is evaluating parallel financing options to ensure it can meet the Q3 2025 delivery schedule regardless of the grant outcome.

Balaton Pack Kft. distributes packaging materials and consumables to food-processing and logistics clients across Hungary and Austria. The supply agreement runs for three years with an option to extend.

title: What We Make and How We Work
text:
PlastiPak Vojvodina has produced rigid plastic packaging from its Subotica plant since 2004. Our core output is injection-moulded polypropylene food trays and lids, sized and toleranced to run on the automated filling lines used by food processors across Serbia and Hungary. We also produce stackable polypropylene industrial crates used in logistics and food transport, and we thermoform PET and PP sheet into custom lid formats for dairy and fresh produce customers.

Our plant runs eight injection-moulding presses ranging from 180 to 650 tonnes of clamping force, plus a thermoforming cell for sheet-fed production. We maintain our own tool room, equipped for EDM and CNC milling, which means we can modify cooling channels, adjust cavity inserts, and carry out routine mould repairs without sending tooling to outside contractors. That capability matters to our customers because it keeps lead times short when a packaging format needs to change.

Quality control follows ISO 9001:2015 procedures. Dimensional inspection is carried out using manual coordinate measurement, and all press parameters are logged continuously through our Fenix DataLog plant-floor system, giving us a traceable record for every production batch.

Our customer base is concentrated in northern Serbia and across the border in southern Hungary. We supply Meridian Retail Group's private-label fresh food programme and several food processors including Danubefresh d.o.o. For crate products we serve logistics operators and export customers through intermediary distributors.

We employ 183 people. Production runs in two twelve-hour shifts, five days a week, with a weekend shift on the thermoforming cell when order volumes require it. If you are a buyer looking for a packaging supplier with short transport distance to Hungary and reliable dimensional consistency, or if you are a technical partner interested in our process improvement challenges, we welcome direct contact through the address on this page.

title: Process Engineer – Injection Moulding (Subotica)
text:
PlastiPak Vojvodina is looking for a process engineer to join our production team in Subotica. The role is on the injection-moulding floor and covers day-to-day process optimisation, first-off and in-process inspection, and support for new product trials.

What you will work on:
- Setting and adjusting process parameters on our 180–650 tonne presses (melt temperature, injection speed, hold pressure, cooling time) to achieve part quality within drawing tolerances
- Investigating and reducing scrap causes, particularly dimensional defects such as warpage and sink marks on polypropylene parts
- Maintaining and interpreting production data in our Fenix DataLog SCADA system
- Supporting in-house mould trials after tool room modifications
- Writing process setting sheets and participating in FMEA reviews for new part introductions

What we are looking for:
- A degree or higher vocational qualification in polymer processing, mechanical engineering, or a related subject
- At least three years of hands-on experience on injection-moulding presses, preferably with PP or PE materials
- Ability to read mould drawings and cooling-circuit diagrams
- Familiarity with basic statistical methods for process capability — we use control charts and Cpk values in our quality reporting
- Experience with mould-flow simulation software would be an advantage, though it is not required; we are open to someone who wants to develop this skill on the job
- Good written Serbian; working English for reading supplier and customer technical documents

We work two twelve-hour shifts. This position is assigned to the day shift with occasional cover on afternoons. Salary is competitive for the Subotica region and is based on experience. We offer a stable production environment, an experienced team, and real problems to solve — our rejection-rate challenge on the food-tray line is something the right engineer can make a measurable difference on.

Send a CV and a brief note about your relevant experience to the HR contact on our website. We will respond to all complete applications within two weeks.

title: Why We Are Pursuing ISO 14001 — and What It Actually Means for Our Plant
text:
We have been manufacturing plastic packaging in Subotica for twenty years. In that time we have invested in presses, tooling, and people, and we have built an ISO 9001 quality system that works. Environmental management has not been a formal priority in the same way — we comply with our permits, we handle waste through licensed contractors, and we have not had regulatory problems. That is changing.

One of our major customers — a German retail chain that takes a significant share of our crate volume — has set a supplier requirement that all packaging manufacturers in their supply chain hold ISO 14001 certification by January 2026. We received that requirement in writing late last year. We are taking it seriously.

We want to be honest about where we are starting from. We have a cooling-water discharge permit that we operate under, but the documentation around it has not been reviewed in some time. We reintroduce production regrind into some of our non-food lines, which is good practice, but we do not have a written procedure for it that would satisfy an auditor. Our pad-printing station generates solvent and ink waste that goes through a licensed disposal contractor, but again the paper trail needs work.

None of these are problems that indicate reckless practice. They are the normal documentation gaps of a company that has grown its production without growing its environmental administration at the same pace.

Over the coming months we are going to do a structured gap analysis, build the documentation that is missing, and work with a certification body toward a formal audit in the autumn of 2025. We are also looking for people and organisations with experience in industrial environmental management who want to work on a concrete, time-bounded project. If that describes you, the contact details are on this page.

For our customers and partners: this process will not change what we produce or how we price it. It will produce better records and, we expect, a clearer picture of where we can reduce waste and energy use in ways that benefit the business as well as the certificate.

title: Environmental and Quality Documentation Coordinator (part-time, Subotica)
text:
PlastiPak Vojvodina is adding a part-time role focused on environmental documentation and quality system support as we prepare for ISO 14001 certification. The position is based at our Subotica plant and is expected to grow into a full-time role once the certification process is underway.

Scope of the role:
- Audit and organise existing documentation related to waste plastic handling, regrind reuse procedures, solvent and ink waste disposal, and cooling-water discharge
- Identify gaps between our current practice and ISO 14001 requirements and maintain a written gap register
- Coordinate with our water-discharge permit holder to confirm current reporting obligations and update records
- Support our quality manager in keeping the ISO 9001 document set current during the transition
- Liaise with external auditors and certification bodies as the project progresses

Background we are looking for:
- Experience with ISO 14001 or similar environmental management frameworks in an industrial setting, either in an internal role or as a consultant or auditor
- Working knowledge of Serbian environmental permit and reporting requirements for manufacturing sites
- Organised, comfortable writing procedures and maintaining a document control system
- Experience with plastics or chemical manufacturing is an advantage but not required

This is a fixed-term contract of twelve months, part-time at approximately 20 hours per week, with the expectation of extension and expansion if the project goes well. The position can be structured around your availability within normal working hours. Travel to Subotica is required at least two days per week; we do not have a remote-only arrangement for this role.

If you have relevant experience and are looking for a focused project with a clear deadline and measurable outcome, please send a short letter describing your most relevant work and a CV to our HR contact. Applications close 30 April 2024.

title: Our Products and Technology
text:
EkoGradnja Sistem produces prefabricated structural panels for residential construction at our factory on Industrijska Street in Novi Sad. We have been making concrete building components on this site for nearly fifty years and the core of what we do has not changed: we cast structural panels that go up quickly, perform reliably and last. What has changed is the materials we put inside them.

Our current wall panel range — the EGS-W series — uses concrete made partly from recycled demolition aggregate, with a hemp-fibre insulation core bonded between the structural leaves. The result is a panel that carries load, provides thermal resistance in a single installation step, and contains a lower fraction of virgin raw material than a standard sandwich panel. We produce these in standard dimensions from 2.5 to 6 metres in length and in widths suited to Serbian and regional grid sizes, with custom dimensions available for projects where the standard range does not fit.

Our floor panel range — the EGS-F series — is a prestressed hollow-core slab produced from a similar recycled-aggregate mix. These are sold to the same residential developers who use our wall panels, allowing a consistent supply relationship across the structural envelope.

All panels are tested in our on-site laboratory before dispatch. We run compressive strength tests on every production batch, and we measure thermal conductivity on wall panels using heat-flow meters. Panels that fall outside specification are recast. Our export clients in Romania and Croatia receive the same test documentation as domestic buyers.

We do not describe our panels as revolutionary. They are a practical response to the fact that construction waste aggregate is available in large quantities across Vojvodina and that biosourced insulation materials can reduce the carbon content of a panel without sacrificing thermal performance — when the production process is managed correctly. Getting that right consistently is the work we are focused on now.

title: Production Process Engineer
text:
EkoGradnja Sistem a.d. is looking for a production process engineer to join our manufacturing team in Novi Sad. This is a full-time permanent position based on-site at our panel production facility.

The role sits between the production floor and technical management. You will be responsible for monitoring cycle times, material yield and reject rates across our three casting lines, identifying where losses occur and proposing and testing changes to reduce them. We have not had a dedicated process engineer before — this function has been absorbed into the production manager's role — and we are creating the position because we need more systematic measurement and improvement than one person can manage alongside day-to-day line supervision.

What you will be doing:
— Mapping current production steps and measuring actual cycle time per panel type on each line
— Tracking material input versus panel output to quantify aggregate waste and cement over-use
— Working with the laboratory team to correlate incoming aggregate test data with final panel strength results
— Maintaining and improving our batch tracking records in ERPAG
— Preparing monthly reports for the technical director on yield, reject rate and energy use per square metre produced

What we are looking for:
— A degree in civil engineering, materials engineering or industrial engineering
— Some experience working in a precast concrete, ceramics, brick or similar factory environment — we will consider candidates two to three years out of university
— Comfort working with spreadsheets; any experience with data visualisation tools is useful but not required
— Serbian language required; working knowledge of English for reading technical standards

We offer a market salary for the Novi Sad manufacturing sector, private health coverage and paid attendance at one technical conference or training per year. Send a CV and a short note explaining your interest to posao@ekogradunja-sistem.rs.

title: Materials Laboratory Technician
text:
We are hiring a materials laboratory technician to join our existing two-person testing laboratory team. The laboratory supports production quality control and occasional product development work.

Daily tasks include:
— Compressive strength testing of concrete cube samples from production batches using our Matest press (EN 12390-3)
— Chloride content determination on aggregate samples from incoming demolition material deliveries, using potentiometric titration
— Thermal conductivity measurements on wall panel core samples with our Netzsch heat-flow meter plates
— Sample preparation, record keeping and issuing test certificates to accompany panel deliveries
— Maintaining calibration records for laboratory equipment

From time to time you may be asked to support work connected to product certification or external audits — for example, preparing sample sets for a third-party laboratory or helping compile test data for a technical file.

We are looking for someone with a secondary technical school qualification in chemistry, materials or construction technology, or a university degree in a related subject. Prior laboratory experience is preferred but we are willing to train a recent graduate who is methodical and careful with records. The job is full-time, Monday to Friday, based at our Novi Sad factory.

The laboratory is equipped with standard concrete testing apparatus, a titration station, heat-flow measurement equipment and basic aggregate grading tools. We do not have advanced analytical instruments — samples requiring XRF or electron microscopy are sent to external laboratories in Novi Sad or Belgrade.

Salary is in line with the local technical sector. Apply by sending a CV to posao@ekogradunja-sistem.rs with the subject line 'Lab Technician 2024'.

title: EkoGradnja Sistem Delivers First Panels to Construcția Vest Project in Timișoara
text:
EkoGradnja Sistem completed the first delivery of EGS-W wall panels to a residential development being built by Construcția Vest S.R.L. on the northern edge of Timișoara last month. The project, a 96-unit low-rise housing scheme, will use our panels across all external wall surfaces, with installation by a local contractor under technical supervision from our export team.

This is our second contract with Construcția Vest. The first, a smaller pilot order of 200 square metres delivered in the autumn of 2022, gave both sides the chance to check that our panel dimensions and reinforcement details were compatible with Romanian structural design norms. After some adjustment to edge connection detailing — worked out between our engineers and Construcția Vest's project architect, Andrei Florescu — the panels were accepted without modification to the production tooling.

The current contract is for approximately 3,400 square metres of wall panel. Delivery is scheduled in four batches between February and June 2024, timed to match the construction programme. Our logistics team is coordinating with a Timișoara-based freight operator, Vest Trans d.o.o., for cross-border transport.

For EkoGradnja Sistem, Romania is currently our largest export market by volume. We have been present there since 2017, initially through a trading intermediary and since 2020 through direct contracts with developers. Construcția Vest is one of three Romanian clients with whom we have a standing framework agreement covering annual volumes.

Our technical director, Dragana Kostadinović, noted that the Romanian market has been consistent in asking for panel-specific test documentation and thermal performance data with each delivery: 'It pushes us to keep our records clean, which is useful discipline for the domestic market too.'

title: What We Learned from Losing a Tender
text:
In October last year we submitted a tender for a large social-housing project here in Novi Sad. We did not win it. The contract went to a company supplying imported panels from Poland at a price roughly twelve percent below ours per installed square metre.

We are writing about this not because we want to complain about competition — imported panels are a fact of life in Serbian construction and we have no argument with that — but because losing on price by that margin made us ask a question we had not asked seriously before: do we actually know where our production cost goes?

The honest answer is that we know our total monthly cost and our total monthly output. We do not know which parts of the production process consume the most time, which steps generate the most waste material, or how much of our cement use is genuinely necessary versus compensating for aggregate variability. Our production manager, Slobodan Mirković, has a strong instinct for the floor after more than fifteen years here, but instinct is not measurement.

So we have started mapping it. We brought in a stopwatch and a notebook and spent two weeks recording actual cycle times per panel type on each of our three lines. We started tracking how much aggregate we discard after each delivery versus how much goes into panels. We are logging every panel that gets rejected and recast. It is basic work but we had not done it systematically before.

What we have found so far is that line two runs about eighteen percent slower per panel than line one for the same product, and we are not yet certain why. We have also found that our reject and recast rate is higher than Slobodan estimated — closer to six percent of output than the two to three percent in our internal reports.

We are not at the point of conclusions. But we now believe the twelve percent price gap is not simply explained by wage differences between Serbia and Poland, and that there is real efficiency to recover on our own floor. We will report back when we know more.

title: EkoGradnja Sistem at the Novi Sad Construction Materials Forum 2024
text:
EkoGradnja Sistem will have a stand at the Novi Sad Construction Materials Forum, held at the Novi Sad Fair grounds on 14–15 May 2024. The forum brings together building materials producers, residential developers and construction contractors from Serbia, Croatia, Romania and Hungary for two days of product presentations, technical sessions and procurement meetings.

We will be showing the current EGS-W wall panel range, including the hemp-core variant that we introduced in 2022, and the EGS-F floor panel series. Physical panel cross-section samples will be on display so visitors can see the aggregate texture and insulation layer directly. Our technical team will be available both days to discuss panel specifications, delivery lead times and integration details.

This year we are also using the forum to introduce our recycled aggregate concrete mix supply service to precasters who do not process their own demolition material. If you are a precast producer in the Vojvodina or Bačka region looking for a consistent supply of graded recycled aggregate with chloride test certificates, come and talk to us.

On the afternoon of 14 May, our technical director Dragana Kostadinović will speak in the 'Materials and Energy Performance' session. Her presentation, 'Recycled Aggregate in Structural Precast: What the Test Data Actually Shows', covers three years of compressive strength and aggregate quality data from our production batches. The presentation will not oversell recycled aggregate — it will show where it works well and where it causes problems, and what we are trying to do about the latter.

title: Šta radimo i kako radimo
text:
GridLogic Systems razvija opremu i softver za aktivno upravljanje distributivnim mrežama. Naš glavni proizvod, VR-400, je uređaj za regulaciju napona koji se postavlja na trafostanicama i dalekovodnim izvodima. Komunicira s centralnim sistemom putem IEC 61850 protokola i prilagođava setpoint vrednosti na osnovu aktuelnog stanja mreže.

Uz VR-400, isporučujemo softverski modul za volt-VAR optimizaciju koji radi kao servis na serveru operatora ili u privatnom oblaku. Modul dobija topologiju mreže i trenutna merenja, izračunava optimalne vrednosti i šalje komande nazad na uređaje — sve bez ručnog unosa.

Telemetrijska platforma prikuplja podatke sa svih terenskih uređaja i prikazuje ih u preglednom nadzornom panelu. Operatori vide trenutno stanje svake lokacije, istoriju alarma i trend ključnih parametara.

Na zahtev operatora, nudimo i uslugu integracije s postojećim SCADA sistemima. Naš tim je do sada radio s tri različite SCADA platforme i zna gde obično nastaju problemi s protokolima i vremenskim sinhronizacijama.

Sedište nam je u Novom Sadu, u okviru Naučno-tehnološkog parka. Uređaji se proizvode kod kooperantskog proizvođača elektronike u Srbiji, a montažu i puštanje u rad obavljamo sopstvenim timom. Za operatore koji žele lokalnu podršku, obučavamo njihovo osoblje za osnovno održavanje i dijagnostiku.

title: Zašto smo prešli s jednostavne baze na TimescaleDB — i šta smo naučili
text:
Kada smo pre dve godine pokrenuli prvu verziju telemetrijske platforme, koristili smo standardni PostgreSQL s ručno definisanim particijama po datumu. Radilo je dovoljno dobro dok smo imali dvadesetak uređaja na terenu. Kada smo prešli na sto i više lokacija, upiti koji su trajali sekund počeli su da traju minut.

Naš backend tim, na čelu s Nenadom Brkićem, istražio je više opcija. InfluxDB smo isključili jer bismo morali da migriramo dosta postojeće logike. TimescaleDB je privlačan jer ostaje u PostgreSQL ekosistemu — isti drajveri, iste SQL navike, samo drugačija organizacija podataka ispod.

Migracija nije bila trivijalna. Najveći problem je bio što neke naše tabele nisu bile modelirane s vremenom kao primarnom dimenzijom — imali smo kombinovane ključeve koje TimescaleDB ne voli. Trebalo nam je oko tri nedelje da prepišemo shemu i prilagodimo upite.

Rezultat: agregacioni upit koji je pre trajao 80 sekundi sada traje oko 4 sekunde na istom hardveru. Upit za poslednju poznatu vrednost svake lokacije, koji koristimo na nadzornoj tabli, sa 12 sekundi pao je na ispod jedne.

Gde i dalje imamo problem je obrada nepotpunih serija — kada uređaj pošalje zakasnele pakete u naletu, baza ih lepo primi, ali naša logika iznad toga još nije dovoljno robusna. Na tome radimo. Lekcija: baza može biti brza, ali pravi problemi su uvek u sloju iznad.

title: About Ekran Media Group – Regional Media Since 1987
text:
Ekran Media Group d.o.o. was founded in Zrenjanin in 1987 by a small team of local journalists and television technicians who wanted to give Banat a media outlet that covered its own towns properly. The company's first product was a weekly half-hour news programme recorded on location and broadcast from a rented transmitter on the outskirts of Zrenjanin. By 1995 we had daily live news, and by 2003 Kanal 7 had become the most-watched local channel in the Zrenjanin municipality according to a regional audience survey.

Banat.rs launched in 2009 as a companion to the television channel and today operates independently, with its own editorial team of twelve journalists led by editor-in-chief Milovan Crnjanski. The portal covers politics, economy, culture, sport and emergency services across Zrenjanin, Kikinda and Pančevo, and regularly breaks stories that national outlets pick up hours later.

Banat Outdoor began in 2016 with eight LED panels in central Zrenjanin. The network now covers 48 locations across three cities and handles campaigns for clients including local retail groups, automotive dealerships, banks and national brands running regional activations.

Banat Programmatic is our youngest unit, launched in 2020, offering display advertising inventory on Banat.rs and a selection of partner local sites to buyers through a real-time bidding interface. Monthly impressions have grown from 1.4 million at launch to over 12 million today.

Our team of 210 people works across three offices: our main production facility and headquarters in Zrenjanin, a sales and outdoor operations office in Pančevo, and a small editorial bureau in Kikinda. We are majority owned by the founding family and have no external investment. We make our editorial decisions independently and publish our ownership structure on this page in full.

title: What 35 Years of Local News Looks Like on a Shelf
text:
Last month our archive coordinator Gordana Nešić asked us to come and see the tape room. Most of the people who work at Ekran today have never opened that door. What is in there is roughly 14 000 DV and BetaSP cassettes stacked in labelled rows under controlled temperature and humidity, covering every significant event in Zrenjanin, Kikinda and Pančevo from 1987 to around 2018, when we moved fully to file-based production.

Gordana has maintained a paper index for years. She can tell you approximately which shelf and which box holds footage of the 1999 floods in central Zrenjanin, or the opening ceremony of the industrial zone in Kikinda in 2004, or three decades of the Zrenjanin City Marathon. The index exists. The footage exists. But none of it is playable without physically locating the tape, loading it into one of our two remaining functioning BetaSP decks and watching it in real time.

A specialist firm that inspected the collection last autumn told us that roughly 2 500 tapes show early binder degradation. Those tapes can still be played, but the window is not infinite. The firm's quote for full digitisation, quality control and basic metadata creation was 280 000 EUR. We do not have that money available as a single budget item.

We are not writing this as a complaint. We are writing it because we think there is a workable path forward that involves digitising the highest-risk and highest-value tapes first, building an indexed digital archive incrementally, and finding partners who understand both the technical and the cultural side of this kind of project.

If your organisation works on digitisation, archiving, audiovisual metadata or related fields and you want to have a practical conversation, write to Gordana directly: arhiva@ekranmedia.rs.

- Integrate the model into our existing Python/Django ad server as a scoring endpoint; latency at inference time must stay under 80 ms per article
- Deliver documentation sufficient for our in-house developer to retrain the model on new data

This is a six-month contract with a possible extension. The work is hybrid: initial requirements sessions in our Zrenjanin office, then remote with monthly check-ins. Rate is negotiable depending on experience and whether you are engaging as an individual or through a company.

title: EdgeWatch Now Deployed at Kovačević Packaging — SOC Service Active
text:
We finished the deployment at Kovačević Packaging's main production facility in late December and the SOC service went live on the second of January. We are writing this up because it is our largest single deployment to date and a few things about it are worth noting.

Kovačević runs a mix of Modbus RTU on older filling lines and a BACnet IP segment for the building management side of the plant — HVAC, access control interlocks, and fire panel interfaces. Those two segments were managed separately and the security team had no unified view of either. Our brief was to change that without touching any of the live process equipment.

The deployment involved four EdgeWatch sensors: two on the production floor Modbus segments, one on the BACnet segment, and one on the network boundary between the OT zone and the corporate IT side. The physical installation took two days during a scheduled maintenance window. Our field technicians worked alongside the plant's own automation engineers, who were helpful and knew their network well.

Since go-live, the SOC has flagged three events worth investigating. Two were benign — a technician connecting a laptop to run diagnostics without notifying the security team first, and a BACnet device that rebooted and re-announced itself in a way that looked like a new device joining the network. The third is still under review and we are not going to say more about it here.

Kovačević's engineering manager, Dragan Milošević, agreed to let us quote him: 'We knew we had gaps but we could not see them. Now we can see them.'

We are grateful for the straightforward working relationship. Deployments go better when the customer's own engineers are involved from the start.

title: What We Do — SecureEdge Labs
text:
SecureEdge Labs builds security monitoring for the networks that run factories and buildings. These are not ordinary IT networks. They carry Modbus commands to motor controllers and BACnet messages to HVAC units. The devices on them are often old, often undocumented, and almost never patched. Standard security tools treat them as a mystery or ignore them entirely.

We do not ignore them.

Our EdgeWatch sensor connects to your OT network as a passive tap. It reads traffic without injecting any packets of its own, so it cannot interfere with your process. It parses Modbus and BACnet at the protocol level, builds a picture of what devices are present and what they normally do, and forwards structured event records to our backend over an encrypted tunnel.

Our SOC service takes those records and puts trained eyes on them around the clock. When something looks wrong — a new device, an unusual function code, a register written to a value outside its normal range — an analyst contacts your designated on-call engineer directly. We do not send you a dashboard and leave you to sort it out.

FloorMap gives you a live topology view of your OT segment without requiring you to walk the plant with a clipboard. PolicyAudit is a fixed-scope engagement where one of our engineers reviews your BACnet or Modbus configuration against a hardening checklist and writes up what needs to change.

We work with manufacturers, district energy operators, and building management companies. Our customers are in the Vojvodina region and we have handled deployments across three countries for customers whose parent companies required consistency.

If you want to talk about your network, contact us at NTP Novi Sad or by email. We do not do high-pressure sales calls.

title: Why Anomaly Detection in OT Is Harder Than It Looks
text:
We get asked fairly often why we do not just use an off-the-shelf anomaly detection library and call it done. The question is reasonable, so here is a plain answer.

The core problem is that Modbus and BACnet traffic is not random. A filling line that runs an eight-hour shift does roughly the same thing every eight hours. The PLC polls the same registers at the same intervals, the same coils get toggled at the same points in the production cycle, and the same set of devices appear on the network. If you build a statistical baseline over a week of this traffic and then look for deviations, you will immediately notice that Monday morning looks different from Saturday afternoon, that the quarterly maintenance shutdown looks like an attack, and that a new product run on an existing line looks suspicious because the register values are in ranges the baseline has not seen.

We tried two approaches to this before landing on where we are now. The first was rule-based: write explicit rules for the things that are clearly wrong, like a write to a read-only coil or a function code the device does not support. This works and we still do it. The problem is that it only catches the obvious cases. A slow scan of device addresses over several days looks completely normal one packet at a time.

The second approach was clustering on feature vectors extracted from ten-minute windows of traffic. This produced clusters that corresponded roughly to operating states, which was interesting, but the boundaries between clusters shifted with production schedule changes and we spent more time explaining false positives to customers than catching anything real.

Where we are now is a combination of explicit rules for known-bad patterns and a baseline model that is trained per-device rather than per-segment, which handles some of the production schedule variation. It is not solved. We are actively looking for better approaches and we are open about that.

title: What We Do — Senzorika Petković i sinovi
text:
We make sensor nodes for farms. That is the short version.

The longer version is that we design and build small battery-powered devices that measure temperature, relative humidity, soil moisture, and canopy conditions, and transmit that data wirelessly to a gateway that the grower can check on a laptop or a phone. We install the hardware, configure the network, and come back when something needs attention.

Our clients are working farmers, not technology companies. They grow peppers, tomatoes, apricots, apples, and table grapes in Vojvodina, mostly in the Banat and Bačka areas. They want to know what is happening in their greenhouse at two in the morning without driving there. They want to catch a frost risk early enough to do something about it. They want records they can show to a buyer or a bank.

We have been doing this since 1998, first with wired systems, then with our own wireless hardware as the radio modules became reliable enough to trust. We do not use off-the-shelf consumer sensors repackaged in a new box. We design our own boards around the measurements that Vojvodina growers actually need, and we build them in our workshop in Zrenjanin.

Every installation comes with the option of a maintenance contract. We visit twice a year to clean sensors, check seals, and recalibrate against reference instruments. If something breaks outside those visits, we respond within 48 hours.

Our team is seven people: three from the Petković family and four technicians who have been with us long enough to know every farm we service by name. We are not going to win any awards for our website, but the growers who have been using our nodes for five or six years tend to renew their maintenance contracts, and that is the measure we pay attention to.

title: Firmware and Electronics Technician — part-time or full-time
text:

What the job involves:

What we are looking for:

- Comfortable with a soldering iron and a multimeter
- Familiarity with LoRa or any ISM-band radio protocol is a strong plus
- Driving licence — site visits are part of the job
- Serbian language required; basic English for reading datasheets is helpful

What we are not looking for:
- Someone who needs a manager to define every task

We are a family business and the atmosphere is informal. Hours are flexible. Salary is negotiable depending on experience and whether the arrangement is part-time or full-time. If you are interested, send a short message explaining what you have worked on before to miroslav@senzorikapetkovicis.rs. No agencies.

title: Field Installation Technician
text:
We install wireless sensor networks on farms and orchards across Vojvodina and we need another person who can handle the physical side of the work.

A typical installation day: you drive to a farm, assess where to mount sensor nodes on greenhouse frames or orchard stakes, run a short survey walk to check signal coverage, mount and configure between 10 and 30 nodes, connect the gateway, and make sure the grower can read their data before you leave. Some days you are replacing a faulty sensor under a maintenance contract. Some days you are helping solder a small batch of boards back at the workshop in Zrenjanin.

What we need:
- Willingness to work outdoors in all seasons — Banat winters are cold and Banat summers are hot
- Basic electrical knowledge — you do not need to design circuits but you do need to wire a 12V power supply safely
- Driving licence, class B
- Patience when working with farmers who are not technical — explaining what the sensor does in plain language is part of the job
- Serbian required

Nice to have:
- Any experience with agricultural machinery or greenhouse equipment
- Experience with hand tools and crimping connectors
- Familiarity with Android apps for basic configuration (we use a simple Bluetooth tool for node setup)

This is a hands-on, outdoor role. We are a team of seven and everyone does several things. The pay is steady and the work is not glamorous, but you will learn how sensor systems are built and deployed from start to finish. Send a brief message to teodor@senzorikapetkovicis.rs.

title: Fifty Nodes Installed at Zeleni Biser Cooperative in Padej
text:
Last month we finished the largest single installation we have done so far: 52 sensor nodes spread across the heated and unheated greenhouse blocks at the Zeleni Biser vegetable cooperative in Padej, about 35 kilometres north of Zrenjanin.

The cooperative manager, Svetlana Ninković, had been tracking temperature by hand with a set of alcohol thermometers since the cooperative was founded. She knew where the cold spots were by memory. When a late frost in March 2023 caught one block unprepared and damaged about a third of that season's early pepper seedlings, the cooperative started looking for something more systematic.

We spent a day walking the site with Svetlana before quoting the job. The blocks are a mix of glass-and-timber structures from the 1980s and newer steel-framed polycarbonate tunnels, so the layout is uneven and gateway placement needed care. We ended up placing two gateways on the water tower at the centre of the site, which gave us clean line of sight to most of the installation.

Each node measures air temperature, relative humidity, and — in the heated blocks — CO2 concentration via a secondary sensor module. Data goes to a gateway with local SD-card backup, so if the internet connection at the cooperative drops, nothing is lost.

Svetlana's comment after the first two weeks: 'I can see every block from my phone at home. I have not slept this well during pepper season in years.'

The cooperative is on a three-year maintenance contract. We will return in October for the first annual calibration check.

If you manage a greenhouse cooperative or a larger private holding and want to talk through what a similar installation might look like, contact us through the form on this page or call Teodor directly.

title: What we learned at the Agro Novi Sad fair this year
text:
We took a small stand at the Agro Novi Sad agricultural fair at the beginning of May, the first time we have exhibited anywhere in about six years. Our previous experience with trade fairs was that they cost a lot and produced mostly business cards from people who never called back. This time was a little different.

We brought two display nodes, a working gateway, and a laptop showing a live data feed from our workshop in Zrenjanin over a mobile connection. Miroslav spent two days at the stand. Teodor joined for the first morning.

The conversations that were most useful came from growers who are already using some kind of sensor system and are unhappy with it — either the vendor has disappeared, the cloud platform changed its pricing, or the hardware simply stops working after a Vojvodina winter. Several people said the same thing: they want a supplier they can actually reach on the phone, not a ticket system in another country. That is something we can be.

We also spoke with two growers from Senta and one from Kanjiža who are interested in apricot and apple orchard monitoring. Orchards are different from greenhouses — the nodes need to survive harsher conditions and the distances between measurement points are larger — but the core hardware is the same. We have done a handful of orchard installations before and the main challenge is frost prediction accuracy, which growers up there care about a great deal.

One unexpected conversation was with a logistics company that moves perishable produce. They asked whether our nodes could be used inside refrigerated trucks. Honestly, that is a different problem and not something we are set up to do, but it was interesting to hear.

We collected around 30 serious contacts. Whether any of them turn into orders we will find out over the summer. The cost of the stand was about what we expected, and we think it was worth it this time.

title: About Us – Agroprerada Kević
text:
Agroprerada Kević started in a rented kitchen in Sremska Mitrovica in 2003. Dragoljub Kević had worked for fifteen years in a large vegetable processing cooperative that closed down, and Milena had grown up watching her grandmother cook preserves every August and September. When the cooperative shut, they decided to do the same thing on a smaller scale and do it properly.

The first products were plum jam and ajvar, sold at the Saturday market. By 2007 we had a dedicated production space on the edge of town, three employees and a handful of specialty shops in Novi Sad taking regular orders. Today we have nine people working with us through the year and we sell through markets, around twenty regional food shops, and our own webshop, which Nikola built and looks after.

Our supply chain is short by design. The plums come from Branko Savić's orchard near Laćarak — we have bought from him since 2005. The peppers for ajvar come from two families in the villages south of Irig. We visit every supplier at least once during the growing season. When a harvest is poor or a field has a problem, we find out early and we adjust.

Production is hands-on. Ajvar peppers are roasted whole, peeled by hand and passed through a hand-cranked mill before cooking. Jams are cooked in open copper pans in batches of 50 to 80 kilograms. Every batch is tested with a refractometer before filling. Jars are filled hot and vacuum-sealed.

We have nine SKUs at the moment. We do not plan to grow that list quickly. Our focus is on keeping what we already make as reliable as possible, which is harder than it sounds when you are working with fruit and vegetables that change every season.

title: Our Quince Cheese Is Now Stocked at Delikatesa Stanković in Novi Sad
text:
From the first week of March, our quince cheese — the firm, sliceable preserve we make every November from Vojvodina quince — will be on the shelf at Delikatesa Stanković on Ulica Miloša Crnjanskog in Novi Sad.

Delikatesa Stanković has been selling regional speciality foods for twelve years and is one of the shops we have wanted to work with for a long time. The owner, Tatjana Stanković, tried our quince cheese at the Novi Sad food fair last October and got in touch shortly after. It took a few months to agree on packaging — she wanted a slightly smaller format, 200 grams rather than our standard 350-gram block, so that customers could try it without committing to a large jar — and we spent part of January adapting our filling process to make that work without creating too much extra waste.

Quince cheese is a product we are quietly proud of. It takes a lot of fruit — roughly two kilograms of raw quince per kilogram of finished product — and the cooking time is long, up to three hours per batch. The result is something that keeps for over a year in a cool place and goes well with hard cheeses, cold cuts or simply on bread. It is the kind of preserve that is common in older Vojvodina households but harder to find commercially.

If you are in Novi Sad, Delikatesa Stanković is open Monday to Saturday. The 200-gram format is exclusive to the shop for the first season; the 350-gram block remains available through our webshop.

title: What Went Wrong With This Year's Ajvar (And What We Are Doing About It)
text:
We want to be straightforward about something.

Some of you who ordered ajvar last autumn have told us it tastes different from previous years — specifically that there is a faint bitterness that was not there before. Three customers wrote to us directly. We have also noticed, looking at our reorder numbers for this season, that the repeat rate is lower than it should be for a product that normally sells well on word of mouth.

We have been cooking ajvar from the same Šorokšar red pepper variety, from the same suppliers, using the same roasting and peeling method for several years. Nothing changed intentionally. But something clearly did change, and we have not yet been able to explain it.

What we have tried so far: we extended the hand-peeling step to remove more charred skin than usual, since charring is a common source of bitterness in roasted vegetables. We also tested a batch with a shorter roasting time. Neither made a noticeable difference in the finished product taste.

Our current thinking is that the peppers themselves may have changed — possibly as a result of this past summer's unusual weather, which was drier and hotter than average in the Fruška Gora area during the critical ripening weeks. Drought stress can affect the concentration of certain natural compounds in peppers. But we are not food scientists and we do not have a laboratory, so this is still a guess.

We are in contact with the Science Technology Park in Novi Sad, hoping to find someone who can help us analyse pepper samples and finished product to identify what is causing the bitterness and whether it can be corrected before next season's harvest.

In the meantime, if you received ajvar from us last autumn and found the taste off, please get in touch. We will send you a replacement jar from our remaining stock of the previous year's batch, which several of us have re-tasted and believe is closer to what you expect from us.

We think it is better to say this out loud than to stay quiet and hope nobody notices.

title: Our autumn-winter 2023 collection sold out in six weeks — and what it cost us
text:
The short version: autumn-winter 2023 was the fastest sell-through we've had. The longer version is more complicated, and we think it's worth being honest about both.

We ran 2,000 pieces across the collection. They were gone in six weeks, which by any measure we'd have used two years ago would count as a success. The extended-size range we introduced — EU 46 through 52 — sold particularly quickly in the first two weeks.

Then the returns started.

By December we were sitting on a 34% return rate for the size-inclusive line. Almost every return note said the same thing: the fit wasn't right. Customers were choosing the size the chart told them to choose and the garment wasn't fitting the way the image suggested it would. We'd graded those sizes ourselves, extending upward from blocks we were confident about at smaller sizes. That was a mistake, and we own it.

The financial reality is that each return parcel from Germany or the Netherlands costs us €6–8 to ship back, before we look at re-processing time. On that run, that's not a small number.

We've since updated the size guidance on the webshop, added more detailed measurement instructions, and are currently working on correcting the patterns before the next run. We've also started talking to people at NTP Novi Sad about whether there are better tools for predicting fit issues before production rather than discovering them at a 34% return rate.

The sell-through speed tells us the demand for this size range is real. We're not stepping back from it. We're going to do it properly.

If you bought from the AW23 size-inclusive line and had a bad fit experience, we want to hear from you. Reach us directly at hello@indigoatelierstudio.rs.

title: About Indigo Atelier Studio
text:
Indigo Atelier Studio started in 2019 with a cutting table, a laptop, and the conviction that it was possible to make clothes worth owning without shipping fabric from the other side of the world or producing more than anyone actually needs.

Marta Vujić had spent six years working in production coordination for larger fashion brands and had grown tired of watching good fabric decisions get reversed because a buyer wanted another €0.30 off the unit cost. Petra Oláh had studied textile design in Budapest and moved to Novi Sad for reasons unrelated to fashion. They met at a craft market, talked for three hours, and started working together the following month.

The first collection in 2019 was 300 pieces sold through a single pop-up in Novi Sad and a basic online store. By 2021 we were shipping to Germany, Austria, and the Netherlands. In 2022 we joined NTP Novi Sad, which gave us a proper workspace and a network of people building things — engineers, data people, biologists — who turn out to think about problems in ways that are useful even when the problem is a dress that doesn't fit right.

We work with mills we've visited. Our main fabric suppliers are a weaving mill in Subotica and a finishing mill across the Hungarian border near Szeged. We know the people who run them. We know roughly what their water consumption looks like and which dye classes they use. We don't claim perfection — textiles are complicated — but we try to make decisions we can explain.

Every collection is small by design: between 1,500 and 2,500 pieces, two times a year. When a style is gone, we don't reprint it. Our customers know this and most of them say it's part of why they buy.

The team today is fourteen people. We're based in Novi Sad and we intend to stay here.

text:
We're a small slow-fashion label at NTP Novi Sad. We sell women's ready-to-wear directly to customers across the EU through our Shopify store. Our social content is working — we get consistent traffic from Instagram and TikTok — but our session-to-purchase rate is 1.2%, well below where it should be, and we haven't been able to move that number despite two layout overhauls and new photography.

We need someone who has actually solved this kind of problem before. Not someone who will redesign the homepage again. title: A German retailer asked us for an LCA. Here's what we learned trying to answer them.
text:
Feldweg Concept Store is a mid-size independent retailer in Germany. They contacted us in January about stocking our spring-summer collection on a wholesale basis. It would be our first wholesale relationship with a German physical retailer and we were glad to hear from them.

Then they asked for a life-cycle assessment document for our core fabric lines.

A life-cycle assessment — LCA — is a structured analysis of the environmental inputs and outputs of a product across its whole life: from raw fibre through weaving, dyeing, cutting, sewing, transport, use by the customer, and eventual disposal. It can cover carbon emissions, water consumption, chemical use, and land use, depending on how detailed the study goes.

We had heard of LCAs. We had not produced one. We called two consultancies — one local, one in Belgrade. The Belgrade firm quoted €12,000 for a full study. That's not money we have available this year.

So we started trying to understand what we actually have. It turns out we have more than we thought, and less than we need. Our mill partner in Subotica provided us with water consumption figures and their dye class certification when we first started working with them. The mill near Szeged has a basic environmental management document they share with buyers. We have fibre origin documentation. None of it is in a format that adds up to anything an LCA framework would recognise.

We've been talking to people through NTP Novi Sad's network about whether there's a methodology that sits between a €12,000 consultancy study and nothing — something we could build ourselves from the data we can actually get from our supply chain, that would be credible enough to satisfy a buyer like Feldweg.

Fieldweg has given us until end of Q3 2024. We're working on it. If you've navigated this for a small brand, we'd genuinely like to talk: hello@indigoatelierstudio.rs.

title: FreshPak Wins Three-Year Supply Contract with Jadran Berry Export
text:
FreshPak Solutions has signed a three-year supply agreement with Jadran Berry Export, one of the larger raspberry and blueberry cooperatives operating out of the Mačva district. The contract covers 125 g and 250 g rPET punnets, anti-fog lidding film, and export cartons for the cooperative's full fresh-fruit output, estimated at roughly 800 tonnes of packaged product per season.

The deal came after a one-season trial in 2023 during which Jadran Berry Export switched two of its German customer lines to FreshPak punnets and lidding film. End-of-season destination reject data showed a drop in packaging-related complaints compared with the previous supplier, according to Jadran's logistics coordinator, Nemanja Štrbac.

"The thing that made the difference for us was being able to call on a Wednesday and have a modified seal spec tested and confirmed by Friday," Štrbac said. "We have had suppliers who are technically fine but operationally slow, and in fresh produce slow costs money."

For FreshPak, the Jadran contract is the company's largest single agreement to date by volume. Production planning manager Jelena Bogdanović said the company will run a second shift on its punnet thermoforming lines from May through August to meet peak-season demand without affecting lead times for other customers.

The agreement also includes a clause requiring FreshPak to present a certified compostable lidding film option for evaluation by the 2027 season, in line with purchasing requirements Jadran expects from its German retail buyers. That clause aligns with a development programme FreshPak already has underway in its quality lab.

Deliveries under the new contract begin with the 2024 raspberry season, starting in June.

title: What We Do — FreshPak Solutions
text:
FreshPak Solutions makes the packaging that gets Serbian fresh produce to Western European shelves in one piece. We focus on soft fruit — raspberries, blueberries, sour cherries — because that is where the margin lives and where bad packaging does the most damage. Growers and packing houses in the Fruška Gora and Mačva regions have been working with us since 2012, and a number of the larger export cooperatives have made us their sole packaging supplier.

Our production floor in the NTP Novi Sad campus runs three lines: two thermoforming lines for punnets in standard and custom formats, and an extrusion and slitting line for lidding films. Everything is checked in our own quality lab before it leaves the building. We test oxygen and CO₂ transmission rates on every film batch, pull-test seals to European standard, and run drop simulations on export cartons before we approve a new format for shipment.

Customers come to us for three reasons. First, we can turn around short customised runs in days rather than weeks. Second, our in-house lab means we can iterate quickly on seal parameters and film spec without waiting for an outside testing house. Third, we understand the cold chain between Novi Sad and Rotterdam because our founders spent years managing it from the logistics side.

We supply:
- Thermoformed punnets in rPET and standard PET, from 125 g to 500 g
- Lidding films with anti-fog treatment and controlled-atmosphere options
- Export cartons in corrugated and solid fibre, rated for refrigerated road and sea freight
- Traceability labels with QR codes linked to lot and grower data
- Foam and pulp tray inlays for premium presentation lines

If you are an exporter preparing for next season or a packing house looking to reduce destination rejects, contact our sales team at the address below. We prefer to start with a trial batch so both sides can see the numbers before committing to a full-season contract.

title: Packaging Materials Technologist — Compostable Films Project
text:
FreshPak Solutions is hiring a packaging materials technologist to join our quality lab team in Novi Sad. This role exists because we are running a two-year development programme to replace our conventional plastic lidding films with certified compostable alternatives, and our current three-person lab team does not have the polymer chemistry background to lead that work.

What the job involves:
You will be the technical lead on compostable film evaluation. That means sourcing and screening candidate materials — primarily PLA-based and PHA-based films and blends — running seal trials on our existing thermoforming and heat-seal equipment, measuring OTR and CO₂TR on every candidate, and keeping records that will eventually feed into an EN 13432 certification submission. You will also work with our production team when a candidate film needs adjustments to seal temperature or dwell time, and you will write the technical reports that go to our key retail customers.

title: What We Learned from Two Seasons of Shipment Temperature Logs
text:
We have been collecting temperature and humidity logs from refrigerated trailers and data loggers placed inside export cartons for two full seasons now. The original idea was simple: if we know what the berries actually experience between the packing house and the distribution centre in Germany, we can make better decisions about film specification. What the data showed was more useful — and more uncomfortable — than we expected.

The first finding was that temperature at the punnet level is not the same as temperature at the trailer probe. In most loads we logged, punnets in the outer columns of pallets ran 1.5 to 2.5 degrees warmer than the trailer setpoint during the first eight hours after loading. That is the period when condensation forms inside the punnet, and it is almost certainly a factor in the mould rates we see on arrival.

The second finding was more straightforward: loads that were pre-cooled at the packing house to below 4 °C before sealing showed consistently lower condensation and lower Botrytis incidence at destination, regardless of which film we used. That sounds obvious, but several of our smaller customers were sealing punnets at ambient temperature and relying on the trailer to do the cooling. The data made the case for pre-cooling in a way that our technologists' verbal recommendations had not.

What we still do not have is a good model linking headspace gas composition — specifically CO₂ accumulation from berry respiration — to mould risk under variable temperature conditions. Our OTR and CO₂TR measurements tell us what a film does at a fixed temperature; they do not tell us what happens when temperature fluctuates over fourteen days. That is the gap we are working on. If anyone reading this has worked on predictive respiration modelling for soft fruit, we are interested in talking.

title: What Actually Happens to a Battery After Two Summers
text:
We have now been doing annual check-ups on systems we installed in 2021 and 2022. For most customers the numbers look about right — panels are within a few percent of their rated output, inverters are running cleanly, and batteries are holding somewhere between eighty-five and ninety-five percent of their original capacity after two years.

But for a handful of customers, mostly on farms with heavy summer loads, the battery capacity has dropped faster. We have seen some units at seventy to seventy-five percent after two years. That is not dangerous and the system still works, but it is not what we told people to expect, and we take that seriously.

The pattern we are seeing is that these are the installations where the battery cycled more than once a day through June, July, and August. A pump running in the morning and again in the evening, combined with a household drawing on the battery at night, adds up to two or three full cycles in a single day. LFP batteries are tolerant of this compared to older types, but they are not unlimited.

When we sized those systems we used a straightforward rule: take the average daily consumption from the bills, multiply by 1.2, pick the nearest battery size. That rule does not account for seasonal peaks or the shape of consumption through the day.

We are currently going through our records — we have data from about sixty installations — to see whether we can identify earlier in the process which customers are likely to hit this pattern. We do not yet have a better sizing method, but we are working on it.

If you are a current SolarStep customer and you want to know how your battery is performing, send us your monitoring data or call us for a check-up visit. We would rather know the real numbers than guess.

title: TalentMost at Zukunft Personal Europe 2023 — What We Learned
text:
Three of us attended Zukunft Personal Europe in Cologne in September, which is one of the larger HR technology trade fairs in the region. It was the first time TalentMost had a presence at an event of that scale.

The honest summary: the fair confirmed some things we already suspected and surfaced one issue we had underestimated.

On the positive side, there is genuine demand among German and Austrian mid-size manufacturers for better structured interview tooling. Most of what is on the market is either built for large enterprises with dedicated HR teams, or it is very generic. Several of the conversations we had were with companies in the 50 to 300 employee range that do not have that infrastructure. They were interested in what we are building.

The issue we had underestimated is documentation. Two separate conversations stalled when potential clients asked about the technical file for our screening battery. One asked specifically for Cronbach's alpha and criterion validity data. We did not have those. We knew the battery was built quickly but we had not fully understood that for buyers in Germany, a screening tool without documented reliability is simply not a product they can use, regardless of how the rest of the platform works. We are treating that as an action point, not just a sales problem.

We also had a useful conversation with a data protection consultant at the fair who pointed out that recording candidate interviews and processing that data for German-resident candidates requires a DPIA under GDPR Article 35. We were aware of this in principle but had not acted on it. We are now.

We will return to Zukunft Personal in 2024 with better answers to both questions. If you met us in Cologne and want to follow up, reach out to marko.lazic@talentmost.rs.

title: About TalentMost — How We Match People to Roles
text:
TalentMost started because hiring in Vojvodina was slow and the tools available were built for markets with very different labour conditions. We are a Novi Sad team and we built the platform here, partly because we know the local manufacturing base and partly because Novi Sad has the technical talent to do it properly.

The core of what we do is straightforward. A hiring manager defines what a role requires, not just a job title and a list of qualifications, but the actual competencies the person needs to perform the job. A candidate uploads a CV or fills in a structured profile. The platform compares the two and produces a ranked shortlist with a competency gap map for each candidate. When the hiring manager runs a structured interview, the platform gives them a scored question guide tied to the specific gaps it found.

We do not promise to automate hiring decisions. We promise to make the information better and the process faster. Our customers report cutting average time-to-shortlist from eleven days to three days across IT and office roles.

Our platform currently handles vacancy matching, structured interview management, and a short screening battery for cognitive and work-style indicators. We serve manufacturers, IT services companies, and logistics operators mostly in Serbia, with an expanding client base in Germany and Austria.

title: Why Structured Interviews Fail in Small Manufacturers (And What We Did About It)
text:
Structured interviews have a good track record in the research literature, but when we started selling to manufacturers in Vojvodina we kept running into the same objection: 'We already tried that. The supervisors hated it and stopped using the scoring sheets after two weeks.'

We spent time in 2022 and early 2023 talking to production managers and shift supervisors at seven companies to understand why. What we found was not that structured interviews are wrong for manufacturing. It was that the implementation was wrong.

Most off-the-shelf structured interview guides are written for white-collar roles. The questions use language and scenarios that feel strange to a supervisor interviewing a press-brake operator or a welding inspector. The scoring scales assume the interviewer is comfortable with behavioural anchors described in HR language. When a supervisor who has been on the floor for twenty years reads a scoring guide that asks him to rate 'demonstrates initiative in ambiguous situations,' he either ignores it or guesses.

We changed how we build interview guides for trades roles. Instead of starting from a competency dictionary and translating down, we start from specific job tasks that the supervisor already recognises. We ask the supervisor to tell us what a good day looks like for that role and what a bad day looks like. The platform structures those into interview questions and anchors, using language that came from that supervisor's own description of the job.

The result is not perfect. The matching side is still weaker for trades than for IT roles and we have said that publicly. But on the interview side, we have seen adoption stay consistent rather than dropping off after the first month. That is progress. We will keep working on the matching side through this year.

title: What We Learned at RehabExpo Maribor 2023
text:
Our team came back from RehabExpo Maribor last month with a notebook full of feedback and a few things worth writing down while they are still fresh.

RehabExpo draws a mix of equipment purchasers, heads of physiotherapy departments and a smaller number of hospital IT managers who are increasingly present at these events. That last group was interesting to us this year because three separate conversations touched on the same topic: EHR integration. Each of the physiotherapy leads we spoke to said that manual data entry between specialist systems and their central patient record is one of the biggest daily friction points in their departments. Two of them specifically mentioned Dedalus. We already knew we needed to move on FHIR integration, but those conversations made clear that it is becoming a procurement requirement, not just a nice-to-have.

On the clinical side, the strongest interest at our stand was in outcome measurement for neurological patients — specifically stroke. Several physiotherapists asked pointed questions about how our symmetry index handles the early post-stroke population. We gave honest answers, which led to good conversations. One attendee from a Ljubljana hospital, who has been a customer for two years, said directly that she has stopped using the symmetry score for her stroke patients because it does not match what she sees in the session. That is a problem we are actively working on.

The positive news: StrideSense's form factor and battery life consistently got strong reactions. Competitors at the show were either treadmill-based or required a wired connection to a trolley unit. The portability of an insole system that pairs in two minutes is a genuine differentiator and physiotherapists notice it.

title: StrideSense and RehabTrack — Gait Analysis Systems for Clinical Rehabilitation
text:
Rehabilitation progress is easier to discuss when you can measure it.

NeuroStep Solutions builds sensor-based gait analysis tools for neurological and orthopaedic rehabilitation centres. Our StrideSense insole system fits into a standard rehabilitation shoe and records pressure, timing and symmetry data across 16 sensor channels at 100 Hz. The data is transmitted wirelessly to a tablet or workstation running our RehabTrack software, where it is processed in real time and presented to the clinician as a structured session report.

RehabTrack stores every session in a searchable patient record, displays trend graphs across multiple visits and generates PDF progress reports that can be attached to referral letters or shared with the patient's GP. The SymmetryView module overlays left-right comparison data as animated pressure maps so that a physiotherapist can see at a glance how load is distributed across a walking cycle.

Our systems are used in fourteen rehabilitation facilities across Serbia, Croatia and Slovenia. They are designed to work in real ward conditions: the insoles are waterproof to IPX5, the battery lasts a full clinical day, and the pairing process takes under two minutes so that a session can begin without disrupting the treatment schedule.

Calibration, maintenance and software updates are covered under our service contracts. Our field technicians are based in Novi Sad, Zagreb and Ljubljana, and response times for on-site visits are typically under 48 hours in all three countries.

For procurement teams: StrideSense and RehabTrack are produced under ISO 13485-aligned quality management and carry CE marking as Class I medical devices. We provide full technical documentation, IFU translations in Serbian, Croatian and Slovenian, and formal user training for clinical staff.

Contact our sales team at sales@neurostep.rs or call our Novi Sad office to arrange a demonstration at your facility.

"The data we get from StrideSense is consistent across sessions and easy to put in front of a patient during the debrief," Vukić noted in her evaluation summary. "That matters when you are trying to explain progress to someone who has just had a hip replacement."

The OrthoKinetica agreement brings the total number of StrideSense deployment sites to fourteen across the three countries and marks our largest single contract to date by number of insole pairs deployed.

title: ClearFrame Bone Now Live at Radović General Clinic — Six Months of Results
text:
Six months ago MedVizion completed the integration of ClearFrame Bone at Radović General Clinic in Novi Sad, our first full production deployment at a public hospital in Serbia. We said at the time that we would report back on how it went. Here is that report.

The clinical context: Radović has a radiology department that handles emergency and elective imaging across roughly 180 studies per day. They were dealing with a backlog on musculoskeletal X-rays, particularly in the overnight shift when senior radiologist cover is limited. ClearFrame Bone was deployed to flag probable fractures for priority review, not to replace the radiologist read.

Volume over six months: 31,400 studies processed through ClearFrame Bone. Of those, 4,870 received a fracture flag. Radiologists confirmed, modified, or rejected each flag before the report was finalised.

What worked: The overnight triage function reduced the time between scan acquisition and radiologist attention on flagged studies from an average of 47 minutes to 19 minutes. The department's lead radiologist, Dr. Jovan Petrović, described the worklist prioritisation as the most useful single change in the deployment.

What did not work as well as we expected: Bounding-box accuracy on low-contrast fractures and fractures at complex anatomy sites — shoulder, pelvis, wrist — was lower than our test set results predicted. Radiologists spent more time correcting annotations than we had anticipated, and our active-learning queue has been slower to improve on these cases than it should be. We are working on this directly.

Next steps: We are extending the deployment agreement at Radović for another 12 months and using the feedback from Dr. Petrović's team to drive specific changes to the annotation pipeline. We are also beginning integration planning at a second Serbian hospital site.

title: What We Do — ClearFrame and the Case for Transparent AI in Radiology
text:
Radiology departments across Central and Eastern Europe are dealing with a straightforward problem: more studies, fewer radiologists, and equipment that ranges from last year's installation to hardware that has been running since 2009. ClearFrame was built for that reality.

ClearFrame connects to your existing DICOM infrastructure — no new hardware, no replacement of your PACS system, no disruption to how your radiologists open and read studies. Once connected, it runs inference on incoming studies, highlights regions of interest, assigns a confidence score to each finding, and places the result directly into the radiologist's worklist. The radiologist sees the flag, reviews it, and makes the call. The system records the outcome and uses it to improve over time.

ClearFrame Bone focuses on fracture detection in X-ray studies and is our most widely deployed module, currently active at seven hospital groups in three countries. It is certified as a Class IIa medical device under EU MDR and operates under ISO 13485 quality management.

DICOM Connect is the integration layer we developed specifically to handle variation in scanner metadata across older equipment. It normalises header information and applies preprocessing before any image reaches the model, which reduces the performance gap between hospital environments.

RadReview Dashboard gives radiology leads a view of worklist throughput, annotation activity, and model confidence distribution across shifts. It is not a management surveillance tool — it is designed to help clinical teams spot bottlenecks and adjust staffing.

We are a team of 34 people based in Novi Sad. If you work in radiology operations or clinical informatics and want to understand whether ClearFrame fits your environment, we are happy to arrange a technical walkthrough with no sales involvement in the first call.

What the work involves:
Our ClearFrame Bone module detects fractures in X-ray studies. It performs well on our internal test sets and less well on scans from older scanners with different reconstruction settings. Your main task will be identifying why that gap exists and building preprocessing or fine-tuning approaches that reduce it. You will work directly with DICOM data, instrument experiments using DVC, and validate results against labelled clinical datasets. You will also contribute to our federated learning infrastructure, which we are beginning to build out to allow on-site training at partner hospitals without moving patient data.

Technical environment:
We train in Python and PyTorch. Data versioning runs on DVC. Deployment is Docker and Kubernetes on hospital-operated servers. Annotation work goes through Label Studio with a custom backend we maintain. DICOM handling uses pydicom and some internal tooling. We do not use cloud compute for patient data — everything runs on-premises or on our own servers.

What we are looking for:
Three or more years of hands-on ML engineering experience, comfort with medical imaging formats or signal data, and some experience debugging performance gaps between training and deployment environments. Experience with federated learning or differential privacy is useful but not required. We care more about how you approach a problem than which frameworks you know.
