title: Zašto nam kal u mlaznicama košta više od goriva — i šta pokušavamo da uradimo po tom pitanju
text:
Ako ste ikada videli dron koji prska usev odmah posle kiše, možda ste primetili da leti nisko — obično između jednog i tri metra iznad krošnje. Na toj visini, u vlažnim uslovima, stajni trap i donji deo trupa postaju magneti za glinasto vojvođansko zemljište.

Prošle sezone smo izmerili da u takvim uslovima moramo da zaustavljamo letelicu i čistimo mlaznice svakih 45 minuta. Uz pripremu, transport i ponovni polet, to je sat vremena izgubljeno na svakih 45 minuta rada. Umesto planiranih osam sortija, realizujemo četiri do pet. I to baš u danima kada su tretmani najhitniji — jer insekti i gljivice ne čekaju da se zemlja osuši.

Isprobali smo nekoliko pristupa. Gumeni zaštitni poklopci na stajnom trapu su smanjili taloženje, ali su dodali 340 grama mase i pomerili centar težišta dovoljno da moramo da reprogramiramo balansiranje — što nije rešenje za celu flotu. Razmatrali smo keramičke premaze za mlaznice, ali nismo pronašli dobavljača koji može da garantuje hemijsku otpornost na kombinaciju glifosata, fungicida i abrazivnih čestica u roku koji nam odgovara.

Nismo još probali aerodinamičke deflektore koji bi usmeravali vazdušni tok od trupa, niti promenu geometrije prečke stajnog trapa. Oba pravca su tehnički moguća bez rezanja u trup letelice, što je za nas tvrdo ograničenje.

Ako imate iskustvo sa zaštitom podvozja u abrazivnim sredinama ili sa materijalima otpornim na pesticidnu abraziju — javite nam se. Tražimo praktično rešenje, ne savršeno.

title: What We Do — AquaCikl d.o.o.
text:
Industrial water is not a disposable input. At AquaCikl we design and run greywater recycling systems that let food processors and laundry operators reuse the same water again and again, with treated water quality good enough to return to their process lines.

Every project starts with a water audit. We take samples from your inlet and your drain, map where your water actually goes, and calculate what a realistic reuse rate looks like for your specific process. Most of our clients achieve between 60 and 80 percent reuse within the first year of operation.

Our systems combine coagulation and flocculation to remove suspended solids and fats, multimedia filtration to handle fine particles, activated carbon to strip odour and residual organics, and reverse osmosis where high-purity recirculated water is needed. We connect everything to a SCADA platform that logs quality and flow data continuously. You can check your system status from a phone. We can see it from our office in Novi Sad.

After commissioning we stay involved. Our technicians carry out quarterly physical inspections, and our remote monitoring team reviews trend data weekly. If a parameter starts drifting, we contact you before it becomes a compliance problem.

We have installed more than forty systems across Vojvodina since 2011. Our clients include poultry processing lines, commercial laundries, and vegetable preparation facilities. Some have been running our equipment for over a decade.

If you are facing tighter discharge limits, rising water tariffs, or a new facility build, contact us for an initial consultation. We will tell you honestly what is achievable and what it will cost.

title: AquaCikl commissions largest installation to date at Zlatna Niva food plant
text:
AquaCikl has completed commissioning of a greywater recycling system at the Zlatna Niva vegetable-processing facility near Vrbas. The installation is the largest the company has built to date, designed to handle up to 480 cubic metres of process water per day.

The project began with a water audit in mid-2023 that identified the facility's main water uses across washing, blanching, and cleaning-in-place operations. On the basis of that audit, AquaCikl designed a treatment train combining dissolved air flotation for fat and suspended solids removal, dual-media filtration, granular activated carbon, and a two-stage reverse-osmosis section for water returned to the highest-purity process steps.

After a six-week commissioning period the system reached a steady reuse rate of 71 percent, meaning Zlatna Niva now draws significantly less fresh water from the municipal supply for the same production volume. The facility's operations manager, Katarina Bjeloš, noted that the reduction in discharge volume had already simplified their compliance reporting under the revised Serbian industrial effluent rules that came into force in 2023.

For AquaCikl the project also served as a field trial for an updated remote monitoring configuration. All key quality and flow parameters now feed into the company's SCADA dashboard in near real time, with automated alerts set to flag deviations before they would reach the discharge monitoring point.

"This was a more complex effluent than we usually see, partly because of the starch and pectin load from the vegetable lines," said technical manager Dragana Feješ. "The system performed within spec from the third week onward, which is a good result for that type of influent."

AquaCikl will operate the system under a five-year service contract that includes quarterly physical audits and all consumables.

title: What we learned at the Regionalni Vodovodni Forum in Subotica
text:
Last month two of us attended the Regionalni Vodovodni Forum in Subotica, a two-day event focused on industrial water management in the Vojvodina and southern Pannonia region. It was a useful way to take stock of where the sector is heading and where the practical gaps still are.

A few things stood out.

First, the updated Serbian industrial discharge regulations from 2023 came up in almost every session that touched on food processing or textiles. The new manganese and iron limits are stricter than most operators expected, and more than one company representative mentioned that their existing treatment systems were not meeting the new thresholds. This matches what we are seeing in our own operations, and it is not a simple fix. The chemistry of manganese removal at low inlet concentrations is specific and not always intuitive.

Second, there was a session on digital tools for water system sizing and bid preparation. Most of what was shown was either very expensive commercial software aimed at large utilities, or very basic spreadsheet approaches. The gap in the middle — something a smaller engineering company could run quickly during a sales discussion — did not seem to have a satisfying answer. We are thinking about this.

Third, and more positively, there appears to be growing interest from industrial park developers in building water reuse infrastructure into new facilities from the start rather than retrofitting it. That is a different kind of project for us, and one we think we should be more prepared to take on.

We came back with some contacts, a clearer sense of what the competition is pricing, and a longer list of questions than we arrived with. That generally means it was worth going.

title: Open day at AquaCikl — see a greywater recycling system in operation
text:
AquaCikl is hosting a half-day open event at one of our operating installations in the Novi Sad industrial zone on 18 June 2024. The event is intended for production and facility managers at food-processing and laundry operations who want to see a working greywater recycling system before deciding whether to invest in one.

The programme will run from 09:00 to 13:00 and will include a guided walk through the full treatment train — from the collection pit through flotation, filtration, carbon adsorption, and the RO section — with stops to discuss what each stage does and what can go wrong. We will also show the remote monitoring dashboard and explain how we track system performance between physical visits.

After the site tour there will be a short discussion on the regulatory context: specifically the 2023 discharge limits, what they mean in practice for Vojvodina-based manufacturers, and what a realistic compliance timeline looks like for a facility that is not currently meeting the new manganese and iron thresholds.

There is no sales presentation. The point is to let you see the equipment, ask the engineers questions directly, and decide for yourself whether what we do is relevant to your situation.

Places are limited to 20 participants. To register, send a short message with your name, company, and the main water challenge you are dealing with to info@aquacikl.rs by 10 June. There is no charge to attend.

The site is accessible by car from the Novi Sad ring road. Parking is available on site. We will send directions on registration.

title: O nama i našim uslugama – Polje Senzor d.o.o.
text:
Polje Senzor je mali tim iz Novog Sada koji pravi hardver za praćenje uslova u voćnjacima. Počeli smo 2021. godine sa jednom jasnom idejom: voćar treba da zna šta se dešava na njegovoj parceli u svakom trenutku, a ne da nagađa na osnovu podataka sa obližnje meteorološke stanice koja može biti udaljena i dvadeset kilometara.

Naša PS-Orchard stanica postavlja se direktno između redova voća. Meri temperaturu vazduha, vlažnost lista i količinu padavina, a podatke šalje bežično preko LoRaWAN mreže svakih petnaest minuta. Voćar prati sve na mobilnoj aplikaciji ili veb portalu, a kada naš algoritam detektuje rizik od mraza, stižu mu obaveštenja na telefon.

Osim stanice, nudimo i PS-Gateway mini – mali LoRaWAN gateway za gazdinstva koja se nalaze van dometa postojeće mreže. Montaža traje manje od dva sata i ne zahteva nikakvo posebno znanje.

Svi naši uređaji prolaze trodnevni test pre isporuke. Podršku korisnicima pruža Milena Savić, koja je prethodno radila na terenu kao agro-savetnik, pa razume šta voćarima zaista treba.

Trenutno sarađujemo sa gazdinstvima od Subotice do Čačka. Naši korisnici uglavnom imaju između pet i pedeset hektara i sami upravljaju zaštitom useva. Cene naših uređaja i planova počinju od razumnog iznosa za porodično gazdinstvo – verujemo da precizni podaci ne treba da budu privilegija samo velikih proizvođača.

Ako imate pitanja ili želite da dogovorite demonstraciju na vašoj parceli, pišite nam na info@poljesenzor.rs.

title: Gazdinstvo Nikolić iz Bačke Palanke prošlo kroz prolećni mraz bez štete zahvaljujući ranom upozorenju
text:
U noći između 8. i 9. aprila 2024. godine temperature u pojasu između Bačke Palanke i Novog Sada pale su ispod nule u ranim jutarnjim satima. Za mnoge voćare to je bila neprijatna iznenađenja – standardne vremenske prognoze nisu predvidele lokalni mraz na ovom terenu.

Obradovalo nas je kad smo ujutru dobili poruku od Jovana Nikolića, vlasnika jabučnjaka od dvanaest hektara u okolini Bačke Palanke, koji koristi naše PS-Orchard stanice od prošle jeseni. Jovan nam je napisao: 'Dobio sam poruku u 2:47 ujutru. Ustao sam, upalio sistem za navodnjavanje kao zaštitu od mraza i vratio se u krevet. Komšija bez sistema je ujutru imao problem sa cvetovima.'

Njegove stanice su izmerile pad temperature na -1,8°C u zoni krošnje, što je dovoljno da ošteti cvetove jabuke u fazi punog cvetanja. Naš algoritam je poslao upozorenje sedam minuta nakon što je temperatura prešla kritičnu granicu.

Ovo je za nas važna potvrda da sistem radi kako treba u realnim uslovima. Nismo uvek savršeni – imali smo i slučajeva lažnih uzbuna tokom zime zbog kondenzacije na senzoru vlažnosti lista, što aktivno radimo na poboljšanju. Ali ova noć nam je pokazala da osnovna namena sistema funkcioniše.

Jovan Nikolić je pristao da učestvuje u testiranju naše buduće kamere za feromonske klopke tokom leta 2024. godine.

title: Bili smo na sajmu AgroNovosad 2024 – utisci i jedan neprijatan razgovor koji nas je naterao da razmišljamo
text:
Prošlog meseca učestvovali smo na sajmu AgroNovosad koji se održava svake godine na Novosadskom sajmu. Imali smo mali štand u paviljonu za agrotehničke inovacije, između prodavca sistema za navodnjavanje i jednog uvoznika gnojiva.

Pozitivno: razgovarali smo sa pedesetak voćara, od kojih su trojica ozbiljno zainteresovana za naše stanice. Marija Petrović iz Fruške gore rekla nam je da je čula za nas od svog suseda i da je godinama čekala nešto ovako. To je lepo čuti.

Manje pozitivno, ali korisno: jedan iskusniji voćar iz Topole, koji je godinama bavio jabučarstvom, postavio nam je direktno pitanje – koliko dugo traju baterije zimi? Kad smo mu odgovorili iskreno, rekao je da to za njega predstavlja problem jer je njegova parcela udaljena četiri kilometra od puta i ne želi da ide tamo po snegu samo da bi zamenio baterije. Razgovor nas je podsetio da ovo nije samo tehnički problem – za nekog ko ima parcelu na teškom terenu, loša baterija zimi znači da sistem prosto nije upotrebljiv.

Odneli smo kući i kontakte triju potencijalnih novih korisnika i jednu listu pitanja na koja još uvek nemamo dobre odgovore. To smatramo korisnim sajmom.

Sledeće godine planiramo da imamo prototip kamere za feromonske klopke koji bismo mogli da pokažemo uživo.

title: Otvoreni dan u NTP Novi Sad – Polje Senzor pokazuje PS-Orchard stanicu uživo
text:
Naučno-tehnološki park Novi Sad organizuje otvoreni dan 5. juna 2024. godine, a Polje Senzor će biti među izlagačima.

Dođite da vidite kako izgleda naša PS-Orchard stanica izbliza. Imaćemo demo postavku sa živim prenosom podataka sa senzora koji će biti montiran u malom testu ispred zgrade NTP-a tokom celog dana. Moći ćete da pratite merenja temperature, vlažnosti i simulaciju upozorenja na fraz u realnom vremenu kroz našu mobilnu aplikaciju.

Naš hardverski inženjer Bojan Đurić biće tu tokom celog prepodneva i može da odgovori na tehnička pitanja o tome kako stanica funkcioniše iznutra – od senzorskog sklopa do LoRaWAN prenosa i cloud-a.

Ako ste voćar koji razmišlja o sistemu za praćenje mikroklime, student koji radi na srodnoj temi, ili jednostavno neko ko je radoznao kako funkcioniše bežična senzorska mreža – dobrodošli ste.

Otvoreni dan traje od 10 do 17 časova. Ulaz je slobodan. Naš štand je u prizemlju, odmah pored recepcije.

Ako planirate da dođete i imate konkretno pitanje unapred, možete nam pisati na info@poljesenzor.rs – pokušaćemo da pripremimo odgovor ili pravi materijal za vas.

title: What We Do — Services and Capabilities
text:
Roboteks builds complete robotic welding and material-handling systems for metal fabricators. We handle every stage: layout design, fixture engineering, robot programming, safety enclosure fabrication, electrical panel assembly, and commissioning. When we hand over a cell, it is tested, documented, and ready to run production.

Our core work is MIG/MAG robotic welding. We integrate 6-axis robots into cells that weld structural steel assemblies, sheet metal enclosures, agricultural machinery frames, and automotive subcomponents. Each cell is designed around your part geometry and your production volume — we do not fit your parts into a catalogue solution.

Material handling is a natural extension of welding automation. Many of our cells include loading and unloading stations, conveyor links, and part-transfer robots that feed downstream operations. We programme the whole sequence on Siemens S7 controllers with touchscreen HMI panels that your operators can actually use without specialist training.

For customers who already have robotic equipment, we offer retrofit and upgrade services. If your robot is performing but the tooling is worn, the program is a patchwork from multiple contractors, or the safety guarding no longer meets current standards, we can modernise the installation without replacing the robot arm.

Every installation comes with a service contract. Our technicians visit on a fixed schedule, and we maintain a stock of common spare parts in Novi Sad for fast response. We currently support active installations across Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the oldest dating back to 2005.

If you have a welding or handling application and want a direct conversation with an engineer — not a salesperson — contact us through the form below.

The core of the job is producing complete, audit-ready technical files for our robotic cells under the EU Machinery Directive and the relevant harmonised standards — primarily EN ISO 10218-1 and -2, EN ISO 13849-1, and EN ISO 11161 for integrated manufacturing systems. title: Completed: Six-Station Welding Cell for Metalotehnika Pančevo
text:
We completed and handed over a six-station robotic welding cell to Metalotehnika Pančevo in March 2024. The project ran over eleven months from signed contract to accepted handover.

Metalotehnika produces structural steel subassemblies for agricultural machinery manufacturers in Serbia and Romania. Their previous welding process mixed manual and semi-automatic stations and was a bottleneck in their production flow. They came to us needing a cell that could handle five different part families with changeover times under twelve minutes between families.

The cell uses two FANUC ARC Mate robots on a shared floor track, with a dual-fixture turntable so operators can load one side while the robots weld on the other. We designed and fabricated all six fixture sets in our Novi Sad workshop. Seam tracking runs on Servo-Robot laser heads integrated directly into the robot program. The whole cell is controlled through a Siemens S7-1500 safety PLC with a custom TIA Portal HMI that shows weld status, cycle counts, and fault codes on a panel at each operator station.

Acceptance testing at our workshop ran for two weeks with parts supplied by Metalotehnika. We hit the twelve-minute changeover target on four of the five part families; the fifth required a fixture adjustment and came in at fourteen minutes, which the customer accepted.

The cell has been running in production since the beginning of April. Stevan Marković, production manager at Metalotehnika, noted during handover that the cycle time on their highest-volume part came in eight percent faster than the figure in our proposal.

This is the third project we have completed for Metalotehnika since 2014. Their maintenance team attended a two-day programming and maintenance course at our facility before the cell went live.

title: Why Our Welding Robots Lose Position During a Shift — and What We Are Trying to Do About It
text:
This is a practical problem we deal with on several of our installed cells, and we are writing about it because we think other integrators and end users probably see the same thing and do not always talk about it openly.

The situation: a robot welding cell is calibrated at the start of a shift. By hour four, the weld start position has drifted by one to two millimetres. On structural brackets with a fillet weld along a long edge, one millimetre of drift is often acceptable. On tight-tolerance parts — thin sheet, short welds, close joint fitup — it causes rejects.

The drift is not coming from the robot arm. Modern 6-axis robots are thermally stable enough over a shift that their contribution to the positional error is small. The drift is coming from the fixture. The steel fixture plate and clamping towers absorb heat from the arc, from the part itself, and from the shop floor environment. Steel expands. A fixture that is 800 mm across will grow by roughly 0.1 mm per degree Celsius of temperature rise. If the fixture heats by 15 degrees during a shift — which is typical on a high-duty-cycle cell — that is 1.2 mm of expansion across the reference datum surface.

What we have tried: the robot controllers we use (FANUC and Yaskawa) have built-in thermal compensation for the arm, but not for external fixtures. We added a contact temperature sensor to one fixture as a trial and logged the temperature against the measured positional drift over thirty shifts. The correlation is clear. What we have not yet solved is how to take that temperature reading and feed an automatic positional offset back to the robot controller in a way that is reliable and does not require stopping the cell.

We are looking for people who have solved this kind of closed-loop thermal compensation problem in an industrial setting. If you have, or if you know of relevant work, we would genuinely like to talk. Our contact is info@roboteks.rs.

title: About PixelForge Studios
text:
PixelForge Studios was started in 2014 in a two-room office at NTP Novi Sad by five people: two illustrators, two programmers, and one writer. The idea was simple — make games that told real stories and looked unlike anything built with stock assets or 3D engines. Ten years later we still work from the same building, though the office is considerably larger and the team has grown to thirty-four.

We make narrative adventure games. Our players follow characters through hand-painted worlds, make choices that matter, and come back for second playthroughs to see what they missed. Our titles have been played in over forty countries, with our strongest audiences in Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and France.

Every visual element in our games is drawn by our own artists. We use a layered digital painting process that starts with rough ink sketches and ends with backgrounds that resemble watercolour illustration. Characters are rigged and animated in Spine 2D. Our engineers build and maintain a proprietary dialogue engine that handles branching, conditional states, and localization across multiple languages.

We have shipped seven titles since 2014. Mireille and the Hollow Road, released in 2019, remains our most-played game. The Cartographer's Debt, our episodic mystery series, is currently in its third episode. Our mobile series, Ashveil Chronicles, releases new episodes roughly every eight months.

We are not the largest studio in the region, and that is not the goal. We hire carefully, train internally, and keep our production scope matched to what our team can do without cutting corners. If you are interested in working with us, our open positions are listed below. If you are a publisher or partner, you can reach our production lead through the contact form.

title: Mireille and the Hollow Road Reaches 80,000 Steam Owners
text:
We hit a number we are pleased with this month: Mireille and the Hollow Road now has over 80,000 owners on Steam. The game launched in October 2019 and has grown steadily through a mix of regional promotions, a free weekend we ran in November 2023, and word of mouth in the story-games community on several forums we did not seed ourselves.

For context, Mireille was our fourth title and the first one where we fully committed to the hand-painted visual style that has defined our work since. Before that we were experimenting with cleaner, flatter looks that were faster to produce but did not feel like us. The art direction on Mireille — led by our art director Sofija Beljanski, who joined us in 2017 — established the process we still use today: rough ink layer, colour wash, detail pass, atmospheric overlay.

The reception among players has been steady. The game holds a rating of 83% positive on Steam across all reviews. The most common praise in written reviews is the writing and the feeling that choices have real weight. The most common criticism is that the final chapter is shorter than the earlier ones — a production constraint we were aware of and have not been entirely able to resolve in patches.

We are not announcing a sequel at this time. What we can say is that the characters from Mireille exist in the same setting as our upcoming untitled PC project, and players who have completed Mireille's story will find references that mean something to them.

Thank you to everyone who has played the game and left a review, positive or otherwise. Honest negative reviews are useful to us.

title: What We Learned from Releasing in French
text:
We added French as a supported language for The Cartographer's Debt in January 2024. It was our third localization after English and German, and the one that taught us the most about where our process breaks down.

The translation itself went smoothly. We contracted a studio called Texte & Jeu based in Lyon, and their team delivered clean, idiomatic French that our narrative lead reviewed and approved with only minor adjustments. That part of the pipeline works.

The part that does not work is lip-sync animation. Our characters have visible mouth movement tied to dialogue audio, and for every new language that means going back through every voiced line and rekeying the mouth shapes to match the new phoneme timing. Our animators use a reference chart that maps French phoneme groups to the nine mouth shapes we use per character. The work is not technically difficult — it is just slow. For the French pass on The Cartographer's Debt Episode Two, which has approximately forty minutes of voiced dialogue, this took just under three weeks of one animator's time.

Three weeks is not catastrophic in isolation. The problem is that we are planning to add Dutch and Italian within the next year. Three weeks per language per episode adds up quickly, and it pulls an animator away from new-content production. We tried one commercially available auto lip-sync solution during the French pass — we are not going to name it here because the problem may be our specific character style rather than the tool itself — and the output did not match our mouth shapes well enough to use without substantial correction.

We are currently looking at building something more specific to our pipeline: a tool that reads an audio file, identifies phoneme timings, and outputs Spine 2D keyframe data matched to our shape library. If you have done something similar or have thoughts on the technical approach, we would genuinely like to hear from you. Reach us through the contact page.

title: AgroLens Completes 2023 Season with 140 Active Farms and Launches Season Report Feature
text:
We finished the 2023 growing season with 140 active farm accounts across Vojvodina and the Hajdú-Bihar and Bács-Kiskun regions of Hungary, up from 97 at the end of 2022. Total area under management passed 190,000 hectares for the first time.

The most-used new feature of the season was the season report export, which we released in April 2023 after repeated requests from customers who needed clean documentation for the Serbian agricultural subsidy system and for their banks. Our field support contact, Milovan Crnobrnja, spent the spring visiting farms and collecting feedback on early drafts of the export format. The final version generates a per-parcel table of all logged operations with GPS-stamped map thumbnails, which several customers told us saved them several hours of paperwork at the end of the season.

On the satellite side, cloud cover over Vojvodina was unusually persistent through May and early June, which reduced the frequency of useful NDVI updates during a critical period for winter wheat. We communicated this directly to customers via in-app notifications rather than staying silent, and we are now looking at whether Sentinel-1 radar data could provide some continuity during cloudy periods. That is an open research question for us and one reason we are currently hiring.

For 2024, our main product priorities are improving the reliability and coverage of health maps during cloudy conditions and beginning the groundwork for a yield estimation feature that we plan to develop through 2025 and 2026. We are also in early conversations with potential distribution partners in Romania.

Thank you to every farm that trusted us with their data this season. Feedback, positive or critical, can always be sent to info@agrolens.rs.

title: What AgroLens Does — Platform and Services Overview
text:
AgroLens Field is farm management software built specifically for mid-size grain operations in Vojvodina and Hungary. If you farm between 150 and 2,500 hectares of wheat, sunflower, maize, or soy, and you want a clearer picture of what is happening on every parcel without hiring a dedicated office administrator, this platform was built for you.

The core of the product is a field record system that works on any Android or iOS phone. Your tractor drivers and agronomists log operations — tillage, sowing, fertiliser applications, spraying — as they happen in the field. Those records sync to a web dashboard where the farm manager sees a running history for every parcel, ready to export at any time for subsidy applications or bank reporting.

On top of the operational records, we layer satellite-derived crop health maps. Every time Sentinel-2 passes over your fields on a clear day, we process the imagery and update your parcel-level NDVI and chlorophyll maps within 48 hours. You can see which parts of a field are lagging behind, compare this season to last season on the same date, and share a map link with your agronomist or input supplier.

The spraying plan module takes those health maps and helps you build variable-rate application plans, which several of our customers have used to reduce fungicide use on lower-risk parcels while increasing protection where the maps show stress.

We are based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad and we have field support staff who visit customers across Vojvodina each season. Pricing is per hectare per year with no long-term lock-in. Contact us through the form below or call our office in Novi Sad to arrange a demo.

title: Why We Are Not Shipping a Yield Forecast Yet — and What We Are Doing About It
text:
Every June we get a wave of messages from customers asking the same thing: can you tell me how much wheat I am going to harvest on parcel 7? It is a completely reasonable question. Our maps show crop health in near-real time, and it is natural to assume that a company looking at satellite data across 190,000 hectares should be able to give a yield number.

The honest answer is that we cannot do it reliably yet, and we think it is important to say so clearly rather than ship something that would mislead a farmer into making a bad contract decision.

Here is the specific problem. NDVI — the greenness index at the core of our health maps — correlates loosely with yield potential, but loosely is the key word. The relationship changes depending on the year, the variety, the sowing date, the rainfall pattern, and a handful of other factors. We fitted a regression model last year using yield-monitor data that a group of cooperative customers shared with us after harvest, and the error range was wide enough that we would not feel comfortable attaching a tonne-per-hectare number to it.

What we are doing: our data scientists, Nataša Korolija and Branimir Šević, are now building a richer feature set that combines satellite time-series, logged field operations, and historical weather data. We are also actively looking for collaborators who have deeper expertise in crop modelling than we do internally. If the 2025 growing season goes well from a data collection standpoint, we believe we can have something worth testing with a small group of early-access customers by mid-2026, ahead of a full product launch in 2027.

If you are a customer and you want to be part of the early-access group — which means sharing your combine yield-monitor data with us under a data agreement — please get in touch. The more ground-truth data we have, the better the model will be for everyone.

'Bili smo zadovoljni konzistentnošću materijala i činjenicom da FlexiPack može da reaguje brzo na izmene dimenzija', rekao je Dragan Popović, menadžer nabavke u Zlatnoj Njivi. 'Za nas je važno i to što pratimo šta se dešava sa EU regulativom o ambalаži — želimo da sarađujemo sa dobavljačima koji razumeju taj pravac.'

Jovana Mirković, osnivač FlexiPacka, istakla je da je ovaj ugovor potvrda da domaći prehrambeni brendovi ozbiljno gledaju na pitanje reciklabilnosti: 'Zlatna Njiva nam nije tražila samo cenu i rok — tražili su dokumentaciju o strukturi filma i pitali su da li smo u procesu sertifikacije. To je za nas dobar znak.'

title: Šta smo naučili na sajmu AmbalaŽex 2024 u Beogradu
text:
Početkom maja smo bili na sajmu AmbalaŽex 2024 u Beogradu — regionalnoj izložbi ambalažne industrije na kojoj smo imali skroman štand, ali bogat program razgovora.

Prvo zapažanje: gotovo svaki razgovor sa prehrambenim brendovima iz Srbije i BiH završio se temom EU regulative. Nije to više apstraktna budućnost — kupci pitaju konkretno: 'Da li vaša ambalaža može da prođe PPWR kriterijume?' i 'Kako ću ja da dokažem reciklabilnost svom distributeru u Austriji?' Mi nemamo sve odgovore, ali dobro je što znamo na čemu treba da radimo.

Drugo zapažanje: postoji interesovanje za kratke serije sa digitalnom štampom. Nekoliko manjih brendova reklo nam je da bi promenili dobavljača ambalаže samo da mogu da naruče 2.000 kesica sa različitim dizajnom bez astronomskog troška. Mi to trenutno ne možemo da ponudimo jer sva štampa ide u Mađarsku, ali potvrdilo nam je da ovo pitanje treba rešiti.

Susreli smo se i sa timom iz kompanije EcoPouche GmbH (Austrija), koji prave bio-bazirane filmove. Razgovor je bio koristan — oni ne rade sa istom strukturom kao mi, ali razmena iskustava oko adhezije slojeva bila je konkretna i bez marketinškog filtera.

Na kraju, nismo se vratili sa potpisanim ugovorima, ali smo se vratili sa boljim razumevanjem šta tržištu treba u naredne dve do tri godine. To je, po nama, pravi razlog za odlazak na ovakve skupove.

Sledeće godine planiramo veći štand i, nadamo se, barem jedan certifikovani reciklabilni proizvod koji možemo da pokažemo sa dokumentacijom u ruci.

title: Our Services — Dunav Kargo a.d.
text:
Dunav Kargo has been operating on the Danube and the DTD canal network for nearly fifty years. We handle bulk freight that needs to move in large volumes at predictable cost — grain, flour, fertiliser, sand, gravel, cement clinker and similar commodities.

Our barge fleet consists of twelve self-propelled and push-convoy vessels with carrying capacities between 600 and 1,400 tonnes per hull. Convoys are assembled at our Novi Sad base and dispatched on fixed weekly schedules to terminals in Smederevo, Apatin, Senta, Zrenjanin and, for international cargo, onward to Budapest and Galați under bilateral transport agreements.

Our road fleet of sixty trucks — flatbeds, tippers and covered curtainsiders — operates as both a standalone service and as overflow capacity when canal conditions restrict barge loading. This combination lets us offer clients a single contract for bulk movements without asking them to manage two separate carriers.

All cargo documentation, phytosanitary certificates for grain, and customs declarations for cross-border shipments are handled by our in-house documentation team. Clients do not need a freight forwarder for standard commodity movements on the corridors we serve.

Our workshop on the Štrand canal bank carries out all scheduled and corrective maintenance in-house. We employ twelve diesel mechanics and hold a stock of critical spare parts for our main engine types. This means a vessel breakdown is usually resolved within 24 to 48 hours without waiting for an outside contractor.

For new enquiries, contact our commercial office at the address below or speak directly with our freight coordinator, Milovan Đurđević, who handles all spot and contract rate discussions.

title: Junior Data Analyst — Fleet Operations (part-time or project basis considered)
text:
Dunav Kargo a.d., Novi Sad, is looking for a data analyst to help us get practical value from sensor data we already collect but do not currently use.

Background:
Over the past five years we have fitted vibration and temperature sensors to the main diesel engines on our barge fleet. Data is logged continuously and downloaded in CSV format during scheduled port calls. We also have two years of GPS and fuel consumption logs from our truck fleet. None of this data is being analysed in any systematic way.

What the role involves:
— Loading and cleaning sensor CSV files (typically 5–15 MB per vessel per month)
— Building simple visualisations that our workshop chief and dispatchers can interpret without specialist training
— Exploring whether patterns in vibration or temperature data correlate with the four engine failures we recorded in 2023
— Documenting findings in plain language

What we are looking for:
— Working knowledge of Python or R for data handling (pandas, tidyverse or equivalent)
— Ability to produce clear charts and short written summaries
— Some understanding of time-series data; prior experience with industrial sensor data is a plus but not required
— Serbian language is useful but not mandatory; we can work in English

What we are not looking for:
— Someone who will build a system that requires constant expert maintenance
— Academic deliverables; we need something a 55-year-old diesel mechanic can act on

Engagement: We are open to a fixed-term project contract of three to six months, a part-time arrangement, or a university collaboration if that is the right structure. Compensation is negotiable based on form of engagement.

Contact: Vesna Latinović, Operations Manager, v.latinovic@dunavkargo.rs

title: Dunav Kargo Signs Three-Year Contract with Zlatna Njiva Agro Group
text:
Dunav Kargo a.d. has agreed a three-year bulk transport contract with Zlatna Njiva Agro Group, a Vojvodina-based grain trading and processing company, covering the movement of sunflower seed, soybean and wheat between storage facilities in Titel and Bačka Palanka and export terminals on the Danube.

Under the agreement, Dunav Kargo will dedicate two push-convoy barge sets to Zlatna Njiva's seasonal movements during the harvest and export windows, primarily from July through November. Outside these windows the vessels return to the general freight pool.

Milovan Đurđević, freight coordinator at Dunav Kargo, said the agreement provides the company with a firmer base for forward fleet planning. 'Knowing two convoy sets are committed for those five months lets us schedule maintenance around the contract rather than guessing at demand. That is useful for our workshop team and for our clients who share the remaining fleet.'

Zlatna Njiva had previously used a combination of spot barge bookings and road haulage for the same movements. Their logistics director, Branimir Kostadinović, noted that consolidating under a single carrier simplified invoice reconciliation and reduced the number of transport documents their team had to process per shipment.

The contract includes a clause allowing volume adjustments of up to 15% in either direction based on crop yields, and a performance metric tied to on-time delivery at the terminal gate. Dunav Kargo estimates the agreement will account for approximately 11% of its annual revenue at current commodity freight rates.

Operations under the contract begin with the 2024 sunflower harvest, expected in late August.

title: What the Summer of 2022 Cost Us and What We Are Doing About It
text:
We do not usually write about operational problems in public. But the low-water situation on the DTD canal in the summer of 2022 was significant enough that some of our clients asked us directly what happened and what we are changing. This post is the honest answer.

From late July through early September 2022, water levels on several sections of the DTD canal dropped below the threshold where we can safely load a barge to standard commercial capacity. At the critical section near Bečej, usable draft fell to the point where we had to reduce cargo per barge by approximately 30%. That meant more trips to move the same total volume, or accepting that some cargo simply waited.

The financial impact came mainly from transport rebalancing. Because we did not have reliable advance warning of how long the low-water period would last, we were late in pre-booking truck subcontractor capacity. By the time we committed to additional road transport, spot rates had risen and the subcontractors with suitable tipper trucks were already partly booked by other clients. We paid more than we would have if we had acted ten days earlier.

We rely on public hydrology data from the Serbian water management authority and on weather forecasts, but neither gives us a reliable two-week outlook specific to the canal sections that matter most to our operations. Our dispatchers make judgement calls based on experience, and those calls are sometimes right and sometimes not.

What we are trying to change: we are in conversation with researchers who work on hydrological modelling to see whether a more targeted forecasting tool is feasible for the DTD system. We are also formalising our pre-booking arrangement with our main road subcontractor, Vojvođanski Transport d.o.o., so that we can call on additional truck capacity at agreed rates during a confirmed alert period rather than at spot prices.

We are not pretending this is solved. The summer of 2024 will be the test.

title: TrasaNet Goes Live in Oradea: Twelve Months In
text:
A year ago this week, the Oradea Metropolitan Transit Consortium switched off its previous scheduling system and moved to TrasaNet for its 87-bus network. We said at the time that the transition would take six months to feel normal for dispatchers. It took four.

The Oradea team came to us with a specific request: they wanted to produce timetables that could legally operate under both Romanian transport regulations and the EU accessibility guidelines their city had committed to meeting by 2025. Their previous software had no concept of accessibility constraints in scheduling — whether a low-floor vehicle was assigned to a route that required it was checked manually by a planner after the fact. TrasaNet encodes those constraints directly in the solver, so an invalid assignment simply does not appear in the output.

Over the first twelve months, Oradea's dispatchers logged 214 incidents requiring schedule adjustments. In 189 of those cases they used TrasaNet Dispatch to implement the change. The remaining 25 were handled manually, mostly in the first two months while confidence in the tool was still building. That ratio has continued to improve.

Consortium Operations Director Florin Baciu told us at our last quarterly review: 'The thing that changed most was not the timetable quality — it was that our planners stopped spending Monday mornings fixing what broke on Friday. The system holds together better across the week.'

We are now in discussions with two further Romanian municipal operators who contacted us after speaking with the Oradea team. We expect to announce at least one of those engagements before the end of Q1 2024.

The Oradea implementation was led by our senior implementation engineer Milovan Toth, with timetable configuration support from transport planning consultant Vesna Ilić.

title: What We Do – Subotička Mobilnost a.d.
text:
Public transport runs on time when the people managing it have tools that match the complexity of the job. Subotička Mobilnost a.d. has been building those tools since 1997, starting from a single timetable editor for the Subotica city bus network and growing into a full suite of planning, dispatch and passenger information software used by fourteen transit authorities across Serbia, Hungary and Romania.

Our flagship platform, TrasaNet, covers the full operational cycle of a bus network: building timetables that balance coverage, cost and driver working-time regulations; assigning vehicles to runs; rostering drivers; and monitoring the live network from a dispatch console. TrasaNet is not a generic logistics tool dressed up for transit — it was designed from the start around the specific rules of public transport: minimum layover times, interchanges, regulatory duty limits, deadhead minimisation and the political reality that some routes must run even when they lose money.

PassengerView connects the back-office data to the people waiting at stops. Display units show the next two or three arrivals on a line, updated from live vehicle positions. The system generates GTFS-Realtime feeds that third-party journey-planning apps can consume.

DataBridge AVL is our onboard hardware and telemetry layer. Units are fitted to vehicles at the depot and communicate GPS position, door events and odometer readings over cellular to our ingestion servers every ten seconds. The data feeds both the dispatch console and the historical archive we use for network analysis.

We work with operators that range from a twelve-bus rural network in southern Serbia to the 300-vehicle Timișoara Metropolitan Authority. Our implementation team handles installation, training and the first twelve months of support directly — we do not subcontract that work. Customers speak to the same engineers who built the system.

If you manage a public transit network and want to talk about scheduling, real-time tracking or passenger information, contact our Subotica office.

title: Backend Engineer – Real-Time Data Processing (Subotica or Novi Sad)
text:
Subotička Mobilnost a.d. is looking for a backend engineer to join the team responsible for our real-time vehicle tracking and passenger information pipeline.

What the role involves:
Our DataBridge AVL units send GPS and event data from 340 buses every ten seconds. That stream lands in a PostgreSQL database and needs to be processed into useful outputs: live dispatch views, GTFS-Realtime feeds and, increasingly, arrival predictions for passenger display screens. Right now the prediction side is underdeveloped and we are actively working to fix that. You would own the ingestion and processing pipeline — keeping it reliable, improving latency and helping us move from a crude position-offset model to something that actually uses the historical patterns in our two-plus billion-row archive.

What we are looking for:
— Solid Java experience; our backend runs on Spring Boot and we are not planning to change that
— Comfortable with PostgreSQL at scale, including PostGIS for spatial queries
— Some exposure to time-series data, whether from transit, IoT or elsewhere
— Python is a plus; our data engineer uses it for preprocessing and analysis
— Familiarity with GTFS or GTFS-Realtime is a genuine advantage, not just a box to tick
— You do not need a machine learning background, but you should be willing to work with someone who has one

What we offer:
A permanent contract, salary in line with Serbian IT market rates for mid-to-senior experience, flexible hours, and a problem that is harder and more interesting than most logistics software jobs. The team in Subotica is eleven people. The Novi Sad office is smaller but possible if you prefer it.

Send a CV and a short note about a data pipeline problem you have worked on to posao@subotickamobilnost.rs. We respond to every application.

title: Transport Planning Consultant – Cross-Border Projects (Subotica)
text:
We are hiring a transport planning consultant to support our growing portfolio of cross-border and international projects, with an immediate focus on the Hajdú Cross-Border Transit Consortium engagement.

The context:
Subotička Mobilnost a.d. has customers in Serbia, Hungary and Romania. Each jurisdiction has its own licensing regime, data regulations and operational standards. Our software handles the technical side well, but navigating the regulatory and planning requirements across borders is a distinct skill set that our current team does not fully cover. title: Subotička Mobilnost a.d. Exhibits at Balkantrans Mobility Forum, Belgrade
text:

It was the largest gathering of that kind we have attended in the past five years, and the conversations were more technical than we expected — operators are past the stage of asking whether to digitise their dispatch operations and are now asking specific questions about data latency, solver performance and cross-border compliance.

We demonstrated TrasaNet Dispatch and the current version of PassengerView at a stand shared with our hardware partner Telematik Sistemi d.o.o. from Kragujevac. title: Why We Still Store Every GPS Ping (And What We Have Not Done With Them Yet)
text:
Since 2021 we have been storing every GPS ping from every DataBridge AVL unit on our network. That is roughly one record per vehicle per ten seconds. Across 340 buses operating an average of fourteen service hours per day, it adds up to about 2.8 billion rows in our archive at the time of writing.

We store them because storage is cheap and because we had a nagging sense that the data would eventually be useful. We were right that it would be useful. We were wrong about how quickly we would figure out how to use it.

For the first two years the archive did one thing: let us replay historical trips for incident investigation. A driver reports that a stop was blocked at 8:47 AM on a Tuesday in October. We pull the replay, we see the dwell time was 40 seconds instead of the scheduled 15, we can correlate it with the delay that propagated through the rest of the morning. That is genuinely useful, but it is not using 2.8 billion rows — it is using maybe ten minutes of them.

The thing we have not done, and that we need to do, is use the archive to understand travel time patterns. The same route at 8 AM on a rainy Thursday takes eight minutes longer than on a clear Tuesday, and our timetable does not know that. Our PassengerView does not know it. When a bus is running late because of conditions that have historically caused that exact delay on that exact segment, we could be telling passengers a realistic arrival time instead of projecting the timetable offset forward.

We have a data engineer, Nikola Horvat, who has started exploratory analysis on a subset of the archive. The patterns are there in the data. The question is how to turn them into a prediction model that runs fast enough to update passenger screens every 30 seconds and that our backend team can maintain without a dedicated data science department.

We do not have a solution to announce. We are writing this because we think being honest about where the gap is matters more than pretending we have it figured out.

title: About Zlatna Njiva — Oils Pressed in Zrenjanin Since 1991
text:
Zlatna Njiva started as a practical decision. In 1991, Dragoljub Kovačević had a building, a network of local seed growers, and a conviction that the oils available in Serbian shops were not as good as what could be made from local raw material. He bought a used screw press, hired four people, and started producing. The company grew steadily through the 1990s and early 2000s, adding a refined sunflower line to keep volume up during slower periods and a cold-pressed range to pursue higher-value retail and export opportunities.

Today we employ 87 people across pressing, filtering, bottling, quality control, logistics, and administration. Milica Kovačević-Petrić, Dragoljub's daughter, has led the company since 2014. The team in production averages over nine years with the company.

Our cold-pressed oils are made from seeds sourced within sixty kilometres of the factory. We know most of our seed suppliers by name. When a batch comes in, our intake team checks moisture and foreign matter content before the seeds go into storage. Cold pressing happens at temperatures that stay below 40°C, verified on every shift. After pressing, the crude oil goes through filtration and then into dark glass bottles with a nitrogen flush before sealing.

Our customers include Merkator Serbia, Tempo supermarkets, and a range of independent health food retailers in Serbia. In export markets we sell through established import partners in Ljubljana and Vienna. We are currently working toward entry into the German organic retail market.

We do not claim our oils are the cheapest on the shelf. We do claim they are made from locally sourced seeds, processed simply, and checked in our own lab before they leave the building. That has been the approach since 1991 and it remains the approach today.

If you have questions about our products, supply terms, or export availability, contact our sales team at prodaja@zlatna-njiva.rs.

title: What We Learned From Our First Full Season Using the New Seed Moisture Protocol
text:
Last year we introduced a more structured incoming moisture check for all seeds arriving at our facility. Previously, our intake team was sampling one bag in ten from each delivery. We moved to a protocol where every fifth bag is sampled using our Dickey-john GAC 2500 analyser, and deliveries with average moisture above 8% are either rejected or directed to a separate drying holding area before going into our main silos.

After running this through a full pressing season, here is what we observed.

First, the number of batches showing elevated free fatty acid values at the point of pressing dropped noticeably. Before the protocol change, roughly one in eight pressing batches for pumpkin seed came out of the press with FFA above 1.5%, which is the threshold above which we see faster downstream degradation. This season that figure was closer to one in eighteen. We attribute most of this improvement to catching high-moisture seed earlier.

Second, the drying holding area created a minor logistical problem we had not anticipated. When we direct a delivery to drying, it can sit for two to four days before re-entering the intake process. During the harvest peak in September and October, this created a small backlog that required our warehouse team to rearrange storage three times in one week. We are planning a modest extension of the holding area before next season.

Third, two of our seed suppliers, both long-standing partners, initially pushed back on rejections. Those conversations were uncomfortable but ultimately straightforward — we shared the FFA data from affected batches and they accepted the reasoning. One of them has since invested in on-farm drying capacity, which should reduce the problem at the source.

We are sharing this not because it is a dramatic story but because it is the kind of incremental, unglamorous process work that actually moves quality in the right direction. The next area we are looking at closely is the nitrogen flushing step at bottling, where we suspect we are leaving more residual oxygen in the headspace than we should be.

title: Terramap Completes Utility Mapping on 4.2 km Road Reconstruction in Kanjiža
text:
Terramap Subotica d.o.o. has completed the pre-construction underground utility survey for the reconstruction of Ulica Maršala Tita and three connecting side streets in Kanjiža municipality. The project was commissioned by Kanjiža Road Maintenance and forms part of a larger EU-co-financed road rehabilitation programme running through 2025.

The survey covered 4.2 kilometres of carriageway with GPR scans at 50-centimetre lane spacing, combined with GNSS-controlled topographic measurements for the road design model. Our crews identified 312 individual utility crossings and longitudinal runs, including water mains, gas distribution pipes, telecommunications ducts, and street-lighting cables. Delivered outputs included a 1:500 utility map, depth profiles at every marked crossing, and a full-coverage DXF file integrated into the client's AutoCAD Civil 3D project.

Project manager Aleksandar Varga noted that the municipality specifically requested a second-pass GPR scan on two sections where previous contractor records were incomplete. The additional scan identified two gas service laterals that were not on any existing drawing.

The survey was completed in eleven field days over December and January, within the contractual timeline despite ground frost that required adjusted antenna-coupling parameters on the deepest scan lines. Final deliverables were accepted by the client without revision requests.

Kanjiža Road Maintenance has been a Terramap client since 2009. This project is the largest single assignment we have completed for the municipality in terms of corridor length, and we expect the as-built documentation phase later in 2024 to follow once construction crews mobilise.

title: Services – What We Do and How We Do It
text:
Terramap Subotica d.o.o. provides land surveying and underground infrastructure mapping services across northern Vojvodina and southern Hungary. Below is a plain description of our main service lines.

**GNSS Land and Cadastral Surveying**
We carry out boundary surveys, parcel divisions, expropriation documentation, and geodetic control for construction sites. Our field crews use dual-frequency GNSS receivers connected in real time to our own reference-station network, which covers the area between Subotica in the north and Bečej in the south. For projects requiring higher accuracy or where satellite reception is limited, we fall back to total-station traverses.

**Ground-Penetrating Radar Utility Mapping**
Before any excavation or drilling on urban roads or near existing infrastructure, we scan the ground with calibrated GPR systems. We map the depth, direction, and approximate diameter of buried pipes, cables, and ducts, and we deliver georeferenced utility maps in DXF or GeoPackage format. Our standard product is a 1:500 scale map with depth profiles at one-metre cross-section intervals.

**As-Built Documentation**
Once construction is complete, we survey the finished structure and produce as-built drawings that conform to Serbian geodetic regulations or, where required, Hungarian EOV standards. We handle utility corridors, road cross-sections, retaining walls, and bridge control monitoring.

**RTK Correction Network**
A limited number of subscriber licences are available for external surveying firms who want to connect to our NTRIP caster and use our reference-station corrections for their own fieldwork in northern Vojvodina.

All deliverables are issued with a full quality-control report, including point coordinate lists, redundancy checks, and the instrument serial numbers and calibration dates used on the job. Our project coordinator, Nataša Fekete, handles all client enquiries and can provide a quote within two working days of receiving a site plan.

title: Terramap at GeoSrbija 2024 Conference in Novi Sad – Notes from the Stand
text:

title: Why Our GPR Archive Might Be Worth More Than We Thought
text:
We have been doing ground-penetrating radar surveys since 2009. Over fifteen years of work we have accumulated roughly four terabytes of raw B-scan files stored on an internal server, organised by project and date. For most of that time we have treated those files as project records: useful if a client calls with a question, otherwise archived and forgotten.

Recently we started looking at the archive differently. On a number of completed projects, we now know what was actually in the ground because construction crews have dug it up. That means we have scan files where we can match what the radar saw to what was physically there. For some sites we detected the utility correctly. For some we missed it. For a few we flagged something that turned out to be a building rubble layer or a dense gravel pocket.

That combination of raw images plus known outcomes is something that does not exist in many places. It took us fifteen years of fieldwork to accumulate it.

We do not yet have a plan for what to do with it. Training an automated detection system of some kind is one idea that has come up internally, though none of us have the background to judge whether that is realistic or what it would require. Improving our operator training materials using real annotated examples is a simpler version of the same idea.

If you work in signal processing, image analysis, or machine learning and find this kind of dataset interesting, we are open to a conversation. We are not looking for a research project that produces a paper. We are looking for something that makes our operators faster and more consistent, and that reduces the chance of a repeat of the incident we had last year. Get in touch through our website contact form or reach Nataša Fekete directly at n.fekete@terramap-su.rs.

title: What We Do — Engineering Simulation and Digital Twins
text:
Orbita Inženjering builds simulation software and digital twins for industrial clients. We have been doing this since 1991, which means we have seen many waves of technology come through manufacturing and we have a reasonable sense of what actually gets used versus what sits in a demo environment.

Our work starts with the physics. Before we write a line of application code, our engineers study the real process — thermal behaviour in a curing oven, mechanical loads in an assembly fixture, fluid flow in a mixing vessel. We build mathematical models of those processes and then we turn those models into software that plant engineers can operate without a simulation background.

The result is a digital twin: a software model that reflects the actual state of a plant in close to real time, connected to live sensor data via standard industrial protocols. Plant engineers use it to test operating changes before applying them on the floor, to plan maintenance based on model predictions, and to train new operators in a safe environment.

We do not sell off-the-shelf simulation packages. Every deployment is custom, because every factory is different. What we do have is reusable solver and visualisation infrastructure that reduces the time needed for each new project.

Our clients are in Italy, France and Slovenia. They are mid-size manufacturers — automotive components, food processing, aerospace supply chain, plastics, furniture. They have engineering departments that know their processes well and want software tools that match that knowledge rather than replace it.

If you are considering a digital twin and want to understand what is actually involved in building one, we are happy to have that conversation. Contact us through the form below or reach our technical director, Bojana Stanković, directly at b.stankovic@orbita-ing.rs.

title: Three Things We Learned at the SIM-IND Expo in Turin
text:
Four of us attended the SIM-IND industrial simulation and digital manufacturing expo in Turin last month. It is the third year we have gone as a company, and the conversations there are useful in a specific way: Italian plant engineers are direct about what they want and what they find frustrating, which is a good corrective if you spend too much time talking to your own team.

A few observations worth recording.

First, the speed expectation has shifted. Two years ago, clients at events like this talked about digital twins as planning tools — something you ran overnight and reviewed in the morning. This year, several conversations started with 'does it run in real time?' before anything else. We heard this from both prospects and from other vendors. It is no longer a differentiator to run in real time; it is becoming a baseline requirement. We are not there yet for our most complex models, and that came up in at least two conversations that did not continue.

Second, the browser rendering question is real. We demonstrated our viewer on two occasions. On the trade fair laptop it was fine. On a plant engineer's own laptop — an ordinary business machine — the model loaded slowly and the fan came on. He laughed but also raised an eyebrow. We knew about this problem before Turin; Turin confirmed it costs us credibility.

Third, ergonomics came up unexpectedly. A Slovenian machinery manufacturer we met — not a current client — mentioned that EU procurement requirements for new equipment are increasingly asking for ergonomic assessment documentation. title: FlowDeck – Workflow Automation Built for Logistics Operations
text:
Running a logistics operation means managing dozens of moving parts at the same time: order intake, carrier selection, booking confirmations, exception handling, invoicing. Most of that work follows rules your team already knows. FlowDeck turns those rules into automated processes that run without anyone having to remember to trigger them.

You draw the workflow. Your team uses a visual canvas to map out the steps — conditions, actions, waits, branches. No programming required. The people who understand the operation build the automation directly, without translating requirements through a developer.

FlowDeck runs it. The execution engine handles timing, retries, and state. When a carrier confirmation arrives, the next step fires automatically. When an exception occurs, the right person gets notified through the right channel.

FlowDeck Live shows you where everything is. Dispatchers get a live map of vehicle positions and predicted ETAs pulled from your existing telematics systems, displayed inside the same platform where the workflows run. No separate tracking tab. No manual status checks.

We built FlowDeck after spending years inside a freight operation ourselves. We know that logistics teams do not have time to learn new software categories. FlowDeck is designed to be configured by an operations manager in a week, not deployed by a consultant over three months.

Our clients are road freight carriers and third-party logistics providers in Germany and the Benelux with between 50 and 500 employees. If your dispatch team is still coordinating exceptions over email and your workflow tools are a mix of spreadsheets and manual checks, we should talk.

Get in touch at contact@krenuti-digital.rs or book a 30-minute walkthrough directly from this page.

title: What We Learned at transport logistic Munich 2024
text:
We sent four people to transport logistic in Munich at the end of May — two from the engineering team and two from the commercial side. It was the first time Krenuti Digital had a stand at a major European logistics trade fair, and we want to share what we actually took away from it.

The good part: the product gets attention. When we showed FlowDeck live — a dispatcher drawing a workflow on the canvas and the engine running it in the same session — people stopped and watched. That was not always our experience at smaller events. Logistics operations people recognised the problem immediately. Several told us they had tried to use general-purpose automation tools and given up because the data model did not fit freight operations. That validation matters to us.

The harder part: we did 23 demo conversations over three days. Eleven of those turned into follow-up requests. Of those eleven, we have had meaningful second conversations with four. That conversion is lower than we expected given the quality of attention we got at the stand. We are being honest with ourselves about why. Running a fast, clear demo in English in a loud exhibition hall, for buyers who are often German-speaking and cautious, is a skill we are still building. The platform works. The story around it needs sharper delivery.

What we are doing about it: we have started working with a presentation coach who has experience with technical founders selling to European enterprise buyers. It is early and we will report back.

On the product side: the most consistent question from floor conversations was about integration with existing TMS platforms. Buyers do not want to replace their TMS. They want automation to sit alongside it. We heard this clearly enough that it has moved up our roadmap. More on that later in the year.

Overall: worth going. Worth going better prepared next time.

title: We Finished the Balogh Kert Online Shop Rebuild

The brief was clear: rebuild the shop so it works properly on phones, connect it to their inventory system so stock levels are accurate in real time and make the checkout process available in both Hungarian and Serbian.

We spent four months on the project. The main technical work was building a custom API connector between WooCommerce and the inventory software Balogh Kert uses internally — a local desktop application that exports data in a format that required some careful parsing. We also rebuilt the entire front end using a clean Vue.js theme that their team can update themselves without developer help.

The language side required more work than we expected. Their inventory system stores all product names in Serbian. We built a small translation layer where the client's staff can enter Hungarian equivalents directly inside the product editor. It is not automated — someone at Balogh Kert has to type the Hungarian name once per product — but it is simple enough that they actually use it.

The shop went live in April. In the first three weeks, mobile conversion was measurably better than their old figures. The client's owner, Tibor Balogh, told us the checkout no longer 'frightens people away,' which we are treating as a compliment.

title: What We Learned From a Bad Translation and a Lost Client
text:
Last year we lost a client over a translation error. We have not talked about it publicly until now, but we think it is worth being honest because the problem is more common than people admit.

The client ran a small online grocery in western Slovakia. We had integrated their WooCommerce shop with a local delivery provider and localised the checkout flow into Slovak. Part of that localisation used a machine translation service to handle the first pass of UI strings, with a plan for a human reviewer to catch anything strange before launch. That review step was done too quickly. A string that should have read 'delivery address' came out as something that a Slovak reader would understand as closer to 'shipping declaration.' It appeared on the final confirmation screen.

Several customers saw it, assumed they were signing something official and left. The client saw a spike in cart abandonment on the confirmation page, investigated and came to us. After a tense conversation, they asked for a partial refund of the integration fee. We gave it to them. They did not renew.

We have since changed our process. Machine translation is now only used for internal drafts. Every string that will appear in any user-facing screen goes through our translators in full before a build is signed off. Releases take longer. We charge slightly more for localisation work. Clients who ask why are told this story.

We are also looking at whether there is a better technical approach — some kind of automated check that flags strings that are technically translated but likely to confuse — before they even reach our translators. We have not found a tool that works well enough on short UI strings in Hungarian and Slovak. If you know of one, or if you work on this kind of problem, we would genuinely like to hear from you.

The lesson is not complicated: moving faster than your quality process can handle costs more than the time you saved.

title: What a Seismic Vulnerability Assessment Actually Involves — and Why Banks Are Asking for Them
text:
Over the past year we have had a noticeable increase in requests for seismic vulnerability assessments on buildings put up in the 1980s and 1990s. Almost every one of these requests comes not from the building owners themselves but from their banks or notaries, who are now routinely asking for this documentation before approving a mortgage or refinancing on older residential property.

We thought it was worth explaining what one of these assessments actually involves, because clients often assume it is a straightforward inspection that takes a day.

For an unreinforced masonry building of four storeys — a common type in Zrenjanin from that period — the process starts with a full architectural and structural survey. We walk every floor, measure wall thicknesses, check window and door openings, look at floor-to-wall connections, examine the roof structure and the foundation type where it is accessible. If original drawings exist we use them, but they are often incomplete or have been deviated from during construction. We photograph everything and record it systematically.

From the survey data we build a structural model of the building and assess it against the seismic hazard level applicable to this region under current regulations. We calculate whether the walls have sufficient area and continuity to resist lateral forces at each floor level, check connections between horizontal and vertical elements and identify any features that represent particular vulnerability: large unsupported wall panels, concentrated openings, soft-storey conditions.

The output is a written report that describes what we found, rates the overall vulnerability level and, where relevant, recommends specific interventions.

For a typical four-storey building this takes our senior engineer the better part of a working week. We currently have a backlog and our honest advice to anyone who may need one of these reports for a transaction is to request it early — at least six to eight weeks before your planned completion date.

If you have a building that might need this kind of assessment, contact us and we can give you an honest estimate of timing and cost.

title: What GrantFlow Does
text:
EU-funded projects involve a lot of paperwork. Most of it is repetitive, some of it is in multiple languages, and almost all of it has to be exactly right before you submit to the managing authority. GrantFlow is the platform we built to handle that part of the work.

Here is what it does in practice. Your team uploads financial reports, narrative reports, and supporting documents directly into the platform. If your project has partners in two or three countries, each partner uploads in their own language. GrantFlow then runs consistency checks across all of the uploaded documents — looking for mismatches between figures, missing mandatory fields, and budget lines that do not add up — and shows you a single list of issues to resolve before you submit.

Every change made inside the platform is recorded in a tamper-evident log. You can export the full history of a document as a PDF for your own records or to share with an auditor.

We currently support Serbian, Hungarian, Croatian, Slovak, and English. Our clients include NGOs running cross-border Interreg projects, municipalities managing structural fund allocations, and a small number of private companies that are partners in consortium projects.

Onboarding takes between one and three weeks depending on the size of your project portfolio. We import your existing data from Excel or from whatever system you were using before. After that, your team works directly in the platform and we handle updates and support.

If you want to see whether GrantFlow fits your situation, you can book a thirty-minute call with one of our implementation consultants. They have both managed EU-funded projects themselves, so the conversation will be practical.

title: Senior Backend Developer (Python / PostgreSQL)
text:
We are a twelve-person software company in Subotica building a compliance and reporting platform for EU-funded projects. We are looking for a backend developer to join the core product team.

What the role involves:
You will work on the server-side of GrantFlow — our main product. That means REST API development in Django REST Framework, database design and query optimisation in PostgreSQL, and contributing to the parts of the system that handle document ingestion, audit logging, and data export. We also have an NLP pipeline built in Python using spaCy that processes uploaded documents; you do not need to be a machine learning specialist, but you should be comfortable reading and modifying that kind of code.

Our current technical focus for the next two quarters is on improving the reliability of our multilingual consistency checker and on hardening our audit trail module to meet stricter compliance requirements from clients. Both of those projects will involve careful database work — schema design, indexing, and thinking about how data needs to be structured to be both queryable and auditable.

What we are looking for:
— At least four years working with Python in a production backend environment
— Solid PostgreSQL knowledge, including indexing, transactions, and writing complex queries
— Experience with Django or a similar framework
— Comfortable working with Docker; Kubernetes experience is useful but not required
— Some exposure to NLP libraries or text processing is a plus
— Good written English, because most of our client-facing documentation is in English

We work mostly remotely with two in-person days per month at our Subotica office. Salary range is 2,800–3,400 EUR gross per month depending on experience. Send a short message about what you have built and your CV to jobs@heliantus-digital.rs.

title: What we got wrong about multilingual consistency checking (and where we are now)
text:
When we built the first version of our cross-language consistency checker, we thought the hard part was translation. It is not. The hard part is that the same concept gets named differently depending on which managing authority wrote the application template.

Our checker compares budget line labels and figures across documents uploaded in different languages. The logic seems simple: if a line called X in one document corresponds to a line called Y in another, and the figures do not match, flag it. The problem is that X and Y might refer to the same thing even though they look completely different, and they might also look similar but mean something slightly different depending on the programme rules.

We built a bilingual glossary covering Hungarian and Croatian — the language pair that causes the most trouble for our current clients — and fine-tuned a spaCy similarity model on about 1,200 labelled pairs we collected from real project submissions. That combination gets us to around 70% precision. Not good enough. Clients started seeing warnings on reports that were actually correct, and once you see enough false alarms you stop trusting the tool. Several clients told us they had switched back to manual checks for the language-matching step specifically.

We ran a test last autumn where we raised the similarity threshold to reduce false positives. It worked for that, but we started missing real errors — cases where two lines genuinely did not match but the labels were similar enough to slide past the higher threshold.

We now have about 4,000 labelled pairs and a clearer picture of where the model fails. The cases it struggles with most are lines where the label is correct but the categorisation under EU budget headings differs between programmes. That is not a language problem — it is a programme-rules problem, and we are not sure a language model is the right tool for it.

We are currently looking at whether a rule-based layer on top of the similarity model — one that is aware of programme-specific budget structures — would get us past the ceiling we have hit. We do not have a solution yet, but we wanted to write this down honestly rather than pretend the checker works better than it does.
