title: About Aroma Natura — Subotica, Since 1975
text:
Aroma Natura a.d. was founded in 1975 as a processing cooperative in Subotica, in the northern part of Vojvodina. The original purpose was simple: take the lavender, chamomile and mint grown on the surrounding plain and turn them into something useful — oils, extracts and basic skin preparations for the domestic market.

Fifty years later the purpose has not changed much, but the scale has. We now employ 214 people across our production facility, distillation unit and offices in Subotica. Our products are stocked in pharmacy chains and health stores throughout Serbia and exported to Hungary, Austria and Romania. Our Austrian distribution partner, Kräuterweg GmbH, has carried our products for over a decade. In Hungary we work through Természet Bolt Kft., a Budapest-based distributor with strong regional reach.

Our formulation laboratory is led by Mirjana Vuković, who joined the company in 2005 and has overseen the development of more than sixty active SKUs. The lab team uses HPLC and GC-MS to verify raw material quality and track active compounds through every production batch.

We own and manage lavender plots near Palić and source chamomile from growers in Bačka Topola with whom we have long-standing purchase agreements. Knowing the origin of our raw materials is not a marketing point for us — it is how we keep the formulations consistent from year to year.

We are currently working toward launching a mineral sunscreen line and continuing to improve the efficiency of our extraction processes. If you are a distributor, a cosmetic ingredient buyer or a research institution interested in working with us, the contact form below reaches our business development manager, Dragan Šević, directly.

title: Job Opening: Cosmetic Formulation Chemist (Stability and Preservation Focus)
text:
Aroma Natura a.d., Subotica — full-time, on-site

We are looking for a formulation chemist to join our laboratory team in Subotica. The role sits within our eight-person formulation and quality group and reports to head formulator Mirjana Vuković.

The main focus of the role is our ongoing stability programme. We run accelerated and real-time stability studies in-house using ICH zone II and zone IV protocols, and we need someone who can take ownership of the study design, data interpretation and formulation adjustment cycle. Specifically, we are working to extend the shelf life of several water-in-oil emulsion products without exceeding EU Cosmetics Regulation preservative limits or altering fragrance profiles. Experience with alternative preservation strategies — water activity management, hurdle approaches, ferment-derived systems — is directly relevant.

Day-to-day tasks include:
— Designing and running stability chamber studies and reading results against specification
— Proposing and testing reformulation options for out-of-specification batches
— Supporting CPNP documentation and EU safety assessment dossiers
— Working with the GC-MS and HPLC operators to track active compound levels across product life
— Coordinating with the production floor on scale-up of approved reformulations

What we are looking for:
— Degree in chemistry, pharmacy or a related field
— At least three years of practical formulation or stability work in a cosmetics or pharmaceutical environment
— Familiarity with EU Cosmetics Regulation (EC 1223/2009), including preservative annexes
— Comfortable working in Serbian; working knowledge of English for reading technical literature

What we offer:
— Permanent contract, competitive salary for the region
— Access to a well-equipped laboratory and a stable production environment
— Real influence on product development decisions

Please send CV and a short cover note to posao@aromanatura.rs. Applications open until the position is filled.

title: Job Opening: Process Technologist — Extraction and Distillation
text:
Aroma Natura a.d., Subotica — full-time, on-site

We are adding a process technologist to our production team with a specific focus on our steam distillation and extraction operations. This is a practical, plant-floor role for someone who wants to improve how things actually work rather than only document them.

Context: our distillation facility uses a 500-litre batch steam vessel that has been in operation since the 1980s. It runs reliably, but we have not done a rigorous process study on it in decades. We know from external benchmarks that our essential oil yields for lavender and chamomile are below what comparable producers achieve, and we believe the gap is in raw material preparation and distillation time-temperature profiles rather than in the vessel itself — but we have not proven that yet.

The successful candidate will:
— Design and execute a structured process improvement study on the distillation line, varying pre-treatment parameters (moisture content, particle reduction, packing method) and distillation profiles
— Use our existing GC-MS data and batch records as the starting dataset
— Work with the lab team to correlate process changes with oil yield and composition outcomes
— Identify whether equipment modification is warranted and prepare a technical brief for management if so
— Over time, take on day-to-day oversight of the extraction line

Background we are looking for:
— Degree in chemical engineering, biotechnology or food technology
— Experience with extraction or distillation processes at industrial or semi-industrial scale
— Ability to design simple experiments and analyse results without needing external support for the basics
— Fluency in Serbian; English reading ability

This is not a supervisory role to start, but there is a clear path for someone who delivers results. Salary is negotiable depending on experience. Send applications to posao@aromanatura.rs with the subject line 'Proces tehnolog — destilacija'.

title: What We Learned at Vivaness 2024 (and One Thing That Surprised Us)
text:
Three of us from Aroma Natura — Mirjana Vuković from the lab, Dragan Šević from business development and our packaging coordinator Ivana Horváth — attended Vivaness in Nuremberg in February. Vivaness is the natural cosmetics trade show that runs alongside BioFach, and for us it is primarily a chance to see what direction the category is moving and to have direct conversations with European buyers we would otherwise only reach by email.

A few observations worth writing down:

Preservative-free claims are still growing but buyers are getting more sceptical. Several German buyers we spoke with said they have had problems with products claiming no preservatives that failed stability at the retailer level. They are now asking harder questions about validated shelf life — real-time data, not just accelerated — before listing a new supplier. For us this was both a warning and a window. If we can demonstrate a clean formula with genuinely verified 24-month stability, that is a stronger commercial argument than it was three years ago.

Mineral sunscreen is crowded but not commoditised. We showed concept packaging for our SPF 30 and SPF 50 zinc oxide formulas to four buyers. Three of them asked about SPF validation certificates immediately. This confirmed what we already knew: the validation step is not optional, and the cost of not having it is lost listings. We came back more motivated to resolve the testing question than when we left.

The surprising part: a Polish contract manufacturer we spoke with at a side event mentioned they had recently invested in in-vitro SPF testing equipment — the spectrophotometric setup for ISO 24443 — and were offering it to smaller brands on a service basis at roughly a third of what the Budapest lab quoted us. We have followed up and are waiting to hear whether their accreditation covers EU market claims. If it does, this changes our timeline considerably.

Overall the trip was worthwhile. We came back with two qualified leads for the sunscreen line and a clearer picture of what Central European buyers actually need from a natural cosmetics supplier our size.

title: Aroma Natura Begins Export to Romanian Market Through New Distribution Agreement
text:
Aroma Natura a.d. has signed a distribution agreement with Floralis Import SRL, a Cluj-Napoca based natural product distributor, covering six SKUs from our lavender and chamomile skincare range. Shipments are scheduled to begin in June 2024, with products entering pharmacy and health store channels in Transylvania and Bucharest.

The agreement follows two years of conversations that began at the Naturalex trade fair in Vienna in 2022, where our export manager Jelena Bošnjak met Floralis founder Adrian Mureșan. A trial shipment of 800 units in late 2023 sold through without returns, which gave both sides confidence to formalise the relationship.

The six products covered by the initial agreement are our 50 ml Intensive Lavender Night Cream, 100 ml Chamomile Daily Fluid, three essential oil singles (lavender, chamomile and peppermint) and our Herbal Steam Blend for home inhalation. Floralis will handle Romanian-language labelling compliance and local regulatory notification.

Dragan Šević, our business development manager, noted that the Romanian market represents our third export destination alongside Hungary and Austria and that the company intends to add further SKUs to the agreement in 2025 if initial sell-through data is positive.

We see Romania as a natural fit. The interest in plant-based skincare is strong there, the distance is manageable for our logistics, and Floralis has the kind of focused approach to distribution that works well with a producer our size. We are not trying to be in every market — we are trying to be in the right ones and do it properly.

Full details of the agreement are not disclosed.

title: What Activora Does — and Who It Is For
text:
Activora is a platform for amateur football clubs that want to reduce training-related injuries without hiring a full-time analyst or buying expensive wearable hardware.

Here is how it works. Players install the Activora app on their Android or iOS phone and carry it in a vest pocket or shorts pocket during training. The app records movement data passively — players do not need to do anything beyond starting a session. After training ends, the data syncs to our servers and the coach sees an updated dashboard within a few minutes.

The dashboard shows each player's training load for that session alongside a four-week history. Players whose load has spiked relative to their recent baseline appear flagged in the weekly summary. The coach does not need to understand the maths behind the flag. They just need to know: this player is carrying more stress than usual this week, consider adjusting their role in the next session.

We also send a Monday morning report by email — a single page covering the whole squad — for coaches who prefer not to log into a dashboard regularly.

Who we work with: we currently serve fourteen clubs in Vojvodina and Central Serbia, ranging from fourth-division sides with forty registered players to smaller community clubs running one senior team and a junior section. Most of our coaches are volunteers or receive a small stipend. They do not have sports science backgrounds. We built everything with that in mind.

What we do not do: we do not replace a physiotherapist. We do not diagnose injuries. We surface patterns in data and translate them into plain language so coaches can make better decisions. If your club already has a physio, we have a separate portal that gives them read access to the same data in a more detailed view.

If you run a regional football club in Serbia or the surrounding countries and want to try the platform, contact us through the form below. The first three months are free for clubs with fewer than fifty registered players.

title: Fourteen Clubs, 340 Players — Where We Are After Two Seasons
text:
When we launched our first pilot in August 2022 we had three clubs, forty-one players, and a model that we knew was imperfect but thought was good enough to start learning from. Two seasons later we have fourteen clubs and 340 players actively using the platform, and we have learned a lot — some of it encouraging, some of it humbling.

The encouraging part: coaches who stay with the platform past the first month use it consistently. Our weekly report emails have an open rate above 70 percent among coaches who are still active at the 60-day mark. Several coaches have told us they would not go back to managing training load by feel alone. One coach at a fourth-division club in Vojvodina — a man who has been coaching for over twenty years — told our customer team in January that last season was the first in five years where he did not lose a player to a muscle tear before Christmas. We cannot claim credit for that with certainty, but we will take the kind words.

The humbling part: our 30-day retention among coaches over 40 is 19 percent. We have a data model that was trained on athletes in a different country playing a different level of football. We have a pipeline that is going to struggle in August if we do not fix it before then.

We are not writing this to perform transparency. We are writing it because the people who might be able to help us with those problems are more likely to take us seriously if they know we have looked at them clearly.

We are at the NTP Novi Sad this spring and open to conversations. If you work on movement analysis, dashboard usability, or high-throughput data pipelines and any of the above sounds interesting, reach out.

title: Senior Backend Engineer — Real-Time Data Pipeline
text:
Activora Sport d.o.o. is looking for a senior backend engineer to take ownership of the real-time data pipeline that sits at the centre of our platform.

We collect accelerometer and gyroscope events from players' phones during training sessions, stream them through an MQTT broker, process them in Python, and store them in a TimescaleDB instance running on PostgreSQL. On a quiet evening one or two clubs are active at the same time. In August, when the new season starts, we expect that to be twelve to fifteen clubs simultaneously. The current pipeline is not ready for that and we know it.

What you will work on in the first six months:
— Audit and rework the ingestion layer so we stop dropping events under concurrent load
— Move time-critical processing out of the request cycle and into a proper async worker setup
— Improve our TimescaleDB schema and query patterns so dashboard queries stay fast as the dataset grows
— Help us put basic observability in place so we know when something is degrading before a coach reports it

What we are looking for:
— Solid Python backend experience, ideally with FastAPI or a similar framework
— Direct experience with either MQTT or another real-time message streaming system
— Comfortable working with PostgreSQL under write-heavy conditions
— TimescaleDB or general time-series database experience is a strong advantage
— You do not need a sports background. You do need to be able to explain a technical trade-off to a non-technical co-founder without making them feel stupid.

Practical details:
This is a full-time role based in Zrenjanin with flexibility for partial remote work. Our current salary band for this position is up to 2,200 euros net per month. We are aware this is below what some companies pay and we are not going to pretend otherwise. If that is a dealbreaker we understand. If you are interested in early-stage equity participation or want to discuss a part-time arrangement, we are open to that conversation.

Send a CV and two or three paragraphs about a pipeline problem you have solved to posao@activora.rs.

title: Senior Backend Engineer — Second Hire, Data Pipeline and API
text:
We are posting this separately because we are looking for two people and the profiles are slightly different.

The first hire (see the other listing) is focused on the ingestion and streaming layer. This role sits closer to the API and the data model — the layer that the mobile app talks to, the layer that feeds the dashboard, and the layer that will eventually serve third-party integrations if we build them.

Current state: our FastAPI backend handles player registration, session management, raw data storage, and computed metric endpoints. It works well enough today. It was not designed for the query volume we will see at the start of next season, and it was not designed by someone who knew we would eventually want to expose data to physiotherapists, club administrators, and potentially federation officials through different permission levels.

What you will work on:
— Review and rework the API layer for performance and maintainability
— Design a permission and role model that goes beyond our current coach/admin split
— Work with the mobile team to agree on a versioning strategy so we can update the app and backend independently
— Help us think through what a simple integration API would look like for clubs that want to pull data into their own tools

Stack: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB, Docker, deployed on self-hosted VPS infrastructure in Novi Sad.

We are a team of nine. There is no separate QA team, no dedicated DevOps function, and no project manager. Everyone does some of everything. If that sounds exhausting, this is probably not the right fit. If it sounds like a chance to have real influence on how a product is built from an early stage, read on.

title: Why We Stopped Calling It a Risk Score
text:
For the first year of the product, our dashboard showed each player a number between 0 and 100 labelled Risk Score. The number came from our injury-risk model. It was colour-coded: green below 40, yellow between 40 and 70, red above 70.

We thought this was clear. It was not clear.

In user interviews conducted in late 2023 and early 2024, we asked coaches what they did when they saw a red score. Common answers: they ignored it because it seemed to contradict what they could see on the pitch. They worried it meant something was already wrong with the player. A few said they had started to distrust the whole dashboard because the scores felt random.

The number was not random. But it was abstract in a way that made it feel random to someone who had not built it.

We have since replaced the score with a plain-language line at the top of each player's weekly card. Something like: Marko has done significantly more running this week than his average over the past month. Consider reducing high-intensity work in Thursday's session. We removed the 0–100 scale entirely from the main view.

Early feedback is better. Coaches say they feel like the app is talking to them rather than reporting a measurement they do not understand.

This did not require any change to the underlying model. It required us to stop designing for ourselves and start designing for the person standing on the edge of a training pitch in November.

We are still working on retention. But changing the language was the right first step and we should have done it earlier. If you work on how people understand data-driven recommendations and you have thoughts on where we go from here, we are genuinely interested in talking.

title: What We Make and How We Work
text:
Košava Tekstil has been making workwear in Zrenjanin since 1991. We produce protective and industrial clothing for clients who need consistent quality, reliable delivery, and paperwork that holds up when an inspector walks through their facility.

Our production covers two sewing lines with a combined daily output of around 350 finished garments, plus an in-house dyeing unit that handles colour matching and finishing for most of our standard product range. Having dyeing under the same roof means we control colour consistency batch to batch without depending on an external supplier's schedule.

Our main product categories are:

— Flame-retardant jackets and trousers tested to EN ISO 11612, used in welding, petrochemical, and utility environments.
— High-visibility sets tested to EN ISO 20471, supplied to logistics and construction clients.
— Chemical-splash coveralls for lighter industrial exposure.
— Standard industrial workwear in custom colours and configurations.

We also take small contract dyeing jobs from other garment producers in the region when our unit capacity allows.

Our clients are mostly mid-size industrial companies in Serbia and Romania. They come to us because we can produce a 200-piece order with a two-week lead time and deliver the test reports and declaration of conformity alongside the goods. We are not set up for fashion retail or consumer orders.

The company is run by the Vujanović family. Nikola Vujanović handles commercial and administrative direction; Jelena Vujanović-Marić manages production day to day. Most of our senior seamstresses and technicians have been with us for more than ten years.

title: What We Learned from Our First EXPO Zaštita Appearance
text:
In early March we attended EXPO Zaštita, the regional occupational safety and PPE trade fair held in Belgrade, for the first time as an exhibitor. We had a stand of 12 square metres, a rack of product samples, and our commercial manager Svetlana Đorđić on-site for both days.

We went with a specific goal: to meet purchasing managers from industrial companies in Serbia and the Western Balkans who buy certified PPE regularly and are looking for a local manufacturer rather than an import distributor.

The two days produced 34 documented conversations with potential clients, of which 11 we would call serious — meaning the person we spoke with had direct responsibility for PPE procurement and asked for a quote or a sample set. Three of those were from companies we had not previously contacted at all.

We also had several conversations that were useful in a different way. Three separate visitors — all of them purchasing staff from subsidiaries of German and Austrian manufacturing groups operating in Serbia — asked us the same question: do your products carry CE marking under EU PPE Regulation 2016/425, and can you supply the same products to our German parent facilities? In all three cases the answer was no, not yet. We gave them our contact details and were honest about where we stand.

Those three conversations have pushed this question up our priority list. We know our EN test results are solid. The gap is the regulatory paperwork and the notified body route for EU market access, which we have not yet found a practical way into.

The fair also reminded us that our printed catalogue is out of date — it still shows an older collar construction on the EN ISO 11612 jacket that we changed 18 months ago. We will have a corrected version ready before the next event.

Overall the trip cost us around €1,800 including stand rental, travel, and materials. Based on the conversations we had, we think it was worthwhile. We plan to return next year with more prepared documentation on our certification status.

title: First repeat order from Hamburg formulator confirms commercial interest
text:
In November 2023 AlgaLux received a second purchase order from NordVital Supplements GmbH, a Hamburg-based nutraceutical formulator we began supplying on a trial basis in June of the same year.

The first order — five kilograms of phycocyanin powder — was conditional on NordVital's internal quality assessment. Their team ran their own spectrophotometric purity check and ICP-MS heavy-metal screen on the batch. The batch passed on metal content. Purity came back at 71%, which NordVital accepted for the trial but noted was below what they would want for a long-term supply relationship.

The November order was for eight kilograms at the same specification. NordVital's purchasing contact, a woman we deal with under the name K. Brandt, confirmed in writing that they remain interested in scaling the relationship if we can demonstrate consistent 95%+ purity. She referenced the upcoming EU revision to maximum levels for certain contaminants in food supplements and suggested that their quality team would reassess all suppliers in early 2025.

For us this is meaningful for two reasons. First, it confirms there is a real buyer willing to pay a reasonable price for Serbian-produced phycocyanin if we can meet the purity threshold. Second, it gives us a concrete deadline: we need a validated higher-purity protocol before NordVital's 2025 supplier review.

We are now treating phycocyanin purification as our primary technical priority for the first half of 2024. We have logged the batch data from both orders and are working through a set of protocol variants internally. If there are people or organisations in the Novi Sad area with relevant separation expertise who want to discuss this, we are open to that conversation.

title: What We Do — AlgaLux Biotech
text:
AlgaLux Biotech grows microalgae and extracts the pigments inside them. That is the short version.

The longer version: we operate a cultivation system at NTP Novi Sad that combines an outdoor open raceway pond with two indoor photobioreactors. The outdoor pond handles the volume work during spring, summer and early autumn. The indoor tanks keep production running in winter and give us a cleaner environment for batches destined for cosmetics customers with tighter contamination specs.

Our two main outputs are phycocyanin powder and astaxanthin oleoresin.

Phycocyanin is the blue pigment that comes from Spirulina. We grow Spirulina platensis, harvest it, break the cells open, and run the extract through chromatography columns to concentrate the pigment. The result is a dry powder that food and supplement makers use as a natural blue colourant or as an antioxidant ingredient. Every batch comes with a certificate of analysis that includes pigment purity by spectrophotometry and heavy-metal content by ICP-MS.

Astaxanthin is the deep-red carotenoid from Haematococcus pluvialis. We produce it as an oleoresin — the pigment suspended in a carrier oil — which is the form cosmetics formulators prefer for incorporation into creams and serums.

We also offer a cultivation service for clients who want biomass grown to a specific specification: particular strains, defined nutrient protocols or documented growth conditions for regulatory submissions. And we run a standalone certificate-of-analysis service — if you buy microalgae biomass from another supplier and want independent heavy-metal and pigment testing, we can do that.

All our work is documented under an ISO 22000-aligned quality system. We do not certify products on behalf of clients, but our batch records are formatted to support clients' own regulatory submissions in the EU market.

If you want to discuss a trial order or a testing request, contact Milena Vukić at the address below.

title: What we learned from a winter of LED lighting data
text:
We installed supplemental LED bars over the raceway pond in October 2022. The idea was straightforward: Spirulina wants light, winter gives us less of it, so add light artificially and keep productivity up.

The result was more complicated than that.

Over the 2022–2023 winter we tracked three things three times a day: pond water temperature, PAR (photosynthetically active radiation) at the surface, and optical density as a proxy for cell density. We ran the LEDs — a mix of 660 nm red and 440 nm blue bars — for 14 hours a day. Cell density did improve compared to the previous winter without supplemental light: roughly 15% higher average OD over the period.

But the electricity bill for October through March was approximately €2,100. Over the same period the extra biomass we harvested translated to pigment revenue of around €2,400 at the prices we were charging at the time. After extraction costs, that net improvement was essentially zero. We did the same experiment in the 2023–2024 winter with a slightly revised lighting schedule and got a similar result.

The pattern in the data is interesting, though. The OD response to LED hours was much weaker in January and February than in October and November, even when we held lighting hours constant. Water temperature in January was consistently 3–5 °C lower than in November. Our working interpretation is that below about 10 °C the cells slow down enough that extra photons do not translate into extra growth — you are just lighting a cold, slow culture.

We now have 18 months of three-times-daily temperature, PAR and OD readings in a spreadsheet. We are not data scientists, and we have not done anything more sophisticated than correlation plots with those numbers. There is probably a better model in there — something that would let us predict on a given day whether it is worth running the LEDs at all given the forecast temperature. If anyone is interested in working with that dataset, we are happy to share it.

title: Downstream Process Technician (part-time, on-site, Novi Sad)
text:
AlgaLux Biotech is looking for a part-time downstream process technician to support extraction and purification work at our NTP Novi Sad facility. This is a hands-on lab and production role.

What the work involves:
— Operating and cleaning ion-exchange and size-exclusion chromatography systems
— Running HPLC analysis to quantify pigment fractions after each purification step
— Preparing buffers, regenerating columns and keeping consumables stocked

We are specifically trying to improve our phycocyanin purification protocol. A lot of the immediate work will involve testing variants in precipitation and column sequencing. You will be doing real process development alongside routine production — not just washing glassware.

What we need from you:

title: What RouteWise Does
text:

title: Why Re-optimising Mid-Route Is Harder Than It Sounds
text:
We get asked fairly often why RouteWise Planner does not just update routes instantly when a new order comes in during the day. The honest answer is that it does update — it just does not always do it fast enough for same-day delivery, and we want to explain why, because it is not a simple fix.

The problem we solve when planning routes is a variant of the vehicle routing problem with time windows. It is well-studied in operations research and it is NP-hard, which means there is no known algorithm that always finds the perfect answer in reasonable time for large instances. What good solvers do is search intelligently and stop when they have something good enough. The trade-off is always between time spent searching and quality of the result.

For overnight planning, you have hours. For same-day planning with orders arriving throughout the day, you might have fifteen minutes between a new batch arriving and needing to redirect a driver who is already at a stop. If you just re-run the full solver from scratch, the time limit you can afford produces a noticeably worse route than the overnight run.

We have tried warm-starting — giving the solver the current solution as a starting point — and it helps, but not as much as we would like when the order set has changed significantly. We have tried decomposing the fleet into smaller sub-problems, which speeds things up but sometimes creates weird zone boundaries that drivers notice.

What we have not yet done is explore approaches that treat the re-planning problem differently from the initial planning problem — methods that specifically focus on making small, local repairs to an existing plan rather than reconsidering everything. That is the direction we are heading in. We will write more about it once we have results worth sharing.

If this is a problem your team works on, we are interested in talking.

title: How PaketBus Works — Services and Coverage
text:
If you need to send a parcel from Subotica to Sombor, Kikinda, Novi Kneževac, Kanjiža, or any of the other eleven towns on our network, the idea is simple: your parcel travels on a bus that is already going there. We have co-loading agreements with bus operators running scheduled intercity routes, and we use the luggage space that would otherwise go empty. This keeps our costs lower than a dedicated courier van, and we pass that saving on to you.

Here is how a standard shipment works. You book online or call our Subotica office before 18:00. We collect the parcel from your address or you drop it at one of our partner bus-station points. That evening our team assigns it to the appropriate departure. By the next morning it is at the destination bus station, where our local liaison hands it to the recipient or holds it for pickup.

We handle parcels up to 30 kg and 80 cm on the longest side. We are not the right choice for same-day delivery or for very fragile goods that need special handling — we are honest about that. We are the right choice if you ship regularly on our routes and want a reliable, lower-cost option.

title: What We Learned from a Year of Tracking Our Reflex Review Flags
text:
Every laboratory that runs automated analysers knows the situation: the middleware flags a result, a technician reviews it, and nothing changes. The result goes out the same as it came in. Multiply that by dozens of samples a day and you have a meaningful portion of your team's time going into reviews that, in retrospect, were not necessary.

We started keeping structured records of our reflex flag outcomes about a year ago. Before that, flags were tracked for quality purposes but the outcome of each review — whether the result was modified, repeated, or sent unchanged — was not systematically recorded. We made a simple change to our technician workflow to capture that outcome in a dedicated field in Deltasoft.

After twelve months of data, the picture is fairly clear. We flag around 60 samples per working day. For roughly half of those, the technician review results in no change to the reported value and no repeat test. The flag was generated by a rule that was doing its job as written, but the rule itself may not have been designed for the population of samples we actually see.

The rules we use were set up when we first configured the current middleware, and while they have been adjusted occasionally, they have never been looked at as a whole against real outcome data.

We are not claiming this is a unique problem — we know from conversations at trade events that many regional laboratories are in a similar position. What we think is different for us is that we now have the data to do something about it. A year of flags and outcomes, linked to patient demographics and test type, is a reasonable starting point for anyone who wants to look at where the rules are calibrated too broadly.

We are not sure yet what the right approach is: revised static thresholds, a more structured decision tree, or something that uses the historical data more directly. If you have worked on this kind of problem in a clinical laboratory setting, we would be glad to hear from you.

title: What We Do — Kriptolog a.d.
text:
Kriptolog builds the hardware and software that organisations use to manage cryptographic keys, issue digital certificates, and verify identities across networks. We have been doing this since 1997, which means we have seen what holds up over time and what does not.

Our flagship hardware product is the KL-HSM line. These are tamper-resistant modules that generate, store, and use cryptographic keys without ever exposing the key material to the host system. The KL-300 is rack-mounted and suited to data-centre PKI roots and subordinate CAs. The KL-500 is a higher-throughput model built for payment processors and national identity infrastructure. Both run firmware we write and maintain ourselves.

Alongside the hardware, we develop and operate CertiCore, our PKI management platform. CertiCore handles the full certificate lifecycle: issuance, renewal, suspension, and revocation. title: What EAL4+ Actually Requires — A Note from Our Hardware Team
text:
We have been working toward Common Criteria EAL4+ certification for the KL-500 for the better part of two years. People sometimes ask what the process involves, so here is an honest account from the people doing the work.

EAL4+ is an assurance level that requires both a thorough design documentation package and physical testing of the product. For an HSM, the physical side is the harder part. The enclosure must demonstrate tamper evidence — meaning that any attempt to open or probe the device leaves a visible mark — and it must do so reliably across the operating conditions the product is rated for.

For us, the critical test is thermal cycling. Our enclosure uses an epoxy potting compound that surrounds the PCB and key storage components. It has to remain intact — no cracks, no delamination — across hundreds of temperature cycles between -10°C and 60°C. That sounds straightforward until you realise that the PCB, the metallic fasteners, and the epoxy all expand and contract at different rates. Managing those differences is a materials problem as much as an engineering problem.

We have been running test samples and adjusting the process since late 2022. We have learned a great deal about what does not work. We are currently in contact with a polymer testing laboratory to get a more precise picture of the thermal expansion mismatch at the points where we see cracking.

Certification timelines are real constraints. Our pre-evaluation agreement sets a date for physical testing, and we are not in a position to slip it by much. If you work in materials engineering or polymer testing and have dealt with similar enclosure problems, we are genuinely interested in talking.

The certification, once achieved, is a prerequisite for the government procurement frameworks we are targeting in Central Europe. It is not bureaucratic box-ticking for us — it is the entry ticket to the market segment we are building toward.

title: CropAir Completes Successful Season with Backa Cooperative
text: After a challenging start in spring—poor fungicide coverage in two early flights—CropAir and our long-term client Bačka Farming Cooperative worked together to redesign our application protocol for the 2023 season. By adjusting flight altitude, reducing airspeed in windy conditions, and increasing nozzle overlap, we achieved an average dose deposit of 87% across 15 subsequent missions, resulting in a 22% reduction in fungal disease pressure compared to the cooperative's five-year average. The cooperative's yields on treated fields were 8.2 tonnes per hectare for wheat (up from 7.4 in 2022) and 58 tonnes per hectare for sugar beet (their best result in seven years). "The precision application saved us approximately 4,200 EUR in prevented yield loss and unnecessary fungicide overuse," said farm manager Radojčić. CropAir's CEO Željko Nikolić noted that the experience has prompted us to invest in wind-adaptive flight control and spray-physics research for the 2024 season.

title: Services
text: CropAir offers three integrated services: drone supply, agronomic advisory, and application execution. We lease our spraying drones on a seasonal basis (April–October) along with pilot deployment to your fields. Before the season starts, our agronomists visit your farm to collect soil samples, review your yield maps from previous years, and satellite data. Using this information, we create a prescription map that specifies the fungicide or herbicide dose at each location—higher rates in areas prone to disease, lower rates where the crop is already healthy or soil conditions are unfavourable. On application day, our pilots follow the prescription map, logging every flight for compliance and performance review. We report dose applied, area covered, and weather conditions for each mission. Our clients are mostly grain and sugar-beet farms between 500 and 2000 hectares in Vojvodina and southern Hungary. The service costs depend on farm size and number of application flights; typical seasonal contracts range from 8,000 to 45,000 EUR. We guarantee in writing that application dose will fall within 10% of prescription (in calm wind conditions), and we reimburse the fungicide cost if we miss that target. title: Why Manual Prescription Maps Are Slowing Us Down—and What We Need to Change
text: Three years ago, our prescription mapping process was a luxury: one agronomist, three days per farm, combining experience and intuition with soil boring data and yield maps. We completed 12 farms per season and felt we were delivering value. Today we have 40 clients and a waiting list of 30 more. Our 14 agronomists are exhausted, and we are turning away revenue because we cannot expand capacity. Here is the problem: most of the work is repetitive data assembly and overlay. An agronomist spends one day collecting soil samples and GPS points. They spend another day in the office manually opening shapefiles, aligning yield maps with field boundaries, checking for gaps, and sketching decision rules (e.g., 'higher dose in low-yield areas with high soil phosphorus'). Only on the third day do they apply actual agronomic judgment. We have the data (four years of field-specific yield, soil, and weather history for each client). We have the rules (written down and consistent). What we lack is a system that can do the assembly and flagging in minutes, leaving the agronomist to review, refine, and sign off. A university partner with expertise in spatial analysis and agricultural decision systems could help us design and validate this workflow. The outcome would be a tool that reduces per-farm mapping time from three days to one, unlocking capacity for 20–30 additional clients without hiring more staff. We believe this is achievable and urgent.

title: ReVita Water commissions new MBR system at Zlatna Livada dairy cooperative
text:
ReVita Water completed commissioning of a new MBR wastewater treatment unit at the Zlatna Livada dairy cooperative near Temerin last month. The installation replaces an ageing aerated lagoon system that had been causing discharge permit issues for the cooperative during high-production periods.

The new unit is sized for a peak flow of 180 cubic metres per day and handles the cooperative's combined process wastewater — wash water, whey spills, and CIP rinse streams — before discharge to the municipal sewer. Zlatna Livada had struggled with COD spikes during summer production peaks, and the lagoon offered no consistent way to manage them.

Our process engineer Milena Đorđević led the design work, which started with a six-week sampling campaign to characterise the actual waste loading across different production shifts. The unit includes a fine-screen pre-treatment stage, an anoxic selector tank to manage filamentous growth, and two submerged hollow-fibre membrane modules.

Zlatna Livada operations manager Branislav Horvat said the plant had been dealing with permit non-compliance notices for two consecutive years and needed a reliable fix rather than another temporary measure. The system passed its performance test in January and is now operating under a three-year service contract.

This is the third dairy-sector installation ReVita Water has delivered since 2020. Dairy wastewater presents specific challenges — high fat and protein concentrations — and each installation has added to our understanding of how MBR systems perform in that environment. We are currently analysing operational data across all three sites to improve our membrane cleaning protocols.

title: Why our dairy MBR membranes foul faster in summer — what we know so far
text:
We have been tracking membrane fouling rates at our dairy plant installations for three years now, and one pattern keeps coming up: fouling is consistently worse in summer, regardless of which plant we look at. Cleaning intervals that hold at ten to twelve days in winter shrink to five to seven days by July. This costs our clients money — more chemical use, more downtime — and it costs us time in additional service visits.

We want to write honestly about where we are with this problem, because we think transparency is more useful than pretending we have it solved.

What our data shows: transmembrane pressure rises faster from June through August across all three dairy sites. The rate correlates loosely with ambient temperature, but not perfectly. One site shows a stronger seasonal signal than the others despite similar production volumes, which suggests the local waste composition might differ.

What we have tried: adjusting aeration intensity to increase scouring of the membrane surface, modifying sludge retention time to change the biology, and tweaking the CIP chemical concentrations. None of these has reliably extended the cleaning interval.

What we think is happening — but cannot confirm: dairy wastewater contains fats and proteins that may behave differently at higher temperatures, either forming a gel layer more readily or changing how the biological community breaks them down. We do not currently have the equipment to characterise the foulant layer in detail.

What we would need to confirm this: proper foulant characterisation — something like autopsy analysis of fouled membrane samples — combined with biological activity measurements at different temperatures. This is outside what our current lab setup can do.

If you work in this area and have thoughts, we are genuinely interested in talking. Contact us at info@revitawater.rs.

title: About Bela Ruža Kozmetika — Handmade Skin Care from Zrenjanin
text:
Bela Ruža Kozmetika started the way most small things start: quietly, at home, out of necessity. In 2008, Dragana Vuković was looking for a soap her youngest daughter could use without the rashes that commercial brands kept causing. She read, she tested, she made mistakes, and eventually she had a bar of soap that worked. Neighbours asked for one. Then their neighbours did. By 2010 she had a regular table at the Saturday market in Zrenjanin and a name — Bela Ruža, the white rose, because the first soap she ever sold was scented with rose water from her mother's garden.

Today we are six people. Dragana runs production and sourcing. Her husband Goran manages deliveries and the van. Their daughter Milica joined us in 2023 and handles quality checks and the webshop. Tatjana Pešić, who has been with us since 2015, leads the soap-pouring shifts. Bojana Ilić and Nenad Crnjak round out the team, taking care of packaging and market days.

We make three product lines. Our soaps are cold-process, using oils we buy from Vojvodina producers wherever we can. Our lip balms use beeswax from Zoran Đorđević's hives in Melenci, about thirty kilometres away. Our body butters are blended by hand in small runs so we can check consistency before anything is jarred. Nothing is made in advance of demand by more than two weeks.

We sell at the Saturday market in Zrenjanin, through fourteen independent stores across Vojvodina, and through our webshop at belaruza-kozmetika.rs. We do not sell through large retail chains and we have no plans to. We would rather make fewer things carefully than more things quickly.

If you have a question about ingredients or want to know whether a product suits a particular skin type, write to us. Dragana usually replies herself.

title: What Soda Ash Actually Is and Why We Cannot Seem to Stop It
text:
If you have ever ordered soap from us and found a white powdery layer on the outside of the bar, we want to explain what that is and why it sometimes happens, even though we know it does not look great.

The white coating is called soda ash. It forms when sodium carbonate — a byproduct of the saponification process — migrates to the surface of the soap before the outer layer has finished reacting. It is not mould, it is not a sign that the soap is wrong, and it washes off with the first use. On skin, the soap underneath performs exactly as it should. But we understand that when you pay for something handmade, you want it to look right, and a bar covered in white powder does not look right.

We have been dealing with this for as long as we have been making soap. Some batches come out clean. Others, especially in winter when our workroom is colder, come out with fifteen percent or more of bars showing the problem. We have tried covering the moulds immediately after pour, spraying the tops with isopropyl alcohol, adding sodium lactate to the water phase, and adjusting our superfat percentage. Nothing has worked reliably across all conditions.

Bars that develop soda ash do not go to waste — we rebatch them, which means chopping them up, reheating and remoulding. The resulting soap is fine. But the process takes time that we could spend on other things.

We are currently looking into whether the temperature variation in our workroom is the main factor, or whether it is something in our water or lye ratio. If you have experience with cold-process production and have solved this problem, we would genuinely like to hear from you. Write to milica@belaruza-kozmetika.rs.

In the meantime, if a bar arrives with a white surface, please know it is cosmetic only. Rinse it once and it is gone.

title: What We Learned Losing a Whole Spring Season
text:
This is not a post we are happy to write, but we think it is worth writing honestly.

In early February 2023 we submitted our annual renewal for the permit to operate guided tours on our Deliblato Sands spring route. We submitted on time, with the same documentation package that had been accepted for the previous four years. In late February we received a request for a supplementary environmental impact assessment — a document we had never been asked for before and that we could not find a published template for anywhere.

We spent March trying to understand what exactly was needed, who to ask, and whether the request was based on a regulation change or a new interpretation of an existing rule. We produced a document in April. It was returned with comments in early May. We resubmitted. The permit was issued on 28 May.

By then, the spring migration season — the main reason international birdwatchers book that trail — was over. We cancelled bookings for six agency partners. We refunded approximately €34,000. We also lost the goodwill cost, which is harder to measure.

We are not writing this to complain about the inspectorate. The people we dealt with were doing their jobs. The problem is structural: requirements change without clear public notice, the process has no predictable timeline, and small operators like us have no early-warning system.

What we are doing differently in 2024: we submitted all three permit renewals in October, two months earlier than before. We have logged every document request we have ever received since 2015 and we are trying to use that record to anticipate what might be asked this cycle.

If anyone has found a better approach to navigating the protected-area permit process in Serbia, we would genuinely like to hear from you.

title: Nature Guide — Fruška Gora and Wetland Routes (Seasonal, April–October)
text:

title: Our Tours and Services — Adria Ecotrail
text:
We run tours in three of Vojvodina's most distinct landscapes: the forested ridges and monastery valleys of Fruška Gora, the shifting sand dunes and steppe of the Deliblato Sands, and the floodplain wetlands of the Tisa and Danube rivers. Each environment has its own seasonal rhythms and its own set of species, and our guides are matched to the terrain they know best.

Day tours run four to eight hours and are available for groups of four to sixteen guests. Multi-day packages range from two to six nights and include pre-vetted accommodation — family guesthouses and small rural hotels, none of them chains — and catering from local suppliers, mostly farms within forty kilometres of the trail. We do not use coaches; transport is by shared minibus, with group sizes kept small enough to reduce impact on sensitive habitats.

Every guest on a guided tour gets access to TrailSense, our nature-interpretation app, which covers 210 species of plants, birds, insects and mammals found in the areas we visit. The app works offline, which matters in the wetlands where mobile coverage is unreliable, and is available in Serbian, English, German, Dutch and Danish.

Travel agencies and tour operators can manage bookings, check real-time availability and download trip documentation through EcoDesk, our B2B portal. Agency accounts are free; contact our office to set one up.

We have been operating since 2007. Our guides are not freelancers hired by the season — most have been with us for four years or more, and several grew up in the villages nearest the trails they lead. That continuity matters. Regular guests notice it, and so do the birds.

title: CardioTrack completes first commercial supply agreement with Dijagnostika Sever
text:
CardioTrack d.o.o. has signed a supply agreement with Dijagnostika Sever, a private outpatient diagnostic centre in Subotica, making it our first commercial customer outside Novi Sad.

Under the agreement, Dijagnostika Sever will order CardioTrack patches on a per-patient basis, with devices shipped from our stock at NTP Novi Sad and returned by courier after the monitoring period. Their cardiologist, Dr. Branko Filipović, will access patient data through the CardioTrack clinician portal.

The arrangement grew out of a three-month informal pilot that began in October 2023, during which Dijagnostika Sever used twelve patches with patients referred for suspected paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Dr. Filipović reported that the portal layout reduced the time he spent reviewing each completed recording compared to the Holter software his practice had previously used, and that the seven-day window captured two AF episodes that a prior 24-hour recording on the same patients had missed.

For CardioTrack, the agreement is meaningful for two reasons beyond revenue. First, Dijagnostika Sever operates in a city with a different patient demographic profile than our Novi Sad pilot sites, which adds variability to our real-world dataset — something our engineering team values as we work on improving the motion artefact classification in the analysis pipeline. Second, it demonstrates that our logistics model — ship, wear, return, upload — works outside the city where we are based without us needing a local technician on the ground.

We are in early conversations with two further private practices in Vojvodina and expect to announce additional supply agreements later in 2024.

CardioTrack d.o.o. is based at NTP Novi Sad and is working toward CE marking under MDR with a target date of 2027. For enquiries about supply arrangements, contact Milena Ðorić at clinical@cardiotrack.rs.

title: What We Do — CardioTrack d.o.o.
text:
Most arrhythmias do not show up when you want them to. A patient sits in a clinic, electrodes on, and the heart behaves perfectly for twelve minutes. They leave without a diagnosis. Two weeks later they are back, same complaint. The standard 24-hour Holter helps, but for intermittent atrial fibrillation it often isn't long enough.

CardioTrack makes a seven-day ECG patch that a GP or cardiologist can apply in under two minutes. The patient goes home wearing it. They sleep, shower, exercise, and go to work while the device records continuously. At the end of the monitoring period, the patient returns the patch, or in some configurations the data uploads automatically over a paired smartphone. Within a few hours, the clinician receives a structured report in the CardioTrack portal with timestamped event candidates ranked by confidence.

The patch itself is built around a low-power system-on-chip and a custom analogue front end developed in-house at our lab at NTP Novi Sad. We do not use an off-the-shelf OEM board. That means we control firmware update cycles, power consumption, and signal quality tuning without waiting for a third party.

The clinician portal runs in any modern browser. Cardiologists we work with have described the layout as closer to a structured report than a raw waveform viewer, because the interface surfaces the segments most likely to be clinically relevant first, while keeping the full trace accessible.

We currently supply private cardiology practices and an outpatient diagnostic centre in Vojvodina. Our quality management system is certified to ISO 13485, and we are working toward CE marking under MDR with TÜV SÜD as our notified body.

If you run a cardiology practice and want to discuss a trial arrangement, contact our clinical liaison Milena Ðorić at clinical@cardiotrack.rs.

title: Signal Processing Engineer (Part-time or Project-based)
text:
CardioTrack d.o.o. is looking for a signal processing engineer to join a focused project aimed at reducing false-positive atrial fibrillation alerts in our ECG analysis pipeline. This is a part-time or fixed-term project engagement based at NTP Novi Sad, with some remote work possible.

Background
Our CardioTrack patch records seven days of single-channel ECG at 250 Hz alongside three-axis accelerometer data at 50 Hz. Our existing arrhythmia detection pipeline is written in Python and runs on AWS Lambda after upload. It uses a combination of R-peak detection, RR-interval variability analysis, and a lightweight TensorFlow Lite classifier. The false-positive rate for atrial fibrillation — driven mainly by motion artefact — is currently around 25 percent of flagged events, and we need to bring that below 10 percent without reducing sensitivity for true AF.

What you will work on
- Analyse our labelled dataset of approximately 1,400 recordings (ECG plus accelerometer) to understand the characteristics of motion-artefact segments that are currently misclassified
- Propose and implement an improved classification approach — this could be a revised feature set, a different model architecture, or a signal quality index that gates the classifier
- Integrate the solution into our existing Python pipeline and document it to IEC 62304 standards with support from our quality team
- Validate performance on a held-out test set and produce a short technical report suitable for inclusion in our technical file

What we are looking for
- Experience with time-series signal processing, ideally physiological signals
- Comfortable working in Python; familiarity with NumPy, SciPy, and either TensorFlow or PyTorch
- Able to work within a regulated medical device environment — we will explain our processes, but you need to be willing to document your work
- Experience with ECG or wearable sensor data is an advantage but not required

Engagement and budget
We anticipate approximately three to five months of part-time work. Compensation is negotiable and we are open to a university collaboration model. Contact jobs@cardiotrack.rs with a short note about relevant experience.

title: What we learned from 1,400 patient recordings
text:
We recently crossed a milestone in our internal dataset: 1,400 completed seven-day recordings, each adjudicated by one of the two cardiologists we work with. It felt like a good moment to write down honestly what the data has taught us, including the things that are not going well.

The good news first. Across the adjudicated recordings, our classifier correctly identified AF in a high proportion of cases where AF was later confirmed. The cardiologists we work with have said they find the portal useful for triage, and the two AF episodes caught by the Dijagnostika Sever pilot that a prior 24-hour Holter missed were a concrete reminder of why seven days matters.

Now the honest part. One in four of the events our classifier flags as probable AF turns out, on review, to be motion artefact. We know this. We have known it for several months. We have tried two things: tightening the RR-interval irregularity threshold, which reduced false positives slightly but also reduced sensitivity in a way we were not comfortable with; and adding a simple accelerometer-gating rule that suppresses detection windows where the accelerometer variance exceeds a fixed threshold, which helped with vigorous exercise but did almost nothing for the slower, lower-amplitude movements that seem to cause most of the problem.

We have the accelerometer data. We log it alongside the ECG for every patient. What we do not have, right now, is the signal processing expertise in-house to build a better solution. Our two biomedical engineers, Nikola and Jovana, are good engineers, but they are currently carrying the hardware work for the next patch revision and neither has spent significant time on learned classifiers for time-series data.

This is why we recently posted a role for a signal processing engineer and why we are also open to a structured research collaboration. If you have worked with wearable ECG or IMU data and want to look at a real, messy, labelled dataset, get in touch. We are not looking for a paper; we are looking for a pipeline that works.

Nikola Petrović, Biomedical Engineer, CardioTrack d.o.o.

title: What We Do — AxleWave Systems
text:
AxleWave Systems builds wireless condition-monitoring hardware and software for commercial vehicle drivetrains. We started in Novi Sad in 2016 because we thought the trucking industry was underserved by the kind of real-time mechanical monitoring that was already common in aerospace and heavy industry. Eight years later, we have sensor nodes running on trucks across six countries and a cloud platform that gives maintenance teams a live view of drivetrain health across their entire fleet.

Our AxleNode sensor unit attaches to the gearbox housing, driveshaft or wheel-end without modification to the vehicle. It reads vibration, temperature and rotational data continuously, and our AxleEdge firmware layer handles initial signal processing on the device before passing data to the AxleCloud platform over LTE-M. Fleet managers see a dashboard showing which trucks are running normally, which show early signs of wear and which need attention before the next long run.

We also offer DriveScore, a driving-behaviour module that uses the same sensor data to score acceleration, braking and cornering patterns. Customers use it alongside maintenance planning to understand whether driving style is accelerating component wear.

For customers who already use a fleet management system, AxleAPI lets them pull our health-status and alert data directly into their existing tools, so our output sits alongside the other operational data their dispatchers already watch.

We do all of this ourselves. We have hardware engineers, embedded firmware developers, backend engineers, data scientists and a product team in one building at NTP Novi Sad. When something breaks in the field, the people who built it are the people who fix it. We think that matters in a domain where a missed alert can mean a truck on the hard shoulder of an autobahn.

title: Edge ML Engineer — Embedded Signal Processing
text:
We are looking for an engineer who can help us move machine learning inference from our cloud pipeline onto the ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller inside our AxleNode sensor unit.

Right now we extract features in the cloud. That works at small scale but it does not work at the scale we are heading toward. We need someone who understands how to take a trained model — likely a compact CNN or a decision-tree ensemble operating on FFT feature vectors — and deploy it efficiently on a device with 256 KB of RAM and no floating-point unit luxury. You will be working closely with our data science team, who own the model training side, and our firmware team, who own the device runtime.

What we are working with: ARM Cortex-M4 running FreeRTOS, C and C++ for firmware, Python and PyTorch on the training side, CMSIS-DSP for on-device signal processing, and our own OTA update tooling for pushing new firmware to deployed nodes.

What we need from you: experience quantising or pruning models for microcontroller targets, familiarity with fixed-point arithmetic, and enough signal-processing background to have a useful conversation about FFT bin selection and windowing. Experience with vibration or audio signals is a genuine advantage.

We are not looking for someone who has done all of this before in exactly this context. We are looking for someone who has done enough of it that they can work out the parts they have not done yet.

This is a full-time role based in Novi Sad. We offer a competitive salary, flexible hours and the option to work remotely up to two days a week. Relocation support is available.

title: Senior Data Scientist — Fault Classification
text:
Our anomaly-detection model tells fleet managers that something is wrong with a drivetrain. We need it to tell them what specifically is wrong. That is the problem you would be working on.

We have roughly 340 labelled fault events in our archive, spanning worn differentials, wheel-bearing fatigue, propshaft imbalance and a handful of rarer failure modes. The dataset is unbalanced and we know it. We also have years of unlabelled signal data from trucks that ran without incident, which we think can be used more effectively than it currently is. You would be responsible for the full lifecycle of the fault-classification work: data preparation, feature engineering on vibration spectra, model selection, validation against held-out customer maintenance records and eventually integration with the AxleCloud alert pipeline.

Our current stack on the data science side is Python, PyTorch, scikit-learn and a TimescaleDB instance holding pre-extracted features. Raw signals live in S3 in Parquet format. We use MLflow for experiment tracking. The team is fifteen people and you would be working alongside engineers who have strong signal-processing backgrounds and others who come more from a software side.

We want someone who takes imbalanced classification problems seriously — not just someone who will run SMOTE and call it done — and who is comfortable reading vibration analysis literature to inform feature choices. A background in mechanical or acoustic signal processing is an advantage but not a strict requirement.

Full-time, Novi Sad-based, with the same remote and relocation terms as our other open roles.

title: AxleWave signs two-year monitoring agreement with Karpacki Przewóz
text:
We are pleased to confirm that Karpacki Przewóz Sp. z o.o., a regional freight operator based in Rzeszów, Poland, has signed a two-year subscription agreement to deploy AxleNode sensors across 120 of its heavy trucks operating on routes between Poland, Slovakia and Hungary.

Karpacki Przewóz operates a mixed fleet including long-haul tractor units and rigid vehicles doing regional distribution. Their maintenance manager, Tomasz Wierzbicki, told us that the decision came down to a simple calculation: their average drivetrain repair cost when a failure reaches the roadside breakdown stage is roughly four times what it costs to catch the same fault during a planned workshop visit. They had been using a time-based maintenance schedule and wanted to move toward condition-based servicing without hiring additional diagnostic staff.

The rollout will be handled in two phases. The first 60 units will be installed during scheduled services over April and May 2024, with the second batch following in the third quarter. Karpacki Przewóz will use AxleCloud directly and has also asked for an AxleAPI integration with their existing fleet management software, supplied by a separate vendor.

This agreement is our largest single deployment in Poland to date and gives us a denser cluster of sensors in a region where winter operating conditions are among the most demanding we see. The data from this fleet will be directly useful for work we are doing on improving fault specificity in cold-climate conditions.

We want to thank the Karpacki Przewóz team for a thorough and straightforward procurement process.

title: What four winter seasons in Poland taught us about sensor housing design
text:
When we designed the original AxleNode housing, we tested it hard. Water immersion to IP67 standard, vibration tables, thermal shock chambers. The units passed. We were confident.

Then we started getting returns from trucks that had spent 18 months operating out of depots in northern Poland. About four units in every hundred showed corrosion on the main PCB. Not catastrophic, but enough to cause intermittent signal loss and, in a handful of cases, complete node failure. That is not acceptable in a monitoring product. If the sensor is not working, the fleet manager has no data — and no data looks exactly like 'everything is fine', which is the worst possible failure mode for a safety-adjacent product.

We pulled the returned units apart. Cross-sections of the potting compound around the cable entry gland showed discolouration and what looks like micro-cracking at the interface between the epoxy and the gland insert. Our working hypothesis is thermal cycling. These trucks see minus 25°C overnight and then run hard enough that the gearbox casing surface temperature climbs to 60°C or above within an hour of starting. Thirty or forty of those cycles per month across a Polish winter adds up.

The problem with a hypothesis like this is that it is easy to believe and hard to prove without the right tools. We know how to build sensor nodes. We are not a materials characterisation laboratory. We are currently working to find a way to properly investigate the failure mechanism — crack initiation point, whether it is the epoxy bulk, the interface, or the gland geometry — so that we can write a proper specification for the next hardware revision rather than just trying a different potting compound and hoping.

AxleNode 3.0 is on the schedule. We want the housing design to be right before it goes to manufacturing. We are being realistic about what we do not know.

title: EkoTok Reaches 340 Active Collection Points After Romania Expansion
text:
EkoTok Solutions passed the 340-cabinet mark in January 2024 following the completion of a 60-unit rollout across Cluj-Napoca, Timișoara and Oradea in Romania. The expansion was partly funded by a grant from the Enterprise Innovation Fund of Vojvodina awarded in late 2022, which covered cabinet hardware and installation costs for the Romanian pilot phase.

The Romanian cabinets are placed at partner locations including the Meridian retail chain and four municipal administration buildings. Under the arrangement with Meridian, collected material is attributed to Meridian's producer-responsibility reporting, with EkoTok providing quarterly data extracts formatted to match the Romanian national waste authority's submission templates.

"Romania was harder to enter than Hungary because the take-back infrastructure expectation was lower — retailers were not used to being asked to host a cabinet and share floor space for it," said Dragan Vuković, EkoTok's head of business development. "It took about four months of conversations before the first partner signed. The second and third were easier."

The company says total material collected across all three countries in 2023 was just under 480 tonnes, up from 310 tonnes in 2022. Approximately 34% by weight was battery packs and cells, which are processed at the Novi Sad facility before recovered fractions are transferred to Halvard Material Group.

EkoTok expects to add a further 40 to 60 cabinets in Bulgaria during the second half of 2024, subject to finalizing a logistics partnership agreement with a local operator. The company is also in early discussions with two Austrian retail groups about a white-label take-back arrangement, though no contracts have been signed.

title: What We Do — EkoTok Solutions
text:
EkoTok Solutions operates a take-back and material-recovery service for small consumer electronics and spent batteries across Serbia, Hungary and Romania.

We place smart collection cabinets at points people already visit — shopping centres, petrol stations, municipal offices, post offices. The cabinets accept mobile phones, tablets, power banks, small household devices and loose batteries of all chemistries. Every cabinet has a weight sensor and a fill-level sensor. When a cabinet is ready for collection, our system routes the next available BrzaTranzit vehicle to pick it up. Items travel to our processing facility in the Novi Sad Science Technology Park.

At the facility, trained disassembly technicians open devices by hand, separate components by material class and remove battery packs. Battery cells go through a voltage-based triage step before being routed either to our grading bench or to downstream shredding through our partner Halvard Material Group in Rotterdam. Metals, plastics and glass are packed and transferred to certified recyclers under documented chain-of-custody records.

We work primarily with three kinds of customers. Municipalities use our service to meet household e-waste collection targets under producer-responsibility legislation. Retailers and electronics importers use our white-label take-back program to satisfy their own EU compliance obligations. And manufacturers with active producer-responsibility schemes contract us to provide the field infrastructure and the material-output data they need for annual reporting.

We are not a waste broker. We handle collection, disassembly and initial material separation ourselves. That means we control the data at every step, which matters as Battery Regulation traceability requirements tighten.

If you represent a municipality, a retail chain or a manufacturer and want to discuss a take-back arrangement, contact our commercial team at partnership@ekotok.rs.

title: Why Open-Circuit Voltage Alone Is Not Enough for Cell Triage — and What We Are Doing About It
text:
Every battery pack that comes off our disassembly floor gets its cells measured before we decide what to do with them. The measurement we take is open-circuit voltage. It takes about four seconds per cell and our technicians can do it without slowing down the line.

The problem is that OCV does not tell you whether a cell is degraded or just deeply discharged. A lithium-ion cell that has been sitting in an unused device for two years can read 2.8 volts — which looks the same as a cell that has genuinely lost most of its capacity. Under our current rules, both go to shredding.

Last year we sent about 22% of cells to shredding that Halvard's lab, when we asked them to spot-check a sample, assessed as having usable remaining capacity. That is a real cost. Black mass recovery from shredding gives us a fraction of the value we would get from selling graded cells to secondary markets, and demand for used cells from local e-bike repair workshops is something we have been watching grow.

We have spent the last few months reading about what faster, floor-practical alternatives exist. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy can identify internal resistance signatures that distinguish degraded cells from discharged-but-healthy ones. The challenge for us is measurement time and equipment cost at scale. Brief pulse-discharge tests are another option — cheaper hardware, but you need to apply a controlled load and log the voltage response curve, which adds handling steps.

Neither is something we can implement alone with our current team. We are looking for a technical collaborator — either a person or a group — who has done this kind of measurement work in a production or near-production environment and can help us figure out what is actually practical at 18 kilograms per worker-hour throughput. If that sounds like something you have worked on, get in touch at tehnika@ekotok.rs.

title: What We Do — VoltCell Storage
text:
VoltCell Storage builds stationary battery systems for farms, food processors and small factories in Serbia and the wider region. Every system we ship uses battery modules recovered from retired electric vehicles — mostly city buses and light vans — that would otherwise be scrapped. We take those modules, test them, grade them, assemble them into cabinets with our own battery management electronics and put a warranty on the result.

Our customers are not large energy companies. They are a sunflower oil mill outside Zrenjanin that wants to shave its peak demand charge, a raspberry cold store near Čačak that loses product when the grid dips, a plastics injection shop in Novi Sad that needs 20 minutes of ride-through while a generator starts. For all of them, a new lithium system from a catalogue supplier costs more than the problem is worth. A VoltCell cabinet typically costs 40 to 55 percent less than an equivalent new-cell system, and the performance warranty means they are not taking a gamble on used goods.

We are based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad, which gives us workshop space, a loading bay and access to a small machine shop. Our team of fifteen people covers firmware, electrical assembly, mechanical integration, procurement and field service. We do our own module testing in-house on rigs we built ourselves.

When a site logs an anomaly, someone on the firmware team digs into the trace data and figures out whether it is a cell problem, a firmware bug or a communication glitch.

title: VoltCell 50 kWh Cabinet Installed at Jovanović Agro Cold Store
text:
We commissioned our seventh customer site last week: a 50 kWh cabinet at the Jovanović Agro fruit storage facility near Bač. The cabinet provides backup power for the refrigeration compressors and peak shaving during the morning harvest intake when three compressors start in close succession and pull the site's demand up sharply.

The project took about four months from first conversation to energisation. The main delay was civil work to install the concrete pad and cable duct, which is outside our scope and always depends on the customer's contractor schedule. Electrical installation and commissioning on our side took two days.

Petar Jovanović, who runs the facility with his brother, told us the main thing he wanted was something simple: a system that works without him having to think about it, and a phone number to call if something looks wrong. We connected the cabinet to their existing SCADA display so the state of charge shows on the screen he already watches. The system has been running for twelve days without any issues logged.

The modules in this cabinet came from a batch of retired Solaris electric bus battery packs sourced through our dismantling partner Reciklažni Centar Dunav in Pančevo. All 24 modules in the cabinet passed our full test cycle with remaining capacity between 81 and 87 percent of original nameplate. Average module age at the time of testing was six years.

We now have a total of 350 kWh installed across seven sites in Serbia. Our target for the end of 2025 is 5 MWh. The gap between where we are and where we want to be is mostly a function of how fast we can screen incoming module batches, which is something we are actively working to improve.

Each channel logs voltage, current and temperature at one-second intervals into a SQLite database via a Python script. Modules sit in custom fixtures with copper bus-bar connections and a thermocouple harness.

Disconnect completed modules, apply our grading labels and move them to the graded-stock area. You will also do basic rig maintenance — contact cleaning, cable inspection, calibration checks.

What we need: Comfortable working with DC voltages up to 60 V under our safety procedures. Methodical about paperwork — every module gets a record and traceability matters to us.
