title: Why Our Module Testing Takes So Long (and What We Are Trying to Do About It)
text:
People who find out we run 20-hour test cycles on incoming battery modules usually ask why we do not just use a quicker method. It is a fair question. Here is an honest answer.

The number we need before we put a module into a warranted cabinet is remaining usable capacity — how many kilowatt-hours the module can actually deliver at a sensible discharge rate. The only way to measure that directly is to fully charge the module, fully discharge it at a controlled rate and count the energy that comes out. At the rates we use to protect the cells, that takes about 20 hours for a 50 Ah module.

We have tried shortcuts. Open-circuit voltage after a rest period is fast and tells you something, but two modules can sit at nearly the same OCV and differ by almost 20 percent in capacity. We spent several weeks last autumn testing a short pulse protocol — ten minutes of charge and discharge pulses, measure the voltage response, fit a simple model. It was faster but our false-pass rate (modules we called good that failed on the full test) stayed around 12 percent. At that rate we would be putting bad modules into cabinets and voiding our own warranties.

We have good data: about 2,400 completed test records with full time-series traces and confirmed capacity figures. We know what a module's voltage curve looks like during discharge. What we do not yet have is a reliable way to predict the full-discharge result from a partial measurement.

We are not going to pretend we have solved this. We are talking to people who work on this kind of problem and we are open to collaboration. If we can get accurate capacity estimates in under two hours per module, we can screen complete incoming batches instead of samples, and our throughput doubles without new hardware. That is a meaningful difference for a fifteen-person company trying to reach 5 MWh a year.

If you have thoughts, our lead test engineer Aleksandar Vrhovac is reachable at a.vrhovac@voltcellstorage.rs.

title: About Us & Services — BrzoPak Logistika
text:
BrzoPak Logistika was started in 2008 by three people with a van, a rented loading bay, and a list of thirty online sellers in Novi Sad who were tired of relying on postal services that took five days to cross the city. Today we run 34 vans and employ 87 people from our main depot at NTP Novi Sad.

We focus on one corridor: Vojvodina and the Hungarian counties directly across the border. We know the road conditions, the address formats, the public holidays on both sides, and the habits of buyers who order online in this part of Europe. That local knowledge is the reason clients stay with us after they try a larger carrier and find that their parcels sit in a regional hub two hundred kilometres away.

Our services cover the full last-mile cycle. We collect parcels from your warehouse or pick them up from our fulfilment shelves if you store stock with us. We deliver next-day to most of Vojvodina and within two working days to the southern Hungary zone. We collect cash on delivery and settle weekly. We handle returns, inspect them against a condition checklist you define, and either put them back in storage or photograph the damage for your records.

For businesses that need an urgent same-day run — a spare part, a document, a small pallet — we keep two vans on a dedicated express schedule.

Our team is based in Novi Sad. Our operations manager Dragana Horvat has run the hub floor since 2019. Our customer service team answers in Serbian and Hungarian and covers 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays.

If you want a courier that will tell you plainly when something has gone wrong and how we are fixing it, contact us at info@brzopak.rs.

title: BrzoPak Signs Three-Year Agreement with Tekstilnica Budanova
text:

Tekstilnica Budanova sells mid-price women's clothing through their own webshop and two regional marketplaces. They were previously managing their own small warehouse and handing off daily to a national postal operator. Delivery times were running at three to five days for Vojvodina addresses, and their return rate from unhappy buyers was climbing.

Starting in February 2024, Tekstilnica Budanova's stock will move to BrzoPak's fulfilment shelves at NTP Novi Sad. Orders placed before 2 p.m. will be picked, packed, and handed to a driver the same afternoon, with next-day delivery to most Vojvodina postcodes.

For Tekstilnica Budanova this means they no longer need to manage warehouse staff or negotiate annual rate reviews with a postal carrier. For us it is our largest single fulfilment client by SKU count, with roughly 340 active product lines.

'We talked to two other fulfilment companies before BrzoPak,' said Jovana Budanov, founder of Tekstilnica Budanova. 'The others were cheaper on paper but both had their main operations in Belgrade. BrzoPak's depot is forty minutes from our supplier. That matters when we need to restock quickly before a weekend promotion.'

The agreement also covers cash-on-delivery settlement and return inspection. We will photograph every returned item and send Tekstilnica Budanova a daily damage report so they can decide on restocking without waiting for the physical parcel to arrive.

Welcome to Tekstilnica Budanova.

title: What We Learned from November 2023 (and What We Are Doing About It)
text:
November 2023 was our highest parcel volume month on record: 71,400 parcels processed through our Novi Sad hub. It was also the month where we made the most mistakes we have made in a single period since 2016.

Our operations manager Dragana Horvat has been going through the numbers since December and we want to share what we found, because some of our clients were affected and deserve an honest account.

Sorting errors: Normally our misrouting rate sits around 3 percent. In the four peak weeks of November it reached 5.1 percent, which meant over 3,600 parcels needed a redelivery attempt. About 400 of those resulted in full refunds to buyers because the second attempt also missed the delivery window. We absorbed that cost. It took our customer service team — which is three people — until the second week of December to clear the backlog of complaints.

Routing: We also tracked fuel usage per parcel in November versus October. The number was 17 percent higher per parcel delivered. Some of that is traffic and weather. Most of it is that our morning route plans collapsed by mid-morning every day and we did not have a fast way to rebuild them.

What are we doing? We have moved our depot into NTP Novi Sad partly for this reason: to be closer to people who can help us fix the sorting and routing problems technically, not just by hiring more sorters and dispatchers. We have posted two new jobs. We are also in early conversations about a small pilot project on automated label reading, which we will write about if it develops into something real.

November 2023 cost us roughly 380,000 RSD in direct extra expense on top of normal operations. We are not going to have another November like that.

title: Products and Services — PrecizMeh d.o.o.
text:
PrecizMeh d.o.o. designs and manufactures precision gearboxes, actuator housings and motion-control subassemblies for customers who need components that perform to a drawing, not just to a catalogue description.

Our RA-series planetary gearboxes run from the RA-20 (output torque to 120 Nm) up to the RA-80 (output torque to 1,800 Nm). Each frame size is offered in single and two-stage ratios from 4:1 to 64:1. Standard outputs are spline or solid shaft; flange outputs are available on all sizes. We stock a limited range of the most common configurations and build the rest to order, typically in four to six weeks.

Actuator housings are machined from customer drawings. We work in cast iron, nodular iron, aluminium alloy and low-alloy steel. Our standard capability on final bore features is IT6, and we can hold IT5 on selected features with process qualification. Every housing ships with a dimensional report against the drawing.

Custom subassemblies — where we supply a complete gear train assembled into a housing, ready for the customer to bolt into their machine — are a growing part of the business. These typically involve closer coordination with the customer's design team from early in the development phase. We prefer to be involved before the drawing is fixed, not after.

Our gearbox refurbishment service is available for RA-series units and, on a case-by-case basis, for competitor units of similar construction. We disassemble, inspect, replace worn components to original specification and test on our run-in stand before return.

For customers supplying Tier 1 or OEM accounts who need dimensional and process traceability, we offer first-article inspection and reporting on third-party components. We use a Zeiss Contura CMM and issue reports in standard formats.

All production is carried out at our facility at Industrijska zona Sever, Novi Sad. We do not subcontract machining operations. Heat treatment is carried out by a qualified external partner under a controlled supplier agreement.

title: Quality Engineer — Process Capability and Documentation
text:
PrecizMeh d.o.o. is looking for a quality engineer to join our team of eleven engineers in Novi Sad. The role has two main areas of work.

The first is process capability. We machine high-precision bores on actuator housings and gearbox bodies, and we want to move from end-of-line inspection to in-process statistical monitoring. You will work with our machinists and process engineers to identify the right control points, set up measurement protocols and turn our existing inspection data — we have several years of CMM and air-gauge records — into something we can use to make decisions about tooling and process adjustments before scrap is generated.

The second is quality documentation for OEM supply. We are preparing for our first PPAP submission to an EU robotics customer. You will lead the preparation of process FMEAs, control plans, measurement system analysis studies and initial process capability reports. Experience with PPAP or a similar structured quality approval process is a significant advantage; if you have not done PPAP specifically but have worked with APQP or equivalent automotive or machinery-sector processes, we want to hear from you.

Required: degree in mechanical engineering, industrial engineering or a related technical field; at least three years in a manufacturing quality role; practical experience with SPC, capability indices (Cp, Cpk) and measurement system analysis; comfortable working on the shop floor as well as at a desk; English sufficient to correspond with customers and read technical standards.

Useful but not required: experience with Zeiss Calypso or similar CMM software; familiarity with AIAG reference manuals; German language.

We offer a permanent contract, competitive salary for the Novi Sad market and the chance to work on technically interesting problems in a company that has been here for over forty years and expects to be here for forty more.

Send CV and a short note about relevant experience to: posao@precizmeh.rs. Applications reviewed on a rolling basis.

text:

On development projects you will work with Mihajlo Stojković, our lead engineer, from concept through to production release.

We are particularly interested in candidates with experience in gear contact analysis or tribology, because we are dealing with some fatigue and thermal questions on our current product range that require more analytical depth than we have been able to apply in-house. Experience with FEA (we use SolidWorks Simulation for structural checks; a candidate who can go further would be welcome) or with lubricant/thermal modelling would be directly relevant.

Required: degree in mechanical engineering; at least two years of design experience in a manufacturing environment; proficient in SolidWorks; able to read and prepare GD&T drawings; Serbian or English working language.

Useful: knowledge of gear standards (ISO 6336 or equivalent); experience with planetary gear arrangements; some familiarity with surface hardening processes and their effect on fatigue life.

This is a full-time, permanent position based in Novi Sad. We have flexible start times and a small but technically engaged engineering team. The work is varied — no two weeks are the same — and there is real scope to influence how the product develops.

Under the agreement, PrecizMeh will supply finished motion-control subassemblies — planetary gear trains assembled into precision-machined housings — at a volume of up to 4,000 units per year. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2025, subject to successful completion of the customer's supplier qualification process.

Dirk Faller, Head of Supply Chain at Robotik Augsburg GmbH, said the decision to source from PrecizMeh followed a two-year evaluation that included on-site audits and sample testing: "We looked at several suppliers in Central and Eastern Europe. PrecizMeh has the machining capability we need and a quality system that gives us a reasonable starting point. The remaining step is completing the PPAP process, and we are prepared to work with them on that."

For PrecizMeh, the contract represents the company's largest single OEM supply commitment to date. Director Zorka Ilić noted that the agreement would require the company to invest in both capacity and documentation processes: "We have the engineering capability and the equipment. What this contract asks us to do is document our processes in a more structured way than we have needed to before. We are treating that as an opportunity to improve, not just a customer requirement to satisfy."

PrecizMeh is currently recruiting a quality engineer with PPAP experience to lead the preparation of the submission package. The company expects to begin the first phase of the qualification process in the third quarter of 2024.

For supply inquiries: prodaja@precizmeh.rs

title: What we learned at the Hannover Messe industrial trade fair
text:
Three of us from PrecizMeh — Mihajlo Stojković from engineering, Dragana Vukić from quality and myself from sales — spent four days in Hannover in April. Here is a short account of what was relevant for us.

On the customer side, we had pre-arranged meetings with four existing contacts and took several unplanned conversations with companies we had not met before. The demand for compact, high-torque planetary gearboxes in collaborative robot applications came up repeatedly. Our RA-20 and RA-40 sizes are relevant here, but the customers asking about this space want very low backlash — consistently under four arc-minutes — and our current production process is not qualified to guarantee that across a full batch. That is something we need to address if we want to serve that segment.

On the supplier side, Dragana spent time at stands showing tooling monitoring and in-process measurement systems. There are now several affordable sensor packages for machining centres that can track cutting force and spindle load in real time and use that to estimate tool condition. We have looked at these before and found them expensive relative to the value they would add at our volume, but prices have come down and the integration with common CNC controllers has improved. We are going to request demonstrations from two suppliers when they visit the region later in the year.

Mihajlo attended a half-day session on gear-contact fatigue, which was directly relevant to an open problem we have with our RA-40 output stage. The session confirmed that the failure mode we are seeing is recognised in the field and that there are modelling approaches available — though applying them requires either specialist software or someone with the specific background to use general-purpose tools appropriately. We do not have that background in-house.

Overall, the fair was useful. It confirmed that the markets we want to grow in are real and that the technical gaps we are aware of are ones we need to close, not work around.

title: What We Do — Sinaps Tech
text:
We build quality-control software for small manufacturers who do not have the budget or the staff for enterprise inspection systems.

Our platform, called Linea, connects an industrial camera and a vibration sensor to a small edge computer that sits beside the machine. The edge device runs our detection models locally — no cloud dependency, no latency waiting for a remote server — and streams a live quality dashboard to any browser on the factory network. When something goes wrong, a supervisor sees it within seconds, not at the end-of-shift scrap report.

Linea is built around three principles. First, it should work on hardware the factory already owns or can buy from a standard industrial supplier. We do not sell proprietary sensor pods or locked-in cameras. Second, configuration should take hours, not weeks. A factory does not have three months to spend on integration before they see any value. Third, alerts have to mean something. A system that cries wolf ten times a shift will be switched off by the end of the first week. We have designed our detection pipeline to prioritise a low false-positive rate even if that means occasionally missing a borderline defect.

We are currently running live pilots at three production sites in Hungary — two metalworking facilities and one plastic-injection shop. Between them they are monitoring eleven machine stations and have logged over six months of production data.

Our team is based in Subotica, Serbia, twelve people in total. Most of us have backgrounds in industrial automation or machine vision. A few of us have spent years on factory floors, which shapes how we think about what operators actually need versus what looks good in a demo.

If you run a production line and want to understand what Linea might look like in your facility, write to us at contact@sinapstech.rs.

title: Linea Goes Live at Kovács Fémipari Kft. — Our Third Hungarian Pilot
text:
We are glad to share that Kovács Fémipari Kft., a sheet-metal fabrication workshop near Debrecen, became the third site to go live with Linea at the end of December 2023.

Kovács Fémipari runs two laser-cutting lines and a press-brake cell. They had been tracking scrap manually — an operator walking the line twice a shift with a clipboard — and losing roughly 2.4 percent of material to defects that were caught too late in the process. Their production manager, Gábor Somodi, told us in our first meeting that he did not want another system his team would switch off after a month. That stuck with us.

Deployment took four days. We installed a Linea unit on each of the two laser-cutting lines, connected them to the factory's existing Wi-Fi, and ran Grafana dashboards on two screens already mounted in the production hall. No new cabling, no PLC integration, no modifications to the machines.

In the first four weeks of operation, the system flagged eleven cutting-head alignment events before they produced out-of-tolerance parts. Somodi's team intervened on nine of those in time to avoid scrap. Estimated material saving in January alone: around 340 euros. Small, but it is one site, two machines, and one month.

We are continuing to collect data and will share more detailed results after the three-month mark. If you are interested in what a pilot at your facility would look like, get in touch.

title: Signal Processing Engineer (Full-Time, Subotica)
text:
We are looking for an engineer to take ownership of the vibration-analysis side of our platform.

The core problem you will work on: our CNC anomaly detector performs well in controlled conditions but struggles in real factory environments where ambient noise from neighbouring machines creates high false-positive rates. We have a large archive of labelled accelerometer data from our pilot sites — roughly 400 GB — and we need someone who can design and validate a signal-separation or noise-cancellation approach that can run efficiently on a Jetson Orin NX with 8 GB of RAM.

You will work closely with our two computer-vision engineers and our embedded-firmware developer. There is no dedicated data team — everyone writes code that goes into the product.

What we are looking for:
- Solid grounding in digital signal processing: filtering, spectral analysis, time-frequency representations
- Experience handling real-world sensor data, preferably from industrial or mechanical sources
- Comfortable in Python; familiarity with NumPy, SciPy, and at least one deep-learning framework
- An instinct for what will actually work under memory and compute constraints, not just in a notebook

Nice to have:
- Experience with vibration analysis for rotating machinery
- Familiarity with MEMS accelerometer characteristics and signal conditioning
- Any embedded or edge deployment experience

We are a small team in Subotica. The work is mostly in the office; occasional travel to our pilot sites in Hungary is part of the job. Salary is negotiable and will depend on experience. We offer equity participation after a six-month probation period.

Send a CV and a short note about a signal-processing problem you have solved to jobs@sinapstech.rs. We do not require a cover letter and will not ask you to complete an unpaid technical task.

title: Junior Computer Vision Engineer (Full-Time or Part-Time, Subotica)
text:
We have a specific gap we need to fill: we want to improve and eventually automate the camera calibration process for our Linea units.

Right now, moving a Linea unit to a new position on a production line requires a full manual calibration that takes around three hours and needs someone who understands camera geometry. That is us. We do the visit, which is expensive and does not scale. We want to change that.

The goal is a calibration workflow that a factory maintenance worker — no specialist background, no calibration software installed — can complete in under thirty minutes, probably using a printed target and a guided process on a tablet or phone. The hard constraint is that the reprojection error has to stay low enough for 0.3 mm measurement tolerance on metal parts at roughly 600 mm working distance.

You will own this project from prototype to production. That includes evaluating approaches (homography-based, structured light, self-calibration from production images), building a test rig in our office, validating on real units, and eventually writing the documentation that a non-engineer can follow.

What we are looking for:
- Hands-on experience with camera calibration — not just calling cv2.calibrateCamera() but understanding what can go wrong and why
- Python and OpenCV, comfortably
- Willingness to work on a problem that is mostly engineering and experimentation, not research

This role can be full-time or structured as a part-time engagement for someone finishing a degree. We are open to discussing the format.

Write to jobs@sinapstech.rs with a few lines about your experience with camera systems.

title: What We Learned at the Hannover Smart Factory Pavilion
text:
Four of us drove to Hannover in March for a two-day visit to the Smart Factory section of the industrial fair. We had no booth. We went to look, talk to people, and figure out where we actually stand relative to the rest of the market.

The honest takeaway: the enterprise end of the machine-vision market is crowded and moving fast. Several large automation vendors are bundling quality-inspection modules into their existing PLC and SCADA ecosystems. For a large automotive supplier that already runs those systems, it makes sense to buy from the same vendor. We are not going to compete there.

But something else was noticeable. Most of the systems on display assumed a clean, fixed production environment — dedicated inspection stations, controlled lighting, static camera positions, a full-time integrator on call. When we talked to smaller manufacturers who had wandered into the hall, the consistent response was that the systems looked impressive but felt like they were built for a different kind of factory.

That confirmed what we keep hearing from our own clients. The three-hundred-person metalworking shop in Debrecen does not have an integration engineer. They move machines around twice a year. Their lighting is whatever the hall has. They need something that tolerates those conditions.

We also had a useful conversation with a product manager from a Slovenian sensor distributor, Meralux d.o.o., who works with exactly the kind of clients we target. We are exploring whether there is a distribution arrangement that makes sense for both sides.

We will go back next year, and next time we will have a booth.

title: Inspekcijska kazna u januaru – šta smo naučili i šta menjamo
text:
Odlučili smo da ovo objavimo jer smatramo da je iskrenost prema klijentima važnija od privida da sve ide glatko.

U januaru 2024. godine jedan od naših vozača, Predrag Đukić, zaustavljan je na rutinskoj inspekciji u Mađarskoj. Inspektor je utvrdio da je u prethodne četiri nedelje kumulativno prekoračeno vreme vožnje za 47 minuta u jednoj kalendarskoj sedmici. Kazna je iznosila 3.200 evra.

Analiza je pokazala da je do greške došlo jer smo ručno računali kumulativno vreme vožnje od ponedeljka do nedelje, ali smo propustili da uzmemo u obzir preklapanje turusa sa prethodne nedelje. Naš dispečer nije pogrešio namerno – model u Excelu koji koristimo jednostavno nije konstruisan da hvata ovaj tip greške.

Kao direktna mera, uveli smo obaveznu proveru pre svakog polaska: dispečer mora da štampanjem iz TomTom platforme potvrdi stanje tahografske kartice vozača za poslednjih 28 dana. Ovo nije idealno rešenje, ali smanjuje rizik dok tražimo bolji alat.

Dugoročno, jasno nam je da nam treba softver koji automatski prati i upozorava na blizinu zakonskog limita. Razgovaramo sa više dobavljača i otvoreni smo i za predloge iz lokalne tehničke zajednice. Ako neko ima iskustvo sa sličnim rešenjima u sektoru drumskog transporta, možete nam se javiti na tehnika@eurofreight-zr.rs.

Naš vozni park čine 28 frigorifičnih poluprikolica u rasponu od 33 do 66 paletnih mesta, sve sa važećim ATP sertifikatima i Carrier Transicold agregatima. Svaka prikolica ima aktivan Comet dataloger koji beleži temperaturu svakih pet minuta tokom celog puta. Izveštaj dobija klijent automatski po isporuci.

Grupažne linije polaze iz Zrenjanina dva puta nedeljno prema Budimpešti i jednom nedeljno prema Minhenu i Hamburgu. Prikolice se pune u našem cross-dock magacinu u industrijskoj zoni, gde možemo da primimo robu na +2°C do +8°C ili na -18°C do -22°C zavisno od zahteva.

Pored grupažnog transporta, nudimo i unajmljivanje cele prikolice za klijente kojima treba garantovana temperatura i rok isporuke. Organizujemo carinjenje i svu ATP dokumentaciju za izvoz i uvoz.

title: Zašto datalogeri nisu dovoljni za upravljanje hladnim lancem
text:
Postavili smo sebi jedan praktičan problem: imamo CSV datoteku sa merenjima temperature svakih pet minuta, imamo GPS trag vozila i imamo dokument o preuzimanju tereta sa tri različita špeditora. Temperatura je u jednom trenutku skočila sa 4°C na 9,3°C i zadržala se tamo 22 minuta. Ko je odgovoran?

Po trenutnoj proceduri, naš magacinski referent Dragana Lukić štampa izveštaj, piše napomenu, i šalje ga šefu pošiljke i osiguravajućoj kući. Svi se pozivaju na to da su oni predali robu u redu. Bez konteksta, bez automatske korelacije sa GPS podacima i bez vremenske oznake preuzimanja na cross-dock tački, ovaj dokument nije dovoljno jak da nešto dokaže.

U konkretnom slučaju iz prošle godine platili smo štetu od 14.000 evra za robu za koju smo bili ubezbeđeni da je ekskurzija nastala na utovarnoj rampi pošiljaoca, ne u prikolici. Ali nismo mogli da to dokažemo u roku koji je osiguravajuća kuća tražila.

Šta bi nam pomoglo: alat koji automatski uzima CSV iz datologera, GPS log iz TomTom sistema i skenove CMR dokumenata, i koji na izlazu daje vremenski niz događaja u kome se vidi gde je prikolica bila u trenutku ekskurzije, da li su vrata bila otvarana, i koji deo puta statistički najviše odgovara uočenoj promeni. Ne tražimo nešto egzotično – tražimo da podatke koje već imamo neko poveže na pametan način.

title: What We Do — Datavox Consulting
text:
We help companies get useful answers out of their operational data. That sounds simple, but in practice it means a lot of work before any model or dashboard appears: understanding where the data comes from, fixing the pipelines that carry it, and making sure the numbers a manager sees on Monday morning match reality. We have been doing this since 2014, mostly for companies in manufacturing, logistics, and retail distribution across the Western Balkans.

Our typical engagement starts with a data audit — two to three weeks where we map your data sources, check quality, and give you an honest picture of what is and is not feasible. From there, projects fall into one of a few categories: building a prediction or classification model that feeds into an operational decision, designing a dashboard that replaces a weekly Excel report with something a team can actually act on, or setting up the underlying data infrastructure that makes both of those things maintainable.

We do not sell licences or proprietary platforms. Everything we build runs on open-source tools your team can inspect and, after a handover period, operate themselves. If you want us to keep running it — monitoring model drift, retraining on fresh data, updating dashboards as your business changes — we offer retainer contracts for that too. About a third of our revenue comes from clients who have been on a retainer with us for more than two years.

Our team of 38 is based at NTP Novi Sad. Every project has a senior engineer attached from kickoff to handover. We do not subcontract the technical core of a project. If a piece of work is outside what we can do well, we say so at the audit stage rather than six months in.

If you want to talk through a specific problem before committing to anything, get in touch. We are used to conversations that start with 'we have data but we are not sure what to do with it.'

title: Datavox signs three-year contract with Koridori Distribucija for demand forecasting
text:
Datavox Consulting has signed a three-year contract with Koridori Distribucija, a regional distributor of fast-moving consumer goods operating across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro. The engagement covers the design, deployment, and ongoing maintenance of a demand-forecasting and inventory-allocation system for the company's 14 regional warehouses.

Koridori Distribucija has worked with Datavox since 2021, when we built the rule-based allocation system the company currently uses. The new contract expands that work significantly: the goal is a planning engine that uses historical order data, current stock levels across all sites, and an advance promotional calendar to generate reallocation recommendations on a rolling 48-hour horizon. Recommendations will be passed automatically to Koridori's existing warehouse management system.

Miloš Vranić, operations director at Koridori Distribucija, said the current system performs well under normal conditions but struggles to respond to the volume spikes that promotional campaigns create. The new system is expected to reduce stockout events during peak periods and lower the cost of emergency inter-warehouse transfers.

The project has a hard deadline: a working pilot must be in place before the November–December peak season. Our logistics modelling team will take the lead, with data engineering support from two colleagues who already know the Koridori data infrastructure.

This contract is the largest single engagement in Datavox's history by contract value and is a meaningful step toward formalising logistics optimisation as a dedicated service line. We will publish a technical note on the project architecture once the pilot is live and the client has reviewed it.

title: Senior ML Engineer — Datavox Consulting d.o.o.
text:
We are looking for a senior machine-learning engineer to join our team in Novi Sad. The role sits inside our modelling team, which currently has five engineers working on projects across churn prediction, demand forecasting, and anomaly detection for manufacturing clients.

What the work looks like day to day: you will own the full lifecycle of one or two models at a time — from feature design through training, evaluation, and deployment into a production FastAPI endpoint, through to monitoring drift and deciding when to retrain. You will work directly with clients during scoping and at review points, so you need to be able to explain a model's behaviour in plain language.

We use Python throughout. On the modelling side the team mostly works with scikit-learn, XGBoost, and PyTorch, depending on the problem. Pipelines run on Airflow; data lives in PostgreSQL or TimescaleDB; everything ships in Docker and runs on Kubernetes clusters, partly on-premise and partly on rented VMs. We use dbt for transformation logic and we track experiments in MLflow. We do code review on all model and pipeline code — this is not negotiable.

We have two open problems right now where we are genuinely stuck and would want a new hire to take a lead on within the first three months: improving recall on an imbalanced classification problem at around 2 million rows, and designing a multi-site inventory allocation system with a 48-hour planning horizon. Both have real clients waiting.

What we are looking for: at least four years of production ML experience, strong Python, comfort with SQL at a level where you can write and optimise non-trivial queries yourself, and experience with at least one pipeline orchestration tool. title: What we learned from six months of model drift in a churn-prediction deployment
text:
We have been running a churn-prediction model in production for a telecom client for about fourteen months. The model flags subscribers at risk of cancelling within 30 days, and the client's retention team uses those flags to prioritise outbound calls. It works well enough that the client renewed and expanded the retainer. But the past six months taught us a few things we did not fully anticipate when we launched, and they are worth writing down.

The first thing was how quickly the population shifted. Telecom subscribers are not a stable group — new tariff plans, competitor promotions, and seasonal patterns all change the distribution of features the model was trained on. We were monitoring overall accuracy and it stayed flat, which gave us a false sense of security. What was actually happening was that precision on the high-risk segment was holding up but recall was quietly falling. We only caught it because the client's retention team noticed their call conversion rate dropping and asked us to look again. The lesson: track the metrics that matter to the client's operation, not just the overall test-set numbers.

The second thing was class imbalance interacting with drift in an awkward way. Our churn rate sits around 6%, and as the feature distribution shifted, the model started under-predicting in exactly the subgroups where churn had increased — younger subscribers on prepaid plans. SMOTE at training time did not carry over to handle a distributional shift post-deployment.

We have since added stratum-level recall tracking to our monitoring dashboard and set up automatic alerts when any defined subgroup drops more than two points in a rolling 30-day window. We are also investigating whether a more frequent retraining cadence — monthly rather than quarterly — helps, though that increases compute and review costs that the client needs to approve.

Recall is still not where we want it. We are actively looking at approaches we have not tried yet. If you have worked on similar problems in high-imbalance binary classification, we are interested in talking.

title: Why Our Receipt Scanner Still Gets Thermal Paper Wrong (and What We Are Doing About It)
text:
About four in ten receipts that our subscribers upload come in as phone photographs rather than PDFs or scans. That is not surprising — most small retailers in Serbia still use thermal printers and hand you a paper receipt, not a PDF. You photograph it with your phone and upload it. That is a reasonable workflow.

The problem is that thermal paper is hard to read optically. The print contrast is lower than inkjet or laser. The paper often curls at the edges. The digits in the total and VAT fields are sometimes smaller than the rest of the text. And if the receipt sat in a pocket or a wallet for a day before being photographed, the image quality drops further.

Our OCR system — built on top of Tesseract with post-processing scripts that Milica wrote — handles clean scanned PDFs well. Thermal paper photographs are a different story. Our internal testing puts the error rate for the total amount field on thermal receipts at around 22 percent. That means roughly one in five thermal receipts comes back with a wrong number. When that wrong number flows into a VAT calculation, the subscriber may not notice until they compare with their bank statement or, worse, until the Tax Administration flags a discrepancy.

We have tried several things. Grayscale conversion and adaptive thresholding improved results on very low-contrast images. Deskewing helped when the photo was taken at an angle. But there is a ceiling to what rule-based image pre-processing can do when the underlying image quality varies as much as it does in practice.

We are now looking at whether a machine-learning approach to the image pre-processing step, or a purpose-trained text recognition model, could move the error rate down significantly. We have a reasonable volume of real receipt images with known correct values that we could use for testing. We do not have the internal machine-learning expertise to build this from scratch, which is part of why we are talking to the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad about finding a research collaborator.

If you are a subscriber and this problem has affected you, we are sorry. It is at the top of our list.

title: NebulaQ Completes First Full Pipeline Delivery for Delfaren Therapeutics
text:
We finished our first end-to-end pipeline delivery for Delfaren Therapeutics, a drug discovery company based in Rotterdam, in January 2024. This is worth writing about not because it was flawless — it was not — but because it was the first time we ran a client's actual molecule through MoleculeQ Pipeline and handed back numbers they used in a real project decision.

Delfaren gave us a target molecule they were evaluating for a binding affinity study. Their computational chemistry team had classical simulation results already and wanted to see how our quantum-based energy estimates compared. The molecule was small enough that we could represent it in twelve qubits, which is manageable on current hardware.

The results were mixed in a useful way. For the lowest-energy conformations, our estimates came within acceptable range of the classical reference. For two higher-energy conformations, the noise in the hardware pushed us outside the threshold Delfaren uses internally. We were transparent about this in the report. Their team appreciated the honesty and the detailed breakdown of where the error came from.

The outcome: Delfaren has renewed their contract for another six months and asked us to focus the next phase on improving accuracy for the higher-energy cases. That is exactly the problem our NoiseShield work is aimed at.

For us, this delivery confirmed that our pipeline infrastructure works end-to-end. It also gave us clean benchmark data on a real client molecule, which we will use internally (with Delfaren's permission, for the conformations they are comfortable sharing) as part of our ongoing error-mitigation development.

We are not claiming this as a breakthrough. It is a first step that went well enough to continue.

title: What NebulaQ Does — Services and Approach
text:
NebulaQ writes quantum algorithms for drug discovery. That is the short version. The longer version is that we take molecular simulation problems from pharmaceutical and biotech companies, convert them into quantum circuits, run those circuits on cloud-based quantum processors, and return energy estimates that slot into our clients' existing chemistry workflows without requiring them to understand anything about quantum hardware.

We built the NebulaQ SDK so that our own physicists could move faster when testing new circuit designs, but it has grown into the foundation of every service we offer. On top of the SDK we run MoleculeQ Pipeline, a managed service where a client uploads a molecular structure file and gets back a set of ground-state energy estimates, along with a short report on which parts of the calculation are being handled by quantum circuits versus classical pre- and post-processing.

We also sell access to NoiseShield, our error-mitigation layer. Current quantum processors introduce errors that make raw circuit outputs unreliable for chemistry applications. NoiseShield applies a configurable set of mitigation techniques before a circuit is submitted and corrects the results statistically after the job returns. It does not eliminate noise — nothing does on today's hardware — but it reduces the gap between raw output and chemically useful numbers.

Our clients are not universities or government labs. They are commercial drug discovery teams that have a specific computational bottleneck and a limited amount of patience for academic explanations. We measure our own work against the same accuracy thresholds they use for their classical simulation tools.

The team is based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad. We have six people: four physicists and two software engineers. We keep the team small on purpose. Every person here writes code or runs experiments; nobody is here just to manage other people.

If you have a molecular simulation problem and want to know whether quantum circuits can help with it today — not in five years, today — get in touch.

title: Why We Track Shot Count as a Business Metric
text:
Most quantum software teams talk about circuit depth or qubit count as their key technical metrics. We track those too, but the number that actually matters for our business is shot count — how many times we have to run a circuit to get a result accurate enough to hand to a client.

Here is why that number is tied directly to our costs. We access quantum hardware through IBM Quantum's cloud service. We pay for compute time. When our error-mitigation approach requires us to run the same circuit thirty times at different noise levels and combine the results, we are paying thirty times as much as we would for a single clean run. On small molecules with short circuits, that is manageable. As the molecules get larger and the circuits get deeper, it compounds quickly.

Our current mitigation approach — a combination of zero-noise extrapolation and partial probabilistic error cancellation — works in the sense that it improves accuracy. But the shot overhead it introduces is large enough that we cannot scale it to the molecule sizes our clients are starting to ask about. A client who wants to study a sixteen-qubit molecule instead of a twelve-qubit molecule does not expect to pay four times more. They expect roughly similar pricing because the molecule is only a little bigger.

So we are actively working on mitigation methods that give us better accuracy per shot rather than just more shots. We have been testing a symmetry-based post-selection approach that throws away results that violate known physical constraints of the molecule, which turns out to filter a surprising fraction of the noise without requiring extra circuit runs. Early numbers are promising but not yet conclusive across our full benchmark set.

We will write more about this once we have results we are confident in. For now: if you are building quantum software for commercial clients, track your shot count. It will tell you more about your business model than almost any other metric.

title: NebulaQ at the Central European Quantum Software Exchange, Vienna
text:
Three people from the NebulaQ team attended the Central European Quantum Software Exchange in Vienna on 17–18 April 2024. This is a small, practitioner-focused gathering — around ninety attendees this year — where quantum software teams from across the region present work in progress and discuss shared technical problems.

Our lead physicist, Tomáš Brežný, gave a twenty-minute talk on our NoiseShield mitigation approach, including the shot-count problem we described in our March blog post and the early results from our symmetry-based post-selection experiments. The talk was well-received in the sense that it generated useful pushback: two other teams in the room had tried similar approaches and hit different versions of the same wall, and the conversation after the session was the most technically dense discussion we have had outside our own office in a while.

We also had a brief meeting with representatives from Varion Quantum Systems, a hardware vendor we have been in early discussions with about backend access. Nothing was formalised at the event, but the conversation moved forward.

One of our software engineers, Milica Savić, attended a session on CI/CD practices for quantum software that she described as directly useful — specifically a discussion about how to structure automated testing when your test results have inherent statistical variance. We are going to apply some of what she heard to our GitHub Actions pipeline.

The event is not glamorous and that is fine. It is one of the few places where you can have a conversation about a specific technical problem with someone who has actually hit the same problem, rather than someone who is projecting about what the problems will be in the future. We will attend again next year.

title: What We Learned at Medicinska Oprema Expo 2023 in Beograd
text:
We exhibited at Medicinska Oprema Expo in November 2023, which brought together medical equipment suppliers, distributors, and procurement staff from hospitals and clinics across the former Yugoslavia. It was our third time at this fair, and a few things stood out as different from previous years.

First, occupational health clients are asking different questions than they were two or three years ago. In 2021, the main question was price and service coverage. This year, the dominant question from occupational health procurement staff was about software: can your system generate longitudinal trend reports automatically, and can it export directly into the national occupational health registry format? We heard this from at least eight different visitors over the two days. Our honest answer right now is: not fully, not yet. We have the data, we have the measurement history, but the automated reporting piece is something we are still working on. That is a gap we need to close.

Second, the conversations about device durability in industrial environments were more specific than we expected. Two visitors described situations where their current equipment — from other suppliers — had problems with humidity in factory medical rooms. We know this problem ourselves; it is something we are actively addressing on the SP-400 turbine assembly. Knowing that competitors have similar complaints does not solve our problem, but it confirms it is a real issue across the market and not something specific to how we design our devices.

Third, interest from North Macedonia and Kosovo was stronger than in previous years. We met four procurement contacts from Skopje and two from Priština who were specifically looking for a supplier with regional service coverage rather than relying on importers from Zagreb or Belgrade who subcontract local repairs.

Overall the fair was worth attending. We came back with twelve qualified leads and a clearer sense of where the product needs to develop over the next two years.

title: About Pulmoteh – Respiratory Diagnostics, Made in Serbia
text:
Pulmoteh d.o.o. was established in 2013 in Zrenjanin by Miroslav and Snežana Kovačević. Before founding the company, the two spent more than a decade servicing spirometry and pulmonary function testing equipment imported from Germany and the Netherlands on behalf of hospitals and occupational health services across Vojvodina. That work gave them a clear view of what local clinics actually needed and what the multinational suppliers were slow to provide: fast repairs, affordable consumables, and documentation that matched Serbian regulatory requirements without translation.

The company's first product was a calibration and maintenance kit for third-party spirometers, which it sold to clinics that could not afford the original manufacturer's service contracts. By 2016, Pulmoteh had developed its first own-brand device, the SP-200 desktop spirometry station, followed by the portable SP-400 in 2017.

Today Pulmoteh sells and services equipment in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. Our 27-person team covers product design, injection moulding of key plastic components, electronics assembly, calibration, and field service. We hold ISO 13485 certification and our devices carry CE marking under the EU Medical Device Directive.

Our customers range from single-physician pulmonology practices to large occupational health services that screen hundreds of workers per month. What they have in common is that they need equipment that is accurate, easy to maintain, and supported by a supplier who understands the working conditions and administrative requirements in this part of Europe.

Pulmoteh is wholly family-owned and intends to remain so. All decisions about product development, pricing, and service commitments are made by the people who will also answer the phone when a customer calls.

title: What We Do — Services Overview
text:
Vojvođanska Energetika d.o.o. offers energy services to industrial and agro-industrial facilities throughout Vojvodina. We are not a consultancy that hands over a report and leaves. We put our own financing into every project and recover it from the savings the project generates. That structure means our technical work has to be accurate; if the savings are not there, we carry the cost.

Our work falls into four areas.

Audit and baseline measurement. We send a team to your facility, instrument the main energy-consuming systems, collect at least three months of load data, and produce a report that quantifies consumption by end use and identifies the measures with the strongest payback. We have done this 130 times across Vojvodina since 1997.

Guaranteed savings contracts. Once an audit is complete and the retrofit scope is agreed, we finance the installation and write a contract guaranteeing a specific saving over the contract term — typically seven to twelve years. Your repayment comes out of your reduced energy bills.

On-bill repayment administration. For clients who prefer to keep the retrofit on their own balance sheet, we manage the repayment structure in coordination with their energy supplier so that the billing stays simple.

Monitoring and verification. For every active contract we maintain sub-metering at the point of each major retrofit measure and produce quarterly M&V reports showing actual savings against the contracted figure.

We work with food processors, oilseed crushers, cold-storage operators, packaging manufacturers, building materials producers, and commercial farms. If your facility runs heavy electrical or thermal loads and you want to reduce what you spend on energy without upfront capital, we are worth talking to. Contact our project office in Novi Sad to arrange an initial site visit.

title: Energy Systems Engineer — Simulation and Analysis
text:
We are looking for an engineer to join our technical team in Novi Sad. The role sits at the intersection of energy modelling and project delivery: you will support feasibility work for new contracts and improve the analytical tools we use across our existing portfolio.

The immediate focus of the role will be developing our capacity to model rooftop PV systems against complex industrial load profiles. We have clients asking whether PV can move them into a lower grid tariff band, and right now we cannot give them a confident answer. You will work with fifteen-minute interval meter data, compressor and refrigeration system specifications, and PV generation models to produce time-resolved simulations we can put in front of clients and network operators.

Over time the role will also contribute to improving our savings baseline methodology for seasonal facilities, which is a persistent source of financial exposure for us.

We use EnergyPlus for thermal modelling, standard power quality analysers for site measurement, and Excel-based M&V tools that we have built and maintained internally. We do not expect you to arrive knowing all of these; we do expect you to be comfortable working with time-series data, to have a working knowledge of electrical load analysis, and to have used at least one energy simulation platform.

Required: degree in electrical, mechanical, or energy engineering; experience handling and processing large meter datasets; ability to write clearly for non-technical readers.

Useful but not required: familiarity with Serbian grid tariff structures; experience with Python or similar for data processing; background in PV system design.

This is a full-time position based in Novi Sad. Salary is commensurate with experience. Send a CV and a brief note on relevant experience to our HR coordinator Jovana Mitrović.

title: Junior Data Analyst — Audit Portfolio
text:
Vojvođanska Energetika d.o.o. is hiring a junior analyst to help us get more out of the data we already hold. Over 27 years of operation we have accumulated 130 facility audit reports, two years of fifteen-minute interval meter data from 40 active contract sites, and a collection of M&V spreadsheets. Most of this information is not easy to access or compare across sites.

The core task in this role is to work with our audit team to develop a practical way of extracting key performance indicators from our PDF report archive and organising them in a form that engineers and project managers can query without specialist help. This is not a large-scale data engineering project; we need something that works with the tools and time we have.

You will also support quarterly M&V reporting by helping to process and quality-check the meter data feeds from our active sites.

We are looking for someone with a degree in a quantitative field, solid skills in Excel and at least one scripting language (Python preferred), and an interest in energy or industrial systems. Prior experience in the energy sector is not required. What matters is that you are careful with data and can communicate clearly about what the numbers do and do not show.

The role is based in our Novi Sad office. It is a good entry point for someone who wants to build a career in energy project analysis. Mentoring from senior engineers including Branislav Čović and project director Milena Savin is part of the offer. Send applications to Jovana Mitrović.

title: Contract Signed with Dunav Hladnjača for Seven-Year Retrofit Programme
text:
Vojvođanska Energetika d.o.o. has signed a seven-year guaranteed savings contract with Dunav Hladnjača, a cold-storage and distribution company operating two facilities near Novi Sad. The contract covers a package of measures including variable-frequency drives on the ammonia refrigeration compressors, LED lighting replacement across the warehouse areas, and insulation upgrades to two cold rooms that were identified in last year's audit as significantly underperforming.

The baseline audit, completed in October 2023 by our team under Branislav Čović, recorded total annual electricity consumption of approximately 4.2 GWh across the two sites. The contracted saving is 18 percent of that baseline, to be measured quarterly using sub-metering installed at each compressor bank and the main distribution boards.

Dunav Hladnjača operations director Svetlana Bojić commented: "We looked at several options for financing these improvements. What made Vojvođanska Energetika the right choice was that they are taking on the performance risk rather than asking us to. If the savings come in short, that is their problem to solve."

Installation of the VFDs and lighting is scheduled to begin in May 2024, with the refrigeration insulation work planned for the lower-throughput period in July. Full measurement and verification will begin once all measures are commissioned, expected by end of August.

This contract brings our active portfolio to 41 sites. We would like to thank the Dunav Hladnjača technical team for their cooperation during the audit and baseline measurement phase.

title: What We Learned from Three Years of Quarterly M&V Reports
text:
We have now run measurement and verification programmes on our retrofit contracts long enough to see some patterns worth sharing. This is not a research paper; it is what our own data tells us after 130 audits and three years of active M&V across a growing portfolio.

The measure that most consistently delivers close to its projected saving is LED lighting replacement in industrial spaces. Across 22 projects where lighting was a significant component, actual savings came in within eight percent of the contracted figure in 19 cases. The two outliers both involved facilities where production hours changed substantially after commissioning — one client moved to a six-day week, one reduced it. When the operating schedule holds steady, lighting predictions are reliable.

Variable-frequency drives on compressed-air and refrigeration systems are more variable. The average saving is in the right range, but the spread is wide. Sites with stable, continuous loads tend to perform well. Sites where demand fluctuates sharply — like seasonal processors — regularly come in below the baseline estimate. This is the area where our modelling methods need the most work, and it is something we are actively trying to improve.

Building envelope and insulation measures sit somewhere between the two. They tend to underperform in the first winter after commissioning and then stabilise. We now build a ramp-up adjustment into the first-year guarantee for those measures as a matter of course.

The broader point is that a guaranteed savings contract is only as good as the baseline model behind it. We have learned to be more conservative in our estimates for variable-production facilities, even when that makes the contract less attractive on paper. A contract we can honour is worth more than one that looks good at signing.

title: What We Make and Who We Make It For
text:
Poljoelektronika Kovačević designs and assembles sensor nodes for working farms. We are based in Zrenjanin, Vojvodina, and we have been doing this since 1993. Our core product is the KV-S3 node: a sealed unit that sits in your field, measures soil conditions and local microclimate around the clock, and sends that data to a base station over a LoRa radio link. You read the numbers on our web dashboard or receive an SMS alert when soil moisture drops below the threshold you set.

Each node measures soil moisture at 20 cm and 40 cm depth, soil temperature, air temperature and humidity at canopy level, and leaf wetness. The housing is polycarbonate with a silicone gasket rated to IP67. We use stainless steel ground stakes. The battery lasts through a full growing season under normal logging intervals.

The base station covers roughly two to three kilometres in open field conditions. Most of our customers run one base station per farm block and connect it to their existing internet router or a mobile data SIM.

Installation takes about 20 minutes per node. Dragan Kovačević or one of our two field technicians handles the first deployment and calibration visit. After that, most customers manage the system themselves.

We sell direct to cooperatives and larger family farms across Vojvodina and into Hungary. We also supply a small number of units through agricultural distributors. Maintenance contracts cover one calibration visit per season and same-week replacement of any failed unit from our stock in Zrenjanin.

We are a family business. Seven of us work here. When you call with a problem, you speak to someone who has stood in a field with one of these nodes in their hand.

title: Embedded Firmware Developer – Part-Time or Project Basis
text:
We are looking for someone who knows low-power embedded firmware and wants practical work with hardware that ends up in real fields.

The job is flexible: we are open to a part-time arrangement, a fixed-term project, or a student placement that runs alongside studies. Location is Zrenjanin, though some remote work is possible once you understand our codebase.

What the work involves:
Our KV-S3 node runs firmware written in C on an STM32L071 microcontroller. The main loop wakes from deep sleep, reads sensors over I2C and a custom analogue front end, packages a data frame, hands it to the SX1276 LoRa radio, then sleeps again. The work right now involves two things. First, we are reworking the power management to reduce average current draw from roughly 45 µA to under 30 µA in sleep mode; there are several peripheral shutdown sequences that are not yet optimal. Second, we want to add a simple over-the-air firmware update path using the existing LoRa link, because travelling to 1,200 nodes for a firmware change is not realistic.

What you need to know:
- C for bare-metal STM32, comfortable reading datasheets
- LoRa or LoRaWAN at the driver level is a clear advantage
- Basic understanding of I2C, SPI, UART
- Git

What you do not need:
RTOS experience, cloud platforms, app development. This is hardware-close work.

We use ST's HAL libraries as a base but the radio driver is our own. The codebase is about 6,000 lines and reasonably documented.

Pay is negotiated based on arrangement. We can provide hardware for home testing.

Contact Milica Kovačević at the address on our contacts page.

title: 200 New Nodes Deployed with Žitoprodukt Cooperative This Spring
text:
We finished the spring installation with Žitoprodukt, a grain cooperative operating across several municipalities in central Vojvodina, at the end of March. This is our largest single deployment to date: 200 KV-S3 nodes across roughly 1,800 hectares of arable land, covering corn, sunflower, and soy blocks.

The project started last autumn when Žitoprodukt's technical manager, Svetlana Marković, contacted us after seeing our nodes at a smaller neighbour's farm. They had been looking at systems from two larger Western European suppliers but wanted something that could be serviced locally and adapted to their specific alert thresholds without a software subscription that cost more than the hardware.

We spent November and December working through their field maps and agreeing on base station positions. Twelve base stations were mounted on existing equipment sheds and water tower structures to maximise coverage. Installation of the 200 nodes ran across six weeks in February and March with our team and two people from Žitoprodukt's own maintenance crew.

All 200 nodes are now live and Žitoprodukt's agronomists are using the dashboard to monitor soil moisture ahead of the first irrigation decisions of the season.

For us this is a meaningful step. Deploying at this scale with one customer has already surfaced a few things we need to improve in our base station configuration process, and Svetlana's team have been direct about what the dashboard is missing, which we appreciate. We will be working through those points over the summer.

The 200 units brought our total active deployment across Vojvodina to approximately 1,200 nodes.

title: What We Learned at AgroTechnika Novi Sad 2024
text:
We exhibited at AgroTechnika Novi Sad for the fourth time in May. Our stand was small, the same six square metres we have booked for years, with a working node on a soil column and a tablet showing live data from the field.

A few honest notes from the three days.

The conversations we had with Austrian and German visitors confirmed something our distributors have been telling us for a while: CE marking is not optional if we want to sell through organised channels in those markets. Two buyers were interested in stocking our nodes but both said the same thing: send us the DoC and the CE-marked label and we can talk. We have been aware of this for over a year and we are now treating it as the thing we fix before autumn.

There was also genuine interest in whether our nodes can report to third-party farm management platforms via a standard API. We have been asked this before and our answer has always been that we have a data export function but not a documented live API. We wrote down every company that asked and we will look at this properly after the CE project is done.

On the positive side, we met the team from a precision agriculture distributor in Hungary, Mezőtechnika Kft., who distribute a compatible base station antenna product. We had a useful conversation and exchanged contacts. Nothing signed, but worth following up.

The two days of driving and the stand fee are always a significant cost for a seven-person business. We will go again next year. The direct feedback is worth it, even when the feedback is about things we are not ready to fix yet.

title: Milica Kovačević Presents Data Archive Project at NTP Novi Sad Open Day
text:
Milica Kovačević attended the Science and Technology Park Novi Sad open day for SMEs in late August and gave a short presentation describing our eleven-year sensor data archive and the question we have been sitting on: whether the microclimate readings our nodes collect carry a usable early signal for pest pressure in corn and sunflower.

The presentation was about ten minutes. Milica walked through the structure of the archive, roughly 800 to 1,200 active nodes over eleven years at 15-minute intervals, alongside the digitised farm-book records we have collected from a subset of long-term customers. She was direct about the limitations: node ID changes across hardware generations, gaps in coverage, and inconsistent terminology in the farm-book data. The point was not to present a finished project but to describe what we actually have and ask whether anyone at the park or connected to it would find that dataset worth working with.

The response during the question session was encouraging. Several people asked about the format of the stored data and what kinds of pest observations were recorded. We were also asked about data access conditions, which is something we had not fully worked out before going in. We are thinking through what a data-sharing arrangement would look like that protects our customers' privacy and our own business interest while still making the archive genuinely useful to a research partner.

If anything concrete comes from the conversations started that day, we will post an update here.

title: Our Services — Pharmacogenomic Testing for Clinics and Pharmacies
text:
GenovaMed offers pharmacogenomic genotyping panels designed for use in everyday clinical and pharmacy practice in Serbia. Our core panel covers the CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 genes, which influence how patients process a wide range of commonly prescribed drugs including certain antidepressants, antiplatelet agents and proton pump inhibitors. We also offer an extended panel that adds CYP2C9, VKORC1 and SLCO1B1, which is relevant for patients starting anticoagulant or statin therapy.

How it works: a saliva or buccal swab sample is collected at your clinic or pharmacy using our collection kit, registered in our secure online portal, and couriered to our Novi Sad laboratory. Most results are available within three working days. Every report is checked by one of our clinical pharmacists before it is released, and we include a plain-language prescriber summary alongside the full genotype detail.

We work with independent pharmacies, specialist outpatient clinics, and general practice centres. For pharmacy partners, we offer a batch billing arrangement so that the administrative burden stays low. For clinics, we can integrate result delivery directly into your existing patient file workflow via our secure portal or SFTP.

Our laboratory holds ISO 15189 accreditation for the panel methods listed above. We are happy to provide our full validation documentation on request.

If you are considering adding pharmacogenomic testing to your service, we offer a no-obligation introductory call with one of our clinical pharmacists, who can walk through the evidence base for the specific drug classes most relevant to your patient population. Contact us at partneri@genomamed.rs or call our Novi Sad office directly.

Their staff took the sample collection training seriously and we had very few pre-analytical issues. Expanding to the full network is a straightforward next step for both sides.'

title: Junior Bioinformatics Engineer — NGS Pipeline Development
text:
GenovaMed is looking for a junior bioinformatics engineer to join our two-person bioinformatics team in Novi Sad. This is a hands-on role focused on maintaining and improving the computational pipeline we use to process short-read sequencing data from our pharmacogenomic panels.

What the work involves:
You will work directly on our Snakemake-based pipeline, which takes raw FASTQ files from our benchtop sequencer through alignment, variant calling, and star-allele assignment to produce structured output files consumed by our reporting layer. Your first project will be profiling the pipeline to find where compute time and cloud cost are concentrated, then testing changes — better instance types, step-level parallelisation, or algorithmic substitutions — to bring both figures down without affecting call accuracy. You will also help maintain our cloud infrastructure on a major European provider and contribute to internal documentation.

What we are looking for:
- Solid Python; familiarity with workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow
- Basic understanding of NGS data formats (FASTQ, BAM, VCF) and standard alignment tools
- Some experience with Linux command line and cloud VM environments
- An interest in the clinical context — you do not need a biology degree, but you should be curious about why the pipeline output matters

Nice to have: experience with cost optimisation on cloud platforms, or exposure to pharmacogenomics tools such as Stargazer or PyPGx.

This is a full-time position based in our NTP Novi Sad office, with some flexibility for remote days. Salary range: 90,000–110,000 RSD gross per month depending on experience. Send a CV and a short note about a pipeline or data engineering project you have worked on to posao@genomamed.rs.

title: What We Learned from Our First Year of Pharmacy-Based Sample Collection
text:
When we designed our panel, we assumed most samples would arrive from clinical settings — a nurse taking a buccal swab in a controlled environment, putting it straight into a stabilisation tube, and handing it to a refrigerated courier the same morning. That is not what pharmacy collection looks like.

In a pharmacy, the sample is often collected by the patient themselves using a self-collection kit over the counter. It might sit in a bag under the pharmacy counter for half a day before the courier arrives. The stabilisation tube might have been stored in a back room that gets warm in summer. None of this is negligence — it is just the reality of a retail environment, and it is different from a clinical lab assumption.

Over our first year of pharmacy-channel work, we tracked every sample that came back with an unresolved allele call. About 3% of pharmacy-sourced samples had at least one position we could not call with confidence, compared with under 0.5% of clinic-sourced samples processed in the same batches. The affected samples showed the kind of signal profile consistent with degraded or low-quantity input DNA.

We have tried a few things. We switched one cohort of pharmacy sites to a different extraction kit with a longer lysis step. We tightened the collection-to-pickup window from 48 hours to 24 hours for one subset of sites. Neither change moved the failure rate in a way that was clearly meaningful, but our sample sizes for each individual change were small enough that we cannot be confident we would have detected a modest effect.

We are now building a more structured experiment — keeping a set of control samples with known genotypes, deliberately varying storage time and temperature, and running each condition through the full extraction and sequencing process. We expect to have preliminary data by early summer. The goal is not a paper; it is a revised standard operating procedure we can hand to every new pharmacy partner. If you have worked through a similar problem in a non-clinical collection setting and want to compare notes, we are happy to talk.

title: Clinical Reporting Pharmacist (Part-Time)
text:
GenovaMed is hiring a part-time clinical pharmacist to support our result review and reporting function. This role is approximately 20 hours per week and can be structured flexibly around other commitments.

About the role:
Every genotype report we issue goes through a clinical review step before it reaches the prescriber. You will check that the automated star-allele call is consistent with the raw data, add any relevant drug-specific flags for the patient's reported medication list where that information is provided, and write or approve the plain-language prescriber summary. You will also be the first point of contact for phone or email queries from pharmacy and clinic partners about how to act on a result.

Over the next six months we also want to develop a plain-language patient-facing explanation of our results for a mobile web app. You will be closely involved in drafting that content and reviewing whether it accurately reflects the clinical meaning of each metaboliser category.

What we need:
- Licensed pharmacist with a clinical pharmacy background, or equivalent postgraduate training
- Familiarity with CYP enzyme pharmacology and drug interaction principles — you do not need prior pharmacogenomics experience, but you should be comfortable learning the star-allele framework quickly
- Clear written Serbian and working English
- Attention to detail and comfort working with a structured checklist-based review process

The role is based primarily in our Novi Sad office, with the option to work remotely on reporting days once settled in. Compensation: 55,000–65,000 RSD gross per month for 20 hours per week. Contact: posao@genomamed.rs with subject line 'Pharmacist application'.

title: Usluge — Datakor Consulting
text:
Datakor Consulting pomaže preduzećima u prerađivačkoj industriji i logistici da od operativnih podataka naprave alate koji se zaista koriste.

Naš pristup je praktičan. Pre nego što napišemo i jedan red koda, razgovaramo s ljudima koji svaki dan rade s podacima — menadžerima smena, kontrolorima kvaliteta, dispečerima. Razumemo šta im treba i šta su već probali. Tek tada projektujemo rešenje.

Šta radimo:

— Prediktivni modeli za industrijsku opremu i procese. Koristimo istorijske senzorske i ERP podatke da izgradimo modele koji upozoravaju na moguće zastoje ili odstupanja pre nego što postanu problem. Modele pratimo i ažuriramo nakon primopredaje.

— Operativni dashboardi. Projektujemo prikaze koji pokazuju tačno ono što menadžmentu treba da prati svaki dan — bez nepotrebnih grafova i bez tabela koje niko ne čita. Radimo s Grafanom i Metabaseom, i integrišemo se s ERP sistemima koje klijent već koristi.

— Automatizovano izveštavanje. Ako vaš tim svake nedelje ručno sastavlja isti izveštaj iz više izvora, možemo to automatizovati. Pipeline koji isporučujemo radi bez nadzora i javlja samo kad nešto nije u redu.

— Upravljanje kvalitetom podataka. Pomažemo klijentima da uspostave procese kojima osiguravaju da podaci koji ulaze u sistem budu tačni, potpuni i konzistentni — bez obzira na format ulaznih fajlova.

title: Zašto naši alarmi više nikoga ne zanimaju — i šta planiramo da uradimo
text:
Ovaj tekst je napisao Nemanja Radić, lead ML inženjer u Datakoru.

Pre nekoliko meseci, jedan od naših klijenata u automobilskom dobavnom lancu — ne mogu da navedem ime — pozvao me je na sastanak koji nisam zaboravio. Menadžer linije stavio je laptop preda mnom i pokazao ekran na kom je gorelo sedamnaest crvenih upozorenja. Pitao me je koliko je njih relevantno. Nisam znao. On je rekao: 'Ni mi ne znamo. Zato smo prestali da ih gledamo.'

Naš sistem za detekciju anomalija tada je imao stopu lažnih pozitiva oko 22% po smeni. To znači da je svaki četvrti-peti alarm bio šum, ne signal. Kada se to ponavlja svaki dan, mozak počne da tretira sve alarme kao pozadinski šum. To je prirodna reakcija. Problem je što prave greške prolaze zajedno s njima.

Šta smo probali: podešavali smo pragove ručno, uveli smo vremenski prozor za potvrdu, čak smo jedno vreme davali operaterima mogućnost da 'obuke' sistem glasanjem. Ništa nije dovoljno pomoglo jer su procesi na liniji zavisni od toliko promenljivih — temperatura u hali, smena, tip materijala — da statički pristup jednostavno ne prati tu dinamiku.

Imamo 18 meseci istorijskih logova i, što je dragoceno, imamo labele — tehničari su retroaktivno označili koji su alarmi bili lažni. To je nešto s čim se može raditi.

Trenutno istražujemo pristupe koji uzimaju u obzir kontekst procesa, a ne samo vrednost senzora u izolaciji. Cilj koji smo sebi zadali: ispod 5% lažnih pozitiva, bez povećanja propuštenih stvarnih grešaka. Ako nekoga interesuje ovaj problem — pišite.
