title: What HidroLogik Does
text:
HidroLogik Net is built around a single idea: all the information a water utility needs to run its network should live in one place and stay consistent. Asset records, pressure readings, meter data and billing exports all talk to the same PostgreSQL database, drawn on the same PostGIS-powered map. When a main breaks on a street, the dispatcher opens HidroLogik Net, finds the affected pipes, traces the isolation valves and sends a work order to the field crew—all without leaving the application.

HidroLogik Billing Bridge handles the back end. Meter readings collected on handheld devices or via AMR systems are validated, aggregated and pushed to the utility's billing software in whatever format it expects. We have written adapters for three different billing platforms currently in use across Vojvodina, and adding a new one takes roughly two weeks.

For engineers who need to model scenarios—planned maintenance shutdowns, new housing developments, fire-flow checks—HidroLogik Sim wraps EPANET 2.2 in a workflow that reads pipe diameters and lengths directly from the asset registry. There is no manual re-entry of network data.

HidroLogik Field is the mobile piece. Crews carry Android tablets, record valve inspections and meter swaps in the field, and the records sync to the main database when they return to coverage. The app works fully offline, which matters in the older parts of networks where mobile signal is poor.

We do not sell per-seat licences. Utilities pay an annual subscription that covers all users, support and updates. A utility with 15 000 connections pays the same rate per connection as one with 60 000. Implementation takes between six and twelve weeks depending on how complete the existing asset data is. We have done four implementations and all four went live within the agreed window.

title: Vodovod Sombor Completes Go-Live with HidroLogik Net
text:
HidroLogik d.o.o. is pleased to confirm that Vodovod Sombor has completed the transition to HidroLogik Net as its primary network management and billing-integration platform. The implementation began in October 2023 and took fourteen weeks, slightly longer than our standard window because Vodovod Sombor operates one of the older pipe networks in the region and a significant portion of their asset records existed only in hand-drawn ledgers that required digitisation before import.

The digitisation work was carried out jointly by Vodovod Sombor's technical staff and our field support team. By the end of the project, 98.4 percent of known pipe segments had been entered into the PostGIS asset registry with confirmed diameter, material and installation-year fields. The remaining 1.6 percent are sections where the physical record could not be located; these are flagged in the map with a distinct symbol so that dispatchers are aware of the uncertainty.

HidroLogik Billing Bridge is now running the nightly import from Vodovod Sombor's existing billing platform. Early figures show a 3 percent reduction in billing-cycle errors compared with the manual import process they used previously, which their billing manager, Milenko Đorđević, described as a meaningful improvement for a team of their size.

Vodovod Sombor has also deployed four additional pressure loggers in their southern distribution zone as part of the project, bringing their total sensor count to eleven. Those readings are now visible in HidroLogik Pressure Console alongside their existing northern-zone sensors.

With this go-live, HidroLogik Net is now in production at four utilities across Vojvodina, covering approximately 120 000 metered connections in total.

title: Why Our Leak Alarms Were Wrong Too Often (And What We Are Doing About It)
text:
A few months ago one of our customers—a utility with about 28 000 connections—asked us to explain why a leak alarm had fired three nights in a row in the same zone and the crews found nothing each time. It was a fair question. We looked at the data and found that the pressure drop that triggered the alarm matched the profile of a large irrigation customer on the edge of that zone who was running overnight watering cycles. The alarm was technically correct—there was a pressure anomaly—but it was not a leak.

That incident made us write down exactly what our current alarm logic does. It compares the rolling seven-day overnight minimum pressure for each sensor zone against a threshold, and fires when the reading drops more than a set number of bar below that baseline. That is all it does. It has no knowledge of consumption patterns, no awareness of season or day type, and no connection to the EPANET model that we already maintain for each of these networks.

The result is what you would expect: utilities that trusted the alarms early on have mostly stopped acting on them, which means we have a feature that exists in the product but is not actually being used.

We are not going to paper over this with a more complicated threshold. What we want to build is something that uses the pressure sensor data together with the hydraulic model and the consumption data we already hold to produce a short list of candidate leak locations, not just an alarm. Crews would go to two or three specific points, not to a whole zone.

We know roughly what this requires: some kind of inverse-problem approach that works backwards from pressure observations to likely pipe conditions. We do not have that expertise in-house. We are actively looking for people who do. If that sounds like your area, our contact details are on the website.

title: New Packaging Programme for Marta & Klen Natural Cosmetics
text:
Vizura Studio has completed a full packaging redesign for Marta & Klen, a natural cosmetics label based in Subotica. The project covered thirty-four SKUs across four product lines: facial care, body care, hair care and a seasonal gift range.

The brief came to us in late spring. The owners, Marta Vujić and Andrej Klen, wanted something that would read as a single family on shelf while keeping enough visual differentiation between the lines to help a shopper navigate quickly.

title: What We Learned From a Colour Problem That Cost Us a Contract
text:
At the end of last year we lost a contract we had been hoping to keep. The client was a Croatian household goods company. The reason was a colour shift between two components of the same shelf system, one printed offset and one printed digitally by a different vendor. Both files left our studio with the same Pantone reference. Both vendors confirmed they were printing to profile. On shelf, the two pieces looked like they had come from different brands.

We have been thinking about how that happened and what to change.

The short version: we had no system for comparing measurements across vendors over time. We own an X-Rite spectrophotometer and we use it at press proofs. But each reading stayed in the project folder for that job, never compared to readings from the same Pantone swatch printed by other vendors in previous months. When one vendor's profile drifted, we had no way to know it until a finished product was on a shelf three hundred kilometres away.

The fix is not expensive equipment. We already have the measurement tool. What we do not have is a simple, consistent protocol for recording readings and a way to flag when a vendor is outside tolerance. We are building that now. It is partly a process change and partly a question of finding the right lightweight tool for storing and comparing spectral data without requiring a full quality-management infrastructure.

We are writing about this not because we enjoy admitting failures but because we suspect we are not the only small studio in this situation. The colour management literature assumes either that you are a large printer with a full ICC workflow team, or that you are a single freelancer who eyeballs things. There is not much written for a fourteen-person studio that does serious print work but does not have a dedicated prepress engineer. If you are working on this problem too, we are interested in talking.

title: What We Do – Vizura Studio
text:
Vizura Studio designs packaging, builds brand identities and makes short-form video. We have been doing this in Novi Sad since 2011, and most of our clients are mid-size companies in Serbia and Croatia that sell physical products to consumers.

Packaging is the largest part of our work. We handle everything from the initial structural brief through to print-ready files and press supervision. We work with cartons, labels, flexible pouches, and multi-unit shelf-ready trays. Our prepress capability is internal, which means we can catch problems before they reach a vendor rather than after.

Brand identity projects usually start with an audit of how a client's mark and colour system behave across the materials already in use. We produce a working guidelines document rather than a decorative brand book, meaning the output is a file set that a printer, a developer or an in-house team can actually apply without calling us first.

Motion graphics and short-form video are a growing part of the studio. We produce animated social content, product reveal sequences and in-store screen loops. Most of this is done in After Effects, with Cinema 4D for projects that require three-dimensional product rendering. We currently use a trusted external collaborator for the more complex 3D work while we build that capability in-house.

Clients tend to stay with us for more than one project. We think that is because our estimates are reliable, our files are clean, and we tell clients when a request will cause a production problem rather than discovering it at proof stage.

If you have a project you would like to discuss, the best first step is to send us a short brief and a list of the substrates and vendors already in your supply chain. That lets us give you a useful answer on day one rather than a placeholder.

title: Tamara Vukić se priključuje timu kao specijalist za izveštavanje
text:
Od septembra 2023. godine Tamara Vukić radi kao peti stalni član tima Analitika Petrović. Tamara dolazi sa iskustvom u finansijskom izveštavanju i radu sa Excel i Metabase alatima, a pre dolaska kod nas radila je u računovodstvenoj firmi u Zrenjaninu.

Njena uloga u timu je preuzimanje izveštajnih zadataka koji ne zahtevaju programiranje — prilagođavanje postojećih izveštajnih šablona, komunikacija sa klijentima oko zahteva za izveštajima, i dokumentovanje sistema koje isporučujemo.

Ovim zapošljavanjem rešili smo deo problema koji smo imali tokom 2023. godine: previše izveštajnih zadataka padalo je na Milicu, koja treba da se fokusira na razvojne zadatke. Sada je podela posla jasnija.

Dobrodošla, Tamara.

title: Završili smo implementaciju sistema za praćenje senzora u Agrozaštita Dunav d.o.o.
text:
U novembru 2023. godine završili smo projekat koji smo s ponosom pratili od prvog sastanka — implementaciju sistema za praćenje senzorskih podataka u skladišnim silosima preduzeća Agrozaštita Dunav d.o.o. iz okoline Zrenjanina.

Agrozaštita Dunav prerađuje i skladišti voće i povrće i imala je problem koji mnoge firme u ovoj branši prepoznaju: senzori su godinama prikupljali podatke o temperaturi, vlažnosti i CO₂, ali te podatke niko nije sistematski čitao. Podaci su bili u nekoliko različitih formata, deo na lokalnim računarima, deo na eksternom disku koji niko nije pregledao od 2021. Naš zadatak bio je da sve to spojimo, očistimo i stavimo u upotrebu.

Instalirali smo TimescaleDB instancu na njihov server, napisali skripte za automatsko unošenje novih merenja i podesili Grafana kontrolnu tablu dostupnu svim tehnolozima iz interne mreže. Mesečni izveštaj koji je ranije zahtevao dva dana ručnog rada sada se generiše automatski.

Na projektu su radili Milica Petrović i Nenad Brkić. Hvala timu Agrozaštita Dunav na strpljenju tokom testiranja — imali smo nekoliko iteracija pre nego što je sve leglo na mesto.

Ovaj projekat za nas nije bio samo tehnički zadatak. Pokazao nam je gde su granice naše sadašnje infrastrukture i šta treba da unapredimo u narednom periodu.

title: O nama i uslugama — Analitika Petrović
text:
Analitika Petrović je porodična firma iz Zrenjanina koja se bavi analitikom podataka i poslovnim izveštavanjem od 1997. godine. Osnivač Dragan Petrović počeo je sa radom sa lokalnim prerađivačima hrane koji su imali pune fascikle podataka, ali nisu imali alat da ih protumače. Od tada smo izgradili sistem rada koji polazi od konkretnog pitanja klijenta — šta zapravo treba da znate? — i odatle idemo unazad do podataka.

Naše usluge obuhvataju:

- Projektovanje i izradu izveštajnih sistema prilagođenih industriji klijenta
- Integraciju podataka iz senzora, mernih uređaja, ERP i računovodstvenih sistema
- Razvoj jednostavnih modela za praćenje i predviđanje procesa
- Vizualizaciju podataka putem Grafana i Metabase kontrolnih tabla dostupnih na intranetu klijenta
- Obuku osoblja za svakodnevni rad sa izveštajnim alatima

Svi naši sistemi rade na infrastrukturi klijenta, bez obaveznog oslanjanja na eksterne cloud servise. Razumemo da mnogi naši klijenti imaju ograničenja u pogledu bezbednosti podataka, troškova i internet konekcije — i projektujemo rešenja koja rade u tim uslovima.

Tim čine Dragan Petrović, Milica Petrović, Jovanka Stanić (analitičar podataka), Nenad Brkić (sistem administrator) i Tamara Vukić (izveštavanje i dokumentacija). Svih pet nas radi iz Zrenjanina.

Ako imate podatke koje ne znate kako da iskoristite, ili izveštaje koji oduzimaju previše vremena, slobodno nas kontaktirajte.

title: Zašto naši izveštaji rade bez interneta — i zašto to ne menjamo
text:
Česta reakcija kada predstavimo naše rešenje novim klijentima je pitanje: zašto ne koristite cloud? Pitanje je razumno, pa ćemo pokušati da odgovorimo iskreno.

Većina naših klijenata su industrijska preduzeća u Vojvodini sa stabilnom ali ne brzom internet konekcijom, sa IT odeljenjima koja imaju dva do tri čoveka i sa politikama bezbednosti podataka koje zabranjuju ili komplikuju slanje operativnih podataka izvan lokalne mreže. Neki imaju i ugovornu obavezu da podaci o procesu ostanu na lokaciji. U tom kontekstu, cloud rešenje nije nemoguće, ali nosi troškove i birokratske prepreke koje mali i srednji prerađivači teško opravdavaju.

Mi projektujemo sisteme koji rade na serverima koje klijent već ima ili koji koštaju koliko jedan rabljeni server — TimescaleDB na Linuxu, Grafana za vizualizaciju, Metabase za izveštavanje. Sve otvorenog koda, sve što se može održavati bez godišnje pretplate.

Postoje granice ovog pristupa. Skalabilnost nije beskonačna, i mi to znamo bolje od bilo koga — upravo se suočavamo sa tim izazovom kod jednog od naših klijenata čija baza raste brže nego što smo planirali. Ali rešenje tog problema ne znači automatski 'idi u cloud'. Znači pametnije upravljanje podacima na raspoloživom hardveru.

Pišemo ovo jer mislimo da ima vrednosti u pristupu koji polazi od realnih uslova klijenta, a ne od pretpostavke da svako može i želi da plati mesečnu pretplatu za infrastrukturu. Ako imate slično iskustvo ili drugačije mišljenje, slobodno nas kontaktirajte.

title: Tražimo: Python developer za analitiku podataka (honorarno ili puno radno vreme)
text:

title: Analitika Petrović na Vojvođanskom sajmu prehrambene industrije 2024
text:

Posetioci mogu da vide kako izgleda praćenje temperature i vlažnosti u realnom vremenu, kako se postavljaju alarmi i kako izgleda automatski mesečni izveštaj.

title: Services – Custom Synthesis and Analytical Characterisation
text:
ChemoSpec Solutions provides custom organic synthesis and analytical chemistry services to clients in the pharmaceutical, agrochemical, and fine chemical sectors. Our work divides into three main areas.

Reference Standards and Certified Compounds
We synthesise organic reference standards to client specifications, typically at the one-to-fifty milligram scale, with full analytical documentation. Each compound is delivered with a certificate of analysis covering structure confirmation by NMR (1H and 13C), high-resolution mass spectrometry, and HPLC purity determination. Turnaround from confirmed order to delivery is typically three to six weeks depending on route complexity.

API Intermediates and Building Blocks
We prepare small batches of API intermediates and synthetic building blocks for clients in early-stage development who need material for formulation trials or stability studies before committing to a larger manufacturing contract. Our team has particular experience with beta-lactam frameworks, protected amino acids, and heterocyclic scaffolds. Batches typically run from one gram to one hundred grams.

Analytical Packages
For clients who synthesise in-house but lack characterisation capability, we offer standalone analytical services: NMR data collection and interpretation, mass-spec analysis, HPLC purity profiling, and basic impurity identification. Reports are formatted to support regulatory submissions under ICH Q2(R1) guidelines.

All work is carried out at our laboratory at the Novi Sad Science Technology Park. We operate under a documented quality system and maintain batch records for every synthesis. Clients receive all raw data files alongside the final report.

We work with clients across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Hungary, and Slovenia. We prefer to discuss each request directly before quoting, since scope and timeline are easier to agree early than to renegotiate later. Contact us by email or through the form below.

text:

What the role involves:
You will carry out multi-step organic synthesis for client orders, primarily reference standards and API intermediates. That means planning routes from literature or in-house precedents, running reactions at the five-to-fifty milligram scale, purifying products by column chromatography or recrystallisation, and handing characterised material over to our analytical chemist. You will also keep accurate batch records and flag any issues with yield or purity to the project lead.

What we use day to day:
- Standard glassware synthetic setup, rotary evaporation, short-path distillation
- Bruker 300 MHz NMR for routine structural checks

You should be comfortable working independently on a route once it has been agreed, and honest about uncertainty when a step is not behaving as expected. Experience with heterocyclic chemistry or beta-lactam synthesis is useful but not required.

We do not expect you to know everything. We do expect careful work and clear communication.

The position is full time, based in Novi Sad. Salary is in line with NTP-sector norms and negotiable based on experience. Send a CV and a short note about your synthesis background to posao@chemospec.rs.

title: ChemoSpec Delivers First Batch of Twelve Reference Standards to Agrovita Group
text:
ChemoSpec Solutions has completed its first supply order for Agrovita Group, an agrochemical company based in Novi Sad that develops and registers crop-protection products in the Western Balkans market. The order covered twelve organic reference standard compounds needed for residue analysis method validation in Agrovita's regulatory submissions.

The compounds ranged from simple aromatic structures to more complex heterocyclic molecules with chiral centres. All twelve were delivered with full analytical packages including 1H and 13C NMR, high-resolution ESI-MS, and HPLC purity data, formatted to meet the documentation requirements Agrovita had been given by their registration consultants.

The project ran over nine weeks from signed order to final delivery. Two of the twelve compounds required route modifications after the initial synthesis attempts gave purity results below specification; both were resolved by adjusting the purification sequence rather than redesigning the route.

Dragana Miletić, ChemoSpec's founding chemist, said the collaboration was a useful test of the team's capacity to run multiple synthesis projects in parallel under a shared deadline. 'We kept all twelve on schedule even when two needed extra work. That's what we built the team to handle.'

Agrovita's head of regulatory affairs, Tomislav Fekete, noted that the documentation quality reduced the time his team spent checking data before incorporating it into submission files.

ChemoSpec and Agrovita are discussing a framework agreement for ongoing reference standard supply covering the next product registration cycle, which is expected to require a further eighteen to twenty-four compounds over the following year.

title: What We Learned from Six Months of Halogenated Solvent Tracking
text:
Earlier this year we decided to start recording our solvent waste volumes more carefully, partly because our disposal costs were becoming hard to ignore and partly because we kept having vague internal conversations about 'doing something about DCM' without any real numbers in front of us.

So we tracked it. For six months, every synthesis batch that used dichloromethane or chloroform at the extraction or workup stage was logged: volume of solvent used, volume of waste collected, and which synthesis route it came from.

The result was clearer than we expected. Two routes accounted for about eighty percent of our halogenated waste. Both are beta-lactam intermediate syntheses that we run repeatedly because they are part of our core service offering. Together they generate somewhere around eight hundred litres of waste per month, which costs us roughly four thousand two hundred euros to dispose of under our current contract.

Knowing that changes the conversation. Instead of a general ambition to 'use greener solvents,' we now have a specific target: those two routes, those two workup steps.

We have started reading more carefully about solvent substitution in beta-lactam chemistry. 2-MeTHF comes up frequently as a DCM replacement in extraction steps and has a more acceptable environmental profile. Ethyl acetate is even simpler. We ran one small substitution trial with ethyl acetate in one of the routes and got acceptable yield but purity dropped in a way we have not fully explained yet.

We are not claiming to have solved this. The ring chemistry is sensitive and we are cautious about changing a step that currently works. What we want is a proper screening study with enough data to make a decision, not a single trial run at two in the afternoon when someone had spare time.

If you have worked through solvent substitution in similar ring-forming reactions and want to compare notes, we would be glad to hear from you.

title: What We Do — Sunčana Mreža d.o.o.
text:
Sunčana Mreža designs, builds, and monitors photovoltaic systems for businesses and institutions across Vojvodina. We have been doing this since 2014 and we have learned a great deal about what makes a solar installation perform well over ten, fifteen, or twenty years — and what makes it underperform.

Our work starts before anyone orders a panel. A site survey team visits your building or land, records the roof structure or ground conditions, maps obstacles that could shade your array, and checks the available grid connection capacity. From that information our engineers produce a detailed electrical design and a yield estimate that we are confident enough to back with a performance guarantee.

Construction is handled by our own installation crews, supported by a network of qualified subcontractors for civil work on larger ground-mounted sites. We coordinate the grid connection application with the distribution operator and stay involved until the system is officially commissioned and handing energy to your meter.

After commissioning, every system we install is connected to SolarPulse, our monitoring platform. SolarPulse reads data from your inverters every thirty seconds, calculates daily and monthly performance ratios, and sends you automated reports. If output drops below expected levels you receive an alert. Our monitoring team reviews alarms and decides whether a remote intervention is sufficient or whether a field visit is needed.

Most of our clients are in food processing, logistics, manufacturing, and warehousing — sectors where electricity is a significant operating cost and where a flat, unobstructed rooftop is usually available. Project sizes typically range from 200 kW to 2 MW, though we have completed smaller installations for municipal clients and larger ones for industrial parks.

Our office is in Novi Sad. Field teams can reach any site in Vojvodina within ninety minutes, which matters when something needs attention quickly.

title: Sunčana Mreža completes 1.4 MW installation at Adriatik Pakovnica facility in Inđija
text:
Sunčana Mreža has completed and commissioned a 1.4 MW rooftop PV installation at the Inđija production and warehousing campus of Adriatik Pakovnica, a packaging materials manufacturer.

The project was contracted in September 2023 and took approximately five months from structural survey to final grid connection approval. The array covers three roof sections across two buildings and feeds directly into the facility's medium-voltage internal network. A dedicated SolarPulse connection gives the Adriatik Pakovnica energy team access to live yield data and monthly performance reports.

The installation presented a number of practical challenges. The older of the two buildings had a corrugated steel roof with non-standard purlin spacing, which required a custom mounting solution developed together with the structural subcontractor. A cluster of large rooftop air-handling units on the newer building created a shading pattern that our engineering team modelled carefully during the design phase to position strings where output loss would be minimal.

Dragan Kovačević, one of the company's founders, said the project was a good example of what Sunčana Mreža tries to do in Vojvodina's industrial sector: straightforward engineering, no surprises at commissioning, and a monitoring connection that gives the client real numbers rather than estimates.

Adriatik Pakovnica's technical director, Branislav Fehér, noted that the company had evaluated two other suppliers before selecting Sunčana Mreža, and that the combination of local presence and in-house monitoring software was the deciding factor.

The system is expected to cover approximately 35% of the facility's annual electricity consumption based on the first full month of metered output.

title: Why our rooftop yield estimates are sometimes wrong — and what we are doing about it
text:
We want to be honest about something that has come up in a few client conversations over the past year: on some of our rooftop installations the actual annual yield has come in below the P90 figure we quoted at proposal stage. In the worst cases the gap has been around 10 to 12%. That is not a small number when a client has made a financial case based on our estimate.

The cause, in almost every case, is shading from rooftop equipment — HVAC units, ventilation stacks, exhaust fans, water tanks, and similar structures. These objects cast moving shadows across the array throughout the day and across the seasons. Their effect on output depends on their height, their exact position relative to each string of panels, and how the inverters respond to partial shading.

We use PVsyst for our yield models, which is a capable tool. The problem is not the software — it is the time required to build an accurate three-dimensional scene of a complex industrial rooftop before a contract is signed. A thorough model of a rooftop with a dozen large obstacles can take a senior engineer three to four hours. At proposal stage, when we may be preparing estimates for several sites in parallel, we usually build a simplified scene. That is where the error enters.

For sites where we have already done a drone survey — which we do for every project before construction — we have detailed point-cloud data. The question is how to turn that data into a shading estimate quickly enough to use it in a proposal, not just after the contract is awarded.

We do not have a complete answer to this yet. We are looking at whether there are faster ways to extract obstacle geometry from point clouds and feed it into a simulation. We are also talking to people who work on this kind of spatial data processing. If you have relevant experience or ideas we would be glad to hear from you.

title: FermenTech Vojvodina Listed with Grünbach Organic Retail — 22 Stores Across Germany from September
text:
We are pleased to confirm that our lacto-fermented red pepper spread and our plant-based kefir analogue drink will be listed in all 22 Grünbach organic retail locations in Germany from September 2023.

The listing came after a six-month trial in four pilot stores, during which both products remained on shelf and achieved reorder rates that met the Grünbach buyer criteria. The pepper spread was placed in the ambient fermented goods section; the kefir analogue in chilled drinks.

Negotiations were handled with the support of our Hamburg-based distributor Nordalto, who has represented our products in Germany since early 2022. We are grateful for their patience and persistence through a buyer review process that took longer than any of us expected.

This listing represents the largest single retail partnership FermenTech has secured to date. Volume commitments for the first six months require us to produce approximately 4,800 units of the kefir analogue and 3,200 units of the spread per month specifically for this channel, which has pushed us toward the 2,000-litre production scale we began commissioning in Q3 2023.

We are aware that retail listings create accountability. Our products carry live-culture and fermented-food credentials that depend entirely on what is actually in the bottle or jar when it reaches a customer. We are investing in process control and shelf-life monitoring to make sure those credentials hold.

For trade and distribution enquiries related to the German or Austrian market, contact our export sales coordinator Bojana Milošević at izvoz@fermentech-voj.rs.

title: What We Learned at Anuga 2023 — A Brief, Honest Report
text:
Three of us attended Anuga in Cologne in October — myself (Dragana Vukić, production), Bojana from sales and our managing director Srđan Kelić. We had a shared stand in the Organic hall, arranged through the Serbian national pavilion. Here is what we actually found useful and what we would do differently.

The useful parts: we had 11 meetings with buyers or distributors that we scheduled in advance via the trade matchmaking portal. Of those, four led to follow-up correspondence within two weeks of the fair. Two of those four are still active conversations as of this writing. The ratio is roughly what we expected — trade fairs are slow funnels, not instant deals.

We also spent time walking the fermented foods, functional beverages and dairy-alternative sections of the fair. The volume of plant-based kefir and kvass-style drinks from Eastern European producers was notably higher than at the previous Anuga we attended in 2019. Competition in this segment is clearly growing. Several of the products we saw carried live-culture claims in prominent positions on the label, which made us think more carefully about how we substantiate and defend our own claims — something we are currently working on.

The less useful parts: our stand graphics were too text-heavy and our product sampling setup was not cold enough for the first two days because the refrigeration unit we rented underperformed. We lost sampling quality at the worst possible time. Next time we bring our own validated cooling box.

Would we go again? Yes, but we would go smaller — two people, pre-scheduled meetings only, no walk-in stand traffic as the primary objective. The real value at a fair this size is in the meetings you planned before you arrived.

If you met us at Anuga and have not heard back, please write to info@fermentech-voj.rs. We are working through follow-ups now.

title: About FermenTech Vojvodina — Who We Are and What We Make
text:
FermenTech Vojvodina d.o.o. is a food production company based at the Novi Sad Science Technology Park. We make lacto-fermented vegetable products, plant-based fermented drinks and functional beverages for health-food retailers and HoReCa operators in Serbia and the European Union.

We started in 2018 with a single 200-litre fermentation tank, a small cold room and a clear idea: use the fermentation knowledge that has always existed in Vojvodina kitchens and apply it consistently and safely at a commercial scale. Six years later we have 34 employees, ISO 22000 certification, regular export to Germany, Austria and the Netherlands, and a product range that is grounded in measurable microbiological data rather than marketing language.

Our production facility sits inside the NTP Novi Sad campus. The location gives us access to technical infrastructure and lets us stay in contact with researchers and engineers working on applied problems similar to our own. We value that proximity.

Every product we make starts with a defined starter culture — a specific blend of lactic acid bacteria that we have selected, tested and logged. We do not use generic off-the-shelf starters for our core range. We track fermentation by pH and temperature from inoculation to filling, and we run colony counts at bottling and through shelf life. When a batch falls outside our parameters, we do not ship it.

Our team includes people who have worked in larger food manufacturing and people who came directly from food science training. Head of production Dragana Vukić manages daily operations and process documentation. Quality manager Tomislav Horváth oversees HACCP compliance, lab testing and customer audit responses. Fermentation technologist Milena Đurić handles starter culture maintenance and in-house product development.

We sell to distributors and directly to retail buyers. Our current retail partners include Grünbach organic stores in Germany and the Zelena Polica chain in Serbia. Our HoReCa volumes go through Nordalto in Hamburg and Adriafresh in Ljubljana.

If you are a buyer, distributor or potential research partner, the contact form below reaches our commercial team directly.

title: Our Services
text:

Our core offering is a Windows desktop application for day-to-day bookkeeping and document handling. It connects to a local or small-server database, runs without an internet connection, and produces reports in the formats that Austrian and Slovenian tax authorities accept. We have been extending and revising the same codebase for over fifteen years, which means it is stable and well understood rather than fashionable.

Alongside the desktop application we offer a web-based document archive module. Scanned invoices, contracts, and correspondence go into the archive; staff can search and retrieve them from any browser on the office network. We also handle migrations when clients move to or from other platforms, and we write custom invoicing or reporting add-ons when the standard module does not cover a client's needs.

Support is direct. When something breaks, you call Dragan or Miroslav, not a helpdesk queue. We answer in German or English and we know your installation because one of us set it up.

If you run a small accounting office and your current software is making your work harder rather than easier, get in touch. We are happy to look at what you have and give you an honest view of what is realistic.

title: What We Learned From 340 Hours of Legacy Migration Work
text:
Earlier this year we quoted 200 hours to migrate twelve years of desktop accounting data for a client in Linz who was moving to a cloud platform. We are now past 340 hours and not finished. We want to write honestly about why, partly because it is useful to us to put it in writing, and partly because if you are considering a similar project you should know what the risks actually look like.

The short version: we sampled the wrong years. We asked for a representative export before quoting and the client sent us three years' worth. Those three years happened to have been managed consistently. The other nine had not.

The specific problems we found:

Field structure changed four times between 2008 and 2016. Two of those changes were undocumented. We found them by comparing row counts against totals in the client's paper records.

Attachments from 2010 to 2013 were stored as relative file paths that pointed to a server that no longer exists. We recovered about 70 percent of them from a backup drive the client found in a cabinet. The rest are gone.

Two years of data had been processed through an intermediate system that added columns with no labels. We eventually worked out what three of the four unlabelled columns contained. The fourth remains unclear and we have marked those records for manual review.

What we would do differently: ask for exports from every year, not a sample. Agree in the contract that unknown format variations will be billed at an hourly rate above the fixed fee. Budget explicitly for manual review.

We will finish this migration. The client has been patient and we are grateful for that. But we will quote this kind of work differently from now on.

title: AquaVoj completes wastewater upgrade for Bečej — plant now meets EU discharge standards
text:
AquaVoj d.o.o. handed over the upgraded wastewater treatment plant in Bečej to the municipal utility JKP Čistoća Bečej on 14 November 2023, following 18 months of construction and an eight-week commissioning period.

The upgraded facility replaces an oxidation pond system that had been in service since 1981 and had not met current discharge limits for biological oxygen demand or total nitrogen for several years. The new plant uses a two-stage activated sludge process with a capacity of 8,500 population equivalents, UV disinfection of final effluent, and automated SCADA monitoring that transmits real-time data to the utility's control room.

Dragan Mirković, chief engineer at AquaVoj, said the project presented specific challenges because the old ponds occupied the same footprint as the new plant, requiring careful sequencing of demolition and construction to keep basic treatment running throughout. The construction phase was completed within the contracted timeline despite three weeks of weather delays in the winter of 2022.

The Bečej municipality director of infrastructure, Lidija Vuković, thanked the AquaVoj team for maintaining open communication throughout the project and noted that the utility's operators had received thorough training before handover.

AquaVoj will provide a two-year operations support contract for the plant, covering monthly performance reviews and on-call technical assistance.

The project was financed through a combination of municipal budget funds and a grant from the Serbian Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund.

title: What We Do — AquaVoj d.o.o.
text:

title: What heavy rainfall does to our treatment plants — and why it is harder to fix than it looks
text:
Every year, as soon as the spring rainfall season starts, we begin watching our manganese readings more carefully. And most years, at least at a few of our plants, we end up in a difficult conversation with an inspector.

Here is the basic problem. Groundwater in parts of Vojvodina naturally carries elevated iron and manganese. Standard treatment — aeration to oxidise the metals, then filtration through sand — works well under stable conditions. Our plants hit their permit limits for months at a stretch with no issues.

Then a heavy rainfall event arrives. Infiltration pushes through the unsaturated zone into the aquifer, changing the redox conditions and, we believe, mobilising manganese that had been sitting in reduced form in the sediment. The raw water chemistry at the borehole changes faster than our treatment settings can follow. Within 24 to 48 hours, treated water manganese is above the 0.05 mg/L limit.

We have tried increasing aeration rates. We have tried extending filter run lengths. We have tried raising pH with lime. Each approach helps somewhat but none of them has solved the problem durably. Part of the difficulty is that we do not fully understand what form the manganese is in during these events — whether it is dissolved, colloidal or partly bound to organic matter — and each form responds differently to treatment.

This is not a new problem in Vojvodina waterworks. But the regulatory tolerance for exceedances has tightened in the past two years and fines are now a real possibility for utilities that exceed limits even temporarily.

We are currently looking for people who have worked on manganese removal under variable raw water conditions and who can help us understand what the chemistry is actually doing before we invest further in equipment changes. If that describes you or your team, we would like to talk.

Contact us at tehnika@aquavoj.rs.

title: Services – Geodata Pro d.o.o.
text:
We offer four main service lines, each built around the idea that spatial data is only useful when it is accurate, current, and delivered in a format the client can actually work with.

**Aerial survey and photogrammetry.** We operate two fixed-wing aircraft equipped with calibrated metric cameras. Flights are planned to client-specified ground sampling distances, typically between three and eight centimetres for urban projects. Deliverables include georeferenced orthomosaics, digital surface models, and digital terrain models, all supplied in coordinate systems agreed with the client before the flight.

**LiDAR acquisition and point-cloud processing.** Our airborne LiDAR sensors record first and last returns at densities appropriate to the application — from two points per square metre for corridor mapping to twenty or more for detailed urban surveys. Point clouds are classified into ground, low vegetation, medium vegetation, high vegetation, building, and noise classes. Feature extraction — building footprints, kerb lines, power-line geometry — is available as an additional deliverable.

**Cadastral and utility GIS integration.** We receive source data from municipal cadastre offices, utility network operators, and road agencies, and we build unified spatial databases in PostGIS or ArcGIS Enterprise. This includes coordinate transformation, identifier harmonisation, topology validation, and attribute schema reconciliation.

**Spatial data quality auditing.** For clients who already hold GIS datasets and need an independent assessment before a major infrastructure decision, we carry out structured audits covering positional accuracy, attribute completeness, topological integrity, and compliance with Serbian and EU spatial data standards.

All projects are managed through a single point of contact and close with a written data-quality report. We do not subcontract survey flights.

title: Geodata Pro completes corridor survey for Vojvodina road agency
text:
We have delivered the final dataset from a 220-kilometre road-corridor LiDAR survey commissioned by the Vojvodina Regional Road Maintenance Agency. The project covered two regional road axes in southern Bačka and was completed across four flight days in March, with ground control established at 38 points by our field team.

The deliverable package included a classified point cloud, a 5 cm resolution digital terrain model, an orthoimage mosaic at 4 cm ground sampling distance, and a GIS layer of detected pavement edge breaks, drainage structures, and overhead obstacle clearances. The agency's asset management team will use the dataset to plan resurfacing priorities for the 2025 maintenance cycle.

Project lead Milica Vranić noted that coordinating the ground control network across a dispersed rural corridor required more pre-flight planning than a compact urban block survey, but that the consistency checks we run between overlapping flight strips caught two areas where ground settlement had affected our reference benchmarks — both were reoccupied before processing began.

The agency has indicated interest in a repeat survey in 2026 to compare change in pavement condition, which would be the first multi-temporal LiDAR comparison dataset we have produced for a road client. We are treating that as a genuine technical interest to explore rather than a confirmed contract.

We have now completed LiDAR or photogrammetric surveys covering just over 4,800 kilometres of road and utility corridors since 2011. Road and infrastructure corridors represent approximately forty percent of our project volume by flight hours. If your organisation manages linear infrastructure and you have questions about what a survey programme would involve, contact us at info@geodatapro.rs.

title: What we learned from two rejected EU project bids
text:
We have been open internally about the fact that we submitted two EU co-funded project bids in the last 18 months and both were rejected on administrative grounds before evaluators read the technical sections. We think it is worth writing about this publicly, because we suspect we are not the only small geospatial firm in the region in the same position.

Both bids were technically sound — we had genuine partners, a clear work plan, and relevant experience. The problem was the consortium agreement. Horizon Europe has specific requirements for how partner liability is structured, how financial responsibility is allocated in the event of a partner withdrawal, and how intellectual property generated during the project is handled. These requirements are written in a way that assumes your organisation has in-house legal counsel who has read the previous version of the agreement and knows where the interpretation has shifted. We do not have that.

We hired external consultants for both bids. On the second bid, the two consultants we consulted gave us different readings of the same clause. We went with the interpretation that seemed more conservative. It was still wrong.

What we are doing now: we have identified the specific sections of the Horizon Europe Model Grant Agreement that caused the problem, and we are looking for someone with direct experience in SME consortium agreements under Horizon Europe — particularly for organisations in associated countries, which have some additional requirements — to work with us on a fixed scope before our next submission. We are not looking for general legal advice. We know what document we need help with.

If you have navigated this successfully and are willing to share how, or if you know someone who works on this specifically, we would genuinely like to hear from you. Contact Dragan Koprivnik at d.koprivnik@geodatapro.rs.

title: About Prosveta Digital — Kits That Take Maths Seriously
text:
Prosveta Digital makes physical game kits that help primary-school children practise mathematical thinking outside the classroom. We are based in Zrenjanin and we sell directly to families across Serbia, with a small number of school orders handled through our webshop.

The business started because our founder, Milena Ostojić, noticed something consistent across eight years of teaching: children who struggled with maths were almost always children who had never had a reason to enjoy it. Tests do not give you a reason. A game where you genuinely need to count, estimate, and compare to win — that can.

Each kit is a self-contained game. The BrojOtkrij Kit is designed for children aged 8 to 10 and covers number sense, arithmetic operations, and basic estimation. The GeoPriča Kit targets children aged 10 to 12 and works through spatial reasoning and introductory geometry using illustrated story cards and a board game structure. Both kits align with the primary mathematics curriculum used in Serbian schools, which makes them practical for parents who want to connect home play to what the child is doing in class.

We also run a free web portal where parents can log which activities their child has completed and get suggestions for what to try next. No account subscription is required — it comes with the kit.

Our kits are used by families in Novi Sad, Zrenjanin, Subotica, and smaller towns across Vojvodina. We have also worked with two primary schools that ran enrichment programmes using our materials.

The team is small by intention. Milena leads curriculum and product development. Dragan Filipović handles all print and graphic work on a part-time basis. Nikola Vranić maintains the web portal. Two part-time colleagues manage packing and orders.

If you have a question about which kit suits your child, or you are a teacher interested in the School Enrichment Pack, you can reach us through the contact form. We answer every message.

title: Junior Developer (Part-Time, Web Portal + App Prototyping) — Prosveta Digital
text:
Prosveta Digital is looking for a junior developer to support our existing developer, Nikola, on a part-time basis. This is a contract role, roughly 10 hours per week, and can be done entirely remotely.

Our current stack: PHP with Laravel on the backend, a WooCommerce webshop running on WordPress, plain JavaScript on the frontend. The web portal is modest in scope — it stores kit activation codes, logs activity completions, and surfaces simple suggestions to parents. There is no mobile app yet.

What we need help with in the short term:
We are prototyping a speech-input feature that would let children read a maths problem aloud and receive a prompt if they skipped or misread key words. Our current experiments using the Web Speech API and a couple of open-source models have not given us usable accuracy, particularly for Serbian-speaking children aged 8 to 10. We want to keep exploring this — testing different model configurations, looking at whether pre-processing the audio helps, and potentially evaluating small self-hosted alternatives. You would work alongside Nikola on this prototype.

You should be comfortable with JavaScript, have some exposure to working with audio APIs in the browser, and be curious about the speech recognition problem even if you have not solved it before. Experience with Python is useful but not required.

This is a small company. There is no complex infrastructure and no team hierarchy. We will explain the context for every task and we expect you to tell us honestly what is achievable within the time available.

To apply, send a short message through our contact form with 'Developer' in the subject. Tell us one thing you have built and one technical problem you did not manage to solve.

title: School Enrichment Pack Now Available — What We Learned from Our First Two Pilots
text:
Last school year we ran informal pilots at two primary schools in the Zrenjanin area. Two teachers — one working with a class of third-graders, one with fourth-graders — agreed to use the BrojOtkrij kit as an optional after-school activity for six weeks. About sixty children took part across the two groups.

We want to be honest about what we found. The children engaged with the game reliably — attendance at the sessions stayed high, and both teachers reported that children who usually avoided maths tasks were willing to keep playing. That part was encouraging.

What we did not find was a clear improvement in arithmetic test scores. Both teachers compared their enrichment group's results to similar classes who did not use the kit, and there was no obvious difference. We think there are a few possible explanations: six weeks may be too short, the test used may measure something different from what the game develops, or the game mechanics themselves may need rethinking. We do not yet know which.

Because of this, we have packaged our materials into a formal School Enrichment Pack — ten kit copies plus a teacher guide — and we are actively looking for a more structured way to measure what children are actually learning. We are talking to the Science Technology Park Novi Sad about whether a research partnership could help us design a proper measurement approach before we approach the Ministry of Education.

If you are a teacher or school coordinator who tried the kit last year, we would genuinely like to hear from you. Our contact form is open and we read everything.

title: The Warped Board Problem — What Happened and What We Are Trying Next
text:
In October last year we shipped fifteen School Enrichment Packs to schools in the Srem district. By the end of the month, three of those schools contacted us to say the game boards had warped to the point where they were not usable. Corners lifting, cards bowing, the whole thing looking like it had been soaked — except it had not been soaked. It had just sat in a school storage room through a mild, damp autumn.

We replaced those three batches at our own cost. It was the right thing to do, and it hurt.

Our print shop in Zrenjanin uses standard 2mm grey board with a matte laminate cover. In most home environments this holds up well — we have kits in circulation since 2021 that still look fine. But school storage rooms in older buildings are a different environment: unheated, inconsistent humidity, sometimes stored against outside-facing walls.

We have been looking at two fixes. The first is a heavier laminate on the same board stock. The print shop quoted an 18% increase in material cost per unit. The second is switching board stock entirely, which comes out at about 22% more. Either of those kills the margin on school packs at current volumes.

A third option we have not fully explored is solving it through packaging rather than the component itself — a moisture-barrier sleeve or a sealed inner bag. We do not know yet whether that is cost-effective or whether it just delays the problem.

We are going to run a small humidity test this spring. We are building a simple chamber with a humidity logger and leaving sample boards in it for two weeks at conditions that replicate what we think those storage rooms were like. We will write up what we find. If anyone has practical experience with moisture-resistant packaging for print products at small volumes, we would be glad to hear from you.

title: About Our Mill and What We Produce
text:
Bačka Mlin Savremeni a.d. has operated from the same site on the southern edge of Subotica since 1975. The mill started as part of an agricultural cooperative, processing wheat from the surrounding Bačka plain and supplying flour to bakeries within a radius of about 150 kilometres. Over the following decades the ownership structure changed, the equipment was modernised in stages, and the customer base grew to include manufacturers in Belgrade, Novi Sad, Niš, and, from the early 2000s, buyers in several EU countries.

Today we process approximately 180 tonnes of wheat per day across two mill buildings and a third building that houses grain intake, storage, and bagging. Our flour is used in sliced bread, rolls, sweet pastry, biscuits, pasta, and a range of confectionery products. We supply both industrial-scale manufacturers and regional bakeries, typically under annual supply agreements with fixed quality specifications.

Our production team works in three shifts, seven days a week. Quality control is integrated into the production flow: every incoming wheat lot is tested for moisture, protein, and falling number before it enters storage, and every outgoing flour lot is cleared against the customer specification before it leaves the site. We use a Perten AM 5200A inline NIR analyser on our two main intake conveyors and a Glutomatic system for wet gluten verification in the lab.

We hold ISO 22000 certification, which we have maintained without interruption since 2011, and an organic processing certificate covering a defined volume of wheat sourced from contracted farms in the Subotica and Kanjiža districts.

If you are a bakery, pasta maker, or food manufacturer looking for a reliable flour supplier with transparent specifications, contact our sales team through the form below or call our commercial office directly. We respond to all enquiries within one working day.

title: We Are Hiring: Process Control Technician
text:
Bačka Mlin Savremeni a.d. is looking for a process control technician to join our production team in Subotica. This is a full-time, permanent position on a rotating shift schedule.

What the role involves:
You will be responsible for monitoring and adjusting our milling process parameters during your shift, working closely with the chief miller and the quality lab. Specific tasks include reading and recording data from our inline NIR analyser, entering results into our internal tracking system, checking pneumatic conveying line pressures, and flagging any deviation from target specifications to the shift supervisor.

We are also asking this person to help us move away from paper-based process logs. Our current ERP is a custom MS Access database that was built in 2009 and is reaching its limits. You do not need to be a programmer, but we need someone who is comfortable working with structured data, can export and read spreadsheets reliably, and would be willing to work alongside an external software partner if we decide to upgrade the system.

What we are looking for:
— Completed secondary technical education in food technology, mechanical engineering, or electrical engineering
— At least two years of experience in a food production or process industry environment
— Familiarity with NIR or other inline measurement instruments is an advantage
— Basic computer skills including MS Excel; experience with any ERP system is a plus
— Willingness to work shifts including nights and weekends
— Good communication with the maintenance team when you spot equipment anomalies

We offer a stable salary, meal and transport allowance, and access to our in-house training programme. If you are interested, send your CV to our HR officer, Ivana Stanković, at the address listed on this page. Applications close 15 March 2024.

title: Seasonal Laboratory Assistant — Quality Control
text:
Our quality control lab in Subotica is looking for a laboratory assistant to support increased sample throughput during the spring and early summer harvest intake period. The contract runs from 1 May to 31 July 2024, with the possibility of extension depending on workload.

The lab operates two shifts and handles incoming wheat testing as well as outgoing flour verification. You will be working under the supervision of our quality manager, Milena Horvatović, and alongside two permanent lab technicians.

Daily tasks will include:
— Preparing and running falling number tests using the Hagberg-Perten method
— Operating the Glutomatic centrifuge system for wet gluten determination
— Recording results in the lab register and flagging any lot that falls outside specification
— Assisting with moisture balance checks and ash content testing on selected samples
— Maintaining cleanliness and calibration logs for lab instruments

What we need from you:
— Final year or recently completed degree in food technology, chemistry, or a related field
— Some practical laboratory experience, whether from coursework or prior employment
— Attention to detail and the ability to follow a documented procedure accurately
— Availability for both morning and afternoon shifts

This position suits a student looking for practical industry experience or a recent graduate considering a career in food quality. We will provide full on-the-job training for our specific instruments and procedures in the first week.

Salary is in line with the collective agreement for the food industry. Apply by sending a short cover letter and your CV to our HR office. We will contact shortlisted candidates by mid-April.

title: Bačka Mlin Renews Supply Agreement with Slovenian Partner for Three Years
text:
We are pleased to confirm that Bačka Mlin Savremeni a.d. has renewed its flour supply agreement with our Slovenian industrial bakery partner for a further three-year term beginning May 2024. The renewal covers bread flour delivered in bulk truck loads of 25 tonnes and represents a significant portion of our total annual export volume.

The agreement includes updated quality parameters that reflect the bakery's current production line requirements. Specifically, the renewed contract formalises minimum falling number and wet gluten band requirements that we have been working toward over the past year. Meeting these parameters consistently is our primary technical focus for 2024.

Our commercial director, Tibor Pap, said: "This renewal matters to us not just as a commercial result but as confirmation that a Serbian mid-size mill can hold its position in a demanding EU supply chain. We have supplied this customer for eleven years. The new contract gives us a clear target and a realistic timeline to upgrade how we make blending decisions."

The Slovenian market accounts for the largest share of our EU export revenue. We also export to Austria, Germany, Hungary, and Romania, though volumes in those markets are currently smaller and based on spot or shorter-term agreements.

Work is now under way internally to address the blending consistency requirement. We are in early conversations with technical partners who may be able to help us build a data-driven support tool for our miller using the grain analysis figures we already collect at intake. We expect to have a working approach in place before the autumn wheat intake season, when incoming grain variability is typically at its highest.

We thank our partners at the Slovenian bakery for their continued trust and their straightforward communication about what they need from us.

title: Nine Bearing Failures in One Year: What We Learned and What We Are Doing About It
text:
Our maintenance foreman Zoltan Fekete has kept a failure log for every mechanical incident on the roller floor since 2015. When we sat down with him in January to review last year's numbers, the picture was not good: nine unplanned bearing failures across our six roller mills, an average of 14 hours of production downtime per incident, and a repair cost that added up to more than half a million dinars over the year.

The machines are 36 years old. That is not a secret and it is not a surprise. What was a surprise, when we looked at the log in detail, was that four of the nine failures happened on the same two mills — units three and five — and almost always at the same bearing positions on the feed end of the roll assembly. Zoltan had noted unusual audible resonance in those positions twice before the failures, but by the time the sound was clear enough to act on, the damage was already done.

We do not have vibration sensors on any of our machines. Every check is done by ear and by hand during walkthroughs. That is the norm in a lot of mills our size, but it is no longer good enough for us.

We have started talking to people who know more about condition monitoring than we do. What we want is practical and proportionate: sensors on the highest-risk bearing points, a simple alert that tells the maintenance team something is changing, and enough lead time to schedule a replacement during a planned stop rather than an emergency one. We are not looking to build a control room. We are looking to stop being surprised.

If you work in this area and have experience with older flour milling or similar heavy rotating equipment, we would be glad to hear from you. Our production manager can be reached through the contact page.

title: PlastiForm Vojvodina renews supply contract with Mira Home Appliances
text:
We are pleased to confirm that we have signed a renewed three-year supply agreement with Mira Home Appliances d.o.o., covering injection-moulded ABS and PP components for their KH and KH-Pro kitchen appliance lines.

Mira Home Appliances has been a customer since 2017. The renewed agreement covers roughly 380,000 moulded parts per year across fourteen active part numbers, including the outer housing shells and internal structural brackets for two new product families Mira will launch later in 2024.

The new contract includes tightened cosmetic-defect limits — the agreed maximum visible-surface defect rate drops from 1.5% to 0.8% for Class A surfaces — as well as a requirement to provide material traceability certificates for each production batch.

Preparing for the new part families has meant tooling investment on both sides. We have built two new two-cavity tools in our in-house toolmaking cell over the past quarter, and a third tool covering the main upper-housing shell is currently in final machining. Press trials for the new tools are scheduled for late February.

Mira's procurement manager Svetlana Đorđević noted during contract negotiations that consistent dimensional accuracy and the ability to handle engineering changes in-house were the main reasons they chose to continue with PlastiForm rather than retendering. We are glad the relationship works for them and we will work to keep it that way.

The new contract runs from 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2027.

title: What We Do – PlastiForm Vojvodina
text:
PlastiForm Vojvodina has been manufacturing injection-moulded plastic parts in Zrenjanin for thirty years. Our 6,400-square-metre facility houses 14 injection presses ranging from 50 to 650 tonnes clamping force, giving us the flexibility to run small precision components alongside large structural housings on the same site.

We work with engineering-grade and commodity thermoplastics: ABS, PC/ABS, PP homopolymer and copolymer, PA6, PA66, glass-reinforced variants up to 30% GF, POM and HIPS. Our materials store is climate-controlled and we dry resin to manufacturer specifications before every run.

Our in-house toolmaking cell is something we consider a genuine advantage. Four experienced toolmakers handle new mould construction, running repairs and engineering changes without relying on an outside supplier. Tools are designed using SolidWorks and Cimatron, and machined on three-axis and four-axis CNC mills together with a sinker EDM. This keeps our modification turnaround inside the production site.

Quality inspection is built into the production process. A Zeiss Contura coordinate measuring machine sits in a temperature-stabilised metrology room beside the shop floor, and all first-off and periodic samples are logged digitally. We hold IATF 16949 certification for our automotive lines and ISO 9001 across the whole operation.

Our customers include automotive Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers in Serbia and Hungary, white-goods manufacturers supplying the European market, and consumer-product companies needing medium-to-high volume moulded housings and sub-assemblies. We are not set up for prototype quantities — our strength is stable, repeatable production from 5,000 parts upward.

If you are evaluating a new moulding supplier or want to discuss moving a tool from another moulder, contact our commercial team in Zrenjanin. We are direct and we will tell you honestly whether the work is a good fit.

title: Why we invested in a CMM — and what it has actually changed on the floor
text:
When we bought our Zeiss Contura coordinate measuring machine in 2019, the primary reason was IATF 16949 certification. We needed a documented, repeatable measurement process for the automotive parts we were supplying, and callipers and go/no-go gauges were not going to satisfy an audit.

Five years later, the CMM has turned out to be more useful than we expected, but in ways we did not fully anticipate at the time.

The most direct benefit has been in first-off sample approval. Before the CMM, a new tool coming off the press meant a full day of manual measurement across thirty or forty dimensions, with the risk of missing something. Now our quality technician Milica Savić can run a full first-off report in under two hours, with a clear pass/fail against the CAD nominal. We find tooling issues earlier, before we have committed to a production run on a tool that needs correction.

The less obvious benefit has been in troubleshooting. When we see a trend in scrap — say, a dimension drifting over a production shift — we can pull CMM data and compare it to process logs from our press controller. That connection between dimensional output and process input is something we are still developing, but it has already helped us understand a warpage issue on a PP part that we had been blaming on the tool when the real cause turned out to be inconsistent melt temperature from a worn screw tip.

We are not claiming the CMM solved everything. It is one tool and it needs a trained operator to be useful. But for any mid-size moulder thinking about whether the investment is justified outside of certification requirements — in our experience it is, once you connect the measurement data to the rest of your process information.

title: PlastiForm at Plastpol 2024 – report from the fair
text:
Four members of our team attended Plastpol 2024 in Kielce, Poland at the end of May — our commercial director Nenad Tomašević, process engineer Dragana Petrović, and two colleagues from toolmaking.

For those unfamiliar with it, Plastpol is one of the larger plastics-industry trade fairs in Central and Eastern Europe, covering machinery, materials, auxiliary equipment and services. We go primarily to look at press technology and to talk to material suppliers, and this year we also wanted to look at what hot-runner system suppliers are currently offering for smaller gate diameters in thin-wall applications.

Notable things we came back with:

Machinery: We had a detailed look at two press manufacturers whose 600–800 tonne machines are on our evaluation list for possible acquisition in 2025–2026. Both had live demonstration cells running. One machine's energy-consumption data during the demonstration was notably lower per cycle than our current press in that tonnage class, which is relevant given that we are now being asked to report per-part carbon footprint by at least one customer.

Materials: We spoke with three resin distributors about engineering-grade ABS with improved flow for thin-wall work, and picked up data sheets and pricing indications. Nothing confirmed yet.

Hot runners: We had a useful conversation with a representative from a hot-runner manufacturer about pin-gate options for small-part tools. We will follow up.

Overall the fair was worthwhile. If any companies or research groups from the Novi Sad area were there and we missed meeting you, feel free to get in touch — we are always open to talking with people working on process or materials questions relevant to injection moulding.

title: What We Do — Konverzija Labs
text:
Konverzija Labs builds and operates conversion-rate-optimisation software for e-commerce businesses selling in German-speaking markets. We started in Novi Sad in 2016 because we could not find a testing tool that worked the way practitioners actually work — with limited traffic, short promotional windows and clients who want answers, not methodology lectures.

Our platform, Konverzija Optimize, lets you run A/B and multivariate tests on product pages, checkout flows and category listings without writing code. You install a single JavaScript snippet, connect your revenue events and you can have a test live within a day. Results appear in a dashboard that shows revenue impact directly, not just click-through rates.

For merchants who prefer not to run tests themselves, our professional-services team takes over. We design the test plan based on your traffic and your current conversion funnel, run the experiments and deliver a monthly report that tells you what to change and why.

We also provide a heatmap and scroll-analytics module. It records where visitors click, how far they scroll and where they leave a page, and that data feeds directly into our reporting process so recommendations come from observed behaviour, not guesswork.

Our clients are online retailers in Germany, Austria and Switzerland with between 500 and 50 000 monthly transactions. Most of them came to us after trying a generic analytics tool and finding that the data told them something was wrong but not what to do about it. We focus on that gap: from data to a specific, testable change.

If you want to speak with someone, contact our account team in Novi Sad or our Vienna office. We do not do hard-sell discovery calls — you book a 30-minute walkthrough and we show you the platform on a demo store so you can decide whether it fits before committing to anything.

title: Konverzija Optimize Now Includes Session Replay — What Changed and Why
text:
At the end of last year we added session-replay recording to the Konverzija Optimize platform. It has been live for six weeks now and we wanted to write a short note on what we built, what we decided not to build and what happens next.

The replay feature records mouse movement, clicks, scroll position and form interactions for a sampled share of sessions — by default five percent, configurable up to 20 percent. Recordings are stored for 60 days and are linked directly to the test variant the visitor was assigned to, so you can watch sessions from variant A and variant B side by side without any manual filtering.

We built this because our analysts were spending significant time trying to interpret heatmap data without context. A cluster of clicks on a non-interactive element looks different when you can see the session: sometimes it is user confusion, sometimes it is a broken link, sometimes it is people trying to select text. Replay makes the diagnosis faster.

What we deliberately did not build: we did not add automatic session scoring or AI-generated summaries. We looked at two third-party APIs that offer this and found the output unreliable on German-language store content. We will revisit that decision once we have more confidence in the quality.

Data-processing note: all session data is stored on our Hetzner infrastructure inside the EU. Recordings are anonymised before storage — no IP addresses, no raw form values. Our legal team has updated our standard data-processing addendum to reflect the new data category. Clients on legacy contracts will receive an updated version by the end of February.

The feature is available to all clients on the Growth plan and above with no additional charge. Clients on the Starter plan can enable it as a paid add-on. Questions can go to your account contact or to support@konverzijalabs.rs.

title: Senior Data Analyst — CRO Reporting (Novi Sad, hybrid)
text:
We are looking for a Senior Data Analyst to join our analytics team in Novi Sad. The role sits inside the professional-services group and your main output is the monthly client reports that tell merchants what their on-site data means and what to test next.

What you will work with daily: ClickHouse for querying event data, Python for analysis and report generation, Metabase for internal dashboards and raw CSV exports from our heatmap module.
