What the job actually involves: most of your time will be spent analysing combinations of scroll depth, click position and session-exit data to identify drop-off patterns on specific page types. We have around 90 active clients and two analysts currently doing this work. Reports take roughly 15 hours per client at the moment; part of your job, over time, is to help us bring that number down through better tooling and smarter processes. This is not a management role — you will be doing hands-on analysis every day.

Required experience: at least four years in a web or product analytics role, strong SQL, Python (pandas, scipy), and practical knowledge of statistical testing — you should be able to explain the difference between a p-value and a credible interval without looking it up. Experience with heatmap or session-replay data is a plus but not required.

We are hybrid: three days in our Novi Sad office, two remote. Salary range is 2 800–3 400 EUR gross per month depending on experience. We offer 25 days leave, equipment of your choice and a learning budget of 800 EUR per year.

Send a CV and a short note (not a cover letter — just two or three sentences about what kind of analysis problems you find interesting) to jobs@konverzijalabs.rs.

title: Junior Frontend Engineer — Platform Team (Novi Sad, on-site)
text:
The platform team at Konverzija Labs builds and maintains Konverzija Optimize — the web application that clients use to set up tests, monitor results and read their analytics. We are looking for a Junior Frontend Engineer to join this team.

Our frontend is written in React. The application talks to a Node.js API layer and reads processed data out of PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. You do not need to know ClickHouse to apply, but you should be comfortable making API calls, handling async state and understanding why a dashboard that loads 400 ms faster matters to a client checking results on a Monday morning.

Day-to-day tasks will include building new dashboard components, maintaining the test-configuration UI, fixing browser-compatibility issues reported by clients (our DACH users have a long tail of older desktop browsers) and contributing to a component library we are in the process of building out.

We do not expect you to know everything. We do expect you to be curious, to ask when something is unclear and to care about the experience of someone using what you build. Our senior engineers do structured code review on every pull request and we run a short internal knowledge-sharing session every two weeks.

Required: solid JavaScript, React fundamentals, basic Git workflow, and genuine interest in web performance. Nice to have: experience with data-visualisation libraries (we use Recharts currently), any exposure to A/B testing concepts or e-commerce.

This is a full-time, on-site role in Novi Sad. Starting salary is 1 600–2 000 EUR gross depending on experience. We are open to recent graduates who can show relevant project work. Applications with a link to a personal project or GitHub profile get priority.

title: What We Learned Running 600 A/B Tests in the DACH Region
text:
Over eight years we have run or supported just over 600 A/B tests on German, Austrian and Swiss e-commerce stores. We do not have a dramatic reveal — most tests do not produce a significant winner, which is itself the finding worth talking about.

About 34 percent of tests in our data produced a clear result, meaning one variant was statistically better than the other and the improvement survived a holdout period. Another 41 percent produced no significant difference. The remaining 25 percent were stopped early — usually because the client ended a promotion, changed the page independently of the test or ran out of time in the testing window.

The early-stop problem is the one we think about most. It is particularly acute for smaller stores. A shop processing 1 500 orders a month running a test on its product-page layout will not collect enough events in a four-week window to say anything reliable. We have been documenting this pattern internally and are working on whether alternative statistical approaches can help. We do not want to overstate what is possible — small samples are genuinely hard — but we think there is room to do better than we currently do.

On the positive side, checkout-flow tests consistently outperform landing-page tests in effect size. The median improvement from a significant checkout test in our dataset is 6.2 percent on conversion rate. The median improvement from a significant product-page test is 2.1 percent. Neither of those numbers should be taken as a guarantee, but they suggest where testing effort is most likely to pay off for a store with limited traffic.

We will publish a follow-up post later in the year with a breakdown by product category. Fashion and home-goods stores show different patterns and they deserve separate treatment.

title: What we learned from a season of override data
text:
Every time a resort staff member sees a fatigue alert on ResortView and decides not to act on it, they can mark it as dismissed. We added that button in the spring 2022 update mostly as a usability feature. We did not expect it to become one of the most useful datasets we have.

Over the 2023 summer season we collected around 74,000 dismissal events across our resort partners. When we cross-referenced those with the session logs and, where available, with post-session guest survey responses, a pattern emerged: our false positive rate was significantly higher for guests who had checked in after 14:00 and for sessions in outdoor pools where ambient temperature varies more than indoor environments. Indoor steam room sessions, by contrast, had a false positive rate roughly half that of outdoor thermal pool sessions.

This tells us our model is probably not accounting well for environmental context. The wristband measures what is happening at the skin surface, but it does not know whether the elevated skin temperature reading is because the guest is genuinely overheating or because they just moved from a 38-degree pool into a 28-degree rest area and the sensor has not caught up.

We have not fixed this yet. We adjusted our smoothing window in the autumn update and that helped slightly, but the aggregate false positive rate is still higher than we want it to be. What we do have is a much clearer picture of where the model is failing, which is a reasonable starting point.

If you work in physiological signal processing and this kind of problem is familiar to you, we would be glad to talk. We are actively looking for people who have worked with wearable sensor data in variable physical environments. Our contact details are on the careers page.

title: How Termalis Works — Products and Services
text:
Spa and thermal resort operators deal with a problem that is easy to describe and hard to solve: every guest is different, and your staff cannot monitor how each person is responding to heat, water and treatment sequences at the same time. Termalis was built to close that gap.

ThermaBand is a waterproof wristband worn during a spa visit. It reads heart rate, skin surface temperature and galvanic skin response continuously and transmits that data to our cloud platform over an encrypted connection. The hardware is designed for wet environments — pool decks, steam rooms, outdoor thermal pools — and the battery lasts a full resort operating day on a single charge.

ResortView is the web dashboard your staff uses. It shows all active sessions on a single screen, flags sessions that may need attention and keeps a log for end-of-day reporting. There are no complicated settings to learn. A front-desk employee can be trained on it in under an hour.

Termalis Go is the app your guests download before or during their visit. It gives them a summary of their session, suggests how long to stay in each zone and keeps a personal wellness history across visits. Guests who return to a partner resort can see how their typical patterns have changed over time.

The DataSync API connects our platform with the booking and property management systems most resorts already run, so check-in automatically activates a wristband profile and checkout closes the session log.

We currently work with fourteen resorts across Serbia, Hungary and Slovakia. If you would like to see a live demo with data from a real resort environment, contact our customer success team.

title: Machine Learning Engineer — Physiological Signal Processing (full-time, Novi Sad)
text:

Our current model uses threshold logic and moving-average smoothing on three physiological signals: heart rate, skin temperature and galvanic skin response. It works reasonably well in controlled conditions but produces too many false positives in real resort environments. You will have access to 14 months of session logs covering over 340,000 sessions, a labelled comfort survey dataset of around 1,200 sessions, and override records from resort staff. The task is to replace or significantly improve the existing model so that the false positive rate drops below 8% without sacrificing sensitivity to genuine fatigue indicators.

title: Agrotrans Vojvodina Renews and Expands KlozuraPro Contract for Third Year
text:
We are glad to say that Agrotrans Vojvodina d.o.o., the Novi Sad-based food distribution company that was our first major client in 2019, has signed a three-year renewal and expanded their KlozuraPro licence to cover their procurement and logistics teams in addition to the central legal department.

Agrotrans started using KlozuraPro to manage supplier agreements, which at the time took an average of eleven working days from first draft to signed copy. Within six months that figure was down to under two days. According to their Head of Legal, Milena Čvorović, the bigger change was not speed but visibility: 'Before, a contract could sit in someone's inbox for a week and nobody knew. Now we see exactly where every document is and who needs to act.'

The expanded licence adds around 120 additional users across two departments and introduces ClauseGuard review for their standard logistics and warehousing contracts. We are also deploying a custom template set aligned with Agrotrans's own standard terms, which their legal team helped us build.

For us, this renewal matters beyond the revenue. Agrotrans gave us detailed feedback throughout 2020 and 2021 that directly shaped several features now used by all our clients — the approval escalation rules and the counterparty tagging system both came from conversations with their team.

We have forty-three clients across Serbia today. Most of them came through word of mouth from clients like Agrotrans. That is still how we grow, and we do not expect it to change.

title: What KlozuraPro Does — Services Overview
text:
Managing contracts manually means someone is always waiting — waiting for a draft, waiting for a review, waiting for a signature. By the time the document comes back, the details have changed or the deadline has passed. KlozuraPro puts every stage of a contract's life in one place.

Drafting starts with TemplateDesk, a library of contract templates built for Serbian law across sectors including distribution, services, employment and leasing. Legal teams pick a template, fill in the variables and have a working first draft in minutes rather than hours.

Review runs through ClauseGuard, which reads each clause and flags deviations from your accepted standard language. Lawyers see exactly which clauses need attention and why, without reading the whole document from scratch. A full audit log records every change.

Approval routing in SignFlow moves the contract through your internal chain — legal, finance, management — with automatic reminders and a clear record of who approved what and when. Electronic signatures are legally valid under Serbian law and comply with the eIDAS-adjacent provisions in domestic regulation.

Once signed, contracts live in a searchable archive. Full-text search, filter by counterparty, date, contract type or custom tags. No more hunting through shared drives.

KlozuraAPI lets you connect the platform to your existing ERP or CRM so contract data does not have to be entered twice.

We work with mid-size companies that have a legal function but are not large enough to run a dedicated contract operations team. Our typical client handles between one hundred and eight hundred contracts a year. Implementation takes between two and six weeks depending on how many custom templates are needed.

For pricing and a demo, contact our sales team at prodaja@lexautomatika.rs.

title: What We Learned at Pravo i Tehnologija 2024 in Zagreb
text:
Three of us — our CEO Dragan Novković, our Head of Product Tatjana Ilić, and I — spent two days at Pravo i Tehnologija, the regional legal technology conference held this year in Zagreb. It was the first time we attended as exhibitors rather than just attendees. Here is what we took away.

The conversations at our stand divided roughly into two groups. The first group were lawyers at larger regional firms who were sceptical that any automated tool could handle the complexity of their contracts. Most of them came in expecting a sales pitch and left having had a fairly technical conversation about how our clause classification actually works. A few were genuinely interested in the false-positive problem — one contracts lawyer from a Croatian manufacturing company said almost exactly what our own clients have told us: 'If it flags everything, I learn to ignore it.'

The second group were in-house legal teams at mid-size companies who were clearly in pain and looking for anything that would help. Several of them had never heard of contract lifecycle management as a category. For them the question was not whether to automate; it was where to start.

The most useful session we attended was a panel on cross-border contract compliance in the region, which confirmed something we already suspected: the legal differences between Serbian, Hungarian and Romanian contract practice are real but not as large as the language barrier makes them feel. That gave us some confidence that our expansion plans are not unrealistic.

We came back with four serious leads, two invitations to present at client sites in Croatia, and a clearer picture of how we want to position KlozuraPro in markets where we are not yet known. We will be back next year.

title: What We Do — FlexBot Systems
text:
Most factory robots are built for one job. They are fast and accurate at that job, and completely useless the moment the part changes. For large manufacturers running millions of identical parts, that trade-off is fine. For the small and mid-size factories that make up most of the industrial base in Vojvodina and across Serbia, it is a real problem.

FlexBot Systems builds tools for those factories. Our AdaptoGrip end-effectors can be reconfigured by a technician in minutes to handle different part shapes, weights, and surface finishes. Our VisionPick software uses a depth camera mounted above the work cell to find parts in a bin, calculate the best pick pose, and hand that instruction to the robot — no fixed fixtures, no hand-coded positions.

We do not sell robots. We sell the gripper and the eyes and the planning software that make a robot genuinely useful in a high-mix production environment. Our FlexCell service handles everything from mechanical mounting to network integration to training your operators.

Since 2019 we have commissioned cells at four manufacturing sites. Our current customers produce stamped metal brackets, injection-molded housings, turned shaft components, and packaged consumer goods. Pick success rates across those sites average 94.3 percent across all part types, and retraining for a new part takes operators an average of 47 minutes using our QuickTrain workflow.

We are based at the Novi Sad Science and Technology Park. Our team of eighteen includes mechanical engineers, embedded software developers, and computer vision specialists. We manufacture prototype and short-run gripper components in our own workshop space at NTP and outsource volume production to a local precision machining shop.

If you run a factory in the region and you are spending time on manual pick-and-place tasks, we are happy to come and look at the line with you. No commitment required.

title: FlexBot Systems Commissions Second Cell at Polimetal Subotica Plant
text:
We installed our first FlexCell system at Polimetal d.o.o.'s Subotica facility in the spring of 2022. That cell handles stamped bracket components coming off their progressive die press line. After eighteen months of operation, Polimetal's production manager Dragomir Fekete agreed to let us share some numbers: the cell has run 94.1 percent pick success averaged over the full period, and line downtime attributable to picking errors has dropped from roughly four hours per week to under thirty minutes.

In December 2023 we signed an agreement to install a second FlexCell at the same facility, this time on a turned shaft component line where operators were spending significant time on manual sorting and orientation tasks before parts moved to the next station.

The second cell presents a harder sensing challenge than the first. Polished shaft ends are among the part types where our current depth camera returns unreliable data, so we are treating this installation as a development site as well as a production deployment. We have fitted the cell with an additional lighting rig and a polarizing filter arrangement to support data collection while the cell runs in assisted mode. Operators confirm pick attempts manually until we have enough data to certify the cell for autonomous operation on the shiny-end geometry.

We expect to reach autonomous operation on all part variants in this cell by the end of Q2 2024.

Thank you to the Polimetal team for their continued collaboration and their patience with a process that involves some real engineering uncertainty. This is exactly the kind of customer relationship that lets us build better products.

title: What We Learned Exhibiting at the Automatika Fair in Budapest
text:
Three of us drove to Budapest in February to exhibit at Automatika, a regional industrial automation fair. It was the first time we had taken a booth outside Serbia and we were not sure what to expect.

The short version: the conversations were useful, the leads were mixed, and we came home with a clearer picture of where our product fits and where it does not — which is probably the most valuable outcome a small company can get from a trade fair.

What worked: our live bin-picking demo drew consistent foot traffic. We brought a real cell — a UR10e arm, one of our AdaptoGrip three-finger heads, a laptop running VisionPick, and a bin of mixed stamped brackets. The demo ran continuously for two days with maybe four interruptions, all caused by a cable-management issue we fixed on day one. Visitors who watched it pick for thirty seconds tended to stop and ask questions rather than walk on. The concreteness of a real part in a real bin seems to matter a lot.

What we learned: Hungarian and German visitors asked about certifications immediately and seriously. IEC 62443 came up in at least eight separate conversations. Two potential customers from the German automotive supply chain were direct about it: they liked what they saw but could not put us on a vendor list without it. We knew this was a gap; the fair confirmed it is not a theoretical gap but a practical barrier to sales that are otherwise within reach.

We also heard a common complaint about competing systems from larger vendors: the onboarding time for a new part is long and requires a specialist. Our QuickTrain workflow drew genuine interest when we explained the forty-seven-minute average. That is a number worth putting in front of people.

Next steps from the fair: two site visit conversations with manufacturing companies in Győr, one of which has already scheduled a date. We will report back on how those develop.

The booth cost us roughly €3,200 all in. Whether it pays off depends on those conversations.

title: BuildTwin completes BIM handover for the Feketić Primary School reconstruction
text:
BuildTwin d.o.o. has completed the BIM modelling and energy audit work for the reconstruction of Osnovna škola Feketić, a two-storey panel-construction school building from 1974. The project was commissioned by the municipality of Mali Iđoš as part of a broader programme to improve the energy performance of public facilities in the region.

The work involved producing a full Revit model of the existing building from a combination of original construction drawings and on-site measurements carried out by our team over three site visits in June and July 2023. The model was used to run thermal envelope simulations in EnergyPlus, comparing the current state against three retrofit scenarios: partial facade insulation, full facade insulation with window replacement, and a combined intervention including a new gas condensing boiler.

The final audit report was delivered to the municipal technical department in October. It shows that the combined intervention scenario would reduce estimated annual heating costs by approximately 54 percent relative to the current baseline, based on current gas tariffs. The municipality has indicated it will use the report as supporting documentation for a capital expenditure application to the Provincial Secretariat for Energy.

The IFC handover package has been delivered to the municipality's facility management team and imported into their building register system.

Dragana Ćirić, project coordinator at BuildTwin, said the Feketić project was a good example of what the team does well: 'The original drawings had gaps, the building had been informally modified twice since construction, and the heating system records were incomplete. We worked through all of that and delivered something the client can actually use going forward.'

BuildTwin currently has three similar projects in progress for municipalities in Vojvodina.

title: Why ranking buildings for retrofit is harder than it looks
text:
We have been asked, more than once in the past year, whether we can help a municipality figure out which of its buildings to retrofit first. The question sounds simple. The answer, in practice, is not.

The core problem is data quality. A city might own 40 school buildings. For five of them, you have complete as-built drawings, measured utility consumption going back ten years, and a recent condition survey. For another fifteen, you have the original 1970s construction drawings and two years of gas bills. For the remaining twenty, you have a floor plan of uncertain accuracy and the memory of the janitor.

If you want to rank all 40 by expected energy savings per dinar spent, you have to do something sensible with that third category. A full EnergyPlus simulation requires inputs you do not have. Making up the inputs produces a precise-looking number that is not actually reliable. Skipping those buildings entirely means your ranking is incomplete.

Our current approach is to run full simulations where the data supports it, and use simplified regression-based estimates for buildings with thin data, with explicit uncertainty ranges attached. It is not a perfect method. The uncertainty ranges on the thin-data buildings are wide. But a wide confidence interval attached to an honest estimate is more useful to a client than a precise number that required us to guess half the inputs.

What we would like to do better: build a method that can learn from the buildings where we do have good data and use that to produce tighter estimates for the ones where we do not. Whether that means some form of statistical model trained on the well-documented buildings in a portfolio, or something else, we are not sure yet. It is the problem we are currently working on, and if you have ideas, or experience with something similar, we would genuinely like to hear from you. Contact us at info@buildtwin.rs.

title: Services – BuildTwin d.o.o.
text:
BuildTwin provides BIM modelling and energy consulting for public buildings in Serbia. We work almost exclusively with municipal clients, school boards, and regional agencies that own or manage buildings constructed between 1960 and 2000 — the era of panel construction and minimal insulation — and need to understand what those buildings actually cost to run and what it would take to improve them.

Our core service is building a detailed Revit model of a facility from whatever source material exists: architectural drawings, site surveys, or in some cases a combination of laser measurements and old blueprints. title: ShiftFrame — Scheduling software built for care homes
text:
Running a care home means dealing with rotas that change every day. Staff call in sick, availability shifts, and labour rules vary depending on where your homes are located. Most scheduling tools were built for warehouses or retail — they treat a nurse the same way they treat a shelf-stacker, and care-home managers end up spending their mornings fixing what the software got wrong.

ShiftFrame was built specifically for residential care operators. You tell it your shift patterns, your staff roles, your site locations, and the rules you need to follow under local employment law. It builds a rota that actually fits, and when something changes it adjusts without wiping out the whole week.

We sell ShiftFrame as a white-label product, which means your staff see your logo and your colour scheme, not ours. If you already have an HR or payroll portal, we can embed the rota view directly into it so your managers do not have to switch between systems.

Onboarding for a home with up to eighty staff takes less than a week. We handle the data migration from whatever spreadsheet or legacy system you are currently using, we configure the rule set for your country, and we stay available by email and video call during the first month of live operation.

Current clients include care-home operators in Hungary and Austria. We work in English, German, and Hungarian.

If you manage care staff across one or more sites and you are still building rotas in Excel, we are happy to show you a live demo. There is no sales process — you speak directly with one of our developers or our product manager, see the real product, and decide from there.

title: What we learned from six months of trying to sell scheduling software to Austrian care homes
text:
We spent most of 2023 making sales calls into Austria. Here is an honest summary of what we found out.

The first thing that surprised us is how many care-home groups of 100–300 staff are still running their rotas in Excel. Not reluctantly — some of them are quite proud of their spreadsheets. The real objection is not that they want to keep using Excel; it is that they have tried scheduling software before and it created more work than it saved. A lot of tools in this space were clearly designed for factories, not care homes, and the process of bending them to fit care-home rules left managers with a system they did not trust.

The second thing we learned is that the absence problem is bigger than we realised. Several managers described their morning routine: check for sick calls, open the rota, find the gap, start calling through a mental list of who might pick up an extra shift. One manager told us she had this routine down to twenty-five minutes on a good day and ninety minutes on a bad one. That is a meaningful chunk of her day, every day.

The third thing is specific to our situation: as soon as a prospect has more than about 150 staff, someone asks how we handle scale. We have been honest that our current system works well below that number and that we are working on the larger-scale case. Some prospects respect the honesty. Others move on immediately. We understand both reactions.

What this means for us in 2024: we need to solve the scale problem, we need to build something useful around absence prediction even with limited data, and we need at least one Austrian reference client above 200 staff to open the next tier of conversations.

None of that is a surprise. Writing it down helps.

title: What we learned exhibiting at SensConnect Leipzig 2023
text:
In September we brought four people to SensConnect, a mid-sized trade fair in Leipzig focused on industrial sensing and wireless connectivity. It was our third time exhibiting there and probably our most useful.

The visitors who stopped at our stand were not looking for catalog products. Most of them had a specific installation problem — difficult RF environments, a sensor that needed to survive a wash-down cycle, a gateway that had to fit inside an existing control-cabinet cutout — and they wanted to know whether someone could actually solve it rather than sell them a development kit and wish them luck. That matches what we do, so the conversations were productive.

Two themes came up repeatedly that we had not expected to dominate the show. The first was cybersecurity certification. Several procurement-side visitors mentioned that their internal policies or customer contracts were starting to require documented security properties on connected devices, with IEC 62443 named more than once. A few years ago this came up occasionally from customers in critical infrastructure. Now it seems to be spreading into general industrial automation. We are taking this seriously and are working out what it means for our product roadmap.

The second theme was supply-chain transparency. Customers want to know where components come from, which suppliers are involved, and what the lead-time exposure looks like. We have always maintained relatively detailed BOM documentation for our own purposes, but the fair made clear that sharing more of this with customers proactively would reduce friction in procurement conversations.

We came back with contact details from eleven companies worth following up with, three of which look like realistic prospects for 2024. We also came back with a clearer sense of where the market is moving, which is sometimes worth more than the leads.

title: Voltara ships first 200 units under renewed contract with Hartfeld Prozessautomatisierung
text:
Voltara Elektronika completed delivery of the first 200 telemetry nodes under a renewed supply agreement with Hartfeld Prozessautomatisierung GmbH, a factory-automation integrator based in Stuttgart. The units are custom LoRaWAN sensor nodes designed to monitor temperature, humidity, and vibration on production-line equipment. They are deployed across three Hartfeld customer sites in Baden-Württemberg.

The order is the third annual delivery under a framework contract that began in 2021. This year's batch includes a hardware revision that reduces standby current draw by 31 percent compared to the previous generation, extending estimated battery life from 4.5 years to just over 6 years under the customer's typical duty cycle. The change was driven by feedback from Hartfeld's field technicians, who reported that battery replacement in some installations required a partial production shutdown to access sensor positions.

Production and functional testing of the 200 units took eleven weeks from purchase-order receipt to shipment, within the twelve-week lead time agreed in the framework contract.

Milan Ćurčić, production manager at Voltara, said the team had also introduced a revised functional test procedure for this batch that checks radio performance under a simulated load condition rather than at idle. 'We found during development of the new power profile that idle-state radio tests were missing a class of intermittent faults. The new procedure catches them before the unit leaves the building.'

The next delivery under the Hartfeld framework is scheduled for Q3 2024. Contract renewal discussions for the following year are expected to begin in early 2024 and will include a review of the customer's emerging requirements around device security certification.

title: What We Do — Voltara Elektronika
text:

Our typical engagement starts when a customer has a measurement or control problem that off-the-shelf hardware does not solve cleanly — wrong form factor, wrong radio, wrong power budget, missing certifications, or simply a supplier who cannot explain what is inside the box. title: Firmware Engineer — RISC-V and Embedded Systems
text:
Voltara Elektronika is looking for a firmware engineer to join our development team in Novi Sad. We build wireless telemetry hardware for industrial clients across the EU, and our firmware runs on microcontrollers from ARM Cortex-M up through newer RISC-V platforms.

The immediate priority for this role is helping us complete a port of our FreeRTOS-based sensor firmware to a RISC-V target. That means writing and verifying startup code, configuring the PLIC interrupt controller, bringing up UART, SPI, and I2C peripherals, and validating timing-sensitive radio driver behaviour. Beyond that initial project, the role covers ongoing firmware development across our product range.

What the work actually looks like day to day: reading chip reference manuals and writing code that matches them, using a logic analyser and oscilloscope to check that the code does what the manual says it should, doing code review with two or three colleagues, and occasionally travelling to a customer site to help with integration.

We use FreeRTOS and are evaluating Zephyr for future products. Our build tooling is GCC-based with CMake. We version everything in Git and do peer review before merging. Debugging is mostly J-Link and OpenOCD.

Requirements: solid C, experience with at least one bare-metal or RTOS-based embedded project, comfort reading a datasheet and turning it into working peripheral code. RISC-V experience is a genuine advantage but not a hard requirement — we can teach the architecture if everything else is strong.

This is a full-time, on-site position at NTP Novi Sad. Salary range is negotiable depending on experience. If you want to know more before applying, send a short message describing a tricky embedded bug you have debugged and how you found it.

title: RF and Hardware Engineer (Part-Time or Project Basis)
text:
We are looking for an RF or hardware engineer who can help us understand and fix packet-loss problems on our 868 MHz LoRaWAN nodes when they operate inside reinforced-concrete industrial buildings. This can be structured as a part-time engagement or a fixed-scope project — we are flexible on the arrangement.

The problem: in open-air tests and in standard brick-and-mortar buildings our packet delivery rate is above 97%. In reinforced-concrete production halls and plant rooms it falls to 82–88%. We have RSSI and SNR logs from multiple sites, gateway event logs, and architectural drawings of two of the most problematic installations. We need someone who can look at this data, identify what is driving the loss, and give us concrete recommendations we can implement: antenna selection or placement changes, gateway positioning rules, spreading-factor and ADR policy adjustments, or whatever else the analysis points to.

We are not looking for a full RF simulation study. We want practical conclusions based on the data we have, with enough explanation that our hardware team understands the reasoning and can apply it to future site deployments.

Useful background: experience with sub-GHz propagation in industrial environments, familiarity with LoRaWAN MAC behaviour (ADR, confirmed uplinks, retransmit policy), and comfort reading network-server logs and gateway statistics. Antenna design experience is a plus but not required — we are not redesigning the radio; we are trying to use what we have more effectively.

Engagement is expected to run four to eight weeks. Work can be partly remote, with at least one site visit to Novi Sad and ideally one to a customer installation in Germany or Austria. Contact us with a short description of relevant experience.

title: What we learned from three pressure incidents
text:
This is not a comfortable post to write, but it is worth writing.

Over the past four years we had three cases where adding a sensor to an existing line caused a pressure spike we did not predict. No injuries. One burst hose. Two unplanned shutdowns. Each time, the problem was an interaction between the new sensor's signal and a part of the pneumatic control loop that we had not mapped completely before we started.

After the first incident we added a step to our pre-installation checklist: ask for the original P&ID before touching anything in a pneumatic circuit. After the second we extended that to include a walk-through of the whole compressed-air circuit with the plant's own maintenance lead. That process caught several things it would have taken us hours to find on our own. The third incident still happened, because the interaction was two control loops removed from the point where we were working and nothing in our checklist pointed us there.

We are not process safety engineers. We are a small integration firm and we do not have that background on staff. What we are doing now: we have written down every interaction that caused or nearly caused a problem in our project history, and we check that list before commissioning. It is not a substitute for a proper hazard analysis, and we know it.

If you work in process safety or instrumentation engineering and you have dealt with this kind of systematic pre-commissioning check before, we are genuinely interested in a conversation. Not looking for a consultant to bill us for a methodology we cannot afford to use on every job — looking for a practical, repeatable approach that a technician can run through on-site in a reasonable amount of time. Contact details are on the site.

text:
Agro-Tech Vojvodina is a trade fair for agricultural and food processing equipment held each spring in Novi Sad. We have attended as visitors for several years and this year we have a small stand in the industrial automation section.

We are not there to sell a product off a shelf. We are there because the people who attend — equipment dealers, plant engineers, maintenance managers from food facilities across the region — are exactly the people we work with or want to work with. In our experience the most useful conversations at these events happen around a specific problem someone is trying to solve rather than around a brochure.

If you manage or maintain a food processing plant and you have a machine, or several machines, that are not connected to anything — no remote monitoring, no historian, no alarm that fires before something breaks — come and talk to us. We can usually tell within fifteen minutes whether there is a sensible project there or not, and we will tell you honestly if there is not.

We will also be interested in talking to anyone working on industrial communication protocols, protocol translation tools, or process safety methods for retrofit projects. Those are areas where we are actively looking for better approaches.

The fair runs 14–16 May 2024 at the Novi Sad fairgrounds. Our stand number will be posted here once confirmed.

title: Neusklađenosti kod farmaceutskog kupca — šta smo naučili i šta radimo
text:
Ovo nije vest kojom se ponosimo, ali smatramo da je pošteno da je podelimo jer direktno utiče na to šta planiramo u narednom periodu.

U prvom kvartalu 2024. farmaceutski logističar MedLogis Panonija evidentirao je dve serije naših kutija kao neusklađene sa zahtevom minimalne tlačne čvrstoće od 3,2 kN. Naše interno merenje pokazalo je vrednosti između 2,63 i 2,79 kN na tim serijama — što je van specifikacije.

Analizom smo utvrdili da su obe problematične serije proizvedene u danima kada je vlažnost u hali bila između 67 i 72 posto. U istom periodu serije napravljene pri vlažnosti ispod 60 posto su bez izuzetka zadovoljile spec.

MedLogis Panonija nije raskinuo saradnju, ali je zahtevao pisano obrazloženje i plan korektivnih mera. Dostavili smo im dokument sa trenutnim podacima i obavezali se da ćemo do kraja jula uspostaviti sistem koji obezbeđuje kontinuirano praćenje vlažnosti i koji nam daje osnov za odluku — može li ta serija da ide u isporuku ili ne.

Currently radimo na tome da pronađemo pravo tehničko rešenje. Kontaktirali smo Naučno-tehnološki park Novi Sad sa opisom problema. Ako iko ima iskustvo s kontrolom mikroklime u lakim industrijskim objektima ili zna nekog ko je rešavao sličan problem u ambalažnoj ili prehrambenoj industriji, slobodno nam se javite.

title: Contract Manufacturing Services — Farmavita d.o.o.
text:
Farmavita d.o.o. offers contract manufacturing for solid-dose pharmaceutical products and dietary supplements from its GMP-certified site in Novi Sad, Serbia. We have been operating under continuous GMP certification since 2001, and our facility has passed inspections by the Medicines and Medical Devices Agency of Serbia as well as audits conducted by several EU-based clients.

Our core services cover the full production chain for tablets and capsules: formulation development support, wet and dry granulation, film coating, capsule filling, blister and bottle packaging, and batch release testing. We operate two tablet compression lines, one pan coater, one fluid-bed processor, and two capsule filling lines. Our analytical laboratory handles dissolution testing, HPLC assay, uniformity of dosage units, and standard stability studies under ICH conditions.

We work primarily as a silent manufacturer for pharmacy chains, wholesale distributors, and supplement brands who need a reliable production partner without the capital cost of running their own facility. Clients provide the formulation and artwork; we provide the documentation, the manufacturing, and the QC sign-off. Where clients need formulation help, our team can support development within certain technology platforms.

All batches are managed in SAP with full electronic batch records. We ship throughout Serbia and across the Western Balkans, and we are currently expanding our client base in Slovenia and Croatia.

If you are looking for a contract manufacturer with a straightforward audit history, competitive lead times, and people who return calls, we are worth talking to. Contact our business development contact, Ana Vuković, at business@farmavita.rs to request a facility overview and capability statement.

title: Process Development Pharmacist — Solid Dose Forms

Day-to-day work includes designing and running small-scale batches in our development lab, setting up dissolution methods on our USP II apparatus, writing development reports for batch records and technology transfer packages, and working alongside production staff when a new product moves to full scale.

title: What We Learned from Two Years of Coating Batch Data
text:
Our pan coater has been running since 2009. Over the past two years, following a batch documentation improvement project, we have been capturing inlet air temperature, outlet temperature, spray rate, atomisation pressure, and pan speed at fifteen-minute intervals for every coating run. That gives us a reasonably detailed process log for around 2,500 batches.

We started this logging exercise because our weight-variation failure rate on coated tablets was sitting at around four percent — higher than it should be for a process we have been running for fifteen years. The logic was straightforward: if we have better data, we can find the problem.

Two years later, we have better data and we still cannot clearly identify the problem. We have looked at each parameter individually. We know our inlet temperature drifts more in winter when the building HVAC is fighting colder outside air, and we know our failure rate is slightly higher in November through February. But the correlation is not clean enough to act on, and when we tightened the inlet temperature control range last spring, the effect was temporary.

What we think is happening is that the failure is driven by a combination of parameters interacting, not any single one. When spray rate and pan speed are both at the lower end of their ranges while inlet temperature is high, something happens to film build-up uniformity that individual control charts do not catch. But we do not have the analytical tools in-house to confirm that, and designing a proper experiment around three or four variables simultaneously is not something our team has done before.

We are writing this partly to document where we are and partly because we are actively looking for someone who works with this kind of process data to help us move forward. If that sounds like something you do, our contact details are on the website.

Ideal background: experience with SAP ECC integration (IDocs, RFC, or REST API approaches), familiarity with GS1 standards and EPCIS event formats, and ideally some prior exposure to track-and-trace or serialisation projects in a regulated industry. Pharmaceutical industry experience is helpful but not required — the compliance logic is well-documented and we can brief the right person.

Engagement: approximately 20–30 hours per week for four to six months, on-site in Novi Sad at least two days per week. Budget is constrained; we are looking for a practical solution, not a premium consultancy rate.

title: What We Do — Paladin Osiguranje Tehnologije
text:
Paladin Osiguranje Tehnologije has been designing insurance products for the agricultural and transport sectors since 2009. We are based in Subotica and licensed by the National Bank of Serbia to write life and non-life business. Our work falls into two areas.

For farmers, we offer parametric crop insurance. That means the policy pays out when a measured weather event — too little rain, a late frost, extreme heat — crosses a threshold we agree on at the start of the season. There is no loss adjustment visit and no paperwork once the trigger is confirmed. The calculation runs automatically through our platform and the payment follows. We currently cover around 18,000 hectares of insured arable land across Vojvodina, and we are expanding into neighbouring countries.

For transport operators and private drivers, we offer telematics-based motor insurance. A small device in the vehicle or our smartphone app records how the vehicle is driven. Customers who drive carefully pay less over time. Fleet operators get a dashboard showing driver scores across their whole fleet, which helps them with safety management as well as insurance cost.

All of our products are sold through the Paladin Broker Portal, a web platform we built and operate ourselves. Independent licensed brokers use it to quote, bind, and service policies without calling us. Around 140 broker offices across Serbia currently use the portal.

We also write cargo-in-transit insurance for road freight companies operating in Serbia and on international routes. This is a straightforward product but we have integrated it into the same broker workflow so operators can manage motor and cargo cover in one place.

Our team of 112 includes actuaries, software engineers, field agronomists, and claims handlers. We have a satellite office in Novi Sad in addition to our Subotica headquarters. We are not part of any insurance group and we make our own decisions about which risks to take and how to price them.

title: Job Opening: Computer Vision Engineer (Vehicle Damage Assessment)
text:
We are looking for a computer vision engineer to join our Novi Sad technical team and take ownership of our automated vehicle damage assessment pipeline.

The role sits within a small team of two data engineers and one data scientist. You will work directly with our claims operations manager and the actuarial team.

What the job involves:

Our customers photograph vehicle damage through our mobile app and we return a repair cost estimate. The pipeline currently uses a fine-tuned object detection model built on a public dataset. It works acceptably on newer vehicles but performs poorly on the older domestic fleet we insure. Your job is to improve accuracy on that older fleet by whatever approach makes technical sense — transfer learning, data augmentation, synthetic image generation, or something else we have not tried. You will have access to roughly 1,800 annotated real claims images and the support of our claims assessors who can label additional data.

Technical environment:
Python, PyTorch, OpenCV, PostgreSQL, Linux. Our inference runs on-premises on modest hardware — we do not currently use GPU cloud infrastructure, though we are open to it if there is a clear case.

What we are looking for:
— Solid Python and experience with at least one major vision framework
— Experience fine-tuning or adapting pre-trained models on small datasets
— Comfortable working with real, messy data rather than clean benchmarks
— Familiarity with model evaluation against business metrics, not just academic ones
— Fluent in Serbian or English; both is a plus

We are not looking for someone to rebuild everything from scratch. We need someone who can look at what we have, understand why it fails on our specific problem, and make it measurably better.

Contract type: full-time, Novi Sad office preferred, some remote flexibility. Salary range on request. Send applications to poslovi@paladin-ot.rs.

title: Job Opening: Agronomist / Field Risk Analyst (Vojvodina Region)
text:

About the role:
Our parametric crop insurance depends on getting the risk assessment right before we write a policy. That means understanding what a farmer is actually growing, on what soil, and what their realistic exposure is to drought, heat stress, or early frost. You will conduct pre-season field visits, review cadastral and soil data, and advise our actuarial team on whether the proposed trigger thresholds are appropriate for a given parcel.

You will also be the first point of contact when a farmer questions a payout decision. When our weather data and the farmer's experience do not match, you need to be able to have a calm, factual conversation and document what you find.

What we need:
— A degree in agronomy, agriculture, or a related field
— At least three years working with grain or oilseed producers in Vojvodina
— Comfortable reading weather data and understanding basic concepts like evapotranspiration and soil water deficit — we will train you on our systems
— A driving licence and willingness to be in the field regularly from March through October
— Good written Serbian for policy documentation

Nice to have:
— Experience with GIS tools or mapping software
— Any exposure to crop insurance or agricultural finance

This role works closely with our two in-house agronomists and with the data engineering team who manage our weather data feeds. You will not be expected to write code, but you should be comfortable working with spreadsheets and our internal portal.

This is a permanent position based in Subotica. Send a CV and a short note about your background to poslovi@paladin-ot.rs.

title: Paladin Signs Broker Partnership Agreement with Vojvodina Agro Mreža
text:
Paladin Osiguranje Tehnologije has signed a three-year broker partnership agreement with Vojvodina Agro Mreža, a network of 23 independent agricultural brokers operating across the Vojvodina region.

Under the agreement, all member brokers of Vojvodina Agro Mreža will distribute Paladin's parametric crop insurance products through the Paladin Broker Portal. The agreement covers the 2024 and 2025 sowing seasons and includes a joint training programme for brokers who have not previously sold parametric products.

Marko Vukičević, managing director of Paladin, said the partnership is a practical step toward reaching more farmers who are currently uninsured against weather risk. "A lot of smaller farms in this region have never bought crop insurance because the traditional loss-adjustment process is too slow and too complicated. Parametric products are faster and more transparent, but farmers need someone they already trust to explain how the trigger works. That is what a local broker does."

Jelena Horváth, coordinator of Vojvodina Agro Mreža, said the network had evaluated several insurance providers and chose Paladin because of the broker portal's practical design. "Our members are not large agencies with dedicated IT staff. The portal has to work simply and reliably. We tested it during a pilot last autumn with three member offices and the feedback was straightforward: it does what it says."

The agreement covers sunflower, corn, soybean, and winter wheat. Paladin expects to add approximately 4,500 hectares of newly insured arable land through the partnership before the end of the 2024 season.

Paladin currently operates the broker portal with around 140 active broker offices in Serbia. The company was founded in Subotica in 2009 and employs 112 people.

title: Why Our Damage Photo Tool Struggles With Older Cars — And What We Are Doing About It
text:
We launched automated damage photo assessment in our motor claims app fourteen months ago. The idea was simple: a customer uploads three photos of the damaged vehicle, and within two minutes they receive a cost estimate and a claim reference number. No waiting for a callback. No scheduling an assessor for a dented bumper.

For a portion of our portfolio it works well. For a large portion it does not.

The honest reason is that the model we built was trained mainly on a dataset of Western European vehicles from roughly the last fifteen years. Clean body panels, standard part geometries, predictable paint finishes. Our actual insured fleet in Serbia looks different. A significant share of vehicles we cover are more than twelve years old, and a meaningful portion are models that were assembled domestically or regionally and are simply not represented in any public training dataset we found.

When the model sees an older vehicle it has not encountered before, one of two things tends to happen: it misses the damaged area entirely, or it produces a cost estimate that bears little relationship to what our assessors find when they inspect the vehicle in person. Neither outcome is acceptable in a product that is supposed to speed up claims for the customer.

Over the past two months our data team has been annotating historical claims images from our own portfolio — we now have around 1,800 labelled images of older-fleet vehicles with assessor valuations attached. That is a start but it is not enough to retrain a model from the ground up.

We are now looking at approaches that make better use of limited data: fine-tuning on our specific distribution, structured data augmentation to expand coverage of vehicle types, and potentially synthetic image generation to fill in gaps. We do not have all the answers internally, which is part of why we are talking to technical teams who work on these kinds of problems.

We are not going to disable the feature. For customers with newer vehicles it saves real time. But we want to expand what it does reliably, and we want to be honest about where it currently falls short.

title: Bili smo na sajmu Aluminium Central Europe u Bratislavi — utisci
text:
Krajem marta ekipa AluStar Profili d.o.o. prisustvovala je sajmu Aluminium Central Europe koji se održao u Bratislavi. Na sajam smo otišli bez štanda — ove godine samo kao posetioci, s ciljem da vidimo šta rade konkurenti i da obavimo nekoliko unapred dogovorenih razgovora.

Trend je jasan: zahtevi za lakšim profilima koji se brže montiraju rastu iz godine u godinu, naročito kod instalatora koji rade krovne sisteme na stambenoj izgradnji. Imali smo i razgovor s predstavnicima kompanije SunRail Systems iz Graca, koja traži dobavljača za rumunsko tržište. Nismo potpisali ništa, ali razgovor se nastavio i po povratku.

Takođe smo primetili da nekoliko kompanija iz Češke i Slovačke reklamira profile s produženim vekom alata i manjim tolerancijama nego pre pet godina. To nam je potvrdilo da naš interni problem s trajanjem kalupa nije jedinstven, ali i da ga moramo rešiti ako hoćemo da ostanemo konkurentni u tom segmentu.

Sledeće godine planiramo da izložimo, ako uspemo da sredimo štand koji zapravo ima šta da pokaže.

title: LearnBit and Adriatic Freight Group Complete Safety Training Rollout Across Four Countries
text:
LearnBit Solutions has completed a twelve-month project with Adriatic Freight Group, a regional logistics operator headquartered in Split, to deliver mandatory safety and compliance training to approximately 1,400 drivers and warehouse staff across Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Slovenia.

The project began in October 2022 when Adriatic Freight approached LearnBit with a specific problem: their existing approach — classroom sessions run by external trainers at each depot — was expensive, difficult to schedule around shift patterns, and produced paper certificates that were hard to track centrally. They needed a system that could deliver consistent content across four jurisdictions, accommodate four languages, and produce a single compliance report that their legal team could use for audits in each country.

The Orbita platform handled course delivery and certification. LearnBit's instructional design team worked with Adriatic Freight's safety officers to convert existing materials into Orbita Author format, which took approximately six weeks. The multilingual version — Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, and Slovenian — was completed and tested by December 2022.

Rollout across all depots finished in September 2023. Completion rates across the workforce reached 91% within the project timeline. Adriatic Freight's compliance manager, Ivana Rašković, noted that the central reporting dashboard reduced the time her team spent preparing for external audits by roughly half.

LearnBit CEO Dragan Vukić said the project demonstrated that mid-size logistics and manufacturing businesses across the region have real demand for compliance training infrastructure that works across borders without requiring a large internal team to manage it. Adriatic Freight Group has signed a two-year renewal for the platform licence and annual recertification cycles.

title: What Orbita Does and Who It Is For
text:
Orbita is a learning management system built for organisations that need to train and certify employees on a regular cycle and do not have a dedicated training department to manage it.

Most LMS products on the market were designed either for universities or for very large enterprises with full-time L&D teams. Orbita was designed for the manufacturing plant in Subotica with 300 workers due for a safety recertification every two years, or the logistics company in Zagreb that needs to onboard 80 drivers before the summer peak. Our clients do not want a feature list. They want their people to complete the training, pass the assessment, get the certificate, and have that certificate appear correctly in a compliance report.

The platform covers the full cycle: a trainer or manager builds a course in Orbita Author using video, text, quizzes, and branching scenarios; learners access it on any device without installing anything; automated reminders chase down learners who fall behind; and Orbita Certify generates the documentation that regulators, auditors, or client procurement teams ask for.

Orbita is multilingual out of the box — Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, Hungarian, German, and English are supported in the current release — and it connects to the HR and ERP systems that are common in Central and Southeast Europe.

We run on AWS infrastructure in the eu-central-1 region (Frankfurt). All data processing agreements are available in English and German on request.

If you want to see how the platform handles your specific compliance requirement, contact our customer success team. We do not do generic demos — we prepare a short walkthrough based on your actual use case.

title: What 18 Months of Clickstream Data Has — and Has Not — Told Us
text:
We have been logging xAPI events on the Orbita platform since July 2022. Every video play, every quiz attempt, every time a learner skips a section or replays a clip — it all lands in our database. Across roughly 12,000 learners and about 200 course versions, that is a substantial pile of behavioural data. We thought it would give us clear answers. It has mostly given us better questions.

The straightforward stuff works. We can see completion rates, average time-on-task per module, quiz pass rates, and drop-off points. We can tell a client that 40% of learners in their warehouse safety course exit before reaching module four, and that module four is the longest one. That is useful. Clients act on it.

The harder question is whether completion means anything. We ran a simple correlation between module completion and post-course assessment scores across three of our larger client datasets last spring. The correlation was weak — weaker than we expected. Some of the modules with the highest completion rates predicted almost nothing about whether a learner passed the final assessment. Some shorter, lower-completion modules correlated more strongly with outcomes.

What does that mean? Probably that some learners click through content quickly and then do fine on the test because they already knew the material. Probably that some modules are well-matched to what the assessment actually measures and some are not. But we cannot say for certain with the methodology we have been using.

We are not writing this to present a solution. We are writing it because we think this is an honest account of where applied learning analytics actually is in a product like ours, and because we are actively looking for collaborators — researchers or data specialists — who want to work on this problem with real-world data rather than a controlled experiment. If that sounds like your kind of problem, reach out.

title: Machine Learning Engineer — Adaptive Learning Systems
text:
LearnBit Solutions is looking for a machine learning engineer to join the product team in Novi Sad and take ownership of the adaptive recommendation layer inside the Orbita platform.

The honest version of the role: our current adaptive engine is rule-based and it is not good enough. We have four static difficulty tiers and a rule that fires on entry-quiz scores. Retention drops sharply by week three and we believe a meaningful part of that is because learners are getting content that does not match where they actually are. We have clickstream data, quiz scores, and time-on-task logs for roughly 12,000 learners going back eighteen months. We need someone who can look at that data, propose a sensible model architecture, build a prototype, and work with our backend team to integrate it into the existing Django/PostgreSQL stack without a full rewrite.

What we use: Python throughout, Scikit-learn for the current prototype, PostgreSQL, xAPI event logs, AWS, Docker, GitLab CI.

What we are looking for: practical experience with recommendation systems or sequential models; comfort working with messy real-world behavioural data; ability to explain model behaviour to non-technical stakeholders; familiarity with model evaluation in a setting where ground truth is noisy. A background in education or training is not required but would be useful.

This is not a research position. We need something in production within nine months. You will work directly with our lead backend engineer, Milena Todić, and the product lead.

Full-time, based in Novi Sad (NTP). Competitive salary for the Novi Sad market. Relocation support available for candidates from the region. Send a CV and a short note about a project you have shipped to careers@learnbit.rs.

title: Junior Learning Data Analyst (part-time or full-time)
text:
LearnBit Solutions is hiring a learning data analyst to help us make sense of the behavioural data we collect from learners on the Orbita platform.

The context: we track every learner interaction — video plays, quiz attempts, module navigation, time-on-task — using xAPI. We have been doing this since mid-2022 and the data is sitting in PostgreSQL. We generate basic completion reports for clients, but we have not been able to answer the harder question: which parts of a course actually drive learning outcomes, and which parts do learners click through without engaging? We need someone to help us build a methodology for that.

Day-to-day work will include: cleaning and exploring xAPI event data; building descriptive analyses and visualisations for internal use and for client reports; working with the product team to define what metrics we should be tracking; and eventually contributing to a client-facing analytics dashboard.

Stack: PostgreSQL, Python (Pandas, Matplotlib/Seaborn), basic SQL. Experience with xAPI or learning analytics is a plus but not required. What matters more is that you are careful with data, honest about what the numbers do and do not show, and comfortable asking questions when something does not make sense.

We are open to part-time arrangements for the right candidate — for example, a current student or recent graduate who wants to build applied data experience. The position is based at NTP Novi Sad. Send a CV and two or three sentences about why this kind of problem interests you to careers@learnbit.rs.

title: O nama i uslugama — Voltis Pay d.o.o.
text:

Za razliku od velikih vendora koji prodaju monolitna rešenja, mi nudimo modularan pristup. Klijent bira koje komponente uvodi i kojim tempom. Svaka komponenta dolazi sa dokumentacijom, sandbox okruženjem i tehničkom podrškom tokom integracije.

— Iniciranje plaćanja: pokretanje prenosa direktno iz vaše aplikacije bez preusmjeravanja na treće strane.
— Poslovni dashboard: analitički prikaz za pravna lica sa pregledom tokova gotovine i planiranim unapređenjem prognoze.

Trenutno sarađujemo sa institucijama u Srbiji, Bosni i Hercegovini, Severnoj Makedoniji, Rumuniji i Slovačkoj. Svi podaci se obrađuju u skladu sa GDPR-om i čuvaju unutar EU ili u Srbiji, zavisno od zahteva partnera.

title: Voltis Pay potpisao ugovor sa Nordelbank AG za open banking integraciju
text:
Voltis Pay d.o.o. je potpisao ugovor o tehničkom partnerstvu sa Nordelbank AG, nemačkom regionalnom bankom sa sedištem u Erfurtu. Ugovorom je predviđena implementacija naše white-label API platforme kao osnove za PSD2-usklađene usluge koje Nordelbank planira da ponudi poslovnim korisnicima.

Ovo je naš prvi ugovor sa finansijskom institucijom van Balkana i CEE regiona u užem smislu. Implementacija je planirana u dve faze: u prvoj fazi, do kraja 2024. godine, biće integrisana agregacija računa; u drugoj fazi, tokom prvog polugodišta 2025, doći će iniciranje plaćanja.

'Razgovarali smo sa nekoliko vendora i Voltis Pay je bio jedini koji je mogao da pokaže funkcionalan sandbox u roku od dve nedelje od prvog kontakta', izjavio je Stefan Molnár, direktor tehničkog razvoja u Nordelbank AG. 'To nam je dalo poverenje da nastavimo razgovor.'

Ivan Crnogorac, tehnički direktor Voltis Pay-a, dodao je: 'Ovo je za nas korak koji potvrđuje da naš pristup ima smisla i van poznatih tržišta. Narednih meseci biće intenzivnih, ali znamo šta radimo.'

Voltis Pay je prethodno realizovao integracije sa Banka Jadran d.d. (Sarajevo), Unia Kredytowa Marek Brzezicki i Partneri (Vroclav) i tri kreditne unije u Srbiji. Ugovor sa Nordelbank AG je po obimu i složenosti najveći do sada.

Sve tehničke i pravne aspekte usklađivanja sa BaFin zahtevima tim planira da finalizuje do trećeg kvartala 2025. godine.

title: Šta smo naučili kada nam je latencija baze prešla 400 ms u produkciji
text:
Pre dva meseca naš monitoring je uhvatio nešto što smo se nadali da nećemo videti pre kraja godine: latencija na pojedinim upitima prešla je 400 ms tokom večernjeg pika, i to na primarnom čvoru PostgreSQL klastera koji inače drži stabilnih 90–110 ms.

Nije bio hakerski napad, nije bio hardware problem. Bio je to rast.

Kad smo pogledali Grafanu, videli smo da se broj aktivnih sesija u intervalu 18:00–21:00 skoro udvostručio u odnosu na stanje od pre šest meseci. Nismo promenili arhitekturu — promenili smo broj klijenata i obim transakcija.

Prvi reflex je bio da proverimo indekse. Pronašli smo nekoliko upita koji su skenirali celu tabelu transakcija umesto da koriste kompozitni indeks. Dodavanje tog indeksa spustilo je najgore slučajeve sa 420 ms na oko 280 ms. Bolje, ali još uvek iznad SLA granice od 200 ms.

Sledeći korak je bila analiza EXPLAIN ANALYZE izlaza za najsporije upite. Otkrili smo da jedan određeni JOIN koji spaja transakcije, korisnike i konfiguracije partnera pravi nepotreban sekvencijalni sken svaki put. Particionisanje tabele transakcija po mesecu rešilo je deo problema.

Gde smo sada: latencija je na oko 230–250 ms u pikovima, što je blizu ali još uvek ne ispunjava SLA konzistentno. Znamo šta je sledeći korak — bolje rutiranje čitanja na replike i potencijalno Redis za određene tipove upita — ali to zahteva pažljivu implementaciju koja ne sme da unese nove probleme.

Ovo pišemo da bude korisno drugima u sličnoj situaciji: rast je dobar problem, ali nije besplatan. Pratite execution planove u produkciji, ne samo u razvoju.

title: Voltis Pay na Finance Forward Balkans 2024 — Beograd, oktobar
text:
Voltis Pay će učestvovati na konferenciji Finance Forward Balkans 2024 koja se održava 17. i 18. oktobra u Beogradu, u hotelu Terminus. Konferencija okuplja fintech kompanije, predstavnike banaka i regulatora iz Srbije, Crne Gore, Bosne i Hercegovine i Severne Makedonije.

Naš tim će imati izlagački prostor u holu B gde ćemo demonstrirati sandbox verziju naše API platforme. Posjetioci mogu da isprobaju simuliranu integraciju i postave pitanja direktno inženjeru koji je razvijao sistem.

Tanja Filipović, voditeljka poslovnog razvoja, drži kratko izlaganje u okviru panela 'Integracija PSD2 u regionalnim bankama — praktična iskustva' u petak 18. oktobra u 11:30. Ako planirate da prisustvujete konferenciji i želite da zakažete razgovor sa našim timom pre ili posle panela, pišite nam na info@voltispay.rs sa naslovom 'Finance Forward 2024'.

Konferencija je otvorena za predstavnike finansijskog sektora, tehnoloških kompanija i regulatornih tela. Više informacija o programu dostupno je na zvaničnom sajtu organizatora.

title: What We Do — Contract Fermentation and Enzyme Production
text:
Ferment-Pro d.o.o. produces industrial enzymes under contract at our facility in Zrenjanin, Serbia. We have been doing this since 1997, and fermentation is the only thing we do. That focus means our team knows the process in detail, from inoculum preparation through downstream concentration to final packaging.

Our two main product categories are bacterial proteases and amylases. Proteases are used by our customers in detergent formulation, leather processing, and protein hydrolysis for food ingredients. Amylases go primarily to starch-processing customers and to bakery ingredient producers who need consistent liquefaction activity across production runs.

We work on a contract basis: customers come to us with a target activity, a volume, and a delivery schedule, and we produce to that specification. We do not sell off-the-shelf catalogue products. This means every batch is tied to a customer order and every batch record is available for customer audit. We have had third-party audits from four different European customers in the past three years, and all have been completed without major findings.

Our fermentation hall currently runs two 5,000-litre stirred-tank bioreactors, supported by seed fermenters, media preparation vessels, and a downstream suite that includes depth filtration, ultrafiltration, and spray-drying capability. We hold relevant Serbian and EU documentation for food-grade and detergent-grade enzyme production.

Customers are typically food processors, detergent manufacturers, and specialty chemical compounders operating in Germany, Austria, Hungary, Romania, and the former Yugoslav markets. Minimum order quantities start at 200 kg of concentrated liquid enzyme.

If you have a fermentation or enzyme supply requirement, contact our production office in Zrenjanin to discuss whether we are the right fit. We prefer to have a direct technical conversation before quoting, so we understand what you actually need.

title: Ferment-Pro Secures Multi-Year Amylase Supply Agreement with Molnár-Stein Kft.
text:
Ferment-Pro d.o.o. has signed a three-year supply agreement with Molnár-Stein Kft., a Hungarian starch-processing company based in Debrecen. Under the agreement, Ferment-Pro will supply a minimum annual volume of thermostable amylase concentrate for use in Molnár-Stein's wet-milling and glucose syrup lines.

The relationship began with a trial order in the second quarter of 2023. After completing internal qualification testing over two production batches, Molnár-Stein's technical team confirmed that Ferment-Pro's amylase met their activity and consistency requirements and formalised the arrangement at the start of this year.

"We have been looking for a regional supplier who could match the technical specification we were getting from a larger Western European producer, at a realistic lead time," said Molnár-Stein's procurement manager in a written statement. "The Ferment-Pro product qualified without modification to our existing process parameters, which was important to us."

For Ferment-Pro, the agreement represents a meaningful increase in committed amylase volume and provides the production planning stability needed to schedule longer fermentation campaigns. Dragan Kovačević, who oversees commercial relationships at Ferment-Pro, noted that the company has been building its presence in the Hungarian market for several years and that this agreement is the clearest result of that effort so far.

Deliveries under the new agreement began in January 2024. Ferment-Pro produces the amylase at its Zrenjanin facility using submerged Bacillus fermentation and delivers in 1,000-litre IBCs by road.

title: Process Biotechnologist — Fermentation and Downstream Processing
text:
Ferment-Pro d.o.o., Zrenjanin
Full-time, permanent

We are looking for a process biotechnologist to join our production and development team. The role sits between day-to-day production support and bench-scale process work, and will suit someone who is comfortable moving between the two.

What the job involves:
— Running and documenting bench-scale (5 L) fermentation trials using our Bacillus strains, including fed-batch experiments and media optimisation work
— Supporting the production team during 1,000 L and 5,000 L fermentation runs, particularly during inoculation, critical feeding phases, and harvest decisions
— Working on cell bank procedures — we need to rebuild our master bank programme and this person will be central to that work
— Collecting and organising fermentation data (pH, DO, OD, enzyme activity over time) and helping the team make sense of trends across batches
— Participating in downstream troubleshooting, particularly around pre-filtration and ultrafiltration performance

What we need:
— A degree in biotechnology, microbiology, biochemistry, or a related field
— Hands-on experience with stirred-tank fermentation at bench or pilot scale — we are not looking for someone who has only worked in a university teaching lab
— Familiarity with enzyme activity assays; experience with proteases or amylases is a plus but not required
— Practical experience with cell banking protocols and cryopreservation
— Willingness to work in a production environment where schedules are set by batch cycles, not office hours
— Serbian language required; working English for reading technical literature and customer documentation

What we offer:
— Permanent contract from day one
— Competitive salary for the Zrenjanin area, reviewed annually
— Real responsibility from early on — we are a small team and there is no large department to hide in
— Direct involvement in projects that affect production outcomes, not background research

Send a CV and a short note explaining your relevant experience to our HR contact, Jelena Ostojić, at the address on our contact page. We do not require a formal cover letter.

title: Quality and Regulatory Coordinator — Enzyme Products
text:
Ferment-Pro d.o.o., Zrenjanin
Full-time, permanent

We are a small company with a flat structure. The quality coordinator reports directly to Nemanja Filipov and will interact regularly with production, logistics, and senior management. The role has real scope to grow as the company grows.

Applications to Jelena Ostojić at our Zrenjanin office.

title: Looking Back at Three Days at FermentaTech Expo, Budapest
text:
Three of us from Ferment-Pro — Svetlana Borojević, Ana Vuković, and myself — spent last week at FermentaTech Expo in Budapest. This is a trade fair aimed at industrial fermentation, enzyme suppliers, and the food and detergent industries they serve, and it runs every two years. We had a small stand in the supplier section.

The fair is useful mainly for the conversations you have at the stand and in the corridors rather than the formal programme. We spoke to procurement people from food companies in Poland, Romania, and Slovenia who were looking for alternatives to their current enzyme suppliers, mostly on lead-time and flexibility grounds. Two of those conversations have moved to follow-up samples. We also met the technical team from a German detergent ingredients distributor, Ritter & Schäfer GmbH, which was interesting given the sustainability documentation requirements that are becoming standard in that market — something we are actively working on.

On the technical side, there were several presentations on continuous fermentation and perfusion approaches that we are not in a position to adopt right now but that are worth following. The conversation around membrane fouling in downstream processing came up in more than one session, which was frankly reassuring — it confirmed that this is an industry-wide challenge rather than something specific to our setup. We collected some references on surface-modified membranes that Ana will look at.

We also spent time at the stands of two membrane suppliers and had a detailed discussion with one of them about pre-filtration configurations that might reduce the fouling load reaching the UF stage. Nothing decided yet, but it was a more specific conversation than we have been able to have remotely.

All in all, two confirmed follow-up leads, a few useful technical contacts, and a clearer picture of where the market is heading on sustainability documentation. We will be back in two years.
