title: What We Do — Mediavox a.d.
text:
Mediavox started as a jingle house. In 1994, two audio engineers with a borrowed mixing desk and a client list of three Novi Sad retailers recorded their first radio spot in a rented basement. That spot ran on Radio Talas for six weeks and the client reported a measurable lift in foot traffic. We have been trying to repeat that outcome, at larger scale and with better tools, ever since.

Today we run three connected businesses under one roof on Futoška Street in Novi Sad.

Our podcast network carries 24 original shows. Topics range from personal finance to regional history to football tactics. The shows are made by our in-house editorial team, not outsourced, and every episode goes through the same review checklist we first wrote for radio in 1999. Combined monthly downloads across the network passed 310,000 in the fourth quarter of 2023.

Our branded-content team works with companies that want a documentary or serialised audio series rather than a standard ad. Recent productions include a six-part series on supply chain logistics for Dunav Credit and a seasonal cooking audio series for Breza Dairy. We handle scripting, recording, post-production and distribution.

Our technology product, SoundSlot, is an audio ad server. We built it internally to manage inventory on our own network, then licensed it to other broadcasters who wanted programmatic insertion without building their own infrastructure. Around 40 publishers now use SoundSlot to manage pre-roll and mid-roll placements.

What holds these three areas together is first-party data. Our listener panel has run continuously since 2015 and currently includes 1,200 active participants across Serbia. That data informs how we programme, how we price and how we advise advertisers. We do not sell the raw data; we use it to provide audited audience insight that media buyers can verify.

Our 87-person team includes audio engineers, editors, developers, a commercial team and a finance function that now spans two countries following the opening of our Zagreb subsidiary. If you are a brand looking for audio content, a broadcaster looking for ad-insertion technology or a researcher interested in audio media, we are straightforward to reach.

title: Veronika Stores Extends Branded Audio Partnership for Second Year
text:
Mediavox has renewed its branded-content agreement with Veronika Stores, the Novi Sad-based retail chain, for a second consecutive year. The renewed contract covers production of a twelve-episode audio series scheduled to launch in the autumn of 2024, focused on consumer lifestyle topics that align with Veronika's product categories.

The first series, produced in 2023 and distributed through the Mediavox podcast network as well as Veronika's own in-store audio channels, averaged 14,200 downloads per episode and generated a measurable increase in traffic to the featured product categories, according to Veronika's internal retail analytics team.

Our head of branded content, Anamarija Čolić, said the renewal confirmed what we have seen with several long-term clients: the second series is typically stronger because both sides understand each other's constraints and there is less time spent renegotiating the creative brief from the ground up.

The 2024 series will include a companion short-form video component for social distribution, the first time Mediavox has bundled video production into a branded audio contract. The video segments will be shot in Novi Sad and edited by our in-house post-production team.

Veronika Stores operates 34 locations across Vojvodina and has been a Mediavox client since 2021, initially for radio spot production before moving to the branded-content format in 2022. The renewed partnership represents the largest single branded-content contract in Mediavox's current portfolio by episode count.

title: Vacancy: Audio Data Engineer (Novi Sad, hybrid)
text:
Mediavox a.d. is hiring an Audio Data Engineer to join our technology team in Novi Sad. This is a new role created to support two parallel projects: improving the automated processing pipeline for field-recorded podcast episodes and developing smarter content-matching features for our SoundSlot ad platform.

What you will work on:

You will take raw audio files — often noisy, always variable — and help design a pipeline that classifies noise types and applies processing without requiring an editor to drive every decision manually. We use iZotope RX today and are open to building on top of it, replacing parts of it or building something new, depending on what the data tells us.

You will also work with our existing episode transcript archive and campaign performance logs to help us build content-classification features. The goal is to improve ad-placement relevance. We are not starting from scratch: we have four years of transcripts, eight years of panel data and a PostgreSQL database that is reasonably well-structured.

What we are looking for:

Experience working with audio processing libraries (we use Python and are open to whatever ecosystem fits the problem). Comfort with signal processing concepts: noise profiling, spectral subtraction, voice activity detection. Some familiarity with text classification or embedding approaches. You do not need to be a machine learning researcher; you need to be an engineer who can take an approach that works in theory and make it run reliably on a production schedule.

Our stack on the technology side is Python/Django for SoundSlot, PostgreSQL for data storage, and standard audio tools for production. We are a media company, not a tech company, which means you will spend time explaining your decisions to non-technical colleagues and that is part of the job.

Terms: Full-time, hybrid from our Novi Sad office. Salary range 120,000–160,000 RSD per month depending on experience. Apply by sending a CV and a short note about a technical audio or signal-processing problem you have worked on to careers@mediavox-ns.rs.

title: Three Things Our Listener Panel Data Actually Tells Us (and Two Things It Does Not)
text:
We have been running a listener panel since 2015. It started as a research project attached to a grant from the Provincial Secretariat for Culture, and it outlasted the grant by several years because the data turned out to be genuinely useful.

The panel currently has 1,200 active participants across Serbia. They complete a short survey after listening to episodes they select from our network, and we run a longer demographic and media-habits survey twice a year. Eight years of that data is a reasonably serious archive, and we want to be honest about what it does and does not tell us.

What it actually tells us:

First, which show formats retain listeners to episode end versus which ones see drop-off in the final quarter. This affects how we schedule ads and it affects how we brief producers. Second, how listener satisfaction scores correlate with social sharing behaviour — the relationship is positive but weaker than most people assume, and it is not linear above a certain satisfaction threshold. Third, seasonal listening patterns at the show level, which matter more for pricing than we accounted for in early years.

What it does not reliably tell us:

First, purchase intent. Our panel participants know they are part of a research panel, and their stated intent numbers are consistently optimistic compared to what we see in client attribution data. We flag this to advertisers but it takes repeated conversations. Second, the panel skews toward listeners who are already engaged with our network. New listener acquisition and the behaviour of occasional listeners are genuinely underrepresented, and any analysis that assumes the panel is representative of the full audience is making a mistake.

We are not writing this to undersell our data product. We are writing it because media buyers who understand the limitations of a dataset make better decisions, and clients who make better decisions tend to stay clients longer. If you want to talk through the methodology before committing to a campaign, our commercial team is available to walk you through it.

title: Vacancy: Podcast Producer — Branded Content (Novi Sad or Zagreb)
text:
We are looking for a Podcast Producer to join our branded-content arm, based either in Novi Sad or our Zagreb office. The role sits between editorial and account management: you will be the person who turns a client brief into a finished audio series.

This is not a presenting or hosting role. It is a production and editorial role. You will write series bibles, conduct or direct interviews, manage the post-production schedule and liaise with the client through review rounds. Our editors handle technical cleanup, but you will be expected to give clear direction on content and pacing.

Current client roster includes companies in financial services, retail and food manufacturing. Series lengths range from three to twelve episodes. Budgets and timelines vary considerably, which means flexibility is genuinely required rather than a phrase we put in job ads.

What we want to see:

At least two years producing audio content in a professional setting, whether in radio, podcasting or branded work. Experience managing client relationships directly, not just through an account manager. Comfort with Hindenburg Journalist or a willingness to learn it quickly — that is our primary editorial tool. Fluency in Serbian and working proficiency in Croatian. English is useful for research and some supplier communication.

The Zagreb option is a smaller office and a more independent working environment. You would report to our head of branded content in Novi Sad and would be expected in Novi Sad roughly once a month for team sessions.

Salary: 100,000–130,000 RSD or equivalent HRK/EUR depending on location, commensurate with experience. We offer 22 days annual leave and a modest professional development budget. To apply, send a CV and links to or files of two pieces of audio work you produced to careers@mediavox-ns.rs. We review applications on a rolling basis.

title: BioVitrum Salmonella Strip Selected for Pilot Programme with Vojvodina Meat Processor Toplinska Klaonika
text:
BioVitrum d.o.o. has agreed a six-month pilot supply contract with Toplinska Klaonika d.o.o., a pork and mixed-meat processing facility based in Temerin. Under the pilot, Toplinska Klaonika will use BioVitrum's Salmonella lateral-flow strip as a rapid screening step at two points in their processing line: incoming carcass swabs and pre-packaging surface swabs.

The pilot covers approximately 1,200 strip tests per month and includes a service component in which a BioVitrum field application scientist visits the facility once a month to review result records and handle any questions from line operators.

Marko Vujičić, operations manager at Toplinska Klaonika, said the decision to trial the strips was driven by a need to reduce the turnaround time between sampling and release decisions. Their current workflow uses an external laboratory with a 24-hour result window. "We wanted to see whether an on-site rapid method could support faster line clearance without adding uncertainty," he said.

BioVitrum's technical team will track concordance between the rapid strip results and parallel ISO 6579 confirmatory cultures throughout the pilot period. The data will feed into the performance evaluation file being prepared for EU IVDR submission.

The pilot is also relevant to ongoing internal work at BioVitrum on false-positive rates in high-fat meat matrices. Toplinska Klaonika processes products ranging from 8 to 28 percent fat content, which gives the BioVitrum team a structured set of real-production samples to work with under controlled conditions.

BioVitrum's commercial director, Jelena Ostojić, said the company is looking for two or three additional pilot partners in the meat processing sector before the end of 2023, with the aim of building a matrix-specific performance dataset that covers the range of products their existing customers handle.

title: What We Do — Products and Services
text:
BioVitrum designs, manufactures, and supplies rapid lateral-flow test strips for detecting bacterial pathogens in food products and food processing environments. Our strips are built for use at the point of need — on a production line, in a receiving bay, or in a field surveillance kit — and deliver a readable result in fifteen minutes without laboratory infrastructure.

Our current product line covers Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes, and coliform hygiene indicators. Each strip is packaged as a single-use cassette with a disposable sample buffer vial. No reader is required for a pass/fail decision, though we also supply a portable reflectance reader for customers who want a numerical signal record for documentation purposes.

All manufacturing steps take place at our facility at the Science and Technology Park Novi Sad. We coat our own nitrocellulose membranes, prepare colloidal gold conjugates in-house, and assemble and cut strips on our own production line. This means we can trace every component lot in a finished product and adjust formulations when a specific food matrix causes interference.

Beyond standard catalogue strips, we offer a development service for customers or research groups who need a custom lateral-flow assay for a specific target. We have completed three such projects to date, producing prototype strips for mycotoxin screening and for a veterinary pathogen target.

Our strips are currently sold under a national conformity mark in Serbia and are used by customers in Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. We are actively working toward EU IVDR registration for the Salmonella strip.

For food manufacturers, we offer a service contract that includes strip supply, application training for line staff, and a quarterly review of result records with one of our field application scientists. For public health laboratories, we supply strips on a framework tender basis and provide method comparison data on request.

title: Quality Engineer — Membrane Processing
text:
BioVitrum d.o.o. is looking for a quality engineer to join the manufacturing team at our facility in the Science and Technology Park Novi Sad. The role focuses on our nitrocellulose membrane coating process and the upstream quality checks that feed into strip assembly.

What the role involves:
- Monitoring and analysing process data from our slot-die coating line, including coating speed, drying temperature, ambient humidity, and material lot records
- Running root-cause investigations when batches fail flow-rate uniformity or line-width specification checks
- Maintaining and improving our statistical process control charts for coating parameters
- Working with the production team to design and run small-scale experiments when process changes are being evaluated
- Supporting internal audits under our ISO 13485 quality management system
- Writing and updating SOPs for coating and incoming material inspection

What we are looking for:
- A degree in materials science, chemical engineering, polymer science, or a related practical discipline
- Hands-on experience with coating or film manufacturing processes — web coating, slot-die, gravure, or similar
- Familiarity with statistical tools for process monitoring: control charts, Pareto analysis, regression, design of experiments
- Comfort working with two years of production logs and identifying patterns that are not immediately obvious
- Experience with ISO 13485 or another quality management standard is useful but not required

We are a team of thirty-four people. The quality engineering function currently sits with one person and you would work alongside them. The role is full time, based on site in Novi Sad. Salary is negotiable based on experience. We are open to candidates who are finishing a master's or doctoral programme in a relevant field and want to move into an industrial role.

To apply, send a CV and a short note on your process experience to posao@biovitrum.rs. Applications are open until the position is filled.

title: Regulatory Affairs Specialist — IVD Registration (Part-Time or Consultancy)
text:
BioVitrum d.o.o. is looking for a regulatory affairs specialist, either as a part-time employee or as an external consultant, to complete the EU IVDR technical file for our Salmonella lateral-flow strip. This is a defined-scope engagement, not an open-ended role, though there is potential for follow-on work on additional products.

Background:
We are registered at the Science and Technology Park Novi Sad and manufacture rapid test strips for food pathogen detection. Our Salmonella strip is currently sold across the Western Balkans under a Serbian national conformity mark. We are preparing for submission to a notified body under EU IVDR as a Class B in vitro diagnostic device. We have a provisional notified body slot in Q4 2024 and need to submit a complete technical file before that date.

Scope of this engagement:
- Review and complete the performance evaluation report in line with IVDR Annex XIII requirements for a Class B pathogen detection device
- Review analytical performance data we have on file and identify gaps that need additional testing
- Complete or revise the risk management documentation to EN ISO 14971
- Check the full technical file structure against IVDR Annex II and III requirements
- Prepare the declaration of conformity template

What we need from a candidate:

- Familiarity with IVDR Annex XIII performance evaluation requirements
- Ability to work with our internal team, who handle the quality system side

title: What We Learned Exhibiting at FoodTech Adriatic 2024
text:
In late March we took a stand at FoodTech Adriatic, a trade exhibition for food processing technology held in Split. It was the second time we have exhibited there, and it was useful enough that we want to write down what we actually observed rather than a promotional summary.

The visitors who spent time at our stand fell into two groups. The first were quality managers from mid-size food manufacturers — mostly in meat, dairy, and ready-meal production — who are under pressure from retail customers to document pathogen testing more thoroughly. Several of them are currently using external laboratory services and are looking at whether a rapid on-site method can supplement or partially replace that. The conversations were practical: they wanted to know test time, sensitivity figures, how many samples a technician can process per shift, and what documentation the strip generates for an audit trail.

The second group were purchasing or logistics managers from food distributors who are being asked by their own clients to provide pathogen testing certificates on incoming goods. This is a segment we had not focused on before. The interest is real but the use case is slightly different — they need a method that works on packaged goods at a receiving bay, not on production-line swabs, which raises some questions about sample preparation that we have not fully addressed in our current protocols.

A few things were harder than expected. Our printed materials are in Serbian and English, and several Croatian and Slovenian visitors switched to English quickly but noted that materials in Croatian would make internal sign-off easier. We will address that before the next exhibition.

We also had three conversations with people who had already heard about false-positive issues on fatty meat matrices — the information is circulating in the sector. We gave honest answers about where we are in resolving it. One quality manager said she appreciated the transparency and would still consider a trial once we publish updated validation data. That is the approach we are taking: do not oversell the current strip in a matrix we know is problematic, fix the problem, and then come back with data.

Overall, FoodTech Adriatic confirmed that the demand for rapid on-site detection is growing in the region. We will be back next year.

title: O nama i kako funkcioniše MlekoSmart
text:
MlekoSmart ogrlica je mali elektronski uređaj koji se pričvršćuje na standardnu ogrlicu krave i šalje podatke na vaš telefon svakih petnaest minuta. Meri koliko se krava kreće, koliko vremena provodi ležeći i koliko puta dnevno preživava. Sva ta tri parametra zajedno govore puno o zdravlju životinje.

Kako to izgleda u praksi? Farmer Jovan Radovanović iz Bečeja nam je rekao: 'Pre nego što sam uzeo MlekoSmart, dok sam primetio da je krava bolesna, već bi bila u lošem stanju. Sada dobijem poruku na telefon i odem da proverim tog jutra.' To je suština onoga što radimo – ne dajemo vam komplikovane grafikone, dajemo vam pravovremenu informaciju.

Ogrlica radi na bateriji koja traje oko devet meseci pri normalnoj upotrebi. Punjenje traje dva sata. Uređaj je prašinootporan i otporan na vodu, testiran u uslovima tipičnog vojvođanskog stočnjaka.

Naša aplikacija je dostupna na Androidu i iOS-u. Postavite je za petnaest minuta, povežite ogrlice i odmah počinjete da pratite stado. Veb portal vam daje dugoročnu istoriju i izveštaje koje možete podeliti sa vašim veterinarom.

Trenutno imamo instaliranu opremu na dvanaest farmi u Srbiji, od manjih domaćinstava sa tridesetak grla do komercijalnih farmi sa više od dvesta krava. Sistem se podjednako dobro ponaša u oba slučaja.

Ukoliko vas zanima probni period, kontaktirajte nas. Nudimo jednomesečni pilot za do deset ogrlica bez obaveze kupovine.

title: Farma Radovanović završila prvu godinu korišćenja – rezultati nas ohrabruju
text:
Januara 2023. godine postavili smo osamdeset MlekoSmart ogrlica na farmi Jovan Radovanović d.o.o. kod Bečeja. Godinu dana kasnije seli smo sa Jovanom i njegovim veterinarom Miletom Stojanović i prošli kroz sve podatke.

Najvažniji nalaz: prosečan broj dana između pada pokazatelja preživanja i dijagnoze bolesti iznosio je 2,1 dan. Farmar je u devetnaest od dvadeset četiri slučaja bolesti reagovao pre nego što bi krava prestala da jede ili pokazala vidljive simptome. Ovo je direktno smanjilo dužinu lečenja i trošak antibiotika, prema proceni samog farmara za oko trideset posto u poređenju sa prethodnom godinom.

Ipak, bili smo iskreni i prema sebi i prema Jovanu: imali smo sedam lažnih uzbuna tokom godine. Sedam puta je Jovan ili Mite otišao da pregleda kravu koja je bila zdrava. To nije katastrofalno, ali nije ni dobro. Svaka nepotrebna poseta košta vreme i pomaže da se farming-sistem koji daje previše uzbuna postepeno ignoriše.

Ovo nam je bio glavni razlog zašto smo početkom 2024. otvorili poziciju za data inženjera. Znamo da imamo dovoljno podataka da gradimo bolji model. Trebamo nekoga ko će taj posao odraditi kvalitetno.

Hvala Jovanu i Miletu na strpljenju i na detaljnom beleženju svakog slučaja tokom godine. Bez takvog labeling-a naš dataset ne bi imao vrednost.

title: Zašto smo izabrali TimescaleDB umesto klasičnog PostgreSQL-a za čuvanje podataka ogrlica
text:
Kada smo 2022. počinjali da gradimo backend za MlekoSmart, naš data inženjer Aleksa Pantić je postavio pitanje: gde čuvamo podatke koji dolaze svakih petnaest minuta sa svake ogrlice? U teoriji, ako imamo hiljadu ogrlica, to je oko hiljadu sedam stotine upisa na sat, ili oko četrdeset hiljada upisa dnevno. To nije ogroman broj, ali kada hoćeš da vučeš trendove za jednu kravu kroz šest meseci, standardni PostgreSQL počinje da se muči bez pažljivog indeksiranja.

Probali smo najpre čist PostgreSQL sa particijama po datumu. Radilo je, ali upiti za trend analizu su bili spori i pisanje tih upita je postajalo komplikovano. Zatim smo pogledali InfluxDB koji je popularan u IoT svetu, ali nismo bili zadovoljni SQL kompatibilnošću i ekosistemom alata oko njega.

Na kraju smo prešli na TimescaleDB, koji je ekstenzija za PostgreSQL. Zadržali smo sav PostgreSQL ekosistem koji znamo, ali dobili smo automatsko chunking-ovanje po vremenu, brže agregacione upite i kompresiju starijih podataka. Za naše potrebe je to bio pravi izbor.

Ne tvrdimo da je ovo jedino ispravno rešenje – za veće sisteme možda ima smisla nešto drugačije. Ali za tim naše veličine, gde svako treba da razume bazu, jednostavnost je bila važan kriterijum.

Aleksa je napisao internu wiki stranicu o tome kako smo organizovali hypertable-ove i koje indekse koristimo. Ukoliko neko gradi sličan sistem i zanima ga naše iskustvo, slobodno nas kontaktirajte.

title: Our Services — Clinical Software Built for Vojvodina's Health System
text:
MediSoft Vojvodina has been writing software for public hospitals and health centres in Vojvodina since 2004. We do not sell generic health IT platforms adapted for the Serbian market; we build and maintain systems that were designed from the start around the way Serbian public health institutions are organised, financed, and regulated.

MediCore HIS handles the full inpatient workflow: admissions, bed management, physician documentation, ICD-10 coded discharge summaries, laboratory order communication, and pharmacy dispensing. It is currently live in six district hospitals and processes roughly 90,000 patient encounters per year. The system runs on standard server hardware that most hospitals already own, with no dependency on cloud connectivity.

TeleKonsult connects rural general-practice teams with specialists for video consultations. A GP in Mali Iđoš can request a cardiology opinion for a patient without that patient spending half a day on a bus. Sessions are logged, and the specialist's notes are written back into the patient record automatically.

MediArh gives outpatient clinics a structured electronic health record that meets the Ministry of Health's documentation requirements and produces the statistical reports required by the Institute of Public Health of Vojvodina.

StatReport automates the monthly and annual reporting obligations to republican and provincial health authorities, pulling data directly from MediCore HIS so that administrative staff do not have to re-enter figures.

All our products are installed and supported on-premises. Our field support team visits sites in person; we do not ask hospital IT staff to manage complex cloud environments. If something breaks at two in the morning before a scheduled admission surge, someone from MediSoft answers the phone.

title: Java Backend Developer — MediMig FHIR Integration Team
text:
MediSoft Vojvodina is looking for a Java backend developer to join the team working on MediMig, our data migration and integration toolkit. This role is based in Subotica with occasional travel to hospital sites in Novi Sad and Zrenjanin.

What the work involves:
You will be writing and testing the mapping logic that transforms records from our existing PostgreSQL schema into valid FHIR R4 resources. Most of the straightforward mappings are already done. The remaining work involves designing FHIR extensions for fields that have no standard equivalent, building a translation-layer API that external systems can query without us having to restructure the live database, and making sure the output passes validation against the national FHIR profile published by the eZdravlje programme.

What we need from you:

— Ability to read technical documentation in English; most of the FHIR implementation guides are not translated

What would be useful but is not required:

— Experience writing ETL pipelines

The team you would join is five developers, currently under real deadline pressure from a Ministry of Health migration requirement. We are honest about that. We offer a permanent contract, a salary in line with Subotica market rates for senior developers, and flexible hours. We do not offer remote-only work for this role because the hospital site visits matter.

title: Data Analyst — Clinical Outcomes and Risk Modelling
text:
We are looking for a data analyst to join our small analytics team in Subotica. The team currently has two people with backgrounds in applied statistics. This is a new position.

Context: We hold anonymised discharge records from three hospitals going back twelve years — close to 480,000 patient episodes. We want to build a readmission-risk tool that ward clinicians can actually use. We have not managed to do this reliably yet, mainly because of data quality issues in the earlier years of the dataset, and we need someone who can help us work through that problem systematically rather than just discarding the older data.

Day-to-day work:
— Exploring and profiling the dataset to understand where the quality problems are and what can be salvaged
— Testing imputation strategies for missing comorbidity fields
— Building and evaluating predictive models in Python or R (we are not committed to a specific tool)
— Working with our clinical contacts at partner hospitals to make sure model outputs make sense to ward staff
— Documenting your methods clearly enough that the Ministry of Health could review them if asked

We want someone who:
— Can write clean, reproducible analysis code
— Is honest about what a model can and cannot do
— Has worked with messy real-world data before, ideally in a regulated context
— Does not need the dataset to be perfect before starting

A background in health data specifically is not required, but you will need to become familiar with ICD-10 coding fairly quickly. We will help with that.

This is a full-time permanent position in Subotica. Hybrid arrangements are possible after an initial settling-in period. Salary is negotiable based on experience.

title: MediCore HIS Goes Live at Dom Zdravlja Senta
text:
MediSoft Vojvodina has completed the deployment of MediCore HIS at Dom Zdravlja Senta, a primary and specialist outpatient centre serving approximately 19,000 residents in the municipality of Senta.

The go-live followed a six-month implementation that included migrating twelve years of patient records from the centre's previous system, a locally maintained Access-based database that had accumulated significant structural inconsistencies. The migration was handled using an early version of our MediMig toolkit, which our team has been developing in parallel with the Senta project. Working through the data took longer than planned — the original timeline was four months — but the centre's administrative lead, Miroslava Fekete, agreed to extend the parallel-running period rather than go live with data gaps.

The installation covers outpatient appointment scheduling, physician documentation with structured ICD-10 discharge coding, referral generation in the format required by the Republican Health Insurance Fund, and automated export to the Institute of Public Health of Vojvodina statistical system.

TeleKonsult is also being piloted at Senta for dermatology consultations with the specialist team at the General Hospital Kikinda. The pilot involves two scheduled sessions per week. Call quality has been acceptable so far, as the centre has a recently upgraded fibre connection, but we are monitoring performance carefully given our known issues with lower-bandwidth sites.

Our project lead for the Senta deployment was Dragan Molnar, who has managed four of our last five hospital go-lives. The support contract runs for five years with a provision for annual system updates.

title: What We Learned Trying to Build a Readmission Model on Twelve Years of Hospital Data
text:
We have been sitting on a large anonymised dataset from three partner hospitals for a couple of years, thinking we should be able to do something useful with it. Readmission prediction seemed like the obvious starting point: if a ward team knows before discharge that a patient has a high chance of returning within thirty days, they can arrange a follow-up call or adjust the discharge plan.

The dataset covers roughly 480,000 patient episodes going back to 2012. In principle, that should be enough. In practice, the first thing our data scientists found when they actually looked at the pre-2018 records was that ICD-10 coding had been done inconsistently across sites. The same condition was coded differently by different staff at different hospitals, and sometimes by the same staff at different times. This is not unusual — anyone who works with real clinical data will recognise it — but it makes building a reliable comorbidity index difficult. The Charlson index, for example, depends on identifying specific diagnosis groups, and if those groups are coded four different ways, you miss a lot of cases.

The second problem was missing comorbidity fields. Fields like diabetes status, renal function category, and heart failure severity were optional in our earlier schema, and optional fields in a busy ward environment tend to stay blank. About half the pre-2018 episodes have at least one blank comorbidity field that would be relevant to readmission risk.

We ran a logistic regression on the post-2018 records only, which gave us a cleaner subset of around 55,000 episodes. The model's discrimination was not good enough for clinical use — AUC around 0.63, which is not much better than chance in this context. Restricting to a smaller, cleaner slice of data reduced the signal too much.

We have not solved this yet. We are currently trying to hire someone with more experience in handling this kind of structured missingness, and we are open to working with external collaborators who have dealt with similar problems in hospital administrative data. If that describes you, we are genuinely interested in talking.

title: Zlatni Klas Mlin Signs Three-Year Supply Contract with Pekara Sunce Group
text:
Zlatni Klas Mlin a.d. has concluded a three-year flour supply agreement with Pekara Sunce Group, an industrial bakery operator running four production sites across central and northern Serbia.

Under the contract, Zlatni Klas will supply Pekara Sunce with Type-500 and Type-400 wheat flour in bulk tanker deliveries, starting in March 2024. Annual volume is expected to be in the range of 9,000 to 10,500 tonnes depending on Pekara Sunce's production schedule.

Branko Savić, director of Zlatni Klas Mlin, commented: 'Pekara Sunce's technical team ran a six-month evaluation of our flour against two other suppliers before they made a decision. The deciding factor, as they explained it to us, was consistency — specifically that our protein and absorption figures held within a very tight band across every lot they tested. That is what our lab and our procurement team work to deliver every day, so it is satisfying when a customer confirms it matters.'

Pekara Sunce's procurement director Miroslav Đurić noted that reliable flour specification is directly linked to yield and waste on automated dough lines, and that variability from inconsistent raw material represents a measurable cost.

The contract runs from 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2027, with annual volume and price reviews. It is the largest single customer contract in Zlatni Klas Mlin's current order book and represents approximately 22 percent of the mill's projected Type-500 output over the contract period.

Zlatni Klas Mlin employs 140 people in Novi Sad and has been in continuous operation since 1974.

title: About Zlatni Klas Mlin a.d. — Fifty Years of Milling in Vojvodina
text:
Zlatni Klas Mlin a.d. was founded in 1974 as part of the Vojvodina agricultural cooperative network. The original facility handled about 80 tonnes of wheat per day using stone-ground technology. Through two full rebuilds — the most recent completed in 2008 — we have grown to a roller-mill operation capable of processing 550 tonnes of wheat daily on a single continuous line.

We are located on Industrijska Street on the southern edge of Novi Sad, close to the main road freight corridor and within easy reach of the Danube grain elevators. That position means we can accept bulk truck deliveries from Vojvodina farms in the morning and dispatch finished flour to bakeries in Belgrade, Subotica or Zrenjanin the same afternoon.

Our product range covers the grades that industrial bakeries and pasta producers depend on: Type-400 and Type-500 white flours, Type-850 semi-white, durum semolina and coarse wholemeal. We also supply packaged retail flour under our own Zlatni Klas label, sold through regional wholesalers and selected supermarket chains.

Quality sits at the centre of how we work. Every incoming wheat lot is tested for moisture, protein content, Hagberg falling number and gluten index in our on-site NIR and wet lab before a single tonne enters the mill. Results are logged against the farm of origin, and we maintain records going back over a decade. Our bakery customers — some of whom have ordered from us for more than twenty years — tell us this consistency is what keeps them coming back.

Director Branko Savić joined the company in 1998 and has led it since 2011. Production manager Jelena Horvatović has managed the mill floor since 2009. Our 140 employees cover milling operations, logistics, quality control, maintenance and administration. We are not a company that chases trends, but we are willing to work hard on problems where the answer is not yet obvious.

title: What We Learned at the Novi Sad Agri-Food Processing Forum 2024
text:
Our production manager Jelena Horvatović and quality lab supervisor Tamara Vukičević attended the Agri-Food Processing Forum held at the Novi Sad Fair in March. This is a post with some plain observations from the two days — not a press release.

The sessions on milling economics were useful mainly because they confirmed what we already suspected: bran valorisation is a topic most mid-sized mills are circling but few have solved. Presentations came mostly from equipment vendors with something to sell, which is fine, but the honest conversations happened in the corridors. We spoke to people running mills of similar scale in Hungary and Romania, and the picture is consistent — the food-grade bran market exists, buyers are real, but the entry requirements around microbial counts, particle size consistency and moisture control are stricter than what animal-feed buyers care about, and most mills have not yet invested in the processing steps needed to meet them.

On energy, there was a half-day session on demand management in continuous food production that was the most practically useful thing we attended. A speaker from a biscuit manufacturer in Subotica described a load-scheduling project they ran using twelve months of sub-hourly metering data and external analytical support. They reported a reduction in their peak demand tariff band of about 18 percent without capital investment in generation or storage — purely through sequencing changes. We have twelve months of equivalent SCADA data sitting in our historian. We came back from the forum more convinced that this is worth pursuing properly.

We also visited the stands of two NIR instrument suppliers and had a conversation about extended calibrations for fibre content measurement, which is relevant to any bran ingredient work. No commitments made, but useful to know what is available.

Overall: worth attending, mainly for the corridor conversations. We will go again next year.

title: About SanaFarma Digitale — What We Build and Why
text:
SanaFarma Digitale started from a straightforward observation: the moment a patient with four or five daily medications leaves a clinic, the system largely stops helping them. The prescription is on paper. The instructions are verbal. Whether the pills are actually taken is unknown until something goes wrong.

We are a small team based in Subotica, working on a practical answer to that gap. Our PillaBox dispenser organises a patient's weekly medications into labelled compartments, reminds them with a quiet alarm and a light when a dose is due, and records whether the compartment was opened. That record goes, via Bluetooth and our backend, to SanaApp — a mobile application for family members and professional caregivers.

SanaApp is built around one question: is my parent on track today? It shows a clear daily timeline, sends a notification if a dose is more than thirty minutes late, and lets a caregiver add a note if they visit in person. It does not show charts or scores or wellness indexes. It shows facts.

We sell to home-care organisations, GP practices, and pharmacies who want to offer their patients something concrete after discharge. We also work directly with families who find us through word of mouth.

Our pilots in Subotica and Sombor involved 60 patients over twelve months. Adherence rates in the pilot group averaged 81%, compared to self-reported rates of around 55% before they started using PillaBox. We are careful about what that number means — it is a small pilot, not a clinical trial — but it is the kind of result that keeps us working.

If you run a pharmacy, a home-care service, or a GP practice and want to discuss a trial, write to us at partners@sanafarmadigitale.rs.

The acoustic part is where we need the most help right now. Our current approach uses a fixed threshold classifier and it does not hold up well in noisy real-world conditions. We want to improve this — possibly by moving to a lightweight learned classifier that can run on-device without a network connection.

— Experience writing embedded C for STM32 or similar ARM Cortex-M devices
— Familiarity with BLE peripheral stacks (we use the STM32WB series)
— Some exposure to signal processing or audio feature extraction, even at a basic level

The role is based in Subotica. Some of the work can be remote, but we prefer someone who can come in to test on physical hardware. We have two dispenser prototypes in the office.

Engagement: contract or part-time employment, roughly 20 hours per week. Compensation depends on experience.

title: PillaBox Pilot Results: What 60 Patients Told Us
text:
We started our first structured patient pilot in the spring of 2023 with 60 participants in Subotica and Sombor, referred through a network of general practitioners and the home-care coordination service Doma Briga. The pilot ran for twelve months. Here is what we found.

The straightforward result: average measured adherence across the pilot group was 81%. Before joining the pilot, participants self-reported taking their medications correctly about 55% of the time. We are not claiming our device is the only reason for that difference — joining any kind of monitored program changes behaviour — but the caregivers and GPs we spoke to at the end said they noticed a real change in their patients.

The more complicated result: our technology failed in ways we did not anticipate.

The acoustic sensor we use to detect whether a pill compartment was actually opened generates false alerts at a rate we cannot accept for a production product. About one in five alerts sent to the family app during the pilot was a false positive. By month three, most family members told us they had turned notifications off. That is the opposite of what we are trying to do.

The app itself lost 40% of patients as active users within three weeks. They did not stop using the dispenser — most continued with that — but the mobile app was too difficult for a large proportion of users over 70 to navigate comfortably.

We are publishing these results because we think it is more useful than writing a press release about the 81% figure. Both things are true: the concept works, and the current implementation has specific, fixable problems.

We are working on both. If you are a researcher, a UX specialist, or an engineer who has worked on related problems, we are genuinely interested in talking.

title: SanaFarma Digitale at MedTech Connections Novi Sad 2024

The practical outcome: we had more than 30 conversations at our table. Most were with other founders or researchers, a smaller number with procurement and clinical staff from healthcare organisations in Vojvodina. Three of those conversations have continued as of this writing.

The less practical but equally useful outcome: we realised how much of our pitch assumed shared context that most visitors did not have. When we stopped explaining the technology and started showing the actual device and walking through a real scenario — a 74-year-old woman who takes five medications at three different times of day, whose daughter lives in Vienna — people's reactions changed. Several visitors said it was the first health-tech product they had seen at the event that they could imagine their own parents using.

We also used the event to have two longer conversations about our current technical challenges. One of those was with a researcher working on audio signal processing who had done work in industrial noise environments. We are following up with her. title: Why We Are Redesigning SanaApp from Navigation Up
text:
When we designed the first version of SanaApp, we built it the way most small development teams build their first app: we made something that worked, showed it to people we knew, fixed the most obvious problems, and shipped it. The resulting application is functional. It is also, as our pilot data showed, too difficult for a significant share of the people who are supposed to use it every day.

The failure mode is not dramatic. Users over 70 do not throw their phones across the room. They open the app, encounter something that does not respond the way they expect, tap something wrong, see a screen they did not intend to reach, and quietly put the phone down. After a few weeks of that, they stop opening it.

We reviewed the screen-capture sessions from our pilot. The problem is not just font size, though that matters too. It is the navigation model. SanaApp uses a bottom tab bar with four icons. Every digital product uses this pattern. For someone who has used smartphones for years, it is invisible. For someone who has used one for eighteen months and primarily for phone calls and messages, the icons are small, abstract, and hard to remember. Our session recordings show users spending 15 to 40 seconds on a screen they did not mean to open, trying to figure out how to go back.

The redesign we are planning will reduce the main navigation to two destinations accessible from a persistent, clearly labelled header. Most users only need to see two things: today's medication status, and the log of the last seven days. Everything else should take deliberate effort to reach.

We are looking for someone who has run structured usability sessions with older adults before, and who can help us validate the new structure before we build it. If that is work you have done, we would like to hear from you.

title: How KreditNova Works — Loans Built Around the Way You Actually Earn
text:
Most loan applications ask you to upload a payslip. If your income comes from invoices, platform payouts, or project fees, that question does not have a good answer — and most banks will stop reading right there.

KreditNova was designed for people in exactly that situation.

Here is how an application works. You fill in a short form: how much you want, how long you need to repay, and some basic information about how your income arrives. The whole thing takes about eight minutes. Our system then runs that information through FlowScore, our in-house scoring model, which looks at patterns in income consistency, spending behaviour, and financial history rather than just a single monthly salary figure.

If you choose to connect your bank account through our open-banking module, we can see a clearer picture of your cash flow, which often means a better offer. That step is your choice.

Most decisions come back in under four minutes. If you are approved, the money reaches your account the same business day.

We lend between 10,000 and 200,000 RSD, with repayment terms from six to eighteen months. There are no arrangement fees hidden in the small print. The interest rate is fixed at the point you accept — it does not change if you miss a payment and then catch up.

If you have a question at any point, you can reach a real person by chat or phone between 8 and 20 hours on weekdays. We do not use automated scripts for complaint handling.

KreditNova is registered with the National Bank of Serbia and operates under the Law on Consumer Credit. Our full fee schedule and general loan conditions are available for download on this page.

title: KreditNova Completes 40,000th Loan
text:
KreditNova processed its 40,000th closed loan in February 2024, a milestone the company marked quietly — with a team lunch and a revised number on the homepage.

The loan, like most of ours, went to a freelancer. In this case, a graphic designer based in Zrenjanin who needed working capital between two project payments. The loan was applied for on a Tuesday afternoon, approved in three minutes, and the money was in her account before the end of the business day.

When we started in 2018, we were not sure anyone would trust a non-bank lender they had found online. The first few months were slow. We made mistakes — our early scoring model was too conservative and we turned away people we should have helped. We rewrote significant parts of it in 2020 after our first full year of repayment data came in and showed us where we had been wrong.

Five years later the picture is different. Our borrower base has grown steadily, mostly through word of mouth and through partnerships with platforms where gig workers are already active. Our repeat-borrower rate sits at around 38%, which we think is a reasonable signal that the experience is working for people.

None of this means the product is finished. Our fraud detection still produces more false positives than we are comfortable with. Our open-banking conversion rate is lower than we want it to be. We have regulatory reporting requirements coming up that will require us to think harder about how we model macroeconomic risk.

But 40,000 closed loans is worth noting. Each one is a person who got a decision based on how they actually manage money, not on whether they have an employer willing to stamp a form.

Thank you to the team, and to every borrower who trusted us with their application.

title: Senior Machine Learning Engineer — Risk Models
text:

title: KreditNova at NTP Fintech Forum 2024 — Talk: 'Scoring the Unscored: Five Years of Lessons'

The original model used seven features. The current production model uses substantially more, with cash-flow variability measures being among the most predictive for our borrower population. The data is useful. Getting applicants to share it is a separate problem. We will share our current conversion numbers and what we have tried.

title: What Three Years of Repayment Data Has Taught Us (And What It Hasn't)
text:
Our head of risk, Dragana Filipović, wrote this post after presenting at the NTP Fintech Forum in April.

When we hit three full years of repayment data earlier this year, I thought we would finally be able to answer the questions that come up most often from our banking partner and from the regulator: how good is your model, really, and how much of your default rate is within your control?

The honest answer is: better than it was, and we are not entirely sure.

The model is better. Our Gini coefficient on the scoring model has improved from around 0.41 when we first deployed it to 0.58 on our most recent validation cohort. That is real progress. The addition of cash-flow features from our open-banking cohort improved the score further on that subset — which is part of why we care so much about getting more applicants to complete that consent flow.

What we cannot yet say cleanly is how much of our year-to-year variation in default rates reflects the model improving versus the economy shifting. Our defaults were higher in 2022 than in 2021. Were we approving worse borrowers, or were the same borrowers facing harder conditions? We have an internal view — we think the macro conditions account for a meaningful share of the variance — but we do not have a rigorous, documented method for separating the two. The National Bank of Serbia has started asking us to show that separation in our supervisory submissions, and we do not currently have a satisfying answer.

We are actively looking for help on this. If you work on credit-risk econometrics and are based in Novi Sad or willing to work with us remotely on a project basis, get in touch.

title: NutriKod Signs Annual Supply Agreement with Alpenfit Handels GmbH
text:
NutriKod d.o.o. has signed a twelve-month white-label supply agreement with Alpenfit Handels GmbH, a sports-nutrition distributor based in Graz, Austria. Under the agreement, NutriKod will produce two SKUs — a vanilla whey-pea blend and an unflavoured pea-only version — at a combined volume of approximately 18,000 sachets per month starting from April 2024.

The partnership began after Alpenfit approached NutriKod through a referral from SupraNutrition GmbH, a German distributor that has sourced from NutriKod since late 2022. Alpenfit's purchasing manager, Thomas Hörmann, visited the Novi Sad facility in November 2023 and completed a supplier audit before the agreement was finalised.

For NutriKod, the contract represents an expansion into a second DACH market and increases total monthly output to a new high. It also introduces stricter packaging specifications, including an oxygen transmission rate requirement of below 0.5 cc per square metre per day, which the company is currently working to meet ahead of the contract's first formal review in October 2025.

"The Alpenfit team was straightforward to work with during the audit," said NutriKod director Jelena Vranić. "They checked our batch records and the dissolution data carefully, which is exactly what we want from a long-term client. The packaging barrier requirement is a challenge we are taking seriously and we are exploring technical options now."

Production of the first Alpenfit batches is scheduled to begin in the first week of April. The initial delivery of 36,000 units will ship to Graz by the end of the same month.

title: What We Do — NutriKod Contract Manufacturing
text:
NutriKod is a contract blending and filling company based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad. We make protein sachets and functional food pouches for sports-nutrition brands that want to sell under their own label without building a production facility.

The process starts when a client shares a nutritional target and a preferred flavour profile. Our formulation team, led by Maja Kovačević, works up a blend specification and produces a 2 kg bench sample within ten working days. The client approves the sample, we agree on fill weight, packaging format and documentation requirements, and then we move to a pilot run of 5,000 to 10,000 units. Full production batches start at 20,000 units.

Every batch leaves with a certificate of analysis that covers protein content by Kjeldahl, moisture, water activity and dissolution time. For clients exporting to Germany or Austria we also prepare the regulatory documentation required for notification under local food supplement rules.

Our filling line runs two shifts and can handle sachets from 20 g to 50 g fill weight in either flat-bottom or pillow format. Nitrogen flushing is standard on all runs. Aluminium-laminate packaging is our default; we can accommodate customer-supplied film rolls if they meet our minimum specification.

Current clients include FormaLine, a Belgrade-based gym network, and two DACH distributors. Combined monthly output is between 50,000 and 70,000 units. Lead time from confirmed order to dispatch is fourteen calendar days for repeat recipes and twenty-one days for new formulations.

If you are a brand looking for a reliable small-to-medium contract manufacturer with documented quality procedures and genuine flexibility on batch size, contact us through the form below.

title: Part-Time Data Analyst — Production Optimisation
text:
NutriKod d.o.o. is looking for a part-time data analyst to help us get more out of the production data we already collect. This is a practical, project-based role rather than a permanent position, and it is well suited to a student in their final year or a recent graduate with some statistical analysis experience.

Background: We run a near-infrared protein analyser on our filling line and collect spectra continuously during production. We also have fourteen months of Kjeldahl reference measurements from the same batches. The problem is that the NIR was calibrated on pure whey and our actual blends mix whey with pea protein in varying ratios. The result is a drift in protein readings across a run that we cannot correct in real time. We want someone to build a revised calibration model that covers the full range of blend compositions we use — roughly 50:50 to 80:20 whey-to-pea by weight.

The work involves:
- Exploring the existing spectra dataset (stored as CSV exports from the instrument software) against our Kjeldahl reference table
- Building one or more regression or chemometric models (PLS or similar) and comparing their prediction error against the current baseline
- Documenting the method clearly enough that our quality manager can apply it without specialist software knowledge
- Suggesting a practical recalibration schedule going forward

Tools: we are not prescriptive — Python, R or any standard chemometrics package is fine. We have a laptop with the instrument software installed that you can connect to during visits.

Time commitment: roughly 60 hours total, spread over two to three months, mostly remote with two or three visits to our facility at NTP Novi Sad.

Fee: 1,200 euros upon delivery of a working model and documentation.

Contact Dragan Miletić at dragan.miletic@nutrikod.rs with a short description of relevant experience.

title: Why Our Sachets Clump in Summer — and What We Are Doing About It
text:
Every summer we face the same problem. The humidity in our warehouse and blending room climbs above 60% relative humidity and the pea protein fraction in our blends starts absorbing moisture before the sachets are even sealed. The result is soft clumps that pass through the filling head but fail dissolution tests downstream.

We started tracking this properly in 2022 when our first chargeback arrived from SupraNutrition GmbH. We mapped warehouse RH against weekly rejection rates and the correlation was clear: below 55% RH, rejection sits under 1%. Between 60% and 70% RH, it climbs toward 8 to 10%.

Since then we have tried three things. First, we added silicon dioxide as a flow agent at 0.3% and later 0.5% by weight. It helped a little — maybe a 1.5 percentage point drop in rejections — but did not solve the problem. Second, we tightened the time window between blending and filling, pushing batches through faster so the powder spends less time exposed. That helped operationally but added stress to the scheduling. Third, we ran a portable dehumidifier in the blending room for the entire summer of 2023. It kept the blending space around 55% RH but the pre-weighed ingredient bags still came in from the main warehouse already conditioned to higher moisture.

Where we are now: rejection is running at roughly 4 to 5% during the current season, down from 8% two years ago, but still above the 1.5% target we need to avoid chargebacks. We have eighteen months of RH logs, aw readings and rejection data sitting in a spreadsheet and we are looking for a better answer — whether that is an engineering fix, a formulation adjustment or a combination. If you have worked on hygroscopic powder handling and want to talk through the problem, reach out to Maja Kovačević at maja.kovacevic@nutrikod.rs.

title: NutriKod at Novi Sad Food & Pharma Suppliers Day 2024
text:

title: About Panonska Slanica — Who We Are and How We Work
text:
Panonska Slanica a.d. was founded in 1975 in Subotica, in the northern part of the Vojvodina region. For nearly fifty years we have made cured and dried meat products using methods that belong to this part of the Pannonian Plain — slow salt curing, cold smoking over beech wood, and long air-drying cycles that cannot be hurried without changing the result.

Today we employ 312 people across our production facility, warehouse and commercial offices. Most of our workforce lives in Subotica and the surrounding villages. Our production runs in two shifts, six days a week, and every batch is tracked from the day of intake through to the day it leaves our loading dock.

Our main products are kulen, slanina and air-dried beef. We sell under the Panonska Slanica label in Serbia through Mercator-S and Univerexport, in Hungary through Auchan and a regional distributor based in Pécs, and in Romania through a wholesale partner in Timișoara. We do not produce for other companies' labels.

We hold BRCGS Grade A certification for food safety, which we have maintained since 2011. We also hold the necessary veterinary export certificates for cross-border trade with Hungary and Romania under EU import protocols.

Commercial director Milena Vukašin and her team manage all retail relationships. Head of production Dragan Kereš oversees the drying, curing and packaging operations. Quality manager Tatjana Molnár runs our internal audit programme and manages the relationship with our contracted laboratory.

We are not a company that sells based on heritage storytelling alone. The products have to arrive in good condition, in the right quantities, on the agreed date. That is what we focus on, and it is what our retail partners expect from us.

title: Panonska Slanica Extends Retail Agreement with Romanian Partner Agrodis SRL
text:
We are pleased to confirm that we have signed a three-year extension of our supply agreement with Agrodis SRL, a wholesale and distribution company based in Timișoara. Under the renewed agreement, Agrodis will continue distributing our kulen and slanina lines to regional retail outlets in Timiș, Arad and Caraș-Severin counties, with the addition of our air-dried beef from the second quarter of 2024.

Commercial director Milena Vukašin commented: 'We have been working with Agrodis since 2018 and in that time we have built up a reliable supply rhythm. Extending the agreement gives both sides a stable basis to plan around. Adding the air-dried beef to the Romanian range is something we have discussed for a while — the product has a following in Serbia and we think there is a real market for it in Banat.'

The Romanian market currently accounts for approximately 14% of Panonska Slanica's total revenue. This agreement is expected to bring that figure above 18% by 2025, supported by the additional product line and a modest increase in weekly delivery volumes.

Agrodis director Florin Costache said the extension reflected consistent product quality and reliable delivery performance over multiple years: 'Panonska Slanica products have built a loyal customer base in our region. The kulen in particular has become a regular purchase for consumers who are familiar with Vojvodina-style charcuterie.'

Logistics for the Romanian route run through our Subotica warehouse, with weekly refrigerated transport arranged through our long-standing carrier, Pannonia Freight d.o.o. of Novi Sad. All export documentation continues to be managed by our compliance team in cooperation with the relevant veterinary authorities.

title: Job Opening: Process Instrumentation Technician
text:
Panonska Slanica a.d. is looking for a process instrumentation technician to join our production team in Subotica. This is a full-time, permanent position.

What the job involves:
You will be responsible for maintaining and calibrating the measurement instruments used across our drying chambers, curing rooms and packaging hall. At present this means analogue thermostats, humidity sensors and the temperature logging system in our cold storage area. Over the next twelve to eighteen months we expect to expand our sensor infrastructure, and you will be part of implementing that.

We will also expect you to work with our production and quality team on identifying measurement gaps — places in the process where we are relying on visual checks or manual logs when an instrument readout would give us better information.

What we are looking for:
— Completed secondary technical education or vocational training in electrical engineering, measurement technology or a related field
— At least two years of practical experience with industrial sensors, PLCs or building management systems
— Familiarity with temperature and humidity measurement in a food, pharmaceutical or similar controlled-environment setting is an advantage
— Willingness to learn; we do not expect you to have done exactly this job before
— Clean driving licence

What we offer:
— Competitive salary based on experience
— Stable employment in a company with nearly fifty years of continuous operation
— On-the-job training and the possibility to work alongside external technical partners

To apply, send a CV and a short cover letter to our HR contact, Ivana Pušić, at the address listed on our contacts page. Applications are open until 28 February 2024.

title: Job Opening: Microbiological Quality Control Technician
text:
Panonska Slanica a.d. is hiring a microbiological quality control technician. The position is based at our facility in Subotica and is full-time, permanent.

Background:
Our quality team currently relies on a contracted external laboratory for all microbiological analysis, including environmental swabbing, product testing and water quality checks. We are evaluating whether to bring some of this work in-house, and this hire is the first step in that direction. The role will work directly with quality manager Tatjana Molnár.

What the job involves:
— Carrying out environmental swabbing programmes in production and packaging areas according to our HACCP plan
— Preparing swab samples and maintaining chain-of-custody records for samples sent to the external laboratory
— Interpreting laboratory results and flagging any trends to the quality manager
— Supporting root-cause investigations when environmental monitoring returns a non-conforming result
— Helping to develop sampling plans and updating them when production layout or processes change
— If we proceed with an in-house lab, helping to set it up and obtain necessary accreditations

What we are looking for:

— Familiarity with Listeria environmental monitoring programmes is a significant advantage
— Careful, methodical approach to documentation
— Ability to communicate findings clearly to non-laboratory colleagues

We offer a competitive salary, a stable workplace and a chance to build something new within an established production company.

Contact Ivana Pušić with your CV. Applications close 22 March 2024.

title: Why We Still Dry for 21 Days
text:
A question we get from buyers and occasionally from journalists is why our drying cycle takes as long as it does. The honest answer is that the physics of drying whole-muscle beef or pork sausage does not change because someone wants the product faster.

What we are doing during those 21 days is removing water from the centre of the product outward, at a rate slow enough that the surface does not dry faster than the interior. If the surface dries too fast, you get a hard outer layer — what people in the trade call case hardening — that traps moisture inside. That moisture eventually causes problems: off flavours, texture defects, in the worst case microbial risk.

The chamber conditions we maintain — temperature between 12 and 16 degrees Celsius, relative humidity between 72 and 82 percent depending on the stage of drying, with controlled airflow — are what keep that balance. The ranges come from decades of trial and adjustment on this specific production floor with our specific product weights and fat covers.

We are aware that this is an energy-intensive process. Eight chambers running continuously for 21 days per cycle represents a significant part of our operating cost, and that cost went up considerably last year. We are actively looking at how to monitor and manage the chambers more precisely — not to cut the drying time, but to run each cycle as efficiently as the process allows.

There is no shortcut version of this product that tastes the same. Customers who buy Panonska Slanica kulen or slanina regularly know what it should be like. Our job is to make sure every batch is consistent. That is the constraint we work within, and we do not think it is the wrong constraint.

title: Panonska Slanica at the Novi Sad Agricultural Fair — Stand Report
text:
Panonska Slanica a.d. exhibited at the Novi Sad Agricultural Fair for the twelfth consecutive year. Our stand in Hall 3 covered approximately 24 square metres and presented our full retail product range alongside two new packaging formats we plan to introduce later this year: a 100-gram resealable pouch for sliced kulen and a wooden gift box containing three products for the holiday retail season.

This year we focused less on consumer sampling and more on professional visitors — buyers from retail chains, food service distributors and colleagues from the processing sector. Milena Vukašin and two members of the commercial team staffed the stand across all five days.

Several conversations worth following up came out of the fair. We met with a buyer from a Belgrade-based speciality food retailer who expressed interest in a premium SKU. We also had a useful discussion with a Slovenian casing supplier who approached us after seeing our products, which is relevant given the cost pressures we have been dealing with on our current casing supply.

On the production and technology side, Dragan Kereš spent half a day walking the machinery and equipment exhibition, looking at sensor hardware and environmental monitoring systems for drying applications. Nothing was ready to buy off the shelf, but a few exhibitors offered to arrange factory visits, which we will consider.

We also met for the first time with a representative from the Science Technology Park Novi Sad, who introduced us to the process of matching industrial producers with applied research capacity. We have since followed up on that introduction. We expect to be back at the fair next year.
